You don’t want to overcomplicate things. We’ve got the garden sorted, I think. I was also thinking about the chickens. They’ve been laying eggs more regularly now. Maybe we should start selling some at the local market?      That’s an interesting idea. I’ve heard about people selling eggs at markets. You could make a bit of extra money. Plus, it’s a way to get them out of the house more.      I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve been telling my mum about it. She says if the weather is good, it’s worth trying. I think we could get a few customers from the local shops.      I think your mum’s right. It’s a great way to get involved and maybe even connect with the community. I’ll help you set it up. I’ve got a few contacts at the market.      That’s a great plan. I’ll check the market schedule and see when we can set up.

Right, so I was just thinking about our school trip to Cambridge last year. You remember, when we had to do that science project on plants and stuff?      Oh yeah! That was a mad time. I remember we had to go to this garden at the university. It was so big, and I couldn’t believe how many plants they had. I tried to take a photo of the greenhouse, but my phone kept crashing.      Haha, I know! I was trying to take a picture of the whole thing and the sun was so bright. I nearly blinded myself. But seriously, it was cool. I even got to touch some of the leaves. You know, the ones that change color in the winter? I think they call them something like… um, maybe  rhubarb ?      No, rhubarb is that red stuff you eat in pies. Those were  autumn leaf plants . I think they were called  maple  or something. Anyway, I remember we had to write a report on the different types of plants, and I got stuck on the science terms. I asked the teacher, and she said, “It’s not about remembering the names, it’s about understanding the process.”      Yeah, I was like, “But how can I understand it if I don’t even know the names?” She said something about the  scientific method . I still don’t get it. I mean, how is that different from just guessing?      Oh, you’ll get it. You just have to keep doing the tests. I’m doing a maths test tomorrow, and I’m so stressed. I’ve been practicing my times tables, but I still get mixed up with 7x8 and 6x9.      I know, right? I was doing that too. I even got a sticker from the teacher for trying. But I’m still terrible at remembering them. Though I heard Ed Sheeran’s new album is out. I was thinking about buying it, but I’m too busy with school stuff.      Oh, I’ve been listening to it all week. He’s got this song called  Shape of You  that’s just  so  catchy. I play it on my way to school every day. It helps me focus.      You’re just trying to make the walk to school go faster, aren’t you?      Maybe. But I think it’s also helping me with my English. I’ve been doing some writing for a school project, and I’m trying to make my paragraphs flow better.

I’ve got a rat puppet, you know, one of them little ones that you can make go ‘squeak’ and do all sorts of funny things. I found it in a charity shop a few years back, and I’ve had it ever since. It’s a real treasure, I tell you. Keeps the kids entertained when they come round.      Oh, a rat puppet? Aye, I’ve got one too, but it’s been in the attic for years. I used to have a bunch of them when I was a child. My mum used to make them for the village fairs. Still, I never did get much use out of them, to be honest.      You should bring it out sometime. The kids love ‘em. I’ve had the same one for ages, and I still get a laugh out of it. It’s got a bit of wear and tear, but it’s still in one piece.      I’ve never had a rat puppet, to be fair. I was more into handbells. I used to ring them in a church when I was younger. I still do a bit now, just for fun. It’s a nice way to pass the time, and it keeps the rhythm in your head.      Handbells, eh? I’ve heard of them, but I’ve never really got the hang of it. I tried once, but I kept missing the beat. Though, to be fair, I was more interested in juggling than bells back then.      Juggling? That’s something I could have done. I used to be able to juggle three oranges when I was a lad. Though I daresay I wouldn’t be able to do it now. I’ve got a bit of an arthritic wrist, I think.      You should get your eyes tested, you know. I’ve been meaning to do that for a while. I’m not sure if it’s just the light, or if it’s something more. I’ve been getting a bit dizzy when I’m out walking.      Aye, I’ve heard that one before. I’ve got a bit of a squint, so I’m always told I need to get my eyes checked. But I keep putting it off. Maybe I should go with you, if you’re going. It’s not fair on the eyes, is it?      I’ll be honest, I’ve been putting it off too.

So, what are we doing today? I was just thinking, maybe we could grab a couple of coffees and wander around the city? I’ve got a few ideas about where to go.      That sounds perfect. I was just thinking the same thing. I’ve got a bit of time today, and I feel like we should make the most of it. You know, before the summer really kicks in.      Yeah, it’s such a shame that we haven’t gotten out much this year. I’ve been so busy with coursework and all that. But I’ve been really looking forward to this. I heard there’s a new café near the canals that serves the best espresso in town.      Oh, I’ve heard about that too. I think they even have a bit of a little bit of an Italian twist to the coffee. I remember when I was younger, I used to go there all the time. It was just the two of us, or sometimes even with some of the other midwives. We’d have a strong coffee and just chat.      Yeah, I remember you telling me about that. It’s funny how things change. I’ve been thinking about how Venice used to be in the old days. I mean, the canals were so busy, people were actually moving around on boats, and the city was really alive.      Definitely. I grew up here, so I always felt a kind of connection. The people were more friendly back then. You could walk down the street and just strike up a conversation with anyone. Now, it’s more of a tourist trap, but I still love it. And the food, oh the food!      Oh, the food! I’ve been dying to try some of the local dishes. I know you mentioned the seafood is amazing, and I’ve heard about this place that serves the best risotto. I can’t wait to try it.      You’ll love it. And there’s this little trattoria near the Rialto market that serves handmade pasta. I’ve taken a few people there, and they always say it’s the best they’ve ever had.      Perfect. I think I’ll make it a day of food and exploration. Maybe after that, we can go check out some of the smaller shops. I’ve heard there are some really unique things to find here.

So, I just wanted to say, I am  so  sorry I missed your workout session last week. I got stuck in a meeting with the client and completely forgot. I feel terrible about it. Are you mad?      No, no, don’t worry about it. Honestly, I was just beginning to think you’d lost interest. You know how hard it is to keep up with that routine. But I’m glad you’re back on track. I’ve actually been thinking about starting a new gym class—yoga and strength training combo. It’s supposed to be really good for core stability. You’d probably like it.      Yoga? That’s different. I’ve only done it once or twice. My friend Lucy did it for a month and got so flexible, she could touch her toes like a tree. But I’m more of a cardio person. Although, I  did  try that spinning class again last week. It was brutal, but I feel amazing afterwards. You should come with me sometime.      I might just do that. I need to get my fitness back on track, especially with the holidays coming up. I mean, we’re not going to be able to keep up with that healthy lifestyle if we’re eating out every night. Speaking of which, have you sorted out your plans?      Yeah, actually, I’m going to York with my cousin for the weekend. We’re staying at her place and then hitting up some of the local pubs and cafes. I think we might even go to the castle. It’s a bit of a tradition, I guess. You should come too—only if you can get away from work, of course.      York sounds lovely. I’m off next week, so I could definitely swing by. It’s just a shame my boss isn’t as flexible as you. I’m trying to get some time off to do something for myself. I’ve been feeling a bit run down lately, you know?      That’s not good. You should take it seriously. I mean, I’ve been working long hours too, and I’m starting to feel the burn. Do you think about your future plans? Like, do you see yourself staying in this industry forever?      Honestly, I’m not sure yet. I love what I do, but I think I want to explore more. Maybe move to a different city, or even take a break to travel.

Well, I just got a card from the grandkids, you know – the ones in France. The little girl got her first birthday last week. I’m so proud of them. I was thinking, how long has it been since I last saw her? I mean, she's been born abroad, so it’s a bit different. But I suppose that’s the way it is now.      Oh, yes. A lot of people have kids overseas these days. Still, it’s a bit strange, isn’t it? You grow up in England, and then you're raising your child in France. You start to think, is that even possible? I remember when I was younger, people didn’t go abroad to have kids like that. It was all about being born in the UK, you know.      Exactly. But I was thinking about the property market down there. I was at a café in Nice last month, and a lady was talking about buying land in Provence. She said it’s all so different from here, even though it's still Europe. And I thought, how do they manage with the bureaucrats and the anarchists? It's like a different world, isn’t it?      Oh, I know. I’ve been reading about it. I’m writing a book about European history, actually. I’m looking at the way different countries handle land ownership and enterprise. France, for instance, is so different from England. You know what I found interesting? The way the cathedral spire in Chichester collapsed last year. They had an architect named Porden who was involved. I remember reading about that in the newspaper.      Yes, that was a big deal. I remember the open day and the photo exhibition. Everyone was taking pictures of the ruins. It was strange to see a cathedral in such a state. But I suppose it's part of the charm, isn’t it? Like, it gives you a sense of history.      Exactly. I think that’s what people love about Europe – the layers of history. But then there's the local housing management. I had a neighbor who moved in with a new landlord, and it’s been a disaster. I’ve been trying to get in touch with him, but he’s not answering.      Oh, I know what you mean. I had a similar problem with my flat in Camden. I had to go through three landlords before I found one who actually cared.

So, I just got my results back from the mock exams. Honestly, I think I did okay, but I got a bit nervous when I saw the history paper. I think I stared at the first question for like five minutes before I even started writing.      Oh no, that sounds like me. I remember when I had to do that English essay about  The Great Gatsby  last term. I just couldn’t get my thoughts straight. I ended up writing about the weather instead of the symbolism.      You’re not the only one. I had a friend who wrote about the colour of the sky in the exam. I mean, it was a metaphor, but I think he got confused. Anyway, that’s not the point. I’m more worried about the school trip next week. We’re going to the science museum, and I’m not even sure what we’re doing there.      Yeah, I heard about that. My brother went last year and he said it was boring. He kept asking, “Why do we have to do this?” I told him, “Because it’s part of your education.” He said, “Well, if I fail, I’m going to start a business and not go to school anymore.”      That’s pretty brave. I mean, I can’t imagine leaving school. I’d probably end up working at a fast-food place like this. It’s actually cool, though. The owner is really nice and gives us free chips sometimes.      Oh, I remember when I first came here. It was my first time eating Chinese food. I was so nervous because I didn’t know what to order. I ended up getting the chicken and broccoli, and I thought it was the best thing I’d ever tasted.      I think you were the only one who actually liked it. I’m still not a huge fan of the veggies. I mean, they’re good, but I’d rather eat a burger. I’m trying to cut down on junk food, but it’s hard.      I’m doing the same thing. I’ve been eating more fruit and veggies, but I still sneak a chocolate bar every now and then. My mum says I’m getting too fat, but I don’t think she’s right. I’m just naturally built like that.      You’re not fat, mate. You’re just a bit of a foodie.

Well, I’ve been going through that old chest of drawers in the attic, and I found a rather peculiar item—like, a box of my old school gym socks. You know, the ones with the funny little logos? They’re faded now, but they still smell like the ’70s.      Oh, I had those too. Though I kept mine—they’re a bit of a nostalgia trip. I’ve even started using them for washing my face. They’re soft and don’t irritate my skin.      Are you serious? I thought that was a myth. I mean, I’ve heard some people do that, but I didn’t think it was actually a thing. I’ve been told to use my old school t-shirts for cleaning my face, but I didn’t take it seriously.      You know, I remember my mother used to say that old socks were the best for facial cleansing, even back when she was a teacher. I guess it’s all about the texture, you know? But I’ve never really got into it. I’ve always preferred a proper facecloth.      I tried once, and then I got a pimple. My face was a battlefield. I didn’t want to go through that again. Though, honestly, I thought that whole thing was just a British myth. You know, like that whole “squares in the pan” thing.      Oh, I remember that one too. Though, honestly, I think the real secret is tea. You know, the stronger the tea, the better it is for your skin. I’ve used it to wash my face for years. It’s a bit of a failsafe.      Well, I suppose it’s all about personal preference. I’ve got a bit of a soft spot for old things, even the ones that might not be the most hygienic. It’s part of the charm, isn’t it?      Exactly. It’s a little bit of nostalgia. I mean, when you’re cleaning out, you’re not just getting rid of stuff—you’re also getting rid of memories. And sometimes, those memories are worth keeping.      Speaking of cleaning out, I’ve been thinking about moving. My room’s tiny, and I’m starting to feel like I’m holding on to things that don’t really belong to me. Maybe I should start clearing out properly.      I think that’s a good idea. I’ve been thinking about it too, actually.

Right, so, like, I’m totally confused about my GCSE options now. I don’t know if I should do English Lit or English Lang. It feels like both are kind of the same, but I guess they’re different. What do you think?      Honestly, I think it’s all about what you’re more interested in. Like, if you love reading books and analysing them, then English Lit might be better for you. But if you’re more into writing essays and getting feedback, maybe Lang is the way to go.      Yeah, but I don’t know what I’m more into. I mean, I like reading, but I also like writing. It’s like I’m split. And then there’s the whole thing about how it affects my future jobs. I heard you can go into teaching or journalism or something with English.      Yeah, definitely. I mean, even if you don’t go into education, the skills you learn—like writing, research, critical thinking—they’re useful in so many careers. But, like, I’ve been thinking about doing a media course or something related to YouTube. You know, like being a blogger or a content creator.      Oh, I know! I’ve been following this YouTuber called – uh –  The Grammar Girl  or something. She’s super smart and she makes these fun videos about grammar and writing. I’d love to be like that. But I’m not sure if that’s a real job.      It is, actually. I mean, some people make a living off it. But you have to be really good at it and have a lot of followers. Not everyone can just make videos and get paid. But the thing is, it’s not just about money. It’s about doing something you love.      Yeah, I guess. But what if I do the wrong thing? Like, what if I pick English Lang and then end up hating it? I don’t want to waste my time.      I get it. It’s so hard to decide. But you’ll find out what you like better as you go along. And if you’re really unsure, maybe you can talk to your teachers or even go to a careers fair. I heard there’s one at school next week.      That sounds like a good idea. I might have to do that. Thanks for helping me think through it.

So, what do you think about that new software they've been pushing at the university? I was trying to update my old files last night and I got stuck on some damn thing called a “cloud backup.” Sounds like a fancy way of saying “get lost.”      I’ve heard of that one. I tried to use it on my tablet last year. It just kept crashing. I reckon the best thing is to keep everything on a physical drive. You know, like the good old days. I still have that old Amstrad computer from the ’80s. It’s been sitting in the attic for years, but it still works, don’t you know.      Oh, I’ve got one of those too. It’s got a bit of a knack for knocking out the odd virus, but it’s a classic. I still use it for my old photo albums. Digital’s all very slick, but there’s something about the smell of a dusty old hard drive that gives you a warm, nostalgic feeling.      Yeah, I used to work with computers back in the day. Before they had all these fancy things. I remember when we had to punch cards. You’d write all your code on these little pieces of paper and then feed them into the machine. It was like magic. And if you messed up, you had to start all over again.      That sounds like a whole different world. I’m more of a modern tech person, but I can definitely see the charm in the old ways. I mean, I still use my old laptop for research, but it’s got a bit of a heart. It’s been through a lot.      Maybe you should start a museum. “The History of Computing in Norfolk.” Maybe we could all contribute. I’ve got that old Enigma machine my dad used to play with. He told me it was used for something important during the war. I dunno, maybe it was just for sending coded messages about the local pub’s closing times.      I’ve heard of that. My granddad used to tell me stories about how he used to send coded messages to his mates in the village. It was all so secretive, and I just thought it was a game. He used to write the codes on the back of old envelopes. It was like a treasure hunt.

So, I was just tellin’ Ann about this bloke I saw deliverin’ a parcel the other day. He was standin’ in the rain, like a right proper malkin, shoutin’ at the dog. “You lot better not eat the parcel, or I’ll fergit to deliver it!” It was ridiculous. I reckon he thought the dog was a thief or somethin’.      Oh, I’ve seen some interesting delivery men. Once, I was out with my cat, and this bloke came up with a parcel, like, “Is this for you?” I said, “No, it’s not.” He said, “Oh, right, I’ll just leave it outside then.” And off he went, not even looking at the door number. I said to my cat, “You know, you’re the only one who’s ever been properly delivered to.”      That’s the kind of thing that happens when you’re out of the loop. I used to work in schools, and I tell you, the way they deliver things now is a bit different. You know, with the emails and the online systems. I’ve got a granddaughter who’s in year seven, and she told me she can’t remember the name of her school. She just calls it “the school up the road.”      Aye, I can see that. When I was younger, you knew your school by name, and you knew where it was. Now, it’s all about the postcode and the website. I tried to get my grandson to look up his school online the other day, and he said, “Granddad, why don’t you just ask the postman?” I said, “Because he’s not the one who runs the school!” We had a laugh about it.      I’ve got a granddad too, and he’s always trying to tell me about the old days. He says, “Back in them days, you didn’t need a mobile phone, you just had to know where the post office was.” I said, “And now you have to know where the takeaway is.” He said, “Well, that’s the way it goeth.”      True enough. But I’ll tell you, even with all the technology, sometimes the old ways are better. I was at the doctor the other week, and the nurse said, “You know, we’ve got this new system for tracking your health.” I said, “Oh, lovely. What’s the password?” She said, “You don’t need a password, just a postcode.”

So, I was just thinking about that snow we had last week. I mean, it was  massive , wasn’t it? I woke up to a world covered in white, and it was like…  midwinter  in the middle of March.      Yeah, I remember. It was ridiculous. I think it actually stopped the university from starting the semester. A lot of people just stayed in their flat, eating chips and watching  Friends  all day.      Sounds like my idea of a perfect winter day. Although, I did get stuck in the car for two hours trying to get to work. My colleagues were like, “Why are you even out? The roads are a complete mess!”      I think the whole city just had a collective panic. My flatmate tried to plant some flowers in the garden, but it was so cold, they just froze. And the birds were everywhere, like they were looking for a warm place to nest.      Yeah, I saw one of those birds land on my balcony and just sat there for ages like it was a throne. I thought it was a little emperor, but it just turned out to be a pigeon.      I’ve been thinking about doing a  Come Dine With Me  thing for the stag do. We’ve been planning it for ages, and I think it’s finally time to book the venue. It just needs to be somewhere quirky—maybe something with a garden? Or at least a place where we can all drink and not worry about the weather.      That sounds good. We could have a garden party. Maybe even some themed food. I know some people are into that. Though, I’m not sure if they’d be up for snow again.      Oh, I think they’ll be fine. I mean, it’s not like we’re going to be outside in  that  weather. We can always have a fire pit or something. But I do need to check with the venue if they have a proper kitchen.      Yeah, I’ll help you with that. I’ve got some contacts in the catering industry. And I’ve got this idea for a menu—maybe some British classics with a twist? Like a truffle-infused shepherd’s pie or something.      That sounds amazing. I think the stag do would be perfect if we all chip in. We could even do a kind of  hen do  for the bride, but I think the stag do is the main event.

Well, I’ve been thinking, lass, you’d think with all this potted meat and pickled eggs in the fridge, we’d be able to cook something decent. But no, it’s all left to rot. Look at this—half a loaf of bread, and it’s been there since last week!      Aye, I know, I’ve been meaning to clean out the fridge. But I’m always so busy with the kids and all, you know. We’ve got three of them and they never stop eating, but they still leave things behind.      I can’t believe you two are still stuck with that kind of food. I mean, I’ve got a microwave and a fridge full of fresh produce. I even cook from scratch, if I can find the time. But then again, I’m a lecturer, so I get to choose when I work.      And I’m a lecturer too, so I have the same problem. I’m always too busy to cook, but I don’t have to worry about rotting food in the fridge. I just throw it away and buy fresh stuff. It’s a bit of a shame, really. I remember when we used to cook proper meals – no pre-prepped stuff, no pickled eggs.      Aye, I can’t stand the pickled eggs, honestly. I used to have a bit of a thing for them when I was a lad, but now they just give me a headache. I think I’d rather have a proper roast than a plate of pickled vegetables and cold meat.      That’s the thing, though. We all had to grow up with what we had. My mum always said that you make do and mend, and we did. I remember she used to cook stew every night, and it was the best thing. The smell would fill the house, and you’d know you were home.      That’s a good memory. I think being able to cook from scratch is something we’ve lost in this modern world. I mean, I can make a good risotto, but I can’t cook a proper Sunday roast. I think it’s something I’d have to learn again.      Yeah, I can see that. I grew up in London, so I was always eating takeaway and fast food. I never learned to cook proper meals like your granddad used to.

So, I tried to make that lasagna again last night, and it turned out... well, let's just say it was more like a lasagna  attempt .      That’s not surprising—remember when you tried to cook it for the first time? You burned the pasta and the sauce was more like a soup.      Yeah, but that was  years  ago. I think I’ve improved. Or maybe I just got better at pretending I know what I’m doing.      Oh, I remember that. I used to help out in the kitchen when you were trying to cook, and I’d always have to step in. You tried to throw the pasta into the pot like it was a game of dodgeball.      Yeah, I still remember that. I said something about not wanting to be hit by a spinning pasta strand, and you just laughed and said it was the  British way .      That’s what I said—“It’s the British way of cooking, Dad. You just throw and hope for the best.”      That’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever heard. I didn’t even know you were trying to cook. I thought you were just tossing spaghetti in the air for fun.      Well, someone had to teach you how to cook. You know, the basics. Like, how to open a can of beans without spilling the contents all over the kitchen floor.      I  told  you I didn’t know how to do that. I just thought you could open a can with your fingers.      Maybe you should just go back to what you know. I always say, the best meals are the ones you can make with what you have. Like your mum’s famous shepherd’s pie.      Yeah, that’s the one. I’ve had that same pie every Christmas for as long as I can remember. It’s basically a frozen pie that’s been reheated, but it’s still amazing.      And it’s got that crust that’s just right. It’s not too thick, it’s not too thin. Just perfect.      I guess I need to start from the bottom up. Maybe I should just go back to basics. Like, learn how to flip an egg without making a mess.      That’s the first step. After that, you can move on to toast, then maybe you can start making toast with jam.      And who knows? Maybe one day you’ll be the one teaching  us  how to cook.

So, I was just thinking about how we could integrate more interactive elements into online learning. I've seen a few viral videos on TikTok where students are using gamified learning platforms—like Duolingo or even some AI-driven tutors. It's pretty cool how they're making education more engaging.      That's interesting, I've heard about some of those platforms too. But I've also been thinking a lot about how students are struggling with traditional lecture-based learning. They’re so used to being passive, and it’s hard to get them to engage. I remember when I was teaching, I tried using some interactive quizzes in class, and even that made a difference.      Yeah, that makes sense. I think the key is to make learning more like a journey rather than a task. I’ve been working on a start-up that uses immersive VR environments for training. It's not just about the content; it's about the experience. You can place students in real-life scenarios—like a business meeting or a science lab—where they have to make decisions in real time.      That sounds like it could work well for applied subjects. But I wonder if it’s scalable. I mean, not all universities have the budget for VR setups. Maybe we could combine VR with existing tools. Like, use it as a supplement rather than a replacement. Or maybe even use mobile apps that offer gamified lessons.      That’s a good point. I’ve been looking at some open-source platforms that could be adapted for different institutions. Maybe we could partner with some universities to pilot a program. I know some students are looking for more flexibility, and blended learning models might be the way to go.      I agree. I think the challenge is balancing structure with creativity. Students need direction, but they also need space to explore. Have you thought about how to measure the effectiveness of these new methods? I mean, how do we know if the gamification is actually helping or just making them more entertained?      That's a solid question. I've been working on some metrics—like engagement levels, time spent on tasks, and even student feedback. We’ve seen a noticeable increase in participation with the gamified elements. But it's still a work in progress. I think the real success will come when we start seeing improvements in retention and performance.

So, I just got an email from the project team about the upcoming deadline. I think we’re going to have to work a bit extra this week, but I don’t know how we’ll manage with the Halloween party on Friday. Do you think we can make it?      Honestly, I’m not sure. I’ve been so stressed with the shift patterns at the hospital. I’ve got two night shifts coming up, and I’m just trying to keep my head above water. If I’m not careful, I’ll be too exhausted to even put on a costume.      Oh no, I can’t imagine. But I’m also worried about the project. I’ve been trying to organise the meetings and get everyone on the same page, but some people are just not responding. I feel like I’m the only one who’s actually pushing things forward.      I get that. It’s so frustrating when people don’t take things seriously. But you’re doing a great job. I’ve noticed how much you’ve been juggling—it’s not easy. Maybe we should plan something simple for the Halloween party, like a themed dinner or just a movie night instead of going out. We can still have fun without the stress of dressing up.      That’s a good idea. I was thinking about doing that anyway. I could cook something nice, maybe some roasted chicken and mash. I’ve been trying to get better at cooking, and I think I’ve got the hang of it now. Plus, I’ve got some new spices from the market. You’d like that, right?      Oh, I’d love that. I’d be happy just to sit down and eat properly without worrying about the hospital. It’s been ages since I had a real meal at home. I’ve been grabbing takeaways all week.      I know, it’s crazy how time flies. I’ve been thinking about where I want to be in five years. I really want to move into a more senior role in project management, maybe even start my own consultancy. It’s a bit ambitious, but I feel like I’m on the right track.      That sounds amazing. I’ve been thinking about going back to study for a master’s in mental health nursing, but I’m not sure if I’ll have the time.

Oh, I remember when I first moved to London, it was like a different planet! I was so used to the quiet of Essex, and then all of a sudden, you're in this buzzing city full of people and noise. I mean, it's not like the countryside, is it?      Yeah, I can imagine. I was born in Lewisham, so I've never known anything else. But I guess it's funny how even though you're surrounded by people, you can still feel quite alone sometimes.      Oh, I know what you mean. I've always been a bit of a loner, really. Even now, I don't get out much. But I do love coming to Cambridge – it's so peaceful here, compared to the chaos of London. You can actually hear your own thoughts without the noise of the city.      You're in Cambridge? When’s the last time you came? I haven’t seen you in ages!      A few months ago, actually. I went to see the gardens, as usual. It's such a treat to get away from the city for a bit. But I do miss the hustle and bustle, in a weird way. I mean, I've got the radio on, and the kettle's on, and somehow it feels like I'm still in London.      You’re full of contradictions, aren’t you? One minute you're craving the noise, the next you're saying you miss peace and quiet.      Well, I suppose it’s about balance. I’ve always liked to have the best of both worlds. But I think I’ve been spending too much time on my own lately. I should start getting out more.      You should. You know, I can take you to some places in London – you know, the places you used to love. I mean, I still go to the same pubs as when I was a student, and it’s like time hasn't moved at all.      That would be nice. I’d like that. It's been too long since we've had a proper catch-up. I could do with a little excitement, you know.      Exactly. So, what do you say? This weekend? We can go to that café near the station – it's got that cosy feel you love.      I’d love that. I’ll bring the tea. I know you’ll be happy to see me.

So, I was just telling my mates about the football match last night — it was a real mess. I swear, the ref was more interested in chewing gum than the game. I think he got a full pack in his pocket before the match even started.      Yeah, I heard about that. I mean, if you're going to be that distracted, you should just call it off and go get a drink. But seriously, did you see what happened with the striker? He took a shot, the ball hit the post, and then the ref blew the whistle like it was a goal. I mean, that’s not even close to a goal.      Exactly! I was like, “Mate, you’ve got to be kidding me.” I don’t know how you can be so oblivious. I mean, it’s not like it’s the first time he’s missed a clear chance. Honestly, I’m starting to think he’s got a bit of a vendetta against the team.      I tell you, I’ve been thinking about uni work lately. Sometimes I feel like I’m trying to translate a whole book just to pass my modules. I’ve got this paper on scientific methods, and it’s like – why is this so hard? I mean, it’s not like we’re studying something new. It’s just like, you have to know what the question is, then answer it, and then explain why someone else might not get it. It’s so frustrating.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve got this band project where I have to write lyrics and then translate them into French. It’s not that hard, right? But then I get to the part where I have to explain the meaning behind each line, and it’s like, “Okay, now I’m confused.” I mean, how do you even explain the meaning of a song? It’s like it’s a different language all together.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? I think we’re all just trying to keep up with the pace. I mean, we’re students, we’re learning, we’re trying to make sense of it all. But I think it’s more about enjoying the journey than trying to get everything right.      Yeah, I think you’re right. It’s not like we’ve got to be perfect.

So, I was just thinking about how weird it is that we have spiders and mice in the house, but not a single bird. I mean, I’m sure there must be birds outside, but somehow they don’t make it inside. It’s like they’re afraid of us or something.      Oh, I don’t know. I think it’s more that we just don’t have the right kind of windows or something. I mean, I’ve seen birds outside my flat, but they never get near the glass. You’d think they’d just fly right through, but no, they always go around.      Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. It’s like they can see us and just decide not to come near. I remember once I left the window open and there was a little bird sitting on the ledge, and I just stood there for a minute thinking, “Oh, come on, fly in, it’s just me.” But it just stared at me like I was some kind of oversized insect and flew off.      That’s funny. I had something like that happen to me last week. I was out washing my car, and a sparrow landed on the bonnet, just like it was on a tiny airplane. I waved at it, and it just hopped off – no chance of getting a ride, I guess.      Yeah, maybe they just don’t like the way we dress. I mean, what with our suits, our shoes, and all that stuff. They probably think we’re not worth the trouble.      Maybe they’d be more friendly if we started wearing more feathers. Or maybe if we had a bird feeder outside. I’ve seen people put up bird feeders, and the birds just love it. I think I should try that.      I might have to do that too. I have this little garden at the back, and it’s pretty much just a mess. I could use a bit of greenery and some seed mixes.      You should. It’s amazing how birds can bring life to a place. I always feel better when there’s a bird outside my window. It’s like a reminder that the world’s still out there, even if it’s a bit messy inside.      Yeah, I guess you’re right. Maybe I’m just being too negative about all the spiders and mice.

Okay, so I've been meaning to ask you about your family tree. I've heard so much about your side of the family from your kids, but I feel like I've only scratched the surface. You know, those stories about your great-grandmother who ran a bakery in the 1920s—was that true?      Oh, it was absolutely true, though I don’t think it was a bakery. More like a small shop that served tea, cakes, and a few hot meals. It was right in the heart of the village, and people used to say she could make a cup of tea so good, it could make you forget about the war. But back to your question—how do you know so much about my family? You’re not even from the area.      Well, I’ve been told I’m a bit of a genealogy enthusiast. My own family’s history is a bit patchy, but I’ve always been curious about where people come from. Speaking of which, I’ve been meaning to ask—your mother, she passed away recently, didn’t she?      Yes, she did. It was a long illness, but she was brave. She had Alzheimer’s, and it got to be too much for her. She was in care for a couple of years before she passed. It was heartbreaking to watch. I still can’t believe she’s gone.      I’m so sorry to hear that. I’ve seen how it affects families. I’m not sure I’d have the strength to cope with it. I’ve been lucky so far—my mother’s still around, but I know it’s not for much longer. My father’s been diagnosed with something similar, and I’m trying to prepare for that.      You’re doing the right thing. I think your mother would be proud of you. You’ve always been so thoughtful. And speaking of careers, what do you do these days?      I’m a teacher, actually. I teach English at a secondary school. I’ve been doing it for over twenty years now. I’ve got a postgrad in education, and I’m still learning. It’s not the easiest job, but I love it. I think it’s the best way I can give back to the community.      That’s a wonderful career. I used to be a teacher too, in a different school, back in the 70s.

So, I was just thinking about that hot air balloon festival we saw last week in Norwich. You know, that one where they had all those balloons floating around like giant jellyfish in the sky. It was absolutely mesmerising.      Oh, I remember! I was actually surprised it didn’t get blown all over the place with the wind that was going. I reckon it must’ve taken years of planning just to get that right.      Yeah, and I bet it’s not just about the balloons. You can imagine how much money that kind of event must cost. I mean, those balloons are huge, and they’ve got to be made of some kind of special material, right? I’ve heard about how they’re regulated, too. You can’t just float a balloon around anywhere you want.      Definitely. I think they’re even tied down with some kind of giant harness or something. And I heard that the ones that go up are usually powered by helium, which is expensive. I mean, we’re talking about something that can carry a whole family up into the sky—what a dream.      It was really special, though. Like, as we were walking through the fields, I could see the balloons from a distance, and they looked like little clouds. It made me think about how much of our lives are controlled by technology these days. I mean, imagine if we had hot air balloons as a primary mode of transport back in the day. Everything would be so different.      That’s true. And not just in terms of transport. I mean, think about the wildlife—those birds, the cows, the sheep, they all just carry on with their lives, not knowing that about five hundred feet above them, there’s a bunch of people watching the sky. It’s wild, really.      I know. It’s a reminder of how small we are, in a way. But then again, we’ve got all this technology and all this modern stuff. It’s funny how quickly things change. I wonder if we’ll ever be able to camp out here without worrying about power lines again. I mean, you’d think with all the countryside, there’d be enough space, but no—everywhere you look, there’s some kind of wire or something.      It’s a bit of a shame, really. I love camping, especially out here in Norfolk.

So, I was thinking about how the weather's changed so much this year. It's been like a rollercoaster—sunny one day, then pouring rain the next. You’d think with all the climate change talk, we’d get used to it by now, but it’s still a bit of a shocker.      Yeah, I can't deny that. I've got a garden at home, and it's like trying to grow anything worth a damn. One minute it's warm enough for a shirt, the next it's freezing. You'd think the seasons would be more predictable. I've been trying to get the kids to plant some herbs, but they keep getting knocked by the weather.      I hear you. I teach language, and I find that the seasons also affect people's moods. Winter is a bit of a downer for some, while spring is a time of renewal. People usually pick up new books or hobbies in the spring. Have you read anything good lately?      Not much, to be honest. I've been quite busy with the gym. I'm an area manager, so there's always something going on. But I did pick up a book on coaching techniques – it's been helping me deal with the team better. You know, managing the staff and keeping morale up.      Oh, that's interesting. I've been researching a bit in my own time. I think coaching techniques can be really useful in any setting, not just at work. I mean, when I teach, I try to be more supportive and encourage feedback. It's a bit like a sport, isn't it? You have to adapt to the players' needs.      Definitely. I think I've been trying to be more empathetic with the staff, especially after the recent changes in the gym's direction. It's not just about the numbers; it's about people too. Speaking of people, have you been to Leeds? I was there a few times as a kid. The weather there is always different, but the people are friendly.      I've never been to Leeds, but I've heard it's quite a lively place. I've been to Manchester a few times, though. It’s got that urban vibe. I guess every city has its own character, and you pick up something new every time you go.      Exactly. It's one of the reasons I like traveling—experiencing different places and meeting different people.

So, I was just telling the lads about the time I tried to teach a kid how to factorise a quadratic equation, and he looked at me like I’d just asked him to explain quantum physics. Not sure if he was confused or just frightened.      Yeah, I remember that. You were really trying to explain it with all that “let’s break it down” stuff. I think I was confused, to be honest. I thought it was a code or something.      That’s the thing with maths, lad. It’s like trying to teach a dog to do calculus. You just have to go slow, and keep repeating it till it clicks. I remember when I was your age, I thought I was going to fail my GCSEs. I couldn’t even remember what a prime number was.      Oh, I remember when I was teaching in the old days, you had to remember that 2 was the only even prime number. And I would always say, “You know, if it’s even and bigger than 2, it’s not a prime.” But back then, people were more likely to get confused by the odd ones.      Yeah, I remember when I was trying to teach my wife about fractions. She was like, “Why don’t they just add up?” I was like, “Because you can’t just add up the denominators, you have to find a common ground.” She just looked at me like I’d said something funny.      Sounds like you all had your fair share of teaching moments. I think I’ve only ever taught myself how to do algebra. I mean, I passed my GCSEs, but I still don’t know why they call it algebra. It just seems like a lot of letters for nothing.      Oh, you’re a student, you think you know it all. I’ve seen you try to explain fractions to your brother, and you just end up confusing him more. He comes to me now and says, “Mum, do you know what 1/2 of 3 is?” I just say, “It’s 1.5, love.”      Oh, that’s because you were a maths examiner, weren’t you? You should be able to do that.      I never said I was good at it, just that I knew how to mark it properly. I remember one time a student wrote “1/2 of 3 is 1.5”, and I thought, “Oh, this is the one that’s going to pass.”

So, I'm sat here in this car, trying to get to that gig in Carlisle, and the satnav keeps telling me to take a route that goes through a mountain pass! It’s like it’s trying to kill me, not get me there.      I remember when I used to drive through those hills. My dad used to say, “If you don’t like the view, you can always turn around.” But I think he was just trying to get me to stop grinding my teeth. You know how it is, don’t you?      Oh, I know. I’ve had a few close calls with the satnav. My last one was trying to get me to a wedding in York and it told me to go through the A66 and then take a left onto a track that looked like it led to a sheep pasture. I nearly crashed into a sheep.      That’s not the first time I’ve heard that story. I once had a satnav tell me to go through the M6, then take a right onto a road that ended at a bus stop. I ended up getting lost for over an hour and had to ask a farmer where the nearest petrol station was. He looked at me like I was a tourist from Mars.      You don’t say. I think the problem is that satnavs don’t understand the nuances of the countryside. They don’t know about the potholes, the bends, the weather, or the fact that you can’t just drive straight into a village and expect to find a pub.      Exactly. I think the real issue is the lack of local knowledge. It’s like a robot trying to understand a human landscape. I mean, I’ve got a friend who’s a local and he can get from one place to another in under ten minutes, but his satnav would take him three hours.      You’re right. We should’ve just taken the old route through the village. It’s slower but safer. And besides, I’ve got a feeling the weather’s going to get worse. The forecast said there’s a chance of heavy rain later on.      Yeah, I’m not liking the look of that either. You know what they say—when the sky turns that grey, it’s like the clouds are putting on a show, but it’s not exactly a celebration.

So, I just got back from the site, and honestly, I was  this close  to booking a coffee with the site manager—just to see if he’s still single. But then I saw him with this girl in a £200 coat, and I thought,  Nope, not today.       You’re still sore about that girl at the last project, aren’t you? The one with the purple hair and the attitude?      Yeah, I mean, she was great in meetings, but she got really defensive when I asked about the structural integrity of the north wing. It was like she thought  she  was the architect.      Fair play. But what’s the point of talking about girls if you’re not even going to ask her out? You’ve got to pick your battles.      I know, I know. But honestly, I’ve been so busy with the university project brief that I’ve barely had time to think about dating. You know how it is.      Yeah, I get it. But you’ve got to balance work and life. I mean, even if you’re still trying to finish off that old project with the council, you can’t let work take over everything.      Exactly. Speaking of which, have you heard about Andy? He’s been struggling with the flat he’s working on. He’s been working 14-hour days, and his partner’s getting fed up.      Yeah, I heard. It’s a shame. He’s a good architect, but he’s too focused on the details. I told him to take a break, but he said he’s just trying to prove himself.      I told him the same thing. Maybe he needs to remember that architecture isn’t just about numbers and sketches—it’s about people. Like, you can’t just build a house if the client doesn’t want it.      True. And don’t forget, we’re all in the same boat. I mean, I had a client last week who wanted a communal living space with a shared kitchen and open-plan areas. It took me three weeks to convince them it wasn’t just a hippie commune.      Exactly! I mean, there’s so much potential in communal living. Imagine a design that’s not just functional, but actually makes people feel connected. It could be the next big thing.      Yeah, maybe. But until then, I think we need to start thinking about our own breakfasts.

Well, I think it’s about time we had a proper chat, love. You’ve been so busy with work lately, and I’ve been meaning to ask you about that new job you’re doing in the civil service.      Yeah, it’s been a bit of a whirlwind. I love it, though. The people are great, and the work is steady. But honestly, it’s a bit of a commute. You know how it is, the traffic in Grantham these days—it’s like trying to drive during rush hour in London!      My, my, I’ve heard enough about traffic from my own experiences! I live in Boston, Lincs, and I used to drive into Lincoln every morning for work. It’s amazing how something as simple as a red light can turn into a full-blown traffic jam. I remember one morning when I got stuck in a queue for over an hour. I was so late I nearly missed the meeting, and the boss was in a right temper!      It’s not just the traffic—it’s the way people drive, too. I was on the way home last week and this man was tailgating me like he was trying to race me. I had to slam on the brakes, and he just kept going. I almost had a panic attack. It’s so dangerous.      I know, love. I always tell people that driving is a skill, not a competition. But I think part of the problem is people are in a hurry and don’t seem to think about the others on the road. It’s like everyone’s in a rush to get somewhere, but no one’s actually in a rush to be anywhere.      I agree. I think it’s about respect on the road. I’ve been told by my colleagues that it’s not just about being polite, it’s about safety. If you’re going to be on the road, you should treat it like a public space, not your own private path. Also, if you’re wearing heels and being a walking disaster, at least you’ll be doing it in style.      Well, I’m going for a casual look. Maybe jeans and a t-shirt. I’m not sure if I want to go all out, but I do wanna make sure I look presentable.      I get that. I mean, I’ve got this black dress, but I’m not sure if I’m gonna pair it with heels or flats. I’ve got a couple of pairs of flats, and I don’t wanna be  that  person who wears heels and then basically walks away in tears.      You’re not that person yet, are you?      No, I’m not. But I also don’t wanna look like I’ve just come from a shopping trip at Tesco.      Okay, so we’re all in agreement – we need to look good, but not too much. Maybe we can all meet up and figure out what we’re wearing?

You know, I’ve been thinking a lot lately about soul mates. Not like that cheesy movie stuff, but more about whether there's actually something deeper than just chemistry. It’s like, is it possible that we’re not just meeting someone we’re attracted to, but someone who’s meant to be in our lives for a reason?      I’ve thought about that too. I mean, I’ve had a few relationships where it felt like we were meant to be, but then there were others where it just didn’t click. I think part of it is how you handle conflict. If you can talk through things and still feel close, maybe that’s the real test.      Yeah, I guess that makes sense. I’ve always believed in soul mates, but maybe I was too picky. Like, I thought if it wasn’t  perfect  from the start, it wasn’t right. But I think everyone has a different rhythm. Some people are more about the spark, others about the slow burn.      Exactly. I remember when I first met you—there was this instant connection, like we’d known each other for years. But it took time to realize that we were compatible in so many ways. We don’t always agree, but we respect each other’s opinions. That’s what keeps it real.      It’s funny, isn’t it? I used to think that if I found the right person, everything would just fall into place. But I’ve realized that it’s not just about finding someone—it’s about being willing to work at it. You have to be open to growing together.      I couldn’t agree more. I think a lot of people are looking for a perfect partner, but they forget that relationships are like a journey. You don’t have to have it all figured out from the start. You just have to keep moving forward, even when the road is bumpy.      Speaking of journeys, I was wondering—what if we had an imaginary party? Like, a time-traveling one. Let’s say we could invite anyone from any era. Who would we pick?      That sounds like a fun idea. I’d invite Gandhi—he’s got a lot of wisdom. And maybe a few scientists like Newton or Einstein. You’d be the queen of the party, though. You’d make sure everyone had a great time.

So, I just wanted to bring up something I’ve been thinking about a lot lately—the state of small businesses in our area. I mean, it’s such a vibrant community, but I feel like there are a lot of challenges. Do you ever feel like the kind of support we get is lacking?      Definitely. I mean, I work for the local council, so I see all the different sectors. A lot of small businesses are struggling with the cost of living, especially with the rise in rent and taxes. I remember one local café that had to close down last year when the landlord increased the rent by 30% without warning. It was heartbreaking.      That’s not just a local issue, is it? I’ve noticed that even in bigger cities, small businesses are under so much pressure. And then there’s the whole language thing—sometimes people from different areas have such different ways of speaking. Like when I was in London earlier this year, I was taken aback by the slang. It felt like a whole different world.      Oh, I can see that. I do sometimes feel like there’s a stereotype around people from the East of England. I’ve heard people say things like, “Oh, they’re all country bumpkins,” or “They don’t know how to speak properly.” It’s frustrating, isn’t it?      Exactly. And I think that’s part of the bigger issue with stereotyping. I’ve had people make assumptions about me just because of where I’m from. But I’m not from the South, I’m from Grantham. I think it’s all about how people perceive accents and dialects. It’s so unfair.      I agree. I mean, I’ve had people from the South of England say I speak like a “chav,” just because of my accent. I don’t know if it’s conscious or not, but it’s definitely a form of prejudice. I’ve even heard some people say that people from the East of England are more aggressive or violent. I think that’s just a stereotype, though.      Yeah, and I think that’s where the violence in society comes in. I’ve heard some people talk about how certain areas are more prone to crime, but I don’t think that’s really true. It’s more about social inequality and lack of opportunity.

So, I was just telling my mates about the flat we saw on Airbnb last week... It was in some weird part of the city, and I swear the toilet was louder than the shower. I don’t know how anyone lives there.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I got an email from my cousin about this place in town that’s a bit run down but super cheap. She said it’s got a weird vibe, like it was built in the 1970s and the walls are still painted in that ugly yellow.      Oh, I know that place. I accidentally walked past it on my way to the shops last week. It looked like it could collapse if you kicked the door. I almost called the landlord and said, “Is this the 21st century or the 19th?”      Yeah, I’d be tempted to do that. I mean, how do you even get a student loan for a flat like that? I was just thinking about the money we’re supposed to be saving for rent. It’s not like we can afford to live in a proper place.      I know, I know. My mates and I were at the pub last night, and we were trying to figure out how we’re gonna split the rent next year. You know what the worst part is? The tax on our student loans. It’s like they're trying to make us pay for everything.      Exactly. And then you have to pay for all this stuff like council tax and insurance. I swear, I’m paying more in fees than I did at home. It’s madness.      Oh, I feel you. I was just in the student union, and they were talking about some new rent control policy. But honestly, I don’t think it’s going to do anything. We’re all still going to be stuck waiting for a proper place.      Yeah, and I heard there’s some protest planned next week. I think it’s about the increase in tuition fees. I’m not sure I want to get involved, but it’s weird how everyone’s just so angry about it.      I can’t wait for the holidays. I’m seriously thinking of heading home for a bit. Even though I hate my family, I miss the food and not having to pay for everything.      I know, I know.

So, I was just telling my dad about the moped I saw in the parking lot—it was like a motorbike, but with more than two wheels. I was like, “Dad, that’s not a moped, that’s a  tricycle !” He just laughed and said, “You’re too young to know the difference.”      Oh, I remember when I was your age, I thought a moped was just a fancy bike. I used to ride to the supermarket with my mates, and when I hit the age limit, I had to get a car.      Yeah, I’ve been trying to get one of those moped thingies. My mates say it’s easier than a car, but I’m scared of the rules. Do you think I should get a learner’s permit first?      Definitely. I did that last year. It’s not too bad once you get the hang of it. Just make sure you wear a helmet and don’t go speeding. I’ve seen some kids out here in Croatia—good thing the roads aren’t too busy.      Speeding? I thought you Brits were more about the rules. I used to ride a motorbike in London, but I always followed the speed limits. It’s not just about the law—it’s about safety.      Yeah, but in my day, we didn’t have all these rules. I remember when I was a student, I used to ride my moped to work and back. It was a bit of a gamble, but I never got stopped.      Wait, what’s this? There’s an app that helps you find the nearest car park? I just used it to check for the cheapest bus route back to the hostel.      You’re such a tech geek. I tried using that app when I was in Manchester. It didn’t work that well.      I use apps for everything—from meal planning to scheduling meetings. But I still prefer a bit of human interaction. I go to the supermarket every week, and I always chat with the shopkeeper. It’s a small connection in a big world.      I agree. I used to work in a hospital, and every day was a reminder that people need connection. Even on the busiest days, a simple smile or a kind word made all the difference.      Yeah, I remember my first time in hospital as a kid. It was scary, but the nurses were really nice.

So, I’ve been thinking about that YHA volunteering in Cornwall, you know. It was a right laugh, honestly. I mean, I hadn’t been on a train since the day I left school, and there I was, off to Cornwall with a bunch of kids who could probably read the timetable better than I could.      You were the most nervous one there, love. I remember you standing outside the station, looking like you’d just seen a ghost. I had to go and comfort you. You said you’d never been that far from home.      Yeah, I know, I know. I’d always fancied a bit of travel, but I’d never actually done it. I mean, I’ve been to the seaside, but that’s not exactly travel. And the lighthouse—oh, the lighthouse! That was something else. I’d never seen one up close before.      You didn’t even know what a lighthouse was, did you, Dad? I mean, it’s not like we don’t talk about it. I remember you saying it was like something out of a storybook.      I remember that. I thought it was a building with a light in it, and I was like, “Oh, that’s clever,” and then I had to go and walk all the way up the hill to see it. It was a right slog, but it was worth it. The view was something else.      And the cycle race? You were so proud of yourself when you got to the top. I remember you saying it was about as far as you’d ever go. But then the next day, you were off again, doing the Yorkshire in a day.      I was. I thought I’d show the lot of you I could do it. I mean, I’ve been a bit of a couch potato all these years, but I thought, “I’ve got to get out there.” And then I came back with photos of crabs and everything.      You even took photos of the crabs, like you were a proper photographer. I still have that photo on my phone. You looked like you were trying to photograph a crab that was about to go on strike.      And you were so proud of yourself. I think you still are. You’ve got that little bit of fire in you still, even if you’re not working.      I think that’s what it is, love.

So, I’ve been thinking, do you ever just  not  want to cook? Like, I mean, I’ve got this chicken curry I’ve been meaning to make for ages, but it’s just… too much effort, you know?      I get that. I’ve been in that place with that same curry. But c’mon, it’s not that bad. I mean, you got the spices, the rice, the naan… it’s like a journey. You just have to take it step by step.      Yeah, but I’m more of a pasta person, honestly. I’ve been thinking about trying that new seafood pasta from the shop down the road. It’s got this sort of creamy sauce, and the prawns are fresh. It’s not like the heavy stuff with all the cheese.      I’ve been wanting to try that too. But I’m not sure if I can handle the indulgence. I’ve got this thing about not eating too much sugar or fat, you know? I mean, I’ve got that wedding coming up next month, and I don’t want to look like a bag of chips on the day.      Yeah, I know what you mean. My cousin tried that and ended up looking like a balloon. He was like, “I just wanted to look good in my suit!” Anyway, maybe we could all just order takeaway? Spaghetti and meatballs for everyone. Easy, cheap, and we can all talk about our relationships instead of cooking.       Please . You know how much I love meatballs. They’re the gold standard of comfort food. But I have to say, I’ve been thinking about my boyfriend again. We’ve been seeing each other a lot more lately. It’s like, we just… click. But I’m worried about how things are going. Are we moving in together? Or is it just… I dunno, a waiting game?      I get that. He’s been pretty committed, but I think he’s still figuring it out. You know, he’s got this job that’s not the most stable, so he’s got his head down trying to get on his feet. I just hope he doesn’t end up treating the relationship like it’s just a phase.      Yeah, and I think that’s the thing, isn’t it? You’ve got to talk about it. Like, if you’re not sure, you gotta tell the other person.

So, I just got back from Barcelona, and I couldn’t stop thinking about it the whole time. It was  so  different from anywhere I’ve been before. I mean, I've been to Paris a few times, but Barcelona felt like a whole other world—more alive, like the streets were buzzing with energy all the time.      Oh, I bet! I’ve wanted to go for ages. I remember reading about those colorful buildings and the beach, and I just imagined how amazing it would be. Did you get to see the Sagrada Família?      Yes, I did! It was absolutely stunning. I mean, I know it's been under construction for over a century, but it’s still so impressive. I even got to meet a couple of tourists who told me the architect was still working on some of the details. They said he’s still alive, which is mind-blowing. I couldn’t believe it!      Wow, that’s wild. I always thought that kind of thing was just in books. I guess I need to start planning a trip soon. I’ve got some time off next month, and I’ve been meaning to do something different. Maybe Barcelona?      You should! I mean, it’s only a few hours from here, and it’s such a fun city to explore. I really hope you get to go. I’m telling you, the food was amazing too. I had this tapas place that made these little bread rolls with all sorts of toppings. I’m still trying to recreate the recipe.      That sounds incredible. I love food, especially Spanish. I’m a big fan of paella, but I never thought I’d get to try it in the country it comes from. Although, I have to say, I’m not sure I’d be able to handle the heat. I’m more of a chilled-out weekend kind of person. Maybe Paris would be better for me?      Well, Paris is definitely a different vibe. I mean, it’s so romantic, but it’s also a bit overwhelming. I had to take a cab just to get around, honestly. I think I’m more of a Barcelona person. I’d love to go back again.      Yeah, I can see that. Maybe if you’re going again, you could invite me? I’d love to go with you. That’d be something to look forward to.

So, I heard you're an entrepreneur. That’s interesting. I’ve always been more of a teacher—what got you into that line of work?      Oh, it’s a long story, but I think it started when I was in university. I was studying business, and I always had this idea of starting my own thing. I didn’t want to be stuck in an office all day. I’ve had a few jobs before that, from retail to event management, but none of them really felt like  mine .      That’s admirable. I’ve always admired people who take the leap. I guess being a teacher is a bit more stable, but it’s not without its challenges. Being a teacher, you’re always dealing with different personalities and having to be on your toes.      Definitely. I think the hardest part of teaching is managing the classroom. But you’re always learning, aren’t you? I mean, with students, you get all sorts of perspectives. It keeps you on your feet.      That’s true. I mean, it’s not all about the kids, though. I’ve also had to deal with the administration, and the bureaucracy can be exhausting. Sometimes, I feel like I’m working more for the system than for the students.      I can imagine. I’ve had to deal with the same sort of thing in my business. You have to juggle so many things—finance, marketing, customer service. It’s not always easy. But I wouldn’t trade it for anything.      I suppose it depends on what you value. I’ve always wanted to make a difference, and teaching allows me to do that. I mean, I know I’m not going to be rich, but I feel like I’m contributing something worthwhile.      That’s a great sentiment. I think that’s what makes people happy in their jobs. When you’re doing something that aligns with your values. It’s not just about money.      Exactly. I hope one day to have that kind of satisfaction in my work. Even if it’s not a business, just something that feels meaningful.      You’re not too far off, really. You go to a school, you help shape young minds, and you know you’re making a difference. That’s a powerful thing.      Thank you. I think I’ll take that as a compliment. I’ve had my ups and downs, but I don’t regret it.

So, I was just thinking, do you reckon we should get a dog? Like, proper, you know, with a collar and everything?      You’re joking, aren’t you? You said that last week. And then you told me you couldn’t even walk the dog without getting covered in mud.      Yeah, but that was before I actually got one! I mean, it’s not like we’ve got a proper place to keep one. We’re still sharing a flat with those two people from the flat above.      And I don’t even know what they do with their dog. From what I’ve heard, it’s like a big, muddy, barking monster that chases the Postman.      Oh, come on, don’t be like that. That’s just their dog. It’s not like it’s a criminal or anything. Besides, we could get a cat. Or a hamster. Or a goldfish?      Yeah, a goldfish. I’m sure your flatmates would love that. It’s got no noise, no mess, and it’s easy to feed. Just put some pellets in the bowl and then it dies in a week.      You’re so mean. You know what I mean. I just think we need something to make the flat feel more like home. We’re still living in that studio with the broken fridge and the oddly-shaped shower.      Yeah, and I still haven’t figured out how to use the oven. I mean, I know how to turn it on, but I don’t know how to make it actually cook anything.      You’re not the only one. I tried to make a toast once. All I ended up with was a charred piece of bread and a lot of smoke.      I could’ve told you that. You’re just as bad as me. But hey, we’re both learning, right?      Yeah, I guess. But I still think we should get a pet. Maybe a bird or something. Just to have some company.      You’re getting more and more weird by the minute. I’m telling you, we’re not ready for a pet. We’re not even ready for a proper meal without burning it.      Well, that’s what I like about you. You’re the only one who can make me feel like a complete failure in the kitchen.      Yeah, and that’s what makes us a good couple.

Well, I’ve been out and about, lass. Felt like I needed a bit of fresh air after sitting in the chair all day. Went to the market, saw a proper variety of things. Not like the ones in the town centre, which are always the same old stuff.      You didn’t miss much, then? I was just about to go out myself, but I thought I’d wait for you. I heard the kettle was boiling, so I thought I’d make us both a cup of tea.      Aye, I saw it too. Thought I’d grab a few bits and bobs, but I ended up buying more than I needed. Still, it’s nice to have a bit of variety. I reckon the kids would have loved it, but they’re all off to work now, aren’t they?      Aye, I suppose they are. I remember when they were little, you’d have to keep the shop open for them. Now they’re all grown up, and I’m just here with you, I think.      That’s the way of it, isn’t it? Time flies. I was just thinking earlier, how the years have been passing by, and I’m still here, trying to keep the place running. It’s not as easy as it used to be, is it?      No, it’s not. But you know what? It’s still nice to have someone to talk to, and someone to share the tea with. Even if we’re both retired and not doing much, it’s about being together.      Aye, that’s true. There’s not much else to do around here, really. The village is quiet, and the days go by so slow. Sometimes I think about the days when we had more going on, but I suppose it’s better this way. At least we’ve got each other.      Yeah, I think we have. It’s not the same as when the kids were around, but it’s different in its own way. You know, I sometimes think about how we used to get up early, make our own breakfast, and have a proper start to the day. Now it’s just us, and the kettle, and some tea.      Aye, and those days are gone. But I wouldn’t trade them for anything, really. You’ve been a good companion these years, lass. You’ve kept me going, I reckon.

So, I was just telling my granddaughter, Ellie, about the time I tried to fix the loo. And I went and got the wrong bit, you know, the one that's for the tap. And I stuck it in and it made such a  clunk . She laughed so hard, she almost spilled her tea. It was ridiculous.      That sounds like a classic North Yorks story. I remember my gran telling me about the time she tried to do the same with the oven. She thought the oven light was a button you pressed to start it. So she pressed it, and the whole thing lit up like a firework.      Oh, I’ve had my fair share of mishaps, too. I remember the time I tried to put the lights on in the hall and I tripped over the cat. And when I got up, I noticed the cat had a bit of a lightbulb in its mouth! That was a real drama.      Ah, the cat, yes! That was a good one. I used to have a cat like that. She used to follow me around like a shadow, watching everything I did. She even used to sit on the loo – just to make sure I was doing it right.      You know what they say about cats – they’re like little teachers. And if they don’t like what you’re doing, they’ll let you know in a very dramatic way.      So, I guess it’s all part of life, isn’t it? You try to do things, and sometimes you end up learning the hard way. But it’s all part of what makes us human.      Yeah, I suppose. My husband used to say that if you don’t mess up once in a while, you’re not trying hard enough. But I think he was just trying to make me feel better about my accident with the lightbulb.      He was a good man. He had a way of making even the worst moments seem a bit lighter.      He was. And I think that’s what makes these moments so special. We’re all just trying to get by, and sometimes we mess up. But we have each other, and that’s what really matters.      Yeah, it’s the family stuff that reminds you why you’re here. Even if the loo’s broken, or the cat’s got a lightbulb, we’re always in it together.

So, I’ve been thinking about that protein powder you were talking about last week. I got one of those shaker bottles, you know, the ones with the little pump thing on the side. It’s £20 for the bottle and the powder. I mean, it’s not that bad, but I feel like I’m paying for the branding more than the actual protein.      Yeah, I got one too, but I just use a regular bottle. I think it’s just the marketing that’s expensive. I mean, when I first started, I thought I needed all this gear, but now I just use a normal one and the powder’s still fine. It’s like that one of those things where you feel like you’re missing out if you don’t have the right equipment.      I’m with you, mate. I still use a basic bottle from when I was in uni. I’ve got a whole collection of protein powders, though, because I’m always trying to find the best one. I even did a bit of research, like reading reviews and everything. It’s like a mini obsession.      I tried that once, mate. I spent a week reading about all these different brands and ended up buying three different powders. Then I tried them all and ended up back at the first one. It’s like the same as trying different brands of tea—there’s only one that’s right for you.      I’m the same. I had a friend who was into all this fitness stuff, and he’d be like, “You need this, you need that.” I nearly bought a whole gym membership just because he said the treadmill was the best. But then I just ended up going to the local gym and using the free weights. It’s not all about the gear, is it?      Yeah, I think you’re right. I mean, it’s all well and good to have the stuff, but if you don’t actually use it, then what’s the point? I’ve been thinking about getting a new laptop anyway—my old one’s starting to slow down. I’ve got this idea to switch to a Mac because I’ve heard it’s more stable. Not sure yet though.      You can’t be serious. A Mac? I’m still using my old PC, and it’s fine.

So, I just swatted a bug off the window. Felt like I was in some kind of action movie. You’d think with all the insect repellent I’ve been slathering on, it’d be a bit more… I don’t know,  effective ?      I’m not surprised. I’ve had a few of those myself. Though I’ve found that a good swat with a piece of cardboard can be just as effective. It’s not like they’re going to run away from a bit of cardboard, are they?      Yeah, I mean, I’ve seen them try to fly away, but they’re like,  “Oh no, not again.”  I got bit last week. My leg was red and swollen for days. I thought I was allergic or something.      I’ve had that too. I once got bitten by a horsefly and thought I was going to die. But, to be fair, I was in a  very  hot place. I think it’s more about the environment than the insect itself.      I guess. But still, there’s got to be a better way than just swatting. I mean, I’m not even sure I’m doing it right. I tried using a fly swatter last time, but somehow it just missed every time. Like it was  cheating  or something.      Let me tell you, a good fly swatter can do wonders— if  you know how to use it. I’ve got one that’s  old  as the hills, but I still use it every day. You just have to aim properly. You don’t just flick it, you  swing  it.      I don’t even know how to use a swatter. My gran tried to teach me, but I kept trying to slap them instead of using it. I ended up knocking over a glass of water. We had to clean up  three  times.      That sounds like a classic family moment. You know, I’ve got this bug spray that’s basically a DIY go-to. I mix it with some lavender oil and lemon. It smells nice and it’s not that bad. Although I’ve got to say, the one from the chemist is  way  better.      Maybe I should just go to the chemist next time. I’ve been meaning to anyway. We need to make a shopping list for tomorrow. I think we’re out of bread and eggs.      Yeah, and I need to buy some more baby wipes.

So, I was just watching this YouTube video about science experiments, and it was like...  so  cool. You know that one with the baking soda and vinegar?      Oh, I saw that! But you can do that in your kitchen, not in a  real  lab. You know what I think? I think your teacher would have a fit if you tried that in class.      Oh, please! Miss Evans would  love  us for being creative. She’s the one who made us build a mini volcano out of clay and red food dye. That was  not  a real volcano.      Yeah, and it exploded all over the table. I still have the stain on my shirt.      I know! And when she said we had to write a report on it, I just wrote, “This was not a volcano, this was a disaster.” And she gave me full marks.      That’s not fair. I think you’re just lucky.      Maybe. But I still think we should do more of these “science” things. Like, what if we tried making slime? I saw a video where you just mix glue and borax and it turns into something gross.      That's what you said last week. And you got stuck with a blob of goo in your hair.      That was  one  time! And I had to spend the whole weekend washing my hair. I even used the special shampoo from the chemist.      Oh, I bet you did. You always do everything the hard way.      Yeah, but it’s fun. Speaking of fun, did you see that Instagram post from Emily? She posted a video of her doing a TikTok dance in the school hallway.      Yeah, and she was like, “Guess who’s trending?” But I think she just wanted to show off her new go-to shoes.      I think she’s just trying to get more followers. You know how she always says, “If you don’t post, you’re invisible.”      Yeah, and she’s right. I mean, we all know the only reason she’s popular is because she’s got a great laugh.      And she’s got that whole “I’m not a fan of the internet” vibe, but she’s still on it.      Yeah, it’s like she’s two different people on different days.      I guess that’s just growing up, you know?      Yeah, and I think we’re both getting better at it.

I swear, I’ve been coughing all day. I think I’ve got a proper cold now. I mean, I’m not sure if it’s a cold or just that weird stomach thing I had last week.
