Did you ever get food poisoning from that street food place in Bristol? I still haven’t fully recovered from that.      Yeah, I remember you talking about it. You were so pale after that. Still, I’d rather have food poisoning than the flu. At least you can tell when it’s coming. But, honestly, I think you’re just faking it. You’ve been doing that thing with your eyes and your hands when you’re trying to sound sick. It’s pretty obvious.      Oh, come on, I’m not faking. I’ve been up all night with a fever. And don’t even get me started on the vaccine. I’ve been reading about it like it’s the next big thing. I mean, I’m not anti-vax, but I still don’t like the idea of sticking a needle in my arm. I’ve got a friend who says it’s like putting your hand in a blender. I’m not sure if that’s true, but it sounds terrifying.      I heard that too. It’s all over the news. They’re saying it’s not just about the vaccine itself, but the side effects. I’ve been watching those TV shows about body language recognition. They say people can detect if you’re lying just by looking at your face. I don’t know if that’s true, but it’s kind of creepy. I mean, are they using cameras in public places to check for lies? That’s the kind of thing that could go wrong.      I guess it’s not just about the vaccine. It’s the whole idea of health and hospitals. I mean, I’ve been to the hospital three times this month. I think I’m just too sensitive. I don’t like the idea of being in a sterile room with people who are sick. It’s not just the smell, it’s the feeling of being watched. I remember watching that show with Lloyd Grossman where he talks about how people can tell when someone’s lying just by looking at their eyes. I think he said something about the left eye, or was it the right?

So, I just used the letter 'Q' and got a massive score. That’s got to be the best move of the game so far. You lot are going to have to beat that, or I’m going to feel like I’ve won.      Well, I’ve got a 'Z' and a 'J' in my rack. Maybe I can make something with that. Not sure yet. I’m not entirely sure if I’ve got the right letters to do anything with them, though. You know how it is, always chasing that big word.      I think I’ve got the 'S' and 'C' and 'R' left. I was trying to make 'scramble' but I didn’t have the 'A'. Wait, I think I just managed to make 'scare' and 'crash'… Hmm, not sure which one would be better.      You’re thinking too hard. Just go with the 'scare' and take the points. You don’t need to overcomplicate it. I used to play a lot more when I was younger, back when I was a schoolmaster. We used to have these long games that would last for hours.      Yeah, I remember when we used to play Scrabble in the staff room. You always had to win to get the last biscuit. It was the only way someone would give you a treat. I think my mum used to play with us sometimes. She was a bit of a Scrabble whiz.      My wife used to be really good. She always used to play with us on weekends. Although, I have to say, she never really got into it when we moved to Manchester. She said the sound of the city was just too distracting for her concentration. She prefers her quiet moments.      I still have my old set. It’s a bit worn, but it’s still in the cupboard. I remember when I was headmistress, we used to play with the staff after school. It was the best way to unwind. I even got a few of the staff into the habit. Though I have to say, the younger ones are so competitive now.      You’re not the only one. I used to have to compete with the headmaster to see who could get the highest score. It was never about winning, it was more about the game itself.      That’s the thing about Scrabble. It’s not just about the game, it’s about the people you play with.

So, you're telling me you once had a successful career in inventing and marketing printing systems? I mean, I never thought I’d hear that from a bloke who’s been long-term unemployed and lives in a caravan in the Somerset countryside!      Oh, I’ve had my ups and downs, just like everyone. I used to work in Germany—no, not just working, I was  inventing  printing systems. You know, those big machines that print books and newspapers. I got into it through a company in Munich. It was a different time, but I had some good ideas.      Sounds like you had a real knack for it. I used to deal in antiques and old art, so I know a bit about craftsmanship, but I never thought of combining that with technology. What made you pivot to printing systems?      Well, I suppose it was a mix of curiosity and necessity. I was always tinkering with things. My father was a mechanic, and I spent a lot of time in his workshop. I got into the mechanics of machines, and it just kind of evolved into something more. Then, in the mid-’80s, I met a guy who was running a small publishing house in Germany. He needed someone with technical know-how, and I was the guy he found.      And how did you manage to market your systems? I mean, not many people would take a retired mechanic seriously in a field like that.      You’d be surprised. I had a good head for business, and I didn’t let my age or background hold me back. I used to travel to exhibitions in Germany and other parts of Europe. I’d set up small demos, talk to publishers, and show them how my system could improve their operations. It wasn’t easy, but I was persistent.      Persistence goes a long way. I suppose that’s one thing I’ve always had. Even when I was working, I never stopped trying to find new ways to bring value to the things I sold.      To persistence then. And to hoping that one day, maybe we’ll get back to doing something we love.      To hoping—and to the chance that maybe, just maybe, we’ll both find a way back into the world of work.      Yeah, maybe. Or at least, we’ll always have the stories to keep us going.      And that’s something we can both claim to have, I think.

Dad, I can't believe you still say “bath” instead of “bathe” – I thought we learned that in primary school!      Oh, I know, love. I still say “bath” like it’s a place, not a verb. I remember my teacher used to get so annoyed with me. She said it was a “misspelling” – but I think it's just a regional thing. You know how we speak in the North, we’ve got our own way of doing things.      Yeah, I get that, but it’s funny because when I was learning English in the sixth form, we had to analyse the etymology of words. You know, like how “bath” comes from the Old English “bathe” and “bath” is the noun. It’s actually the same root. So it’s not a misspelling at all.      Oh, interesting. I never looked at it like that. I always thought it was just a silly way of saying it. But I guess you get into all that in school. I left school at 16, so I never got to university. But I’ve always wanted to. I mean, I’ve got a good head for numbers, and I know I could do it, but I never really thought about it. You, though – you're going to uni, aren't you?      Yeah, I’m applying for a philosophy course in Bristol. It’s got a really good reputation. I thought it’d be cool to study something like that. It’s not exactly practical, but I love thinking about big questions. Like, what is the meaning of life? Or why do we even care about the meaning of life?      That’s the kind of stuff that gets you into trouble at school. But I like it. I always thought philosophy was the best subject. Though I never actually studied it. I told myself I’d take it up when I was older, but I never did. Maybe I should’ve.      You never know, Dad. Maybe you can do it. I mean, you’ve got experience in customer service, so it’s not like you’re starting from scratch. You could even use your skills there.      I suppose. But I’ve got this holiday to think about. We’re heading to Cornwall, right? I’ve never been there. I think it’s got those big rocks and the sea. Is it like that?      Yeah, it’s got those big rocks and all that coastline.

So, what’s for dinner, then? I was just gonna make a stir-fry, but I thought maybe we could all chip in and make something a bit more substantial.      That sounds good, but I wouldn’t say no to a good old roast. I’ve been meaning to try making one proper.      Roast sounds good. I love a good roast. My nan used to make the best one. She’d do a whole leg of lamb, and it was always so juicy.      Oh, really? I’ve never actually had lamb, to be honest. I’m more of a turkey or chicken person.      You’re missing out. Lamb is proper food. It’s got that rich taste, you know. But I suppose it depends on how you cook it.      Yeah, it’s all about the seasoning. My nan always used rosemary and thyme, and a bit of garlic. She’d say it’s all in the aromatics.      That sounds fancy. I’ve never really thought about it like that. I just throw some herbs in and call it a day.      You’re not really cooking, you’re just tossing ingredients in a pan. You need to cook with intention, you know.      That’s the way it is. I remember when I was younger, I tried to cook for my mates, and it ended up being a disaster. One of them nearly choked on a piece of meat.      That’s what you get for not cutting it up properly! I’ve had that happen to me before. I tried making a stew and forgot to chop the potatoes, and it was like eating a brick.      I’ve had worse. Once I tried making a cake and it ended up being more like a rock. My mum said it was a new kind of digestive.      That’s not a bad idea. Maybe you should start a line of rock cakes. It’s got a market, I reckon.      You’re right. Maybe we should all start a food business. I’ve got the organisational skills, you’ve got the cooking skills, and I’ve got the connections from work.      You’re on. I’ll make the meat, you’ll handle the logistics, and I’ll take care of the marketing.      And I’ll be the judge of the taste. If it’s not good, I’ll be the first to say so.      Deal.

So, I heard you're teaching English now. How’s that going? I mean, I thought you were into more... creative stuff?      Oh, I still love the creative stuff—writing, art, all that—but teaching gives me a different kind of satisfaction. It’s like helping people see the world through language. And honestly, I’ve always been passionate about how language shapes identity.      That makes sense. I guess it’s like being a bartender—everyone comes in with their own story, and you just have to listen. Though I’d never say I’m a good listener, honestly.      I’m sure you’re a great listener when it matters. I mean, you’ve been working at The Silver Spoon for months now, right? How’s the gig? Still loving it?      Yeah, it’s alright. I like the rhythm of it, you know? The people, the energy. It’s not the same as being a teacher, though. I mean, I never thought I’d end up in a bar. I was going to be a writer, like, full-time.      You were? That’s cool. I mean, I always thought you had the kind of brain that could write books. You have that way of putting things together.      Maybe. But I got sidetracked. I mean, I did a degree in English, then a postgrad in linguistics. It was all theory, though. No real world application. So I figured, why not try something practical?      I get that. I had a similar path. I studied languages and then moved into teaching because I wanted to be around people. And honestly, it’s not all theory here. You get to learn new things every day.      To the unpredictable paths of life.      And to the fact that sometimes the wrong path leads you somewhere amazing.      Yeah, I guess it does. Though if you ever need a barista for your language classes, I’m your guy.      I’ll keep that in mind. And if you ever want to write, you know where to find me. I’ve got a few students who’d love to read your stuff.      I’ll keep that in mind too. Maybe I’ll write a story about a bartender and a language teacher.      Please. That’s a cliché. But hey, if you do, I’ll be the first to read it.      Deal.      You know, it’s funny. We’re both kind of stuck in the middle—between dreams and reality.

Right, I'm just about to do that – I've got the mug in my hand, and I'm just about to pour the coffee. I think it's going to be a proper cup, not one of them instant ones, like the children used to have.      I don’t think you need to explain that, love. You’ve been known to make that coffee for years. I remember when we first got married, you used to make it so strong it made the whole kitchen smell like a café.      Yes, like the sort of coffee you'd get in a place like Munchausen, if you know what I mean. Though, I have to say, I think the one you make is better.      Oh, you're just saying that because you've never had it when it's been properly made. I remember when I was in Gambia, I used to make coffee with the locals – not the way we do it here, but it was different. I suppose it's all about the beans, isn’t it?      Yes, and I think the best part is how you can make it in such a humble way. I remember when I was a childminder, I used to bring coffee to the parents, and they’d say, “What a lovely cup you’ve made.”      I think the real key is the coffee machine. You know, the one you’ve had for years, and it’s like it’s a part of the family. I still have mine from when I was in the business, and it’s been through a lot.      Right, I need to be heading off. I’m late for break time, and I don’t want to be the one who’s always running late. I’ve got that donation box to sort out.      Oh, you’re doing the donation box again? I thought that was done.      Yes, and I think the banners are going to be a good idea. We could put them up by the entrance so people know what it’s for.      I think it's a good idea, but I’ll be honest, I’m more worried about the plants. I’ve had a few go out of their pots, and I’m not sure what to do with them.      You’ll get the hang of it. I think it’s all about the bell ringing, really.

So, I just got this new mobile app that’s supposed to help you track your fitness goals. It’s called  FitTrack , and honestly, I’m already regretting downloading it.      Oh no, you’re not going to like it then? I’ve heard of that one. It’s all about counting calories and tracking steps, right?      Yeah, that’s the thing. I tried it once, and after a week, I was so obsessed with my step count that I started running to the shops just to get more steps. It was kind of fun at first, but then I got burned out.      That sounds like a typical  FitTrack  experience. I think the app is designed to make you feel like you’re failing if you don’t reach your targets. It’s a bit sad, honestly.      Yeah, and then there’s this feature where it reminds you to drink water every hour. I’ve got a water bottle on my desk, but I still forget to drink it. It’s like the app is trying to take over my life.      I can relate. I’ve tried a few fitness apps, but they all end up feeling like a chore. I think the key is to make it fun. Maybe if we all agreed to do a challenge, like a weekend fitness journey or something.      That’s a good idea. I’d actually love that. I’ve been meaning to start working out more, but I never get the motivation. If we all commit to something, it might help.      Or maybe we could do something non-fitness related. Like, a movie night where we all watch a scary movie together. I heard the new  Halloween  movie is really intense.      Oh, I’d love that. I haven’t seen a proper horror movie in ages. Maybe we could do that after our fitness challenge.      I’m in. But I’m warning you, I’m not going to be scared. I’ve seen too many horror movies.      Yeah, you’re not the only one. I’ve got a few friends who say they’re brave, but when the lights go out, they run for the door.      Exactly! I once watched  The Conjuring  with a group of friends, and half of them ended up crying. It was ridiculous.      That’s the kind of thing I was thinking of. Maybe we can talk about our favorite scary movies later.

Well, I don't know what’s come over me, but I’ve been thinking about buying a car. I mean, I’ve had mine for twenty years, and I’ve had to do a few bits and pieces here and there. But I’ve been driving it as long as I can remember, and it’s just beginning to fall apart.      You know, I reckon it’s time you thought about it. I’ve been reading about these new electric cars, and they don’t need as much maintenance. You know, no oil changes, no exhausts, just plug it in and go. Sounds like a dream, but I guess it’s not for everyone.      Oh, I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve got this old Ford, and it’s been giving me trouble for ages. You know, it started making that knocking noise when I first started the engine, and now it’s just been getting worse. I’ve been trying to get it fixed, but the garage says it’s too old and they can’t even get spare parts.      Yeah, I’ve been thinking the same thing. I’d rather get something modern, something that’s reliable. But I’ve got to be honest, I’m not sure I can afford it. I mean, I’m retired, and I’ve got no income. I just rely on benefits, and they don’t cover much. I’ve been telling myself that if I can’t afford a new car, I’ll just keep the old one for a bit longer.      I know what you mean. I’ve been doing the same. I had this old Rover, and I used to be able to drive it all over the countryside, but now it’s about as reliable as a sack of feathers. I had to sell it last year, and I’ve been taking the bus ever since. It’s not the same, but at least I don’t have to worry about the cost.      I’ve been considering taking the bus too. I used to drive a lot when I was working, but now I just stay local. I mean, I can walk to the shops, but getting home from the village is a different story. I’ve got to take the bus, and sometimes it’s late, and sometimes it’s full. It’s not really convenient.

Well, I think it’s time we actually made a decision about moving house. I’ve been thinking about it for a while, especially since I’m retired now and not tied to a job anymore.      I can see where you’re coming from, but I’m still not sure about the whole moving thing. I mean, I’ve got a stable place here, and I don’t want to uproot everything just because you’re retired.      Yeah, I get it. I’ve been through this before. When I left the oil industry, I thought moving would be a fresh start, but it turned out I just ended up in the same old rut, just in a different place.      You were in the oil industry? I remember you talking about that once. It must have been a different world.      Oh, it was. I mean, it was technical, but there was a lot of pressure. You had to be on call all the time. I think that’s why I got burnt out. I tried to move to a smaller town, but it didn’t work out. I just ended up in a place where I felt like I didn’t belong.      I can imagine. I’ve been in the transcribing world for a while now, and it’s not exactly the most exciting career, but it’s stable. I mean, I have a good place to live here, and I like the routine.      That makes sense. But the thing is, I’m not looking for a routine. I want something different. Maybe closer to the countryside, or near a lake. I’ve always loved the idea of being near water.      You know, I was thinking about that too. I tried to find a place near a river once. It didn’t work out, but maybe there’s something out there.      Maybe it’s time we all start looking. I mean, the weather is getting colder, and I think it’s time we all got out of this house. It’s been too long since we’ve done something like this.      You’re right. We’ve been stuck in this house for too long. It’s time we did something about it. Maybe even take a trip somewhere.      Yeah, I’ve been thinking about a short trip to the coast. Maybe Cornwall. I could do with a change of scenery.      That sounds amazing!

Right, you were so upset when your bike got stolen last week. I remember you were shouting at the top of your lungs, like you’d seen a ghost.      You don’t even know what I went through. I had to walk two miles to school every day. I was so stressed, I even started skipping some classes.      I know, I know. But I was talking to the police, and they said they found the bike. It was in a junkyard near the old car park, near the beach.      Wait, really?      Yeah. One of the officers said he saw someone trying to sell it on Facebook Marketplace. They tracked the transaction and got the bike back. It's in the garage, waiting for you.      Oh my God. I can’t believe it. Thank you so much for helping me sort it out. I didn’t know where to start.      You don’t have to thank me. We’re family. But also, you need to be more careful with your stuff. I remember when I was your age, I used to lose my wallet all the time.      Yeah, you always said you had the attention span of a goldfish.      Exactly. But it’s funny, isn’t it? My bike got stolen once too. I had to borrow one from my friend for a month. It was a disaster.      So you’re telling me I’m not the only one who’s had a bike stolen? That makes me feel a little better.      You’re not alone. And hey, you’re getting your bike back. That’s the main thing.      I can’t wait to ride it again. I’ve been dreaming about it all week. I was going to buy a new one, but this one’s way better.      Just make sure you keep it safe. I’ve learned my lesson. No more biking without a lock, no more leaving it outside.      I promise, I won’t make the same mistakes again. I’ve had enough of walking to school.      Good. Now, let’s get you back on two wheels. And maybe we can go for a ride this weekend. The weather’s looking nice.      That sounds perfect. Just don’t expect me to be the one doing all the work this time. I’ll be the one holding the handlebars.      Deal. I’ll be the one waiting with the coffee. That’s how it’s going to be.

So, I just had the most ridiculous idea about the train dynamics. You know how when you’re on a train and you’re trying to find a seat, and someone just  slips  into it? Not like they’re being polite, but they just  slide  in like they own the place.      Oh, I know that feeling. I once saw a woman do that on the  GWR —she was so fast, she nearly knocked over someone’s coffee.      That’s the  GWR ? I thought that was just a  regular  train.      It’s  GWR , the Great Western Railway. It’s not just any train. It’s got the charm of a 19th-century steam engine and the efficiency of a modern tram.      I remember when I was in Singapore, the trains there were so fast, they didn’t even have the same kind of dynamics. You’d just walk on and off like you were in a movie.      I’ve never even taken a train. I’ve always taken the bus. But I’ve heard stories from the support workers about how the buses are  always  late, and the trains are  always  full.      Yeah, I think the real problem with trains is the  schedule . They’re supposed to be reliable, but they’re not.      Exactly! And it’s not just the schedule. There’s also the  culture  of trains. You’ve got people with their headphones on, people eating chips, and then you’ve got the people who just  take over  the seat.      I once sat next to someone who was playing  Monopoly  on their phone. They were so into it, I thought they were actually playing it in real life.      That sounds like something I would’ve seen in Singapore. The people there are always so  efficient , but also  very  territorial about their space.      I think I get it. It’s like a microcosm of the world in a small space.      Yeah, and when you have a big group, like when we’re playing  Ticket to Ride —it’s like a train journey. You’ve got to plan your route, but also deal with the  dynamics  of the game.      Exactly! And if you get too ambitious, you might end up with a  straight line  to nowhere, like that one time I tried to connect Paris to Moscow.      Oh, that was a disaster. You ended up with a red route that just looped back to the starting point.

So, I think I’ve finally figured out why you hate the game  Monopoly —it’s not just the luck of the dice or the board, it’s the whole damn concept of wealth accumulation. It feels so… unfair, you know? Like, you’re not just playing a game, you’re  pretending  to be a capitalist.      Oh, come on, love. It’s a metaphor, isn’t it? It mirrors real life—people do get ahead, and others don’t. Didn’t you grow up with that idea? I mean, we all know how the  real  world works, right?      Please, I grew up in Norwich, not London. I was more interested in the Postman Pat cartoon than the cutthroat of the world. But even so, it’s just not fun to watch someone win by pure chance. I mean, I’ve seen you throw a dice and roll five sixes in a row. It’s not fair.      That’s the joy of it, though—there’s always a chance. You can’t control everything. It’s like life. You’ve got your skills, your luck, and sometimes, you just have to take the win. Or lose gracefully.      Yeah, but don’t you think it’s kind of… toxic? The whole idea of hoarding money and pushing people out of the game? It’s not just a game—it’s a lesson in inequality. I mean, you know, I’ve been in the real world and seen how that plays out.      I agree. That’s why I prefer  Catan —it’s more about strategy and trading. You can be successful without trampling over others. Plus, it’s less aggressive. You don’t have to  buy  your way to victory.      Exactly! I love how you can build settlements, trade resources, and still come out on top without being a complete jerk. It’s like a more civilised version of the real world.      And I think it’s also the drinking culture that makes me prefer it. You know, after a few glasses of wine, I just want to play a game where I can actually  win  without being a complete capitalist villain.  Monopoly  just feels too… oppressive.      True. I mean, I’ve seen you get so frustrated when someone just landed on your property and you couldn’t afford to buy it. It’s like a miniature version of being evicted, only with more board game stakes.

So, I just got an email from the council about the bins. They said we need to order new ones because the old ones are being phased out. I’m not even sure what they mean by that.      Yeah, I read that too. It’s one of those things that’s supposed to make things more efficient, but honestly, it feels like just another hassle. I’ve been trying to order a new fridge online, but every time I click “buy,” there’s a 20% surcharge for delivery.      Oh, don’t get me started. I had to replace my old fridge last year, and the whole process was a nightmare. I had to go through three different retailers before I found one that actually had the right size and features. And then there was the problem with the installation. The company sent someone, but they couldn’t fit the fridge in the kitchen because the wall was too thin.      That sounds like such a pain. I’m not even sure we need a new fridge yet. We have the old one, and it still works, even if it’s a bit outdated. But I guess it’s just one of those things you have to keep up with.      Exactly. I remember when I was doing my project co-ordination work, we had to manage a lot of small but frustrating tasks like that. It’s like the bigger picture is always what matters, but the details can really trip you up.      Speaking of details, have you two heard about the new local chef who’s been doing a series of pop-up dinners? I think he’s from Swansea, like me. I went to one last week, and it was incredible. He used local ingredients and everything.      That sounds amazing. I’ve been wanting to try something new with cooking. I’ve been doing a lot of experimenting with herbs and spices lately. Maybe I’ll try making my own pasta sauce next week.      That sounds great. I’ve been meaning to start cooking more instead of just relying on takeaway. I even bought a new set of cookware last month. It’s a bit of an investment, but I think it’s worth it.      You know, I’ve been thinking about doing some DIY improvements around the house. Maybe I’ll paint the kitchen walls, or even try my hand at a bit of carpentry.

Man, I swear the traffic in this city is getting worse every year. I don’t know how you ever managed to get around in this area when you were a kid, Mum. It’s like the roads are designed to make us late.      Yeah, I know what you mean. When I was your age, we didn’t have all these traffic lights and all the congestion we see now. It was easier, you know. We’d just drive straight to wherever we needed to go, no queues, no stress.      That’s the thing, though—those days are gone. It’s like the city’s turned into a maze. I’m starting to think I need a GPS just to find the postcode of my own house.      You’re not alone in that. I used to have a paper map, and it’s amazing how often I’d get lost even with that. Now I just rely on my phone. But I still miss the feel of reading a paper map—there’s something about holding a physical copy.      I get that. I mean, I still have a few books from my uni days, though I mostly read e-books now. It’s just easier, you know? But I don’t know, there’s something about the smell of a real book.      Yes, there is. I still have my old TLS magazine on the shelf. It’s a bit outdated, but I still look at it every now and then. You know, it’s about the same as your dad’s old TLS from when he was at university.      Wait, you still have that? I thought he left it to the charity shop.      No, he left it to me. I think he thought it was a bit of a treasure. You know how he is.      He always did have a thing for old English magazines. I remember him going on about how they were the best.      Exactly. I think he’d be so proud of you, really. You’re a bit of a bookworm yourself, even if you prefer digital.      Yeah, I guess I am. I mean, I do love to read, but I’ve got this thing about the convenience of e-books. I’m always on my phone or tablet.      And that’s fine, but don’t forget the charm of the old ways. It’s just like how I still write letters sometimes—I think there’s something special about that.

So, I was sat on the beach in Cornwall, just trying to get a tan, when this massive wave came out of nowhere and drenched me! I was like, “Oh, this is just the start of my holiday!” and then I looked over and saw my mate Dave in a wetsuit, like he was surfing, and I thought, “Oh no, I’ve been outsmarted by a wave.”      You’re not the first to get soaked by a wave, mate. I once tried to chase a crab on the shore and ended up getting frozen to the sand. I was like, “I’m not moving, I’m not moving,” and then my mate Steve came over and said, “You’re not moving because you’re already in the water.” D’you know what I did? I screamed. Like a banshee.      That’s classic. I once tried to take a selfie with a seagull and ended up with a bird on my shoulder. I was like, “Okay, I’m just gonna walk around with this bird for the next hour,” and then it flew off and left me with a photo that looked like I was holding a mini helicopter.      Yeah, but I reckon you all had it easy. I was in Barcelona, and the weather was perfect. All I did was sit under a parasol, sip a sangria, and look at the people walking by. One guy looked so suspicious that I thought he was going to run up and rob me. Then he just smiled and said, “Hola, bon dia.” That was the highlight of my day.      That’s not the worst, though. I had a guy in Italy who thought I was a tourist and tried to sell me a fake watch. I said, “No, mate, I’m not buying that.” He looked at me like I was stupid. Then he said, “You’re not from around here, are you?” I said, “No, I’m from Warrington.” He said, “Oh, I’ve been to Warrington! It’s a bit of a weird place, but I like it.”      You think that’s weird? I once went to a pub in Manchester and the landlord asked me if I was from Warrington. I said yes, and he immediately said, “Oh, you’re one of them, then.” I said, “What, like a tribe?” He said, “Yeah, we’ve got a few of you round here.

So, I’ve been thinking about that wild winter camping trip we talked about last week... You know, the one with the tent, the fire, and no phones.      Yes, I remember. You were all worked up about it, like it was the next big adventure. But I still say it’s a bit reckless for someone your age, Dave.      Oh, come on, Mairi. It’s not reckless—it’s just different. I mean, what’s the point of being outdoors if you don’t get a little uncomfortable now and then?      That’s the thing about nature, isn’t it? It doesn’t care what you think you know. You go out there, and it shows you exactly what you’re made of.      Well, if you’re going to take that attitude, you’d better make sure you’re properly prepared, Dave. I’ve seen what happens when people underestimate the cold.      I’ve been prepping for weeks. I’ve got the tent, the sleeping bag, the fire starter, the proper food...      And the warm socks, the thermal layers, the GPS, and the first-aid kit?      Oh, you’ve been reading my mind.      It’s my job. I’ve had to talk to plenty of people who think they’re ready for the wild but aren’t.      I guess it’s just the way I grew up. Both my parents were into the outdoors. We went camping every weekend when I was a kid. No tents, just the woods, the stars, and the quiet.      That’s the beauty of it, really. There’s something about being in nature that makes you feel... connected to something bigger.      I suppose it’s also a form of therapy, in a way. Being away from the noise, the deadlines, the constant stimulation. It’s like your brain gets a reset.      Exactly. That’s why I’m doing it. I need to get back to that feeling. The one where you’re not just surviving, you’re thriving.      Then I say go for it. Just make sure you don’t go alone. Safety first, Dave.      And take someone who knows what they’re doing. Maybe even me? I’ve got a couple of clients who’ve done wild camping, and they’re all raving about it.      You’d be the first person to join me, Mairi.      Then I’m in. I’ve been wanting to try it myself.

So, I was just thinking about that film we watched last night,  The Lighthouse . You remember, the one with the two guys and the lighthouse? It was  so  intense, wasn’t it?      Yeah, it was pretty heavy. I mean, mentally, I felt like I’d been on a boat for hours. But honestly, I couldn’t stop thinking about it. That ending—do you think they actually went mad, or was it just the isolation?      I think it was a bit of both. You know, like how the more they isolated themselves, the more the lines between reality and madness blurred. And that one scene where they were arguing about who was the real captain? It was so creepy.      Yeah, and the way they talked about the lighthouse like it was a living thing. Like it had a will of its own. It felt like it was almost a character in the film. I mean, not just a setting, but almost like it was controlling them.      Definitely. It reminded me of  The Wicker Man , in a way. You know, that whole idea of being trapped in a place that’s not quite real. But I think  The Lighthouse  was more about the psychological toll of isolation. Like, how long can you go without human connection before you start losing your grip on reality?      That’s a good point. I mean, I can relate. I’d been working on a project for weeks with no one to talk to, and I started getting these weird thoughts about things. I even checked the date a couple of times to make sure I wasn’t in the wrong century.      You’re not the only one. I’ve been reading that book by that writer— The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo —and it was just as intense. It’s like, you’re waiting for someone to come in and save you, but they never do. It’s so draining.      Yeah, I’ve read that. I thought it was a good read, but it didn’t really get me thinking about anything. I mean, I respect the author, but I’m more into books that make you question the world.      I get that. I like books that make you think, but I also like ones that make you feel something. Like,  The Kite Runner —that one really hit me emotionally.      I’ve read that one. It’s a classic.

So, I was telling the kids earlier about the time I tried to teach my first ever lesson and I completely blanked on the lesson plan. I stood in front of the class, looked at the board, and honestly, I couldn’t remember what I was supposed to be teaching. It was terrifying! I thought,  “Oh no, I’ve completely forgotten what I was going to say!”  And then I just started talking about the weather. I mean, it wasn’t even relevant. But the kids were so nice—they just nodded and said, “That’s interesting, Miss,” and then one of them even asked, “Do you like the weather?” I was like, “Oh, yes, I love the weather. It’s so changeable, isn’t it?” And then I just blundered through the rest of the lesson. I think I turned it into a discussion about the seasons instead. It was a disaster, but somehow, I think they all still passed the exam.      Wow, Miss? You were  Miss ?      Yeah, I was their teacher. Anyway, I’ve learned to be more prepared now. Although, I did have this one time where I tried to use a PowerPoint presentation and it completely crashed. I was standing there with a laptop, and the screen just went black. I thought,  “Oh no, not again!”  So I just sat down and read the lesson off a piece of paper. It was the same lesson I’d given the week before. It just goes to show, sometimes the simplest things are the most effective.      I like when you read stories. I like the ones about dragons.      Oh, I like that. I think you’ll be a great storyteller one day. You just need to practice. My sister used to tell the most amazing stories. She’d make up whole worlds and characters. One time, she told us about a dragon who could fly backwards. I mean,  backwards ! It was so bizarre, but it was funny. We all believed her for a week.      Do you think the dragon would be scary?      If you wanted to be scared, yes. But if you wanted to be adventurous, it could be a lot of fun. Anyway, I’m going to go check on the kids' Xbox. They’ve been playing for hours. I think it’s time for bed.      Can we play Lego tomorrow?      Only if you finish your homework first.

You know, I was just thinking about that old house in the village—ANON’s place. It’s been on the market for ages, hasn’t it? I’ve been meaning to pop over and see it, but with all the roadworks going on, it’s like trying to walk through a war zone.      Yeah, I saw that. A lot of people have been asking about it. They say it’s got character, but I bet it’s got more damp than a London cellar. Didn’t you hear about the last guy who tried to sell it? He ended up offering it to a charity for a hundred quid just to get rid of the ghosts.      Ghosts? I’m not sure about that, but I’d say the place has more history than most of the houses in Bradford. You remember when we used to walk past it on our way to the market? It was all boarded up, and the garden was full of weeds.      I do. I remember the old man who lived there. He used to grow fruit. He had this little orchard, and the apples were so good—like they’d been picked by the angels. You could taste the sunlight in every bite.      Oh, I remember that. He used to bring the fruit to the market in a cart, all by himself. He never had a driver. Spent his whole life growing apples and plums. He must have had a good ear for the soil, if you ask me.      He even had a few of those old medieval villages nearby. I’ve been reading about them. Some of them were abandoned centuries ago. You know, the ones where the houses just fell into disrepair and were left to rot.      Yeah, that’s what I was thinking. It’s sad how time can just take something and leave it forgotten. I mean, I’ve seen places like that in rural Yorkshire. Even the roads are just potholes and dust.      But you know what’s funny? The number of people who still live on those roads, sending junk mail to houses that don’t even exist anymore. It’s like they’re trying to keep the ghosts alive.      I’ve had more junk mail than my tea ration since I moved to Bradford. But I tell you what, if there’s one thing I’d like to grow in my garden, it’s herbs.

So, I was just telling my sister about the time I tried to cook that new recipe from the glossy magazine— that  was a disaster. I mean, I thought I was being clever, but I ended up with a sticky, inedible mess that looked more like a science experiment than a meal.      I know what you mean. I once tried to make a “delicious” shepherd’s pie, and I burnt the top to a crisp while undercooking the filling. My wife nearly hit me with a ladle. Still, I think it’s part of the charm, isn’t it? That sense of pride in trying something new.      I get it. I’m not great in the kitchen, but I love experimenting, even if I end up with something that tastes like regret. Although, I do have this breakfast recipe—this avocado toast with a sprinkle of chili flakes—that’s pretty much perfect.      Oh, that’s lovely. I’ve been thinking about getting a new recipe book, though. My mum always says that cooking is a way to show love, and I’d like to be better at that. But I’m not sure if I’m up to it.      You know, I think the best thing you can do is just start small. Maybe try something simple, like a stir-fry or a soup. I’ve been starting with those lately. It’s less pressure, and you can always adjust the taste as you go.      Yeah, and if you make a mess, there’s always a way to recycle it. I’ve had a few failures, but I’ve turned some of them into new dishes. Like that time I scorched a lasagna, I just turned it into a baked pasta scramble.      That’s more resourceful than I’d ever be. Do you think I could try something like that? I mean, I’m not good at following instructions, but maybe I can improvise?      Absolutely. You don’t have to be perfect. Just be creative. And if you go wrong, it’s not a failure—it’s just a learning curve.      Exactly. And besides, what’s life without a little mess?      True. I think I’m going to start with a simple soup, just to be safe. Maybe a classic tomato soup.      That’s a good plan. And if it turns out bad, we can always use it for something else.

Right, so I’ve been thinking about the new series on BBC Three.  The Checklist —you watched it, didn’t you?      Yeah, I did. It’s pretty decent, isn’t it? The way they combine comedy with real-life issues is refreshing. I mean, it’s not just laughing at people—it's actually making you think. You’ve seen the episode with the couple who were always arguing about chores?      Oh,  that  one! Didn’t that end with them both just walking out? I swear, it was like  The Office  meets  Fleabag . But honestly, it made me think about how much I’ve been arguing with my roommate over the last month. We’re like,  The Checklist  characters.      You’ve been living with her long enough to know that? I mean, I’ve been in a flat with people for five years and we’re still not there yet. But I guess it’s just the early stages of cohabitation, right? You know, figuring out whose turn it is to do the washing up, and when.      Oh, it’s not just the washing up. It’s the shared Netflix account, the last night of the month, and the fact that I have to explain to my parents why I’m still living with someone who’s not my boyfriend. It’s like,  we’re not even dating, but I’m not moving out.       Exactly! And now you’re looking at moving out, aren’t you? I heard you’re thinking about about renting a place in Shoreditch.      Yeah, I’ve been looking at places. It’s a bit of a step up, but I think I’m ready for more independence. Plus, I’m trying to save up for the next phase of my career. I’ve got this copywriting job, but I want to start my own business one day.      That’s great! I mean, I’ve got my Masters, but I’m still working part-time. It’s tough, but I’m not giving up on my own business idea. I’m just waiting for the right opportunity.      You’re doing what you can. I think we both have big plans, but we’re just figuring out the steps to get there. You know, it’s all about taking it one day at a time.      Yeah, I suppose that’s the thing about being young. You’re always trying to figure out what you want, and how to get there.

So, I was just thinking about how we haven’t really had a proper chat about our health lately. I mean, I’ve been trying to get back into exercise after that long break, but it’s been a struggle. I’ve been running a few times a week, but honestly, I can’t keep it up. Do you ever feel like you’re just not motivated enough?      Honestly, I’ve been there too. I’ve been doing a bit of cycling recently, but I’m not sure if it’s the right fit for me. I tried running a few times, but my knees started acting up, and I just didn’t want to risk injury. I think I’m more of a walker, to be honest. My doctor even said I should just keep it light.      I know what you mean, lads. I’ve been doing a bit of yoga and some light swimming. It’s not intense, but it’s good for me. I’ve been reading a lot about how exercise is more about consistency than intensity, and that helps me feel less guilty when I can’t do something more rigorous.      Yeah, I think that’s a good point. I remember when I was younger, I used to think that if I wasn’t doing something extreme, I wasn’t really exercising. But now I’ve come to understand that even a daily walk or some gentle stretching counts. Still, I find it hard to stick to a schedule.      I know the feeling. I’ve been trying to get back into a routine, but work just keeps pulling me in different directions. I’d love to be more consistent, but it’s tough when you’re juggling so many things.      That’s the thing, though. It’s not just about the exercise itself—it’s about how you fit it into your life. I’ve started doing short workouts in the mornings, even if it’s just ten minutes of stretching or a quick walk. It’s surprising how much of a difference that makes.      I suppose I need to take a page out of your book. I’ve been thinking about getting a gym membership again, but I’m not sure if I’ll be able to commit.      Maybe you could try a class or something? I’ve been going to a local fitness group, and it’s actually been a lot of fun.

You know, I’ve been meaning to come here for ages. The whole place is so peaceful, especially after the week I’ve had at work. It’s like a total reset button.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been twitchy all week too. My project deadlines are killing me. I’ve been working non-stop since the Budget announcement. I mean, the government’s been talking about cutting public spending, and now we’re seeing the effects. Didn’t even get a proper budget for the next quarter.      Yeah, the Budget’s been a bit of a shock. My boss was pretty concerned about how it might affect our department. I mean, we’re in the public sector, so it’s not like we’re immune to the cuts. They’ve been saying we need to streamline operations and cut costs. It’s like a bit of a nightmare.      I can’t even imagine. I’ve been trying to stay positive, but the way things are going, I feel like I’m working harder than ever to keep my job. Plus, with the economy as it is, it’s hard to see a light at the end of the tunnel.      It’s really tough. I’ve been trying to find ways to manage my expenses too. I mean, I’m not exactly in a position to just walk away. But I also feel like there’s not much we can do about it. You ever think about the impact it’s having on people’s lives?      I do. I mean, I’ve got a good job, but I know people who are struggling. My mum’s been cutting back on things she used to do, like going out to see musicals. She used to love them. I remember her going to  Cats  at the Cambridge Theatre. She told me how amazing it was.      That’s such a shame. I love musicals too. Even though I’ve been busy with work, I’ve been thinking about going to  Hamilton  in London. It’s been on my bucket list for ages. But I don’t know if I’ll get the time or the money.      You should do it. It’s worth it. I mean, I’ve seen it and it’s mind-blowing. I think you’d love it. Maybe we can go together sometime? I mean, if the budget doesn’t kill me first.

You know, I was just thinkin’, mate—what if the council decides to knock down this whole back yard and build a gym or somethin’? I’d hate to lose this spot. I mean, it’s been part of the family for generations.        Well, that’d be a shame. A lot of people would love that—fitness, ya know. But I reckon they’ll leave it as it is. It’s not like the area’s runnin’ short of space. You know what’s funny? My nephew’s been talkin’ me into gettin’ a gym in the back. He says it’s a good investment.        You? Doin’ push-ups in the back yard? I’d be worried about the gutters gettin’ clogged with sweat and all. You’d need a proper gym, not a shed. But I tell you, you’d be a legend in the area. I bet the blokes’d come from miles to see you lift weights.        Yeah, right. But I tell ya, it’s not just about the gym. I’ve been thinkin’ about startin’ a small business—sellin’ second-hand stuff. You know, bits and bobs. I’ve got this old camera, and a few books. I could turn it into a little shop, maybe even in the back yard. It’s a bit of a risk, but I’ve got the space, and I’m not afraid to put my money where my mouth is.        That’s a solid idea, mate. I’ve always thought about doin’ the same. I had this old projector I bought for a few quid, and I’ve been thinkin’ of runnin’ some film nights. People love that kind of stuff. You know, a bit of culture in the neighborhood. I’d even do some acting—maybe get a few mates together for little plays.        That’s a good point. You’ve got the flair for the dramatic, I’ve no doubt. I mean, you used to act in school plays, didn’t you? I remember that one with the goat—awkward, but you nailed it.        Oh, that one was a disaster. I had to get a special costume and all. But I was proud of it. Anyway, I think we’ve got a bit of a plan here. Maybe we can team up somehow. You do the shop, I do the films. We could even have a little acting group.

So, I just saw this really weird sign off the motorway. It said “Tarnow – 40km.” But I thought it was like 60km away. Maybe the sign is wrong? Or maybe I’m just getting too used to driving in the UK, where the signs make more sense.      You’re not the only one who’s confused. I’ve been on a few trips through Poland, and sometimes the directions are just... odd. But I think you’re right—40km sounds too short. Maybe the sign is from a different route or a new road?      I don’t know. I just wanted to check because I’ve got this weird feeling like we’re missing a bit of the journey. You know how sometimes you just feel like you’re being rushed or something? Like, I’m not sure if we’re making the most of the trip.      Yeah, I get that. I think part of it is the clutter we’ve been clearing up back home. I mean, I still haven’t sold that old sofa, and it’s been in the hallway for months. It’s like we’re all holding on to stuff, even when it’s not useful.      Exactly. I remember when I got out of work, I felt like I had to let go of everything. But it’s hard. You start to think, “What if I need it later?” But then again, you’re not in a rush anymore. You just travel, and you see things differently.      I think that’s what’s happening here. We’re in a campervan, driving through Poland, and it’s like we’re not in a rush. I even met a hitchhiker the other day. A man from Germany, in his 50s, heading to Kraków. He had a classic Volkswagen van, all patched up.      Hitchhikers are such a mix of experiences. Some are really friendly, others are just looking for a lift. I once had a guy who tried to sell me a map and then just disappeared. But that guy from Germany? He was great. He told me about all the best places to stop and eat.      That’s the thing about traveling with friends—sometimes you end up meeting people who become part of the journey. It’s like we’re all just exploring together, even if we’re not sure where we’re going.      Exactly.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we got lost on the way to the Hay Festival? I swear, we turned down every single side road for like twenty minutes before we found the right one.      Oh, don’t even start. I was so desperate to get there on time I nearly pulled the car off the road. I remember you were shouting, “Left, left, left!” like it was a race.      Yeah, and when we finally got there, the queue was longer than the one to get into the cinema. I swear, you were so excited, you nearly wet yourself.      Oh, come on, you know I love the Hay Festival. I still have that little notebook from the first time I went. It was about a book on the history of British literature—maybe that’s why I still can’t get over it.      I remember that. You were so determined to find the author’s signing table, and then you got lost again. I think you even asked a stranger for directions.      And that’s when we met that guy who said he was a ghost hunter. I swear he was just trying to get us to stop for a drink.      Oh, he was so convincing! I thought he was real for a minute. Anyway, I also got a book from that festival. It’s been on my shelf ever since. I think it’s still there.      What was it called again?       The Story of the English —or something like that. It was about how storytelling shaped the country. I read it every year on my birthday.      Sounds like a good one. I used to read a lot as a kid. My mum would read to me every night. She had this voice—like she was actually in the story.      That sounds nice. I wish I had that. I just remember my mum saying, “You’ll never be a proper reader unless you read every day.”      I think that’s the key. You have to make it a habit. Even now, I still have that habit. I read a book every night before bed. It’s like a ritual.      That’s the way to go. I tell you, my daughter’s got that same habit. She’s always got a book in her hand, even when she’s on her phone.      Yeah, I’ve seen her. She’s like a bookworm on steroids.

Oh, I just had the most ridiculous idea about technology. You know that new smart fridge we’ve been talking about? I was thinking, what if it starts talking back? Like, you put the milk in and it says, “No, you shouldn’t have. You’ve had enough today.”      That would be funny, but I reckon it’s more likely to start listing your grocery list before you even open the door. You know how those things are—always trying to help.      Exactly! And then you’d have to argue with it. I mean, I’ve had enough of arguing with my own grandchildren.      Grandma, you’re getting too old for this. I’d argue with a fridge, and I’m only 15!      Oh, you’re just bitter because you can’t argue with me anymore. And speaking of which, I saw your Grandpa the other day. He was trying to fix the TV with a hairdryer.      Oh no, not again. I told him that the remote control was the only thing that would work.      He said, “It’s just a remote—it’s not like it’s got a brain.” And then he started trying to plug it in the wall!      That’s what I do with my phone. It just sits there, blinking at me like it’s judging me.      That’s your mental illness, mate. You’re just being paranoid.      I’m not paranoid. I’ve had enough of that in my life. I think it’s more like... I’m just not  with  it anymore.      I know. I’ve been thinking about that too. I don’t know how to explain it, but I feel like I’m not connected to the world anymore. It’s like I’m stuck in a different time.      I get that. Sometimes I feel like I’m not really here. Like I’m just... waiting for something.      That’s not normal, lad. You should talk to someone.      Yeah. I know. I’m not sure I’ve got the strength, though.      You’ve got to take care of yourself. You both do. You’re not alone.      Thanks, Grandma. I think I’ll try that.      And if you need someone to argue with about the fridge, I’m here.      Oh, you’re in for a fight, mate. But I’ll be there to help.      Good. I’ve got a feeling I’ll need it.

Right, so I’ve got this new laptop, and it’s got this thing called Windows 11. I’ve been trying to set it up, but it’s been a right pain in the arse. I don’t know why it’s so complicated.      I remember when I first got my laptop, it was like trying to solve a Rubik’s cube with one hand. I ended up just using my old desktop instead. It was easier, honestly.      Yeah, but you can’t really work from the desktop these days. I mean, I still use my old PC, but only for basic stuff. I’ve got a laptop now, but I still use it for gaming.      Gaming? You? You’re a gardener, for God’s sake. What’s the point of gaming if you’re just messing with plants?      I didn’t say I was a pro. I just play a bit. I do like the way it tunes your brain, you know? Helps with focus.      Maybe. But I’m not here to talk about gaming. I’m trying to get this laptop to connect to my old external hard drive. It won’t recognize it.      Oh, that’s a common one. Try using the disk management tool. Sometimes it just doesn’t show up unless you manually add it.      I tried that. It just says the drive is unallocated. I’m so confused.      Maybe the drive’s formatted in a different file system. Windows 11 might not support it. I had that problem once with a Mac drive.      Oh, right. I used to work with Macs at uni. You know, back when I was an art student. I used to hate the Macs, but the design software was so much better.      I told you, you’re an artist. You should be using something more creative.      I know, I know. I’m trying to switch back to Windows. It’s just that this laptop’s a bit of a pain.      Yeah, I get it. I’m an English teacher, and I use a lot of software for lesson plans and stuff. It’s not that different from what you’re doing.      I’m just trying to keep my things in order. You know, like my garden. If I don’t keep things tidy, they just go to hell.      You’re not wrong. I’m starting to feel like I’ve got a garden in my head.

So, I just wanted to say, I think the bistro’s a bit of a miracle. The first day, the place was packed with locals and even a few tourists! I mean, it’s not exactly in the centre, but the vibe is so welcoming. It’s got that  cosy  feel that makes you want to stay for hours.      Yeah, I’ve been there a couple of times. It’s actually got a really good selection of Polish and British dishes. I was surprised how well it’s been received. I mean, for a new place in Tarnow, it’s doing pretty well.      I know, it’s the kind of place that makes you feel like you’re in a small English village, but with the added perk of being in Poland. It’s kind of nostalgic, but also fresh. I think the owner must have a real passion for food and community.      I agree. They’ve even got a little barista section with proper coffee. I mean, not just the usual instant stuff. It’s a nice touch. I do miss the coffee shops back home, though. I mean, the ones with the  real  espresso machines and baristas who know what they’re doing.      I know, it’s one of those things that you take for granted. I’ve been thinking a lot lately about my own life. I mean, I’m not working, and I’m not sure what I’m going to do next. It’s like I’m in limbo. I keep thinking about my old job, the one with the kids, and how different things could have been.      I get that. I’ve been thinking about my own dreams too. I always wanted to teach English, and now I actually do. It’s not what I expected, but it’s better than nothing. Still, I sometimes feel like I’m not living up to my potential.      I hear you. You know, I was always the type to have dreams, but I never really pursued them. I just… drifted. Maybe that’s what happens when you’re unemployed for so long. It wears you down.      It’s a tough place to be. But I think we’re both still fighting. Even if it’s just staying active, going to the gym, or just making sure we don’t fall into old habits. I’ve started going to the gym again, actually.

So, I’ve been thinking about going to the Dorset Steam Fair next week. I got the ticket sorted, but I was wondering if we could bring my mum’s old cat, Whiskers, along with us? She’s not too old, and she’s pretty chill.      Oh, you want to take Whiskers to the Steam Fair? I remember when I used to take my old cat, Puddles, to the fair. He’d curl up under the trestle tables like he was sleeping. But I don’t know if the fair has any facilities for disabled people or pets. I’ve heard some places are strict about that.      Yeah, I agree. I think the Steam Fair might have some wheelchair access, but I’m not sure about pets. I remember when I had my dog, Max, and I tried taking him to a local fair once. They said no pets unless it was a service animal. I guess cats are not considered service animals, so maybe they’d say no.      That’s a shame. I really want Whiskers to come. He’s been so lonely since my dad passed away. I mean, he’s got his litter box and all, but he’s just not the same. I was thinking maybe we could bring a small carrier and keep him in the car. Would that be allowed?      I’d say it’s worth a call. Let me check the Steam Fair’s website real quick. Wait, I can’t remember what it’s called. I think it’s called the Dorset Steam Fair – yeah, that’s it. Let me recall, did they have any info about pets? I think the contact details were on the back of the ticket. Maybe you can call them and ask directly.      Yeah, that’s the way to go. I’d suggest you call them and ask about their pet policy. And also ask about disabled facilities. I’ve heard some people say the fair is pretty accessible, but others say it’s a bit of a maze. If you’re using a wheelchair, maybe you should get an accessible route mapped out in advance.      Thanks, I’ll do that. It’s just so hard to leave Whiskers at home. I don’t want him to feel left out. Maybe we can bring some of his favorite toys too to keep him entertained.      That’s a kind heart.

Well, I do hope the postman’s feeling better, love. He’s been so grumpy lately, and I’ve got a feeling it’s all because of that      Yes, he said something about a sore foot. But it’s not that bad, is it? I mean, he’s got that little garden he’s so proud of.      Does he still use that old lawnmower? I saw it in the garden the other day and thought it was a dinosaur.      Oh, he still uses it, but he’s been trying to get a new one. Said the old thing’s not worth the effort. I told him to just throw it away and buy a new one, but he said it’s sentimental.      I know, he’s got this whole collection of odd things in his shed. I think the last time we were over, he showed me a tin that he claimed was from the First World War.      You don’t say! I still remember when he took us to the war memorial in town and started telling us about his great-uncle. It was amazing – he had a story for every stone.      He’s got that whole thing about the war memorial down to a T. I think he’d be proud to be someone’s ancestor.      He’s got a point. Though I’d rather have a grandchild than a great-uncle, I suppose.      That’s the spirit! Anyway, what about this weather? It’s been so gloomy all week. I think I’ve seen more rain than sun.      Yes, it’s like the sky’s depressed. I told my mum it was a sign that something was wrong with the world, but she just said I was being dramatic.      She’d say that. I mean, she’s got a tin roof over her head and a garden that’s growing like a jungle.      If it was my roof, I’d be in a panic. But I think she’s just happy to be alive.      She’s got that spirit. Anyway, I was thinking, do you think we should start looking for a new house? I’m not sure about staying in the same one forever.      That’s an interesting idea. I was thinking the same. I mean, the garden’s lovely, but maybe it’s time to move somewhere a bit more modern.      Yeah, I think it’s about time.

So, I was just telling the kids about the dentist. You know, that first time they go in, they’re all so nervous. But I think it's actually the  second  time for Ashaad. He’s been going since he was three. Just like the other kids in his class—except he  always  has a sore tooth. I think his parents are starting to think he’s a vampire or something.      Oh, you mean Ashaad? He’s always been like that. Every time he gets a new tooth, he’s like a squirrel with a nut. But I think it’s just his way of showing he’s growing up. You know, like that one time when he screamed so loud at the dentist that the whole room heard him.      Yeah, and he’s got that weird habit of licking his teeth. Like, it’s not normal. I mean, I do it sometimes, but not like  that  much. I think he’s just trying to make sure he doesn’t lose another tooth.      Exactly! I mean, we all know that’s how you get the most  vibrant  teeth, right? But it’s funny because when he got his first hearing test – that was a disaster. He couldn’t hear the whisper test, and he thought it was a game. He kept saying, “I can hear it, I can hear it!” until the tester just gave up.      Oh, he’s so dramatic. But you know, Mom, he  is  the one who got the most creative birthday presents. Last year, he got a doll that could walk and talk. And the year before that, he had a cake with a  whole  chocolate fountain. I think he’s trying to outdo his sister.      Yeah, and they both have birthdays on the same day. It’s like they’re competing for attention. I mean, yesterday, I found them both arguing over who got the bigger slice of cake. They both had the same birthday, but they keep thinking it’s different.      I know. It’s like the universe is testing us. But I think it’s more about sibling rivalry than anything else. Although, I did notice that they both like the same things—Monet, Maths, and Easter chocolate. Maybe that’s why they’re fighting over the same things.      Oh, they even like radishes. I bought some at the market the other day, and they were both eyeing them like they were gold.

So, I was just telling my mum about the time I tried to cook that lasagna from the supermarket, and it turned out like a brick. I mean, it was  so  orange, it looked like a sunburned pizza.      Oh no, that sounds like one of those 'I tried to be a chef' disasters. I remember when I tried to make a roast dinner for my first job interview. I burnt the potatoes and forgot to season the meat. My boss was like, "I hope you're not planning to cook for me too."      That’s brutal. I feel like everyone has a story like that. Anyway, I’m trying to get back into cooking now. I’ve got this recipe for homemade bread that I found online. It’s supposed to be super easy, but I’ve got this massive loaf that’s taking over my kitchen.      You’re not the only one. I’m working on a new recipe for my mum. She’s got this thing about 'traditional' meals, and I’m trying to introduce her to a bit of global cuisine. She’s not too keen on the spicy ones, though.      Yeah, I know what you mean. My family’s all about the classics. I mean, I’m trying to be more adventurous, but they’re like, ‘What’s the point? It’s just food.’      I get it. But I think it’s good to mix it up a bit. You know, being flexible. Especially with all the work we’re doing these days. I’m actually thinking about taking a break for a few weeks. I’ve had this idea for a new therapy program that I want to try out.      That sounds exciting. You’ve always been so passionate about your work. I’m just worried about how the financial stuff is going to work out.      Yeah, it’s not easy. I’ve been saving up, but I’m not sure if it’s enough. I mean, I’d love to do something different, but I don’t want to leave my job just yet.      I get it. It’s tough. But you’ve got the skills, and your passion is obvious. I just hope you can make it work.      Thanks. I’ve got a lot to think about, but I’m excited about the future. And I’m so glad I got to reconnect with you.

Well, I just thought of something. You know when we were kids, we used to do that long cycle ride from Almondsbury to Winchcombe. It was a bit of a trek, but we’d cycle all day, stop for a picnic, and then come home exhausted but happy. I was always the one who’d get a bit lost on the way, but somehow we always found our way back.      Oh, I remember that! I think I had a flat tire halfway through. I was so frustrated. But you were the one who knew the way. You always had that knack for getting around, even when you didn’t have a map.      I had no idea where we were going half the time, honestly. I just followed the others. But I do recall the scenery was beautiful—those hills, the way the light hit the fields. It was like a different world. I think it was the first time I felt truly free. No exams, no deadlines, just the wind in my hair and the road ahead.      That sounds like paradise compared to what I do now. You know, I still get the occasional nostalgic moment when I think about my early days as a dentist. There were these perks in the NHS, you know. I remember when I got to sail on the – what was it called? – the ‘Dental Cruiser’? It was this old ship that sailed up and down the coast. You’d have lectures all at sea with your oral surgeon, and you’d get free drinks and food. It was a way to relax and catch up with colleagues.      Oh, that sounds amazing. I wish I’d had something like that when I was teaching. Though I did enjoy the summer holidays, the chance to travel without the hassle of booking. I remember a trip to Prague with a group of teachers. It was the late ‘80s, and the place was so different from now. The architecture was pristine, the people friendly. I still remember the red rooftops and the narrow streets.      I’ve been thinking about doing a bargain trip to Prague again. You know, with the travel deals coming up. I heard there are some amazing theatres and exhibitions there, but you have to book well in advance. I tried to get tickets for a play last week, but it was already booked out.      I’m actually planning a jive event in the converted barn down by the river.

So, I was just thinking about how social media can be such a double-edged sword when it comes to building real relationships. I mean, it’s easy to connect with people across the globe, but sometimes it feels like we’re just sharing curated versions of ourselves.      Absolutely, I agree. I’ve noticed that even with my students, some of them are really good at using platforms like Instagram or TikTok to showcase their work, but when it comes to face-to-face interactions, they can be a bit hesitant. It’s like they’re used to communicating through screens more than through actual conversation.      That’s interesting. I’ve been thinking about how we can use social media as a tool for deeper connections, not just for marketing or self-promotion. Maybe we could create a platform or a community that’s focused on learning and collaboration. Think of it as an online space where educators and learners can share resources, discuss ideas, and even collaborate on projects.      That sounds like a great idea, especially for remote learning or blended learning environments. I’ve been working on some case studies about how video content can be used in education, and I think a digital hub where people can upload and access these case studies would be really valuable.      Exactly. And it doesn’t have to be formal. It could be more like a social network with a focus on education. You could have sections for different subject areas, or even for different age groups. People could follow other educators, share their own teaching strategies, and even crowdsource ideas for lesson plans.      I like the crowdsource idea. It would make it more interactive and engaging. Plus, it could help teachers who are looking for new ways to incorporate multimedia into their lessons. But how do we get people to use it?      That’s the challenge, isn’t it? We need to make it easy for educators to find and use the resources. Maybe we can partner with some educational organizations or universities to promote it. Or even integrate it with existing learning management systems.      Yeah, and maybe we could start with a pilot program. Test it with a few schools or colleges, gather feedback, and then scale it up. I think it could work, especially if we go for a more community-driven approach.      I’m really excited about this.

So, I was just thinking about that weekend trip we took to the coast last summer—the one with the family. It was so nice to get away, you know? I mean, it’s been a while since we’ve done anything like that.      Yeah, it was great. I still remember the way the sea looked at sunrise. It was like the sky and the water were blending into one. I’ve never seen anything so peaceful.      I know, right? It was like time stood still. We even walked along the cliffs for a while. I remember how the wind was blowing so hard, but it felt invigorating, you know? Like it was cleaning your mind.      Exactly. I think that’s what I missed most—just being out there, not worrying about anything. It reminded me of when we first met, actually. We used to take walks by the sea when we were students. You’d always say, "Let’s go there," and I’d groan but then end up loving it.      Oh, I remember that! I think it was the first time I properly noticed how much I loved the sea. It’s such a powerful force, isn’t it? You can’t help but feel small in front of it. It’s humbling.      Definitely. And it’s so different from being in the city. You know, London, all the noise, the traffic, the never-ending deadlines. It’s like the sea is this reminder that there’s more to life than work.      I couldn’t agree more. I’d love to go back again. Maybe with some friends? I was thinking about inviting the Hughs for a weekend trip. They’ve been talking about wanting to go somewhere different, and the coast would be perfect.      That sounds like a great idea. You know, I’ve been thinking about that too. Maybe we could all go together. It would be nice to have some time away from the usual routine. Do you think they’d like it?      I’m sure they would. I’ll ask them next week. It’d be nice to have some quality time with friends, just like we did last summer. You know, before everything got so busy again.      Yeah, it’s easy to get caught up in work and responsibilities, but moments like that—being with friends, on the coast, just chatting and watching the waves—it’s what keeps things balanced, don’t you think?

Right, I just saw this outfit on the telly, it’s mad. That girl in the white coat with the oversized sunglasses—what’s even going on? It’s like she’s trying to be a character from a 90s movie or something.      Yeah, I saw that too. It’s one of those looks that’s supposed to be edgy but ends up just looking like she’s too confused to wear anything. I don’t get it. Why would you wear a white coat with a neon green shirt? It’s like the colours are fighting each other.      Oh, I think it’s called "vintage meets modern." Like, you take something from the 70s and then throw in some glitter and call it a day. I’ve seen that look on a few people in the city. It’s trendy, I guess.      Trendy? It’s more like desperate. I mean, if you want to be fashion-forward, maybe go for something that actually fits. I’ve had to dress like that for work once—except I had to do it in a boardroom, not on a street corner.      You’re telling me. I once showed up to a meeting in a graphic tee and cargo pants because the weather was too hot. My boss didn’t look too happy, but he didn’t say anything. I think he just wanted someone to be an example of what not to wear.      I had to wear a suit to a primary school event once. It felt like I was in a museum. I nearly cried. I mean, I love fashion, but sometimes the rules are just too strict.      Yeah, I get it. But we’re all just trying to find our own style. I mean, I’m into more casual stuff. I think the key is to be comfortable and confident. If you look good, people will notice.      Yeah, confidence is everything. Even if the outfit is a little off-the-wall. I think the more you express yourself, the more people start to like you.      Exactly. It’s about being true to yourself. I mean, I’m a primary teacher, so I can’t exactly walk around in jeans and a hoodie every day, but when I get off work, I like to wear something that makes me feel like me.      I think that’s the key. You can dress up for work, and then when you’re off, you can be whoever you want.

So, I was just telling my mum about the photos I took at the beach last weekend. You know, the ones where I tried to capture the sunset, but ended up with a bunch of blurry blobs? She said I should have just taken a proper photo instead of trying to make it look “artistic.”      Oh, I know that look. I used to do that too. I think it's just the phase where you're trying to be a bit more creative. But you have to remember—sometimes the best photos are the ones that look like they were taken by someone who actually knows what they're doing.      Yeah, I guess. But I still think you can be creative without being bad at the technical side. I mean, I’ve been reading these books about photography and I think it’s just about understanding the rules before breaking them. Though I’m not sure I’ve actually broken any yet. Maybe I should try something more daring, like jumping in front of the camera or something?      Oh, you would do that, wouldn’t you? Remember when you were eight and you tried to take a photo of the garden, but kept getting the lens dirty? You were so determined. I remember you even got your dad to hold the camera for you while you stood in front of it, wearing a crown made of daisies.      Yeah, and you posted that on Facebook and said it was “one of the best photos ever.” Of course, it was just a blurry mess with a crown made of flowers. But I still think it’s a masterpiece in its own way.      You always have a way of making the mundane feel magical. I think that’s part of what makes you such a good photographer. You’re not just taking pictures—you’re capturing moments. That’s what makes the difference between a snapshot and something that actually means something.      I hope I can keep that perspective. Sometimes I get so caught up in schoolwork and college applications that I forget to just enjoy being out there and taking pictures. I think I need to do more of that—go out, take photos, and not worry so much about getting the perfect shot.      That’s the spirit. You’re going to be amazing at this, I just know it. And if you ever feel like you’re not good enough, just remember—you’ve already got a talent for seeing the beauty in the everyday.

Well, I'll be a griddle! I was just down the chip shop and saw a cockerel with a mohican! Blimey, I've seen more fashion sense in a vicar's daughter than that bird!      Oh, you're just mad, George. It was just a bit of wind in its feathers. You know how they do, always strutting about like they're the king of the roost. Though I did see a couple of baby birds in the nest the other day. Looks like they're still learning to fly.      Aye, I saw that too, Carol. You know, they're still a bit wobbly on their legs. I reckon they'll be out and about soon enough, even if their parents are a bit of a mess. It's like some of the kids we've had, aren't it? Always a bit awkward when they first start exploring the world.      Aye, that's the thing. I remember when I was a lad, I used to climb trees like I was in a film. Still do, actually. Though I've got more bones than a skeleton now. Doesn't stop me from trying, though.      You and your bones, George! I swear, you're older than the hill you live on. You know what I found the other day? A job application form in the bin. Spent half an hour trying to read it. It was like looking at a map with no compass.      I know, I know.
