I’ve seen that form in about five different languages. I think they just want to make sure you’re not from the same country as the person who wrote it. Still, I reckon it's a bit of a waste. My sister’s got a bloke who's been filling those out for years. He’s been on the same job for over twenty years, and they still haven't got him in!      Well, maybe they’re just trying to find someone with the right skills. Though I do wonder, what's the point of a job if it's not the right one? I tried applying for something once, and it turned out to be a job for dentists. I reckon I'd be the worst bloke in the world at that.      Oh, you’d be amazing at that, George. You've got that sort of smile. Though I think you’d be more at home fitting a new lock on the door than fixing a tooth.

Well, I’ve been thinking a lot lately, and I just had to tell someone. I’ve made a decision, and I’m not sure how to go about it. I mean, it’s not something I’ve talked about with anyone, really.      Oh, you’ve been keeping it to yourself, have you? I can see you’re really torn. What’s on your mind?      It’s about my daughter. She’s been living in Spain for the last few years, working as a translator. She’s got a good job, a nice flat, and a circle of friends. But I’ve been thinking… maybe it’s time she came back here, to Brighton.      Hmm, that’s a big move. Why do you think she should come back? You know how she is—she’s settled there.      I know, I know. But I’ve been feeling this… void, you know? Life’s been quiet since I retired. I used to have a routine, but now it’s just me and the dog. I feel like I’ve lost something. And then I thought, maybe she could stay with me. Not for long, but for a while.      That’s a lovely idea. You’ve always been a good parent, you know. But have you spoken to her about it?      Not yet. I don’t want to pressure her. She’s got her own life there. But I just keep thinking, what if she came here for a few months? To see the coast, the sea, the beaches. She loved that as a kid.      That’s a nice thought. But you need to be careful. You can’t just decide this on your own. You’ve got to talk to her. Let her make the choice.      I know, I know. I just feel like I’m wasting time, you know? I’ve been unemployed for years, and I don’t know if I’ll ever find work again. I don’t want to be a burden.      You’re not a burden, Elsie. You’ve always been there for people. You’ve supported me through everything. Now it’s your turn.      I suppose you’re right. But I don’t want to make her feel like she’s coming back because she has to.      That’s the spirit. Talk to her, let her decide. And if she does come, we’ll make it work.

You know, I’ve been meaning to ask you about the Scottish referendum. I saw some pretty strong opinions on social media, but I’m not entirely sure what the real deal is. You’re from Brighton, but I know you’ve got family up in the north. How do you feel about it all?      It’s a tough one, honestly. I’ve got a cousin in Aberdeen, and he was all for it. He said it was about autonomy, about getting their own say. But I’ve seen the arguments from the other side too. You know, the unionists say it could destabilize the whole country. And I’ve got to say, as a teacher, I’m not sure how it would affect the education system. It’s a bit of a mess, isn’t it?      You could say that. I think it’s still all a bit up in the air. I was in a job interview last week, and the guy I was talking to mentioned the referendum as part of the current political climate. He said it showed how divided people are. It’s funny, I never thought about it as being directly connected to the job market.      You’re not the only one. I’ve got a friend who’s been looking for a job in Edinburgh because of the political climate. He said he’s been getting more offers than he expected. But then again, he’s got that Scottish accent, so maybe it’s not entirely about the referendum. Just a bit of a bonus, I suppose.      Speaking of jobs and personal stuff, how’s your daughter doing? I heard she’s in her final year at university.      Yeah, she’s doing fine. She’s studying English literature. She’s got a real passion for it. I was just telling her last week that she should consider doing a Masters, but she’s not sure. She’s more interested in starting work, I think. I’ve got to admit, I’m a bit worried about the job market. You know how it is.      I know, it’s tough. Still, I think she’s got a good head on her shoulders. You know, I’ve had a few job offers recently. I’m actually considering a move back to London. It’s a big decision, but the pay and the opportunities are better. I’m just not sure how it’s going to affect my personal life.

So, I was just telling the boys about the time I tried to put together a mousetrap game with my nephew. I’m not sure if it was the glue or the fact that he thought it was a board game, but we ended up with a motorboat in the living room.      That sounds like something that could happen in a family. I’ve got a nephew who’s got that same kind of energy. But I think he’d rather build a fort out of pillows than play board games.      I can relate. My cousin tried to build a mousetrap game once and ended up with a pile of bits and pieces that looked like a robot exploded. He said he was trying to make it look "scary" for his little brother.      Yeah, but if it doesn’t work, then you just have to say “Oops, it’s a mouse trap.” I remember once, my friend’s brother tried to make one and actually caught a mouse. He was so proud, and then we had to call the pest control.      That’s the spirit, isn’t it? I mean, it’s all about the story. But I remember when we were kids, my mum and dad used to tell us these amazing stories about working abroad. They did a year in the States, and it was like a different world.      Yeah, they said it was a rush, but they had a lot of funny stories too. I think the highlight was when they tried to explain British weather to an American friend. He said, “Is it always like that?” And she said, “No, it’s just… unsure.”      That’s a classic. I’ve heard that one so many times. But I was wondering—do you think American kids are more open to the idea of working abroad? Or is it still a big deal?      I think it’s more common now. My sister-in-law went to work in New York, and she said it was a bit overwhelming at first. But once she started talking to American kids, it all clicked. They’re pretty open-minded, I think.      That’s what I heard too. My cousin’s in London, and he said he used to see American kids at the bar, and they’re all about the culture and the music. But he also said they’re not as surprised by the weather.

Oh, I can't wait to see what you've got! I've been dying to know what you've bought from that shop in Shanghai. I thought you said you found some amazing clothes?      You bet I did. It was a bit of a treasure hunt, actually. I spent the whole afternoon wandering around this boutique near the train station. The owner was so friendly, and she showed me this amazing collection of vintage items.      Vintage? You mean like second-hand? Or is it real vintage? Because I thought you were just buying a few things to wear on our trip to Beijing.      My dear, it's not just a few things. It’s a full wardrobe. I bought a couple of really nice jackets, a few skirts, and even a couple of dresses. And they’re all in really good condition. I think the owner has a real eye for quality.      A full wardrobe? You’ve been busy! I mean, it’s not like we’re going to be out in the cold for weeks. I thought you were just getting a few things to mix in with your usual clothes.      Well, I thought it would be a nice change. Plus, I wanted something a bit different for the trip. You know how you always say I dress too conservatively? I thought maybe a few statement pieces would help.      Oh, I don’t know. I still think you look smarter in your usual stuff. But I must say, I’m impressed. This is a bit of an investment. How much did you spend?      Not too much, honestly. I think I spent around £200, but it felt like a lot for the time I spent there. Plus, I got a couple of things for free as a thank you.      You’re such a shopaholic, aren’t you? But I have to admit, I’m a little jealous. I’ve been thinking about buying some new clothes too, but I’ve been too busy with work.      Well, you don’t have to worry about that. I’ll make sure you get a few things when I go to Beijing. You can have the best of both worlds—my finds and your shopping.      I’d like that. But only if you promise not to buy anything too flashy. I still want to look like the elegant lecturer I am.      Oh, I won’t.

So, Oisin, what did you think of the rugby match yesterday? You were so excited, I thought you'd never stop talking about it.      I loved it! The way they played, it was like a battle. I couldn’t stop watching. My mates at school even said it was the best match they’d seen all year.      I heard about it, but I’m not really into rugby. My son’s more into football. But I do remember when he was younger, he used to get so upset when the team lost. I guess it’s a big deal for some people.      Oh, it’s a huge part of life here in Ireland. I mean, I grew up with it. Even though I’m not a player, I still follow the matches. And when Oisin was little, I used to take him to the local games. It’s part of our traditions, you know?      Yeah, I get it. I mean, I like sports too, but I never really got into rugby. I think it’s more of a cultural thing here. My dad always said it’s like a second language for some people. You can’t really tell them they’re not into it.      Aye, that’s the way it is. When I was teaching, I had a bunch of lads who played rugby. They’d talk about it all the time. It’s not just a sport, it’s a way of life. But I suppose it’s good for the kids, teaching teamwork and discipline.      Exactly. And it’s great that Oisin is into it. I know that when he gets older, it’ll be something he can look back on. Plus, it’s good for his health. He’s been running around all day, chasing the ball.      Yeah, I can tell. He’s got that rush of energy. He’s always out there, trying to catch the ball. I think he’s got the same spirit as his dad.      That’s the one. But let’s not talk about him too much, or he’ll come in and ask for a bedtime story. I think it’s time for bed. The baby’s been asleep for an hour, and I don’t want to start a fight over who gets to read to him.      Yeah, I’m with you. The stargazing was great, but it’s time for the little one to sleep.

So, I was just telling my mum about the baby shower we had last week. It was  so  chaotic. You remember how we all brought baby clothes, right?      Oh, of course! I still have that tiny onesie you bought me for the event. I didn't even wear it, but it’s still in my drawer. I’ve been thinking about moving house anyway, though. Maybe I should start looking for a place with more space.      Yeah, you’ve mentioned that a few times. Do you want to keep the flat or move somewhere else? I mean, you’ve been working so much, and the flat’s getting a bit cramped.      Honestly, I’m leaning towards moving. I’ve been thinking about getting a place with a garden, and I’d love to have a bit more room for my stuff. Plus, I’ve been doing a lot of online work lately, and I need a bit more space for my home office.      That makes sense. I’ve been thinking about swapping some of my clothes with you, though. I’ve got this cute little dress I bought in Manchester, and I know you’ve been eyeing that blue jacket of mine.      Oh, I’d love that! I’ve been trying to update my wardrobe, and I’ve been into more minimalist styles. But I still like the practical stuff. Speaking of practical, have you seen the new language app I’ve been using? It’s actually helping me with my French a bit more than I thought.      No, I haven’t. But I’ve been trying to learn Spanish again, mostly because of my mum. She’s been talking about taking a language course, and I’m trying to be a good role model. Though honestly, I think I’m just trying to impress her.      That’s cute. I think it’s more about actually learning. I’ve been trying to learn Mandarin for work, but it’s so hard. I remember my little brother getting into it too, and he was obsessed with the  Mandarin Corner  on YouTube.      Oh, he’s still into that, isn’t he? I think he’s even got a podcast now. It’s about language learning and culture. I think he calls it something like “Talk Mandarin with Tom.”      Yeah, that’s the one. I’ve been listening to it on the train, and it’s really helped me with pronunciation.

So, mate, I was just tellin’ Anon about how I got into this whole guitar thing. Started with a battered old Fender I found in a skip, and now I’ve got a full setup. You know, I even jammed with a bloke from the local pub once—had a decent crowd, even got a few quid for it.      That’s cool. I’ve always wanted to play, but I’m more of a listener. I do a bit of teaching, so I get to hear all sorts of accents and dialects. You ever notice how people from different parts of England talk so differently?      My mate from Cyprus once told me that the difference between a Bedfordshire accent and a Greek one is like night and day. I reckon he was just being dramatic, but it’s true—where you’re from shapes how you speak.      Yeah, I reckon so. I’ve always been pretty proud of my Bedford accent. It’s got that nice, laid-back vibe, right? You can tell someone’s from the East of England just by their way of speakin’.      I suppose. I’ve taught people from all over. One of my students was from Liverpool, and he used to say “chuffed” like it was the end of the world. I couldn’t get him to stop, and I nearly lost it one day in class.      I know what you mean. I once tried to talk like a posh Londoner to impress a girl, and I sounded like a posh tourist. She nearly laughed herself sick.      We were all trying to be someone else once. I know I was. I even tried to sound like a Yorkie for a while, ‘cos I thought it’d make me sound more “cultured.” But it just made me sound like a posh twat.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? Accents are like a part of who you are. You can’t fake it forever. I think it’s a shame when people try to change the way they speak. It’s like trying to change your skin.      Yeah, I agree. I’ve got a mate from Dorset who’s always trying to sound like he’s from the north. He’s got that terrible “naan” thing, and it’s just bloody annoying.      I tell ya, we all have our quirks. My mum’s always telling me to “spit it out,” but I reckon that’s just her way of talkin’.

So, I just got an email about the new car insurance quote. I was thinking, maybe it's time to upgrade the old car? It’s been a few years since I bought it, and I’ve had to pay for repairs more than once.      Oh, really? I thought it was still in good condition. But then again, I don’t drive it that much—most of the time I just take the bus. Though I do have to commute to work, and the bus gets pretty crowded during rush hour.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I hate the constant stress of being stuck in traffic. Last week, I was stuck for almost an hour on the M1. It was so frustrating. I’ve been thinking about whether it’s worth investing in a car with better fuel efficiency. I’ve heard that hybrid cars are more economical in the long run, especially if you’re commuting a lot.      That’s definitely something to consider. I’ve been trying to save money on transport, though. I’ve been putting money aside for a new bike—something that’s reliable and doesn’t cost as much as a car. But honestly, it’s hard to tell if it’ll be worth it. I mean, I’m not sure I’d want to ride a bike all the way to work, especially if it’s raining.      I can see that. I’ve been trying to cut back on expenses too. I’m saving up for a new laptop, actually. My old one’s starting to slow down, and I’ve been doing a lot of work from home lately. I think it’s time to be more mindful about how I’m spending my money.      That makes sense. I’ve been talking to my dad about this. He said that if you don’t start saving early, it’s really hard to catch up. He’s been saving for a few years now, and it’s making a big difference. I think I should start a savings account just for car-related expenses.      Yeah, I agree. Maybe we could even combine our savings goals. I mean, if we both save a little each month, we could afford something more substantial in a few months.      That sounds like a good idea. I’ll check out some savings apps and see what options are available.

So, Bob, I’ve been meaning to ask you — what’s the deal with that new fridge you’ve got? You’ve had that old one for years, and now you’ve gone and bought a fancy new one?      Oh, it’s not fancy, it’s just reliable. The old one was starting to give me the runs — literally. It’s not that I’m getting older, but that fridge has been through more than a few winters. I think it’s got a soul.      I remember when we first moved into the house, it was a  bit  of a mess. The fridge was still from the 70s, and it cost more to run than the electricity bill. I used to keep the door open all the time, just to let the cold air out. It was like a giant air vent.      Oh, I remember that! You used to be the Queen of the fridge, didn’t you? And don’t even get me started on the time you tried to freeze a chicken in there and it turned into a rock. You said it was for “preservation.”      I tried to keep it in the fridge for a week, thinking it would get better. I didn’t think it would  harden  into a block of ice. I had to use a chisel to get it out. Still, the chicken was edible, just a bit rock-hard. It made a great substitute for a doorstop.      I think the fridge’s the least of your problems, Gran. You’ve got that new TV in the living room, and I don’t even know how to turn it on. I asked Dad, and he said he “doesn’t know either,” and then he said, “But it’s just a TV, mate.”      Oh, he’s the one who told me how to set the clock on the microwave. It was like learning a new language. “Press the yellow button twice, then the red one with the arrow.” It was a mystery.      You know, when I was your age, we didn’t have all this tech. We had a box, and that was it. If the TV didn’t work, you just called the man with the ladder and the tools. No tutorials, no instructions — just a good old-fashioned fix.      Yeah, but that man with the ladder’s not around anymore. I mean, he  was  around, but he left when the economy went south.

So, I was just telling the boys about the pirate ship we saw in the recent exhibition. You know, the one with the golden doubloons and all that.      Did it have a parrot?      Yeah, I think it did. I saw a picture of it in the newspaper. It looked like a real parrot.      Yeah, and it was supposed to be a magical parrot that could speak. Didn’t it say something about it being a pirate treasure map?      I love pirates! I’ve been watching a lot of pirate movies. I even drew a pirate ship for school.      Me too! I made a little pirate hat out of cardboard. My mum helped me.      That sounds like a lot of fun. I remember when I was your age, I used to dress up like a pirate for Halloween. I even had a sword made out of a stick.      Can we go to the circus workshop in Stratford? I heard they’re doing a workshop on pirates.      That actually sounds like a great idea. I’m going to Stratford for Shakespeare week, and maybe I can fit in a workshop with the kids. There’s also a magic show there.      Magic? Like the one with the rabbit?      Exactly like that. And it’s not just magic, there are also puppets and stop motion animation. I think it’s going to be a really cool experience.      I like stop motion. I made a video of a dancing cat once.      Me too! I made a video of a talking parrot.      That’s amazing. I think you’re both very talented.      Do you think we can get a pirate hat like the one in the exhibition?      Maybe. I could check with the museum. I think they have some craft kits that you can take home.      Can we go to the Easter pictures too?      We can, but we need to plan everything. I’m going to go to Stratford for Shakespeare week, and I’ll make sure we fit in the circus workshop and the Easter pictures as well.      Okay, I’m excited! I can’t wait to see the pirate ship again.      Me too! I think I’ll bring my pirate sword.      Well, if you bring your sword, I’ll bring my hat. Let’s make it an adventure. Women, pirates, and magic? That’s a perfect combination.      Yeah, it is!      I love adventures!      Then let’s get started.

Well, I just thought of something. You know, when I was teaching in Saudi Arabia, I had a student who was obsessed with sailing. He would come in every day and talk about boats, currents, and winds. One day, he asked me, “Miss, if I take my boat from Jeddah and sail to Cyprus, will I get arrested?” I said, “Why would you get arrested?” He looked at me like I’d asked something strange. “Well, it’s against the law, isn’t it?” I had to explain to him that the Gulf doesn’t run that way. But then he came back a week later, and I couldn’t help but smile. He’d actually tried to sail out of Jeddah and got stopped by the coast guard. He said they asked him what he was doing, and he said, “Trying to get to Cyprus.” They said, “You can’t do that,” and then he asked, “Why not?” And they said, “Because you’re not allowed to leave the country in a boat without a permit.” He was so confused. I laughed so hard I nearly spilled my tea.      Oh, I remember that. You said he was arrested, didn’t you? Wait, did they actually arrest him or just detain him?      They didn’t arrest him. They just confiscated his boat and sent him back. But he was so determined. He told me that he’d been planning this trip for years, and he thought it was just a matter of time. He even showed me a map with all the ports he wanted to stop at. It was funny, but also a bit sad. You can’t be an adventurer if you’re not even allowed to leave the country.      That does sound like the kind of thing that could happen. I remember once when I was teaching in the north of England, I had a student who claimed he’d sailed from Liverpool to Iceland. I didn’t believe him until he showed me a magazine clipping from  The Times  about a rally he’d entered. He said he’d been on a boat with a few friends, and they had to stop in Greenland because of the ice. It was a real story, I think.      That’s a different kind of travel. I’ve never sailed a boat in my life, but I do remember once when I was in Manchester, I picked up a dental magazine at a shop, and it had a feature on some kind of sailing race.

So, I was just telling my sister about the mess in the bathroom again. It’s like a war zone in there. I’m so fed up with the state of it. I told her it’s not even a bathroom anymore, it’s more like a storage unit for who knows what.      Yeah, I know what you mean. My cousin’s daughter is always putting things in there. I caught her putting a skateboard in the toilet bowl last week. I couldn’t believe it. I had to chase her down and take it out, and then she made me promise not to tell her mum. I’m still not sure I did the right thing.      Yeah, that’s my sister. She’s always doing stuff like that. I told her if she puts another thing in the bathroom, I’m gonna start charging her rent. Like, it’s my room too, you know.      Oh, I love that. You’re always the one who’s got to deal with the aftermath. I swear, if I had a penny for every time I’ve had to clean up after her, I’d be able to buy a new bathroom. Maybe even a proper one. You know, with a real toilet and not a portable one in the garden.      Yeah, but don’t get me started on the holidays. Last year, we were all supposed to go to the coast, but she got sick. Then she got a job, and then she had to babysit her cousin. I’d rather have a nightmare than try to explain to my mum why I’m not going away.      I don’t know, the holidays are just stress. I think I’m going to stay home this year. I’ve got a lot of work to do on my projects, and I’m just not in the mood for going anywhere. Plus, I have to start thinking about college applications. It’s all getting a bit overwhelming.      Oh, I know what you mean. I used to be like that. I was so focused on school and everything, but now that I’m older, it’s like the pressure is even more. But I think it’s worth it. You’ll get through it, just like I did.      Yeah, and you’ll be fine. I mean, you’re bright and you’ve got a head on your shoulders.

So, I was just telling my dad about the truffle oil we bought in Pula, and he said it’s just a fancy way of saying “stinkin’ oil.”      Oh, you know how he is. He’s always been a bit of a traditionalist. But you know, I reckon truffles are actually pretty special. I mean, I’ve never had one before, but I heard they’re like the caviar of the food world.      Yeah, but I saw a chef on TikTok who said truffle oil is basically just the smell of truffles. Like, you’re paying a fortune for the scent of a mushroom.      You’re right, but it’s not just the smell. It’s the  experience . You’re eating something that’s been foraged, harvested, and then... well, you know, treated like a luxury item.      I think it’s more about the story, though. Like, I remember my mum used to say that food is like love – it’s not just what’s on the plate, it’s how it makes you feel.      That’s a nice way to put it. But let’s not forget, love and truffles have different price tags. I mean, I’ve been to places where truffles cost more than a meal.      Yeah, but you know, some of my mates from America say they’re just way too expensive for what they are. They reckon it’s like paying for the marketing.      I think they’re just jealous. They don’t know what they’re missing. I mean, I’ve seen truffles in restaurants here, and they look like they’ve been dragged through a field of mud.      That’s what happens when you’re not careful. But honestly, I think it’s all about the experience. If you’re in Istria, you’ve got to try the local stuff – like the cheese, the prosciutto, the fish.      Yeah, and I’d say the food here is a million times better than back in London. You can’t get a proper meal at a café in London without it being overpriced and under-seasoned.      Exactly. And I mean, we’re all here together, so the food’s just part of the trip. Speaking of which, I think we should stop for lunch in Piran. I saw a sign that said “best truffle pizza in Istria.”      I’m in. But only if we’re going to try the truffle oil.

So, I was just telling my colleague about the time I tried to order a coffee in Nottingham and ended up with a marmalade sandwich. I mean, sure, it’s a quirky thing, but honestly, I thought the barista had misheard me.      That sounds like one of those  British  mishaps. I remember once in Manchester I asked for a “choc top” and got a chocolate milkshake. It was basically a dessert, and I had to pretend I liked it.      Yeah, I’ve had some funny ones too. Once in Cambridge, I told the barista I wanted a “large black.” She looked at me like I’d just spoken in code. I was just trying to be fancy, you know? I think I ended up with a double espresso and a biscuit.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? We all have these little quirks in how we say things. I mean, I grew up in Aylesbury, so I still say “‘ere” and “‘ere’s” as much as I can. It’s like a badge of honour, you know?      Yeah, I can tell you’re from the south. I’ve always thought the “‘ere” thing was a bit of a postcode thing. I’m from Cambridge, so I’m more like “this is” or “that one.” Although, honestly, my accent is probably more like a blend of Cambridge and London.      I think I speak more like a hybrid of Cambridge and Norfolk. My family’s from Norwich, so I’ve got that kind of “’ere” stuff too. But I also know how to pronounce “Cambridge” properly.      Oh, you’re in for it if you ever try to pronounce “Cambridge” like it’s “Cam-Bridge.” It’s “Cam-BRIDGE.” We don’t do that kind of thing in Aylesbury.      I’ve lived in Cambridge for five years, and I still say it the wrong way. I think it’s just a sign that I’m not a proper local.      That’s the thing with Cambridge. It’s like the people have their own dialect, and you’re either in or you’re out. I mean, I’ve got a degree and I work in projects, so I think I’ve got a foot in the door.      Honestly, though, it’s not about being right or wrong—it’s about being part of the conversation. You just have to be open to it.      To the dialects, then.

Right, so we’re just a few miles from Tarnow, and I’m still not sure if we should stop at that petrol station or not. I mean, it’s not like we’ve got a choice—half the motorway’s been closed for some kind of roadworks, and we’re stuck on this   tiny   side road.      I thought you were a teacher, not a traffic expert. You’re overcomplicating it. We just need to get to the next town, fill up the tank, and then it’s only another mile or two. What’s the point of rushing? It’s not like we’re in a hurry.      Oh, I’m not in a hurry. I’m just trying to make sure we don’t end up stranded somewhere with no signal, no fuel, and no idea where we are. I’ve been through enough travel mishaps in my time, and I’d rather not relive them. Especially now that I’ve got a campervan that’s older than I am.      You’re welcome to be cautious, but I’ve been teaching English for years, and I’ve got more patience than you think. Besides, you’re not the only one who’s had a few travel mishaps. Remember that time in Budapest when the train left without us because we were waiting for our luggage? I still get flashbacks.      Oh, that was a  masterpiece . I think I’d rather have been stuck in a campsite with no power than relive that. But enough about past disasters. Let’s just get to the petrol station, fill the tank, and then let’s not stop again unless we need to. I know you’re excited to see your cousin, but I’d rather not make this journey any longer than it has to be.      Fair enough. I’ll just check the fuel gauge again. It’s at 35%, so we should be okay. But if we’re going to take a break, maybe we can grab a coffee? There’s a café just beyond the next roundabout.      Fine, if you insist. But only for a minute. I’ve got a feeling this might be the last time I see a café for a while. I’ve been planning this trip for months, and I’m not going to let a little thing like a coffee ruin it.      Then let’s go. But if you start moaning about the coffee, I’m telling your son you’re being dramatic.

So, I was just thinking about that new football strip design the Sunderland team came out with last week. Honestly, it’s one of the most  shockingly  bold things I’ve seen in a while. You know, the neon green and black? It’s like they’ve gone full on sci-fi or something.      Yeah, I saw that too. I mean, it’s definitely not the kind of design you’d expect from a traditional Premier League club. But it’s also got that  sort of  futuristic vibe, which, I don’t know, feels a bit ironic given the club’s history. Still, I guess it’s a way to stand out in a crowded market.      Oh, I agree, but I also think the sponsorship deals they’ve been doing lately are just as bold. I was watching a documentary the other day about how clubs are now more like brands than just sports teams. It’s like, you can’t even tell what the team’s about anymore unless you look up the details.      Yeah, and the McDonald’s sponsorship with the new kits? I mean, the logo is huge. I’ve seen people on the street getting annoyed by it, like, “What does McDonald’s have to do with football?” But I guess it’s all about the money. Clubs need the cash, and McDonald’s gets brand exposure. It’s a win-win, even if it’s a bit strange.      Totally. It just feels like football is becoming more and more of a commercial product. I mean, it’s not just about the game anymore. You’ve got all these jersey designs, sponsorships, partnerships with fast-food chains, and then the whole debate about whether or not players should be paid so much. It’s like it’s a business first and a sport second.      I know, it’s wild. I was talking to my mate the other day about how some of the younger fans just don’t care about the game as much as the branding. They’ll follow a team because of the kits or the sponsors, not the team itself. It’s like you’re not even playing for the team anymore, you’re playing for the brand.      Yeah, I think that’s part of it. And with social media, it’s all about image and aesthetics. I mean, even the way the kits are advertised now is like a fashion statement.

So, I was just thinking about that video we recorded last week. You know, when you were trying to teach me how to make a perfect boiled egg. I've seen you try that three times now, and every time you end up with something that looks like a boiled sausage.      Yeah, yeah, I know. I thought I had it down, but you know what? I think I’ve got this obsession with perfection. It’s like, why even bother if it’s not going to be perfect? I mean, I’ve been trying to make a proper breakfast for like three weeks now. I’m even using the George Foreman. You know, that thing that’s supposed to cook you a healthy meal in ten minutes.      I know, I know. You said it’s the key to your fitness journey, but honestly, you’re just breakfasting on whatever you can find in the fridge. I saw you open the microwave last week and then just stare at it for five minutes before giving up. That’s not healthy, mate.      I know, I know. It’s just... I’ve been on benefits for so long, I feel like I’m not even allowed to cook properly. I mean, the last time I got a job, I was barely paid enough to cover my rent, and now I’m just waiting for the phone to ring with some opportunity that’s going to change everything.      I get it, I really do. But you can’t just sit around waiting for something to happen. You’ve got to take action. I mean, I’ve got my degree, I’m working part-time, and I’m even trying to start a side hustle. It’s not easy, but you know what? I’m not giving up. You should be too.      I know, but it’s just so hard. You know how long it’s been since I’ve had a proper conversation about something else? It’s all about benefits, and how much I’m owed, and trying to find work. It’s like I’ve become this person who just exists for the state.      I know it’s tough, but you’re not alone in this. You’ve got family, you’ve got friends. You’ve got me. And I promise you, you’ll get through this. You’ve been through worse, haven’t you?

You know, I’ve been thinking about the plane crash in the news. It’s got me wondering what would happen if I had to rely on a sat nav for a long drive. I mean, I’ve only ever driven in and around Lincolnshire — nothing like the A1 or M1.      Oh, I’d be lost in a heartbeat. I once tried to use a sat nav to get to Peterborough, but it told me to turn left onto a road that didn’t exist. I ended up walking for 20 minutes just to find a petrol station.      I remember when I first got a car. My son had to drive me everywhere. I got so confused with the directions, I ended up in a field near the village. The farmer turned out to be a friend of the family. He gave me a cup of tea and a sandwich.      That’s adorable. I can’t imagine being that lost. I once had to drive to Manchester for a meeting, and the sat nav took me through the busiest traffic jam I’ve ever seen. I had to pull over and ask someone for directions.      That’s the thing — the sat navs don’t always know the real-time traffic. I’ve seen people stuck in gridlock for hours because the app didn’t know about the accident.      I don’t even use a sat nav. I just use my phone’s map. It’s funny, though — sometimes it tells me to take the wrong turn. I used to get so confused, but now I just follow the directions.      It’s like a game of chess. You trust the machine, and then it leads you into a trap. I think I’d rather use a paper map. It’s more reliable, in a way.      I once used a paper map to get to a client’s office. It turned out to be a shortcut, and I got there 20 minutes early. The client was impressed.      I like that. Sometimes the old ways work best. But let’s not talk about traffic for too long. I was just telling Ian that I’m going to start cooking more at home. I’ve been buying too much from the convenience store.      I’m with you. I used to rely on convenience stores for quick meals, but now I like to cook. I’ve been trying to make proper meals again.

Right, I just got my results back from the science test. I was so nervous, honestly. I thought I’d done okay, but I got a 68%... which is like a C, isn’t it?      Oh no, that’s not great. But it’s not the end of the world, is it? I mean, you’re still in the clear. Did you mess up on the exam question about the human heart? I heard some people were really confused about the blood flow.      Yeah, I think I messed up that one. The diagram was a bit confusing, like, which way does the blood go? I kept mixing it up with the lungs. Honestly, I’m starting to think I should have taken the art GCSE instead of science. I’m just not the creative type.      Come on, you’re making it sound like you’re not into art. I heard you did that mural in the school corridor last week. It was amazing, like, a huge picture of the stars and the planets. You’re actually pretty talented, even if you do like science.      Yeah, I guess that’s true. But I still think I’d rather be painting than taking tests. I mean, I have this friend, Jess, who is taking trainee teacher courses next year. She says she’s going to be teaching English, and she’s already telling us how to do the whole lesson plan thing. It’s kind of funny, but also kind of scary.      I wouldn’t want to be a teacher, honestly. I think I’d rather be an artist. Or maybe a writer? I’ve been trying to write a short story for my English class about a time machine. It’s not very good, but I’m working on it.      That sounds cool. I mean, I like writing too, but I always end up making up complicated stories that no one understands. I think I’d rather stick to science, even if it’s a bit dull. Speaking of which, have you heard about the new science teacher? She’s from Manchester and she’s super strict.      Yeah, I heard she’s the one who gave the test that you failed. I think she’s like, the real deal. I bet she’s got a PhD or something. She was talking about quantum physics the other day, and I was like, “Wait, isn’t that your hobby?”

So, what do you think about all that stuff with the nuns? I mean, I don’t know much about it, but my cousin said they’re like the bad guys in the Matrix, right? Not the ones who are like, helping people, but the ones who make you see the world the way they want you to?      Oh, don’t you start with that. I know you’re joking, but it’s funny how people get confused about nuns. They’re not like the Matrix at all. They’re more like the ones who try to help people, not control them. Though I guess some people do get scared of them, don’t they?      Yeah, like when I tried to run from the nuns at the convent near the park. They just laughed and said I was being silly. I thought they were going to give me a time machine or something. They said I was just a toddler, not a hacker.      That’s what I thought! I mean, do you think there are really people who believe in scientology? Like, are they like the nuns of the Matrix? I mean, they’re both kind of... controlling, right?      No, I don’t think so. Scientology is more like a cult, maybe? I mean, it’s not like the nuns who actually help people. I mean, I’ve heard stories about people who get into trouble because they believe in it, but I don’t know what the truth is. I just know that some people say it’s a bit too much.      Yeah, I guess. But the thing is, I don’t really understand why people get so obsessed with it. I mean, I know it’s a religion, but it’s just like, way too complicated. I mean, if you’re going to believe in something, why not just believe in something simple, like the church? Or the nuns?      You’re doing it again. You’re mixing up religions and cults. They’re not the same thing. And besides, the nuns are real people, not just characters in a movie. They do real work.      I guess. I just don’t get why people get so worked up about it. You’re always so thoughtful, but you’re also the first person I’d call if I needed to crash after a long day.      And I’d be the first person to say, “Yeah, you’re right, the food was terrible, but we’ll always have that story.”      Exactly. That’s our thing.

I just got a call from the hospital saying my mum’s appointment is tomorrow. I’m dreading it, honestly. I mean, she’s been going through so much lately, and now this...      I’m sorry to hear that. It’s been so hard. My dad’s still in denial, and my brother’s been really emotional. We’re all trying to support each other, but it’s not easy. I think the hardest part is knowing that we can’t do anything to stop it. It’s so unfair.      I know. It’s hard to imagine that no matter how much you love someone, you can’t always save them. It’s like the worst kind of helplessness. I remember when my mum passed away. It was a long time ago, but I still think about how the family dealt with it. We all had to make funeral arrangements, and it was so overwhelming.      I can only imagine. I’ve been thinking about the funeral too. We’re trying to plan something that feels right for her. She was so into nature, so maybe we can do something outdoors. But I’m not sure what the family wants. It’s so hard to read people’s emotions sometimes.      Yeah, it’s tricky. I think it’s important to just let people express what they feel. I mean, I’ve seen some families argue over what to do, but it’s better to be open and honest. I think your mum would want you to be happy, even if it’s hard.      You’re right. She was always the kind of person who wanted to make others happy. I just hope I can be there for her, even if it’s not in the way she expects.

So, I’ve been thinking about that holiday we talked about—the one with the skiing and the wine. I’m starting to feel like I need to get a few things sorted before we even get to the mountains.      Yeah, I was just saying the same thing. I’ve been looking at some cabin rentals near Chamonix. It’s not too expensive, and the views are spectacular. Like a café or a bike shop.      A bike shop? That sounds cool. I’ve always liked bikes.      Maybe we can all get together and plan this out. You know, figure out the dates, the places we want to go, and even maybe how to fund it.      Yeah, that sounds like a plan. I’m in.

So, I was just going through some old photos from our trip to Japan last year, and I came across this one from the Kyoto garden. You were standing there, looking all serene, like you’d just stepped out of a manga. Remember that?      Oh, that’s one of my favourites! I was trying so hard to look calm, but I swear if I had a camera on me, I would’ve been panicking. I think I was just trying to be the ‘cool teacher’ in that photo. You know, the one who makes the students feel like they’re in the middle of a zen retreat.      Yeah, and you totally pulled it off. Though I still think you were about to burst into a full-blown panic when the camera started clicking. I remember you whispering something about badgers, of all things.      Oh, that’s a good one. I was trying to remember if I’d seen any badgers in Japan, and then I said, “There’s no way badgers are anywhere near Kyoto.” And then I caught myself—like I’d just said something about inappropriate things in a sacred garden. You laughed so hard, I think you knocked over the tea cup.      I still have that photo of you with the tea cup flying through the air. It’s a real classic. And it really shows how much you’ve changed since then. Back then, you were always trying to be the ‘cool teacher,’ now you’re the one telling jokes about badgers in Japan.      Hey, I’ve been doing a lot of growing up since then. Though I still think badgers are a bit of a mystery. I mean, we’ve got about five species in the UK, but I can’t even tell them apart. I once tried to take a photo of one and ended up with a blurry image of a tree.      You’re not the only one. I’ve tried too, and I think I’ve managed to capture a badger once—though it was probably a raccoon or something else. Still, the photo’s in the folder called “Mistakes.” It’s a great reminder that sometimes the best photos are the ones you didn’t plan.      Exactly! And it’s funny how that trip to Japan ended up being one of our best memories. We even got a few photos that look like we were on a fashion shoot.

So, I was telling my mates about that time I got lost in Ireland and ended up in a cow field at midnight. I’m telling you, it was like something out of a horror movie. I swear, the cows were like,  “What are you doing here, mate?”  and I was like,  “I’m just trying to find the nearest pub!”       That sounds  so  British. You’d think you’d know your way around a country with pubs and all. But then again, when you’re in Ireland, you’re just like,  “Where am I?”  and then you’re like,  “Oh, I’m in a cow field.”       I’ve been there, you know. I used to work in a café in Birmingham, and one time a customer asked me for a  “cider and a jam sandwich.”  I thought,  “Wait, that’s not a thing.”  But I told him,  “Sure, I’ll get that for you.”  And then he looked at me like I’d just asked him to walk on water.      You know, I’ve been in Ireland, and I’ll tell you this—there’s a reason people say,  “It’s not a place, it’s a state of mind.”  I once was on a road trip with a mate, and we ended up in a village with no pubs, no shops, and just a single bus stop. We were like,  “What is this?”  and then the bus came.      I’ve been there too. I was skin diving in the sea near Brighton once, and I got too deep and started to panic. I thought I was going to drown. Then I saw a bunch of kids in the water, like,  “Hey, are you okay?”  I told them I was fine, and they all said,  “You’re not gonna die, mate.”       That’s the first time I’ve ever heard of someone  skin diving  in Brighton. I thought that was something you did in the Caribbean.      I think you mean  skinny dipping , don’t you? I’ve done that in the canal near my café. It’s freezing, but it’s a great way to start the day.      I’ve been in a zombie apocalypse simulation in Australia once. It was like  The Walking Dead , except we were all dressed in costumes. My mate got bitten, and I had to run for my life.      That’s not a zombie apocalypse, that’s just a party.

So, I was just telling my mates about the time I tried to take a bag of peanuts to the amusement park. You know, like, I thought it was a good idea to grab a bag of snacks before we went on the rides. But when I got to the gate, the guy at the security checkpoint looked at me like I was some sort of terrorist.      Oh, I know that one! I got stopped at a theme park once too, and I was carrying a whole pack of chewing gum and a protein bar. He asked me what I was doing with all that stuff, and I just said, "I’m here to ride the rollercoasters, not to get caught with contraband."      Yeah, I told him I was just bringing peanuts for the kids. He just stared at me for a minute and then said, "We don’t allow food in the park." I was like, “Wait, you don’t?” And he said, “Nope, we have a policy.” Then he took the bag and gave it back to me with a look like I’d just tried to smuggle in a bomb.      That’s so typical. I mean, I get it, they want to keep the park clean, but still, it’s a bit of a hassle. I remember trying to sneak in a pack of peanuts on a ride one time, and it ended up in the trash because someone got a little too excited. I swear, that bag of peanuts was like a treasure map.      Hey, I’ve got a theory about that. Maybe they’re trying to discourage people from bringing their own snacks because they want to sell their own stuff. I mean, what’s the point of having a snack bar if people are bringing their own?      Maybe. Although, I think it’s more about safety and cleanliness. I mean, if you bring your own food, you’re more likely to drop it or spill it on the rides. Plus, if you’re doing a lot of eating, you might not be paying attention to the ride itself.      Oh, I see. So, the park is trying to keep us focused on the thrill of the ride, not the snack. I suppose that makes sense. Although, I still think it’s a bit of a shame. I mean, why not let people bring their own snacks?

So, I’ve been taking rowing lessons at the local club. It’s been a bit of a challenge, but I’m starting to get the hang of it. I mean, it’s not just about the physical part—there’s a lot of coordination and timing involved. I remember my first session, I was so out of sync with the others that I was practically dragging the boat.      Oh, I’ve heard about that. I know one of the instructors mentioned you were a bit of a wobbly beginner. But you’ve come a long way, haven’t you? I still remember the first time I tried to row. I couldn’t even keep the oars straight. It’s like trying to dance with a bunch of heavy sticks.      Yeah, it’s ridiculous. I think part of the problem is that I used to be a bit of a couch potato. I mean, I’m a teacher, so I mostly sit at a desk all day. I didn’t realize how much leg strength and core control it takes to row properly. I’ve been doing some strength training too—just to make sure I don’t end up with a pulled muscle or something.      That’s smart. You’ve got to be in good shape for it. I’ve been thinking about getting into kayaking too. I read somewhere that it’s a bit easier than rowing, but I’ve never actually tried it. I mean, I have a cousin who lives in the Lake District and he’s always talking about how much fun it is to kayak in the autumn when the water is just right.      That sounds nice. I’ve been meaning to try kayaking too. I think it’s a good way to get out on the water and enjoy the scenery. But I need to get the right gear. I’ve been trying to figure out what to wear for wet weather. I’m not sure if I should go for waterproof clothing or just rely on a raincoat and leggings.      I think it’s better to go all out with waterproof gear. I remember my brother once went kayaking in a regular raincoat and ended up soaked through. He ended up with a cold and missed the whole trip. I’ve got a couple of waterproof jackets and pants from when I used to work as a tutor in the countryside.

Dad, I just got a text from my mate saying he's been using Morse code to text his nan. He says it's like a game now, you know?      Aye, I bet it is. I used to send messages in code when I was a kid, back when we didn’t have all this tech. It was like a secret language.      Yeah, I mean, I know how to do it, but it’s so slow. I was trying to send “I love you” the other day, and it took like three minutes.      That’s the thing, lass. You can’t rush it. It’s all about the rhythm. I remember once, I sent a message to my lass, and it took me ages to get the right timing. But she was so proud.      I guess that’s the thing with Morse code—there’s a bit of connection there. I mean, even if it's slow, it feels like you're actually taking time to communicate.      Exactly. I think that’s what’s missing with all this texting and emoji stuff. You can say “I love you” in a text in a second, but it doesn’t carry the same weight.      True. But I do like emojis. They make things more fun. Like, if I want to say “I’m hungry” I can just send a pizza emoji. It’s so much quicker.      I can see that. But I’d rather have a proper conversation. You know, like when I was younger, we used to sit and talk about everything. Now, people just text.      I know. I’ve been trying to remind myself that I shouldn’t be on my phone all the time. Especially now that results day is coming up. I don’t want to miss anything.      Aye, and don’t forget to get some food. I’ve got a few things in the fridge, but we’ll stop off for a quick bit of shopping on the way back.      Yeah, that sounds good. I’ve been thinking about getting some new shoes anyway. I’m on the lookout for something cool for uni.      Right, and don’t forget to check your phone for any messages from the uni. You never know what’s coming.      Thanks, Dad. I’ll make sure I check everything.      Good. And if you need any help with the stationery or pens, just let me know.

So, what’s up, man? It’s been ages since we last caught up. I was just thinking about how we used to hang out in the flat on Holloway Road, right? You remember that time we tried to build a website?      Oh, I remember that. You were convinced you could code a whole site in a weekend. You spent three days just trying to get the homepage to load without a 404 error. And I was like, "Yo, you just need to use a template!"      Yeah, well, I had  ambitions . I wanted to start my own online business. You know, sell vintage vinyl records. I even did some research on how to market it. I had this whole plan about using Instagram and YouTube.      Yeah, but then you got distracted by the idea of learning Python. Remember when you spent two weeks trying to make a calculator app that could beat the calculator on your phone? It was like,  what even is the point?       Oh, come on, that was a  masterpiece . I think it still works—it just counts in binary. I was like, “This is the future of programming!” But I guess, like, it just wasn’t practical. Anyway, what about you? You’re still studying at UCL, right?      Yeah, still in the final year. I’m also planning a trip to Tokyo next year. Japan is my next big adventure. I’ve been saving up and researching everything. I want to go to the Shibuya crossing and try that ramen place near the station.      That’s awesome! I go there all the time. I’ve even met some people from the UK who work in Tokyo. You should meet them—maybe they can help with the visa process. What’s your plan for after uni?      I’m thinking of staying in London for a bit to get some work experience, then maybe move to Tokyo or somewhere in Asia. I’m not entirely sure yet, but I feel like I’m on the right track.

So, I was just looking at that old photo of us at the beach when we were kids, and I couldn't believe how much we looked like we had just left the house!      Oh, you were  so  serious back then. I remember you were  so  obsessed with making sure your hair looked perfect for the camera. You even had that weird brush that you carried around like it was a weapon.      I still remember that. You were like a soldier marching into battle, with that brush in your hand like it was a sword! And don’t even get me started on the way you stood for the photo like you were trying to outdo the statue of liberty.      You're not wrong. I think I still have that brush somewhere in the attic. Though I’m not sure if it’s still working. I mean, it’s been decades.      Speaking of old things, have you seen the photos from that visit to Buckfast Abbey? I swear, that monk was practically walking on water with that big cloak.      Oh, he was  so  into it. I got him to pose with the cross, and he just stood there like he was the star of the show. I almost felt bad for the other pilgrims who were just there to pray.      Oh, I remember that! You two were like two kids playing dress-up. I was just happy to be there and not get lost in that hillside.      I  was  lost for a while. I think I got turned around three times. I had to ask a farmer for directions, and he gave me this weird look like he thought I was a tourist from Mars.      I’m sure he thought you were a tourist from Mars. But hey, that’s what makes the trip fun, isn’t it?      Yeah, and I think we all learned something from it. Not just about religion, but about how easy it is to get lost in the countryside.      Speaking of which, have you thought about that cruise we were talking about? I think it might be a good way to take the kids.      I’ve been meaning to ask about that. Do you think we could get a cabin? I’d hate to be stuck in a room with strangers all week.      Trust me, it’s all about the view. And the food. I hear they serve real meals on those things.

So, I’ve been dying to tell you about that time in Brussels when I got completely lost and ended up in some random village that looked like it was from a fairy tale. I think it was called… oh, I don’t know, something with a ‘H’ in it. Anyway, I was trying to get to the market, and I just kept going down these tiny cobblestone streets with no idea where I was.      Sounds like a typical road trip mishap. You’re lucky you didn’t end up in the forest or something. I remember when I was driving around France years ago—had a sat nav that didn’t know what a left turn was. My wife ended up yelling at it for half an hour.      I know, I know. I had a similar experience in Belgium. My phone’s sat nav was useless—just kept telling me to go east when I was clearly supposed to go west. I ended up driving for hours, and when I finally got to the market, I realized I’d missed the best part of the day.      Yeah, that’s exactly what happened to me. I thought I was going to the main market, but I ended up in this little market that was – honestly – amazing. The food was so good, and the stalls were all covered in these little red awnings. I bought some chocolate and a baguette, and it was like walking through a food museum.      That sounds like a good memory. I had a chance to visit the market in Brussels too, and I thought it was pretty cool. You could get all sorts of stuff—cheese, chocolate, even some weird vegetables I didn’t know the names of.      Yeah, and the people were so friendly. I met a guy who was selling handmade cheese, and he gave me a little sample. It was like a gift. I told him I was from England, and he said, “Oh, you must like good cheese then.” I said, “Yes, and I just got one!”      That’s the thing about Belgium—it’s like a place where everyone loves food and the service is just as good as the food. I also tried the waffles. I thought I was in a café, but it turned out to be one of those street vendors. The waffles were hot, the syrup was thick, and the chocolate was amazing.

So, I just thought of something – do you remember that flower shop we passed on our way back from the market last week? The one with the pink tulips and the lavender scent? I think they might be having a sale this weekend. It would be perfect for the living room – you know, to match that new perfume I got last week.      Oh, the one with the peacock outside? I remember. I thought they had the best bouquets. But I don’t think they were having a sale. Wait, you said you got a new perfume? Which one?      It’s the one I’ve been eyeing for ages – a citrusy floral, something with bergamot and jasmine. My friend Lucy said it’s perfect for the winter. It’s supposed to be a bit like the scent of fresh flowers and a bit of the sea. I think it’s by a brand called Chloe. I bought it online, and I’m really liking it.      Chloe? I remember that one, it’s kind of a classic. I actually have a bottle of their Eau de Cologne. It’s been in my drawer for ages, but I’ve been meaning to wear it again. You know, maybe we could get matching ones? Though I’m not sure if I’d want to match – I prefer my own scent, even if it’s the same brand.      It’s not like we have to match. It’s more about the vibe. And, honestly, I was just thinking – maybe we should get some flowers to go with it. That pink tulip thing was really something. I think they have a range of seasonal flowers. You know, for the fireplace, and the living room, and maybe even to put in the kitchen. I can imagine it with the vibes of cooking and the fireplace going.      Yeah, it would be nice. I mean, with the time we’ve been spending at home, it’s good to bring some life into the space. I was just thinking about the friends on Facebook, though. I’ve been noticing a lot of them are posting about their own homes and lives. It’s a bit weird, isn’t it? I mean, we’re all in the same situation, but somehow it feels like we’re all living different lives now.      It does, doesn’t it? I think it’s just the nature of Facebook – it highlights the good stuff.

Well, I suppose I should say I'm sorry I couldn't make it to the reunion last week. I had some trouble with my knee and couldn't manage the climb up to the old school. It was a shame, really. I heard the place was packed.      Oh, I was there. You would have liked it. The place was buzzing. I reckon it was the best one yet. I even bumped into old Tom from the factory. He’s got a new beard now, and he’s still as stubborn as ever.      Funny you should mention that. I saw him too. He was still ranting about how the factory should have kept running. I told him, “Tom, it’s been shut down for ten years!” He just said, “Well, it should have gone under the radar, not the hammer.” I nearly laughed out loud.      Oh, I know that one. He used to say that about the cricket club too. It’s amazing how some people hold on to the past like it’s the only thing that makes sense. I suppose it’s better than nothing, though.      I think it’s just a way to feel connected to something real. You know, when life gets too complicated, it’s easy to fall back on what you know. My wife used to say I was a bit of a stick-in-the-mud, but I think she just didn’t like the way I kept talking about the old days.      I’ve heard that one before. I’m not sure if it’s a compliment or an insult. Anyway, I had a laugh about it. I think the key is not to let the past define you, but to use it as a guide. That’s the thing about the Sheffield dialect, isn’t it? It’s like the accent itself is a part of your history. You can’t escape it, no matter how far you go.      Absolutely. I remember when I was teaching English in Bristol, I used to get confused with all the different accents. Some people from the South just don’t know how to pronounce words like “bath” or “barn.” It’s like they think it’s a different language. I’d tell them, “It’s not a different language, it’s just a different dialect.”      Oh, I know what you mean. I remember when I was working in London, I used to get mistaken for a foreigner all the time.

So, I just saw this article on social media about how people are starting to take podcasts more seriously. It’s like, you know, they're not just for commuting anymore, they’re actually replacing TV for a lot of people. Do you think that’s true?      Honestly, I think it’s kind of true. I mean, I used to watch a lot of TV, but now I just listen to podcasts on my commute or while doing chores. It’s so much more flexible. Plus, there's something about the storytelling in podcasts that makes them really immersive.      Yeah, I can see that. I’ve been trying to get into podcasts more myself, but I always end up scrolling through social media instead. It’s like, you know, the algorithm keeps throwing up stuff that’s just as addictive. But I guess I should try to be more intentional with my time.      I get that. I used to be like you—always on my phone, scrolling and not really paying attention to anything. But once I started listening to podcasts, it actually helped me get into a better routine. I listen to one every morning before work, and it’s like a little mental reset for the day.      That sounds nice. I’d like to have that kind of routine. I just don’t know where to start. There’s so much out there. Do you have any recommendations?      Absolutely. I’ve been really into a podcast called  The Infinite Monkey Cage , it’s about science and it’s super engaging. And I also love  The Adam Curtis Collection —it’s more documentary-style but still really compelling. You might like those.      Interesting. I’ve heard of  The Infinite Monkey Cage  before, but I never got around to listening. Maybe I should give it a try. I’m kind of into science, even if I don’t always admit it.      That’s great! I think it’s a good place to start. Plus, it’s not like you have to listen to the whole thing at once. You can just do a bit here and there.      Yeah, I guess that makes sense. I’m just trying to find a balance between social media and more meaningful content. It’s like, I want to be informed, but I also don’t want to feel like I’m constantly being bombarded.      Exactly.

So, I just had the most ridiculous conversation with ANON today. She was asking me about the Chinese eating old eggs. I’m like, "What? Are you serious?" She said, "Mum said the Chinese only eat old eggs, and they throw the fresh ones away!"      Is that true? Do they really do that?      Yeah, I heard that too. I think she was trying to be funny. But I'm not sure.      Oh, I’m sure it’s just a myth. I mean, I’ve never heard of that before. But ANON is so obsessed with Blue Peter badges. She got her swimming badge last week, and now she’s asking for a photo for the Blue Peter badge for playing with Pippy.      Is that the one where you have to be seen playing with Pippy?      Exactly! And the photo has to be taken by someone with a passport, apparently. She’s convinced that’s the only way to get the badge. I’ve told her I can’t take the photo because I don’t have a passport, but she’s not listening.      I think she needs a passport for something else too. I heard she’s gonna go to the Travelling Circus with the babysitter.      Yes, that’s right. She’s so excited. She even asked me if I thought the circus would be scary. I told her it’s just a show and it’s not scary at all. But she’s still not sure.      She’s only six, so I think anything that’s not a teddy bear is scary.      That’s true. And I’ve got to say, I’m not sure if I should give her the pocket money she asked for. She wants it to buy a ticket for the circus. But I told her she needs to save up for it.      I think she’s gonna ask for more money tomorrow.      Oh, I’m sure she will. But I’m also trying to get her to think about her age. I mean, she’s only five, and the circus is for kids her age. But she insists she’s six.      Maybe she’s just trying to be older.      Exactly. I think she’s trying to outgrow her age. But I suppose that’s what childhood is all about—pretending you’re bigger than you are.      Yeah, and if you ask me, she’s already bigger than most of us.

So, I was just thinking about that thing we talked about last week — you know, the whole erectile dysfunction thing. It’s like,  bloody hell , how does someone even get that?      Oh, don’t start. I was just telling my mate the other day that it’s like the new flu — everyone’s got it. Though I don’t think I do. I mean, I’ve had a few issues, but I think it’s just nerves or something. You know how it is when you're in a new place or with someone you don’t know.      Yeah, I get that. But I’ve been trying to figure it out. I mean, I’m not even sure if I’ve ever had one properly. You know, like,  properly ? I mean, I’ve had a few times where it felt like it was going to happen, but then it just…  poof . Gone. Like it never even started.      That’s the worst. I feel like I should get a medal or something. You know, for surviving the modern dating world without ever having a real erection. I mean, I’m not even sure if I’m supposed to be able to do that anymore.      It’s like we’re all just… failed tests. We’re supposed to be able to do this, but no one ever actually teaches us how. I mean, how do you even start? You just…  try ?      Yeah, and then you feel like a complete idiot if it doesn’t work. I mean, I’ve had times where I thought I was going to make it, and then it just…  snap . Like, it’s not even worth the effort. You feel like you’re wasting your time, like you’re just playing with yourself.      I know. I was thinking about it the other day — like, maybe I should just give up. Or maybe we’re just not built that way anymore.      I don’t know.

So, I just got my latest Slimming World  booklet, and I was like, ‘Oh, look at all the free food options!’ You know, like the extra portions of veg or the ‘healthy extra’ things. But honestly, I feel like I’m being sold a bit of a scam. It’s like, if you  don’t  use the free food, you’re basically paying full price for the same thing. A bit of a gotcha, don’t you think?      Oh, I know, I’ve been there. I tried this new ‘0 calorie syrup’ they’re pushing, and I thought, ‘Oh, this is so clever, no sugar at all, no calories!’ But then I had one, and it was like drinking a bowl of instant noodles. I’ve been trying to make more of the roasted veggies and that cauliflower cheese with the roast. I’ve got all this double peas in the freezer, and I’m not sure what to do with them. Maybe I can make a sort of pasta dish or something? I’m just being stubborn with the fried chicken with frylight. It’s better than the real thing, honestly.      I’ve been using the spice mix to make things more interesting. It’s like a game of trial and error, but I think I’ve got the hang of it. Oh, and I’ve been using Siri to set reminders for my exercise targets.

So, I was just thinking about our holiday plans for next year. I know it's still a bit early, but I've been trying to imagine where we could go. Maybe somewhere a bit different from the usual? I mean, we've been to the coast a few times, and I think it's time we tried something more...  exotic ?      Exotic? You mean like Thailand or something? I thought we were just going to do a short break in France or maybe even a trip to Cornwall. You haven't been to Cornwall in ages, you know.      I know, I know. But I've been reading this book about a place called Oman, and it's got these amazing deserts and mountains. I’ve never been to the Middle East, and I thought it might be a nice change of scenery.
