I guess it’s not a bad idea, but I’m not sure about the politics of the place. I mean, I know it’s a lot more stable than some other countries, but I still worry about the safety. I don’t want to take the kids to somewhere where there’s a lot of unrest or something.      I get that, but the country is pretty safe overall. I did some research, and it’s not like the Middle East. It’s more like a middle ground. And also, we could always plan a couple of days in the city and then head out into the desert. You know, it doesn’t have to be all or nothing.      Fair enough. Maybe I should look into some more details.

Well, I’ve just got a postcard from the Highlands. Beautiful place, really. They’ve got a little café there with some really good local cheese and whisky. I can’t wait to try it myself, but I’m not sure if I’ll have the chance before the next holiday.      That sounds lovely, but I’m still not sure about the holiday plans. I’ve been thinking about a trip to the Lake District. The kids have been asking for it, and it’s been a while since we did anything like that.      The Lake District is a good idea. It’s not too far, and you can do a bit of hiking. But I’ve been thinking about something else too. My son’s birthday is coming up, and I’m trying to work out how to make it special.      Oh, your son’s birthday is coming up? That’s right, isn’t it? You need to do something for him. He’s been working long hours lately, and I think he’d appreciate a bit of a break.      I know, and I’ve been thinking about taking him to that music festival in Manchester. He’s always loved the live music scene. But there’s something else I’ve been meaning to bring up.      What’s that?      I was thinking about the Scottish independence issue. It’s been making quite a stir lately. I understand the arguments on both sides, but I still think Scotland is better off as part of the UK. It’s a bit of a sensitive topic, though—especially with the younger generation.      I agree with you, to an extent. I think people are more divided than ever. My cousin’s daughter voted for independence, and she’s really passionate about it. It’s quite an emotional subject.      Definitely. I just hope there’s some kind of resolution soon. But back to the original topic—birthday arrangements. Are you free next weekend? I was thinking of having a small gathering at my place.      I’m free, but I’d need to check with my wife. She’s been looking forward to a weekend away. Maybe we could do something together?      That’s fine. I’ll let you know once I get the final details. I just need to make sure the food is good, and the atmosphere is relaxed.      Sounds like a plan. I’ll let you know my availability by the end of the week.

I was just thinking about the chair we saw in the newspaper—those Syrian refugees in the camp, you know, the one with the broken legs.      Oh, the one with the red chair? I drew that on my page. I think it was a very old chair, like from the museum.      Yeah, that one. I drew a chair too, but I put a smiley face on it. I thought maybe they’d feel better if it had a smile.      That’s sweet, isn’t it? I mean, we can’t always fix the problems, but even little things like drawing a chair can help.      But why do they need a chair? I mean, doesn’t everyone have a chair?      Well, not everyone. In some places, especially where there’s been a lot of fighting, things like chairs can be really scarce. They don’t always have sturdy furniture, or sometimes they have to reuse things.      But isn’t that just because they’re in a refugee camp? I mean, isn’t it supposed to be better than being in a war?      It’s not easy, no. There’s a lot more to it than just having a chair. But still, even small things can make a difference. Like, when we donate school supplies, or when we teach kids how to draw.      I drew a school bus too. I think the girls in the refugee camp can go to school. I read it in the paper.      That’s right! The UN is helping set up schools. It’s important for kids to learn, even if they have to leave their homes.      I think I’ll draw a chair for them too. Maybe a yellow one. I like yellow.      That’s a lovely idea. You know, I once taught a class where we made chairs out of cardboard. It was a project about design. Maybe something like that could help in the camp too.      Can we make chairs at school? I can help!      You might have to wait a bit. But I’ll talk to the principal. It’s a great idea—using creativity to make a difference.      I’ll bring my crayons.      That’s the spirit. Let’s get started on this project. And maybe, one day, we can even bring one of those yellow chairs to the camp.      Yeah, let’s make it happen!      I can’t wait.      Me neither. Let’s get drawing.

So, I was just thinking about how things have changed since we first met. You remember when we were both just starting out as lecturers, and we used to meet up every weekend to swap stories about teaching and our friends? It feels like it was just yesterday.      Oh, I remember that well! I think we were both so full of energy back then. We'd talk for hours about everything—teaching, our courses, even the mess we'd get into with our friends. It was such a different time. We didn't have the same pressure now, did we?      Yeah, I guess things have changed a bit. I mean, we’re both in our late thirties now, and the lectures are more intense than ever. Plus, we’ve both got more responsibilities—like the kids, the house, and all that. But somehow, we still find time to catch up.      Exactly. It’s been a while since we last talked about our friends, though. I was just thinking about how many of them have had babies over the last few years. It’s like, one after another, and now we're in the middle of it all.      You're right. It's crazy how fast time has gone. I was just at a coffee meet-up the other week with Sarah and Tom, and they had this adorable baby, Lily. She's nearly two now, and already she's got her own personality. You know, it's so rewarding, but at the same time, it's exhausting.      I know. I was at a similar gathering with Mark and Lisa the other day. They told me their baby, Ethan, is starting to make noises like he's trying to talk. It’s so cute, but honestly, I'm trying to keep up with my own life. I’m still trying to get my research done, and I've got that upcoming conference to prepare for.      I feel you. I’m trying to balance it all too. But you know, talking to you about it makes it easier. It’s like, we’re not alone in this. Even though we’re both lecturers, and we're used to being busy, it’s the friends and family that keep us grounded.      Definitely. I think that's why we've stayed close for so long—because we understand each other’s lives. And even with all the babies and the responsibilities, we still find a way to make time for each other.

So, I was telling my sister about that time I got stopped by a policeman on holiday in the Lake District—just after I’d run into a sheep. I was so flustered, I dropped my camera, and then the sheep ran off with my sandwich.      Oh no, that’s bad. Did you actually get stopped? Or did the sheep just take off?      I got stopped. The policeman was very friendly, actually. He said, “You look like you’ve had a bit of a rough day.” I told him about the sheep, and he just laughed. Said he’d had the same thing happen to him when he was a kid.      That’s classic. I remember my uncle once told me about how he used to chase cows in the countryside and end up with a cow’s udder in his hand. He said it was the most humiliating thing he’d ever done.      That’s a good one. I think I’d rather be chased by a cow than a sheep. Although, I’ve got to say, the sheep in Norfolk are  very  cheeky. Last week, I was walking along the coast path and one of them just walked up to me and started nibbling my boot.      Oh, I’ve heard about those. My cousin once tried to take a photo of a sheep and the thing just stared at the camera for five minutes. Spooked the hell out of her.      That’s funny. I’d say it’s a form of superstition—like, if you make eye contact with a sheep, it’s bad luck. Or at least, it’s definitely bad for your camera.      Maybe that’s why they’re called "sheep"—because they’re always watching. I’ve always thought that.      I’m not sure if it’s superstition or just general paranoia. I mean, you can’t trust a sheep in the countryside. They’re like the local police.      Well, if they’re like the local police, maybe they’re not evil. Maybe they’re just doing their job. I mean, if you’re a sheep, you have to look out for the farmer, right?      Exactly. But if you’re a sheep and you get too close to a lecturer, you might end up with a sandwich in your mouth and a lecture on the dangers of wandering off the path.      That’s the kind of thing that makes a good story.

Dad, you remember that phone you bought last year? I think it’s still on the kitchen table. You said it was the best one ever, but now I've got this new phone and it's got all these fancy apps.      Yeah, I remember that. I thought it was a miracle, but I reckon it just broke down on me after a week. I should've listened to you, lass. You always said it was too complicated.      Well, I never said it was easy, but at least I can use it without getting lost in the settings. You know, I’ve been thinking about getting a van for moving things. I’m gonna be living with my new boyfriend’s family in Dorset, and I need to get all my stuff there.      Oh, a van! That sounds like a good idea. I used to have a van in my youth. I even used to take people on fishing trips. You know, I still remember the time I caught a cod bigger than my head.      That’s one to tell the grandkids. But seriously, I’ve been looking at van hire places. I saw an ad for one that costs about £50 a day. I was thinking, maybe I could get it for the weekend and move everything in one go.      Sounds like a plan. But you’ll need to be careful. I once rented a van and it had a flat tire halfway through the journey. Just had to push it to the nearest garage. Still, it was worth it because I got there in time for the Great Dorset Steam Fair.      Oh, I’ve been looking forward to that! I think I’ll take the van to the fair. I heard there are some amazing antiques there. And maybe I can even meet some of the family. I’ve got a cousin who lives there, and I haven’t seen them in ages.      That’s a good idea. You’ll have to keep an eye out for the lottery numbers too. I heard you can get a ticket at the fair. Maybe you’ll win something and then you won’t need that van after all.      Don’t get your hopes up, Dad. But if I do win, I’ll make sure to buy you a new phone. You’ve been using that old one for years now.

So, I just got an email from the local council about the library. They’re saying it’s under threat of demolition because they want to redevelop the area. It’s ridiculous. I mean, how can they even consider tearing down a library that’s been a cornerstone of the community for decades?      Yeah, I know. I read about it in the paper this morning. It’s really sad. I remember when I was a kid, the library was my second home. My mum used to take me there every Saturday. We’d sit in the reading room, and I’d get lost in books for hours.      I remember that. I used to go there too, even though I was older. The older kids would hang out in the corner, and the librarians would just let us be. It was like a safe space. I think the council is just trying to make it look like they’re modernizing, but honestly, it’s just a way to make money off the land. They’re planning to build some shopping centre or something.      That’s what I was thinking. They’ve got this new policy about "urban regeneration" that’s been going on for years. It’s all about making everything look fresh and new, but it’s just a way to push out the old buildings. I can’t believe they’re even considering demolishing the library. It’s not like the building is in bad shape.      It’s not. The building’s been renovated a few times, and it still looks pretty good. But maybe they think it’s outdated? I mean, the council’s always talking about how they want to bring in more people, but they don’t seem to care about preserving the identity of the area. I think the real issue is the lack of funding. They’re trying to make up for budget cuts by selling off public spaces.      Exactly. I was thinking about that earlier. When I was looking at some upholstery fabrics for the living room, I couldn’t help but think about how the library was once a place where people could just sit and read without worrying about their budget. Now, everything’s about spending and profit.      It’s so sad. I think there’s a real disconnect between the council and the community. Maybe it’s time for the locals to stand up and fight for the library.

So, I was just thinking, do you two know what I got for my birthday? It was a CD by some indie band I’ve been trying to find for years. You know, that one with the upbeat guitar riffs and the singer who sounds like he’s shouting from a rooftop. I’ve been listening to it all week, and it’s been giving me the best vibes.      That sounds like  The High Kings . I think you mentioned them a few times. You’ve been trying to track them down for ages. Did you finally get it?      Yeah, I think he did. I remember you saying you’d like to support local artists. I guess that’s what they are, right? Indie bands. I still don’t get why they’re not mainstream. They’re so good.      I know, I know. They’re not in the charts, but they’ve got heart. You know, the kind of music that makes you want to dance in the kitchen with the door closed.      I still don’t get why you’re so into that. I mean, I like music, but that kind of music is just noise to me. I prefer something with a bit more structure. You know, like the old classics. It’s got more meaning.      Oh, come on, Phil. You’re just too old for that. You used to like rock ’n’ roll, remember?      I still like rock, but it’s got to be something I can actually relate to. And I’m not talking about  any  rock. I mean  real  rock. The kind that you can listen to while you’re working. You know, something that doesn’t put you to sleep.      You’re like a man who only eats steak. You like it, but you don’t want to admit it’s not the only option.      Well, I do like the classic stuff, but I think there’s room for everyone. I mean, I got that CD for my birthday, and it’s been great. I think I might even bring it to the pub next week.      You have to, seriously. I think you’d love it. And if you don’t, I’ll just say it’s not for you.      I’ll be there, but I’m not promising anything.      That’s the spirit. Now, what about presents? You two got anything good?      I got a book from a friend.

Oh, I’ve been trying to get that bloke in the garage to fix my car for weeks now, but he keeps saying he’s got more important things to do. You know what he said the other day? “I’ve got a family to feed, not a car to fix!” I don’t know if he’s joking or if he’s just got his priorities wrong.      I can imagine that. My dad used to say the same thing. He’d always be like, “I’d rather spend my money on fish and chips than get the car sorted.” But I reckon he’s just being stubborn. I mean, I’ve got to get to school, and without the car, it’s a bit of a problem.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to get my son to help me out with the car, but he’s got his own things going on. You know, he’s busy with exams and all. I told him, “You can’t skip the car exams, or you’ll end up with a learner’s permit for life.”      That’s what I tell my mates. I’m starting to think I should just take the bus. It’s not that bad. Yeah, it’s slower, but I can read, watch a book, or even catch up on some TV. Plus, I don’t have to worry about petrol prices or insurance.      That’s a good point. I’ve been thinking about car insurance lately. You know, the rates have gone up again. I thought it might be cheaper if I had a younger driver, but then I remembered how much I paid for my own when I first got my licence. It was like a fortune.      I heard that too. My mum said she’s been looking for cheaper insurance. She reckons if she takes a basic driving course, maybe she could get a discount. I think it’s called a no-claims bonus or something like that.      That’s right. It’s all about how long you’ve been driving without making a claim. The longer you go without one, the lower your premium gets. But I still think it’s a rip-off. If I was a younger person, I’d probably be paying even more.      Maybe. But I guess it’s just part of life. I mean, you can’t really escape it.

So, I was just thinking about that talk we had about the workplace stress. You know, the one where I said I was more stressed than I’ve ever been in my life, and then I went out and bought a new suit and a brand new watch.      Yeah, and then you said you were just “organizing your thoughts.” You don’t need a watch for that.      Oh, come on, you know you were trying to impress the boss. That’s called “professional grooming,” Mink.      Okay, fair enough. But the real point is, how do we even measure stress? I mean, I’ve got my left arm in a sling because I pulled it trying to lift a box, and I’m still getting emails at 10 PM about deadlines. How do we know when we’re actually at the edge?      I mean, we can look at the symptoms. Like, the heart racing, the sleep issues, the constant anxiety. But sometimes, it’s just the way you carry yourself. You know, like, when you’re always fiddling with your collar or looking at your watch.      Exactly. And don’t even get me started on the way you use your words. You’re like a dictionary now. “Stress,” “burnout,” “overwhelmed.” It’s like you’re writing a book.      Hey, I had a degree in IT. I can’t help it if I want to be precise. Although, I did get a bit of a shock about the Irish Present. I thought you could get it at 18, but turns out you have to wait until you’re 18 and a half. What’s the deal with that?      I think it’s some kind of stupid bureaucratic nonsense. I mean, if you’re 18, you’re an adult in most countries. Why not give it to you then?      Maybe because the politicians want to keep the cash in the system a little longer. You know, like the Green Party or whatever.      You mean the ones who just passed the equality vote? That was a big deal, wasn’t it?      Yeah, it’s a huge step. I mean, even though it was already legal, it was still a big cultural shift. I think my dad still struggles with the idea.      He’s been trying to get me to talk to him about it. I mean, he’s not against it, but he just keeps saying, “It’s not like we’re all going to be running around with rainbow flags.”

So, I was just thinking about that time we drove up to the hilltop village last summer and got stuck in a traffic jam because of the weather. You remember, it was that day when it started raining so hard, and the roads were like a puddle.      Oh yes, I remember that. I was so glad we had the car with the heated seats. I swear, if I had been wearing a top, I’d have been shivering like a leaf.      You were shivering like a leaf? I thought you were just being dramatic. I was stuck in the car with you and my dad, and you kept saying, “It’s freezing! I wish we were in the UK!”      Oh, come on, I was just making a point. It was  so  cold that day. I mean, it was early in the morning, and the sun hadn’t even come out yet.      I still can’t get over how cold it was up there. I’ve been to some of the most remote places in England, and that was probably one of the coldest.      You know, I actually think the reason it was so cold was because of the weather patterns. It was that time of year when the air pressure was low and everything was just damp and chilly.      Wait, what does that even mean? I mean, I know about the weather, but I don’t really understand the science behind it.      Yeah, it’s all about the atmospheric pressure. When it’s low, it means the air is rising, which causes clouds and rain. It’s like the air is being pushed up, and that makes the temperature drop.      Exactly. And it also affects the wind. If the pressure is low, you can get strong winds, which make it feel even colder.      I guess that’s why we always have such drastic weather changes in the North. You can have a sunny day, and then it’s overcast and freezing within an hour.      I think I’m going to start calling that "the Bolton weather." It’s like it’s planning to mess with us.      Oh, you’re on. I’ve already started doing that. I told my mates it’s "Bolton weather" when it goes from sunny to stormy in five minutes.      I think I’ll have to start doing that too. It’s just the way we’ve grown up here.

So, I just read this article about the new lab-grown meat thing. You know, the 'shmeat' they're talking about. I’m like,  this is it , right? No more cows, no more ethical issues. No more animal cruelty. It's like the future of food.       laughs  Yeah, I read that too. It's so weird, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve been vegetarian for a while, but I still find it hard to wrap my head around the idea of eating something that’s not animal-based. But if it’s grown in a lab... like, is it even  meat ?      That's the thing, isn’t it? It still has all the proteins and nutrients of regular meat, just without the ethical baggage. And honestly, I think it’s going to be a game-changer for the environment too. Less land use, less water, less carbon footprint.      Exactly. And I mean, I’m not even sure I’m fully vegan anymore. I take some vitamin tablets, like B12, because I know my body needs it. I don’t want to be missing out on nutrients just because I’m trying to be ‘pure’ about it.      Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that too. I’m not a strict vegan, but I do try to minimize my impact. It’s not just about the animal cruelty, it’s about the whole ecosystem. And I mean, even if someone is vegetarian, they still have to eat something—so maybe lab-grown meat is the way forward.      I think the key is transparency. Like, if you’re eating something that’s made in a lab, you should know what you’re putting in your body. It’s not like you’re eating a cow that’s been raised in a factory farm. It’s more controlled, more ethical.      I guess. But I still feel like there’s a lot of hype around it. Like, everyone’s talking about it, but how long until it becomes mainstream? And how do you even get it in the shops? I mean, I’m a pharmacy dispenser, so I’m used to dealing with supplements and medications, but this is a bit different.      Yeah, I can imagine. It’s going to take time. But I think the younger generation is more open to it. Like, when I was younger, you couldn’t even get vegan options in most places.

So, I just got this massive delivery of stuff from internet shopping, and it's all over the house. I can't even find my own clothes anymore.      You’re not the only one, mate. Christmas. Yeah, go on, get your own phone. It’s not like you’re going to be in the holiday season without one.      Yeah, and you’ll be missing out on all the Christmas movies. I mean, it’s not like you can binge-watch  Home Alone  without a proper screen.      I think I’m going to have to get a new phone just so I can watch  Home Alone  properly.      That’s the spirit, mate. We’re all just here for the movies, the shopping, and the occasional game.

So, I just got back from my holiday in Spain, and I have to say, it was absolutely  mad . That sounds like a breakfast, not a night out! But seriously, I’d love to go. I’ve been thinking about visiting somewhere new this year. Maybe the Canary Islands? I went to Tenerife last year, and it was just so different from anywhere else I’ve been. Yeah, he’s got a point. But hey, you’re worth the risk. Now, let’s just hope the massage therapist doesn’t turn out to be a lecturer in disguise.      I’d be fine with that.

You know, I’ve been thinking about this migrant crisis in Calais. It's been on the news a lot lately, and I can't help but feel a bit helpless. I mean, how can we just ignore it? Well, I’ve been thinking about redecorating the bathroom. It’s been a bit of a mess since I got the new shower unit installed. I’m not sure I like the modern look, though. It feels too stark. So, I was telling my wife earlier about the time I tried to cook curry and ended up burning the house down. You know, that one time when I thought I was being clever with the spices...      Yeah, you told us that story. You accidentally set the kitchen on fire with the curry sauce and had to call the fire brigade. It was a real showstopper. I wouldn’t even try that. I think I’d rather drink something. You know, like that terrible history science book you told us about. The one with the terrible experiments?      Yeah, that one. I tried to read it once and it made me feel like I was in a nightmare. It was so dull, I could barely stay awake. I think I ended up falling asleep in the middle of it.      That’s not true! You were so into it! You were the one who said it was the best book you’d ever read.      Okay, maybe I was a bit into it at first. He’s got so much energy, he might actually get through it.

So, lass, what’s the talk about this year? I’ve been thinking about Halloween and how it’s changed since I was a kid. I remember one year I dressed up as a chicken and ran around the street shouting “Baaaack! Baaaack!” and it made the whole village laugh. My dad was so embarrassed.      That sounds like you. So, I just got a ticket for parking outside the fair, and it’s like,  what even is this?  I’m not even sure if it’s a valid disabled parking spot. Yeah, it’s like they’re just saying, “We care, but we can’t afford to.” But how are we supposed to live like this? I mean, I’ve got a car, but I can’t afford to fix it. You know, I’ve been thinking about starting an allotment. It’s got to be the best way to get back to nature, isn’t it?      Absolutely. I’ve been meaning to get one myself. It’s a bit of a journey, but I think it’s worth the effort.      I’m ready to jump in. Maybe we could even help each other out. You’ve got more experience, after all.      I’d be happy to help. It’s about time I gave gardening a real go.

So, I was just thinking, have you ever had that moment where you’re like, “I’m gonna be friends with this person forever,” and then a few months later, you’re like, “Wait, who even are they?”      Oh, I know exactly what you mean. Yeah, I’ll text you back.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to play  Call of Duty  together last week? I’m telling you, it was chaos.      Oh, I remember—  you   were the one trying to rush through the level like it was a race, and I was just trying to actually survive.      Yeah, that was a disaster. I swear, you thought you were in a movie, not a multiplayer game.      You were like a kid with a toy gun. I swear, you were more excited about the gun than the game itself.      Yeah, I mean, I was just trying to be the hero, you know? But then you screamed “Ow, watch out!” and I got shot.      Oh no, the hero has fallen!      And I was just sitting there watching, like, “This is going to be a long one.”      You were like a proud parent watching your kid get into a fight.      I don’t know, I think it was just a bad day. I was stressed about exams and just wanted something to take my mind off it.      Yeah, I get that. I was like that last week too. I tried to play  Fortnite  with my mates, and it ended up being like a  Sims  game because we were all just arguing about what to build.      I remember that. And it’s better than trying to do anything else. I mean, I tried to cook last week, and it ended up being like a science experiment.      I can only imagine. Yeah, and sometimes it’s better than the stories we tell in real life.      That’s one way to look at it.

Oh, I remember when we first met. You were just this wide-eyed girl with a camera and a heart full of dreams, and I thought, “Here comes someone who’ll probably disappear in a year.”      You were the one who told me I should stop taking photos of the same tree every day and actually go out and meet people. You were a bit of a drama queen back then, weren’t you?      Oh, I was! I used to get so worked up about the weather. You know, you were the one who dragged me to that film festival in Edinburgh. I was so nervous, and you were like, “You’ll be fine, just act like you belong here.” And then, when I got on stage and forgot my lines, you were in the front row cheering so loud, the whole audience looked at you.      Yeah, and don’t forget, you were the one who told me, “You don’t have to be perfect, just be real.” That’s what got me through my darkest days. You’ve always had a way with words, even when you didn’t mean to.      I never thought I’d be the one to help you. I mean, you were the one who always knew how to fix things. You were the one who told me I needed to take up photography, even when I didn’t think I was good enough.      And you were the one who kept me grounded. I don’t know what I’d do without you. You’ve always been like that – full of energy and always trying to make the best of things.      I think we’ve both grown a lot since then. I still get nervous sometimes, but I don’t let it stop me. And you? You’ve still got that same fire, even though you’ve stopped chasing storms.      You’re not wrong. And I think that’s what makes us work – we balance each other out. You’re the spark, and I’m the flame.

So, I just got back from this weekend trip to the spa. I know it's not exactly the first thing you'd think of when you're hanging out with friends, but it was actually pretty chill. So, I was just telling my mum about the washing machine—the one we got last week. She’s like, “Oh, you’ve got a washing machine now? I thought you were still using that old thing from your flat in Sunderland!”      Yeah, I can imagine. You always told me how you used to have to do all the washing by hand in that tiny flat. It was so cold in the winter, and I’d be like, “I’m not doing this again.” But now, with the washing machine, I can just chuck everything in, press a button, and forget about it.      I know, it’s amazing how much simpler it’s made life. Although, I still can’t help but feel like I’m wasting water. But honestly, it’s just part of modern life. It’s one of those things that’s so taken for granted now. Speaking of which, have you seen the new film  Everything Everywhere All At Once ? It was like a rollercoaster of emotions. I think the whole thing was just a way to talk about family and identity, right?      Exactly! And the food they served in the film, it was like a whole new world of cuisine. I’ve been trying to recreate some of those dishes. You know, the chicken with the peanut sauce—wild, but delicious.      I’ve been into that too. I tried making it last week, and it turned out okay. Although, I think I used too much soy sauce. My flatmate said it was like “a punch in the gut.”

So, I heard you mentioned the VW scandal last week, Sarah. I was just reading about it in  The Guardian —it's absolutely ridiculous how they managed to get away with it for so long. That’s the thing, isn’t it? I mean, the whole thing’s a bit of a scam. Everyone knew, but no one really did anything about it. It’s like the system made it possible. I suppose that’s part of the problem. There’s a huge amount of pressure to perform, especially when you’re in a high-stakes job like that. It’s not just about individuals—it’s the system that enables it. I’ve always thought that way.      I can’t help but think about how things are changing. I’ve been thinking, luv. I don’t know how we’re gonna get through this next bit. The pension’s not enough, and I can’t see how we’re going to manage with the housing developments all over the place. I heard from the postman yesterday, he said the council’s even talking about changing the rules for B&Bs. Now they’re making it harder for people like us to keep our little places running. I was planning on staying in one of those for a bit, but now I don’t know.      Yeah, and I’ve been thinking about computers too. I’ve got this old laptop that’s been sitting in the corner gathering dust. I tried to use it last week, and it just kept crashing. I don’t know how to fix it, and I don’t know anyone who can help me. They’re all about the gadgets, but I’m just waiting for them to come back from school and tell me about the latest game or app. I’ve got a feeling it’s going to be a long time before I catch up.      I suppose we just have to keep going. If we can’t stay in our own homes, maybe we can find a place to stay in a B&B.

So, I just saw this video online about evolution and human biology. It was like, explaining how humans evolved from apes and all that. It was pretty interesting, but I still can’t wrap my head around how we got from monkeys to people in such a short time.      Yeah, I saw that too. I mean, it’s one thing to know that we share a common ancestor with apes, but the whole idea that we evolved so fast is confusing. I remember my teacher saying something about natural selection, but I don’t think I got it.      Oh, I think it’s like, the more complex organisms are, the longer it takes to evolve, right? But humans are kind of unique because of our intelligence. So maybe that’s why we evolved faster?      You know, I think it’s not really about how fast we evolved, but about how much we changed. Like, we didn’t suddenly jump from apes to humans in a week. It was a gradual process that took millions of years. But the video made it sound like it was like a few thousand years, which is way too short.      Right, that’s what I was thinking. But then, I’ve also heard people talk about how society is changing so fast now. Like, with the internet and everything, people are getting more educated, more connected, and more aware of issues like racism and sexism. Is that kind of like evolution in a way?      That’s a funny way to put it. Like, society is evolving? It’s a bit of a stretch, but I guess you could say that. I mean, people are more open-minded now than they were, like, 20 years ago. I think that’s the kind of evolution we’re seeing.      Yeah, but I don’t think it’s just society. I think it’s also how we handle issues like feminism and equality. Like, more people are speaking up about gender issues now. I remember hearing about a campaign where people used social media to protest against sexism in schools. That was really powerful.      And that’s probably why people are talking about it more now. The internet gives everyone a voice. It’s like, no one can ignore the conversation anymore. I mean, it’s wild how something can go viral and change people’s opinions so quickly.      Exactly.

I was just telling Fran about that time I had an infection that took weeks to clear up. I thought I was just coming down with a cold, but it turned out to be a nasty bacterial infection. I had to go to the doctor and get some tablets.      I know the feeling. I had one of those infections last year that just wouldn’t go away. I went to the doctor, and they said it was something called  Strep  or  Staph . I had to take antibiotics for a month.      I had one of those too, love. I got it from a small cut on my hand. It turned into a big red thing with a head on it. I had to go to the hospital and get it drained. It was terrible.      I remember when I was younger, I used to get those infections all the time. When I was a lorry driver, I didn’t take care of myself. One time, I had a boil on my back, and it was so bad I couldn’t even sit down.      I think we’re all a bit too old for that sort of thing. I’ve started taking some vitamins and doing some acupuncture. I read somewhere that it helps with the immune system.      I’ve tried acupuncture once. It was weird, but I felt a bit better. I think it helps with the stress too. I’ve been feeling so much better since I started seeing that acupuncturist.      I used to have a friend who always said she could cure everything with a teaspoon of honey and a bit of rest. Maybe there’s something in that.      I used to say that too. "Just rest and take some tablets," I’d tell the kids. But I think I was just trying to avoid going to the doctor.      I can’t say I’ve ever avoided the doctor. I’ve got an appointment next week for my annual check-up. I’m a bit nervous, but I think it’s good to go.      I think I’m going to go too. I need to make sure I’m not getting any of those infections again. I’ve been feeling a bit off lately.      I’ve been meaning to go, but I’m always too busy. I like to stay out of the hospital unless it’s absolutely necessary.      Same here.

You know, the people who lived in the Americas a long time ago didn't always have the same rights as everyone else. Some people were treated very badly because of the color of their skin.      Was it like they were taken away from their homes?      Yes, some people were taken from their homes in Africa and forced to come to the Americas. They were made to work very hard on farms and in big houses, and they weren't paid for their work. It was a terrible thing.      Why did they do that?      It was because some people thought that people of a different color were less important. They believed that they could own other people, which is something that is wrong and has been proven wrong over and over again. That is what we call slavery.      That sounds so mean. Why wouldn't they just let them go?      It was a very old system, and it took a long time for people to realize that it was wrong. It was a very dark part of history, and it caused a lot of pain and suffering. People fought very hard to end it, and that’s why we now have laws that protect everyone, no matter what color their skin is.      So it was like a big mistake that people had to fix?      Yes, exactly. And because of that, we remember it and teach our children about the importance of fairness and respect for everyone. It’s part of why we are all learning about different cultures and histories now.      Do you think people still do that now?      No, not in the same way. But there are still things we need to learn about being fair and kind to everyone. It’s a journey, and we’re all on it together.      I think it’s important to remember what happened so we don’t let it happen again.      That’s exactly right. And that’s why we talk about it, and why we learn from the past so we can build a better future. Do you want to read a book about it tomorrow?      Yes! I like books. Can we read one about the people who fought to end slavery?      I think that’s a great idea. Let’s make it part of our bedtime story tonight. We can learn something new together.      I like that. I think I’ll remember this conversation forever.

So, I was watching that new drama on the box last night,  The Halting Point —you know, the one with that actor from  Sherlock ? It’s a bit slow, but the way they built the plot up, it’s got me hooked. I mean, I’ve only seen two episodes, but I was like, “This is gonna be something.”      Yeah, I saw the trailer. It’s got that kind of gritty, real-life feel, doesn’t it? But I’ve got to say, the slow burn is killing me. I’m like, “Where’s the action?” But I’ll give it a go. I’ve got that one episode on my list to catch up on.      I didn’t even know it was on. I’ve been so busy with work, and my flatmate’s been pestering me about this new series she’s obsessed with. I think it’s called  The Midnight Spectator . It’s got a bunch of weird, surreal scenes, like, I don’t even know what’s going on half the time. But she says it’s  so  good.      You know, I was just thinking about that. My nephew mentioned it to me the other day and said it’s  exactly  the kind of show he used to watch when he was a kid. He said it’s like that mix of horror and comedy, but with a twist. Honestly, I think he just wants to talk about it because he can’t stop watching it.      You know, I’ve never been a fan of all that TV drama. I used to watch telly when I was working in catering, you know—that kind of old-school stuff.  Coronation Street ,  EastEnders . I mean, they’re not exactly  art , but they passed the time. These modern shows, they’re all about holding your hand and telling you what’s going to happen.      You’re telling me! I used to watch  Doctor Who  with my mum when I was a kid, and it was something else. Now, it’s all about the gothic vibes and deep life lessons. I mean, I appreciated it, but it’s not the same.      Yeah, but I think the younger generation has a different taste. I mean, my niece watches all this stuff, and she’s like, “This is where storytelling is at.” I think it’s just a reflection of how we all consume media now.

So, I was just telling the kids about George Stephenson—the man who built the first proper steam engine, you know. I’m trying to make it interesting for them, but they’re more into Harry Potter.      Yeah, I was just telling my sister about the Hogwarts Express. She thinks it’s real!      I think it’s real! I mean, I saw a train with a dragon on it once!      Didn’t you just get off the school bus? You’re still in primary school! But I can see why you’d think that—those trains do have some pretty cool designs.      I just think the steam engine would be way cooler than a magical train. I mean, imagine if you could ride a real steam train!      Exactly! George Stephenson was a genius. He built the Rocket, which was the first steam locomotive to win the Rainhill Trials in 1829. It was super fast for its time.      What’s a Rainhill Trials?      It was a competition to find the best steam engine for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway. There were a bunch of engineers trying out their designs, and the Rocket won because it was faster and more efficient.      So he was like a racing car driver, but with steam engines?      In a way, yes! He was one of the first people to really make steam power useful for transportation. Before that, people were using horses or carts.      So, was it dangerous?      Oh, definitely. Steam engines can be dangerous if they’re not handled properly. There were a lot of accidents back then, but Stephenson was really careful. He even designed the first safety valves to prevent explosions.      So he was like a superhero?      Sort of. He was a real pioneer. I think it’s amazing how he changed the world with his inventions.      I want to be an engineer when I grow up.      That’s great! You’ll have a better chance than me—my job is much less exciting.      Yeah, you’re just a teacher. We’re the future!      I’m the one who’s got the kids interested in science. That’s not exactly unexciting.      Yeah, but you still have to unload the dishwasher.      Ah, there you go. Back to the real world.      I can help!      Alright, let’s get this done. Next, we can talk about the next big invention—maybe something even cooler than a steam engine.

So, I just got a message from my mate on Words With Friends — he’s gone and used the word “malarkey” as his move, and I’m like, “What even is that?!”      Oh, he’s been watching too many old British TV shows. “Malarkey” is basically his way of saying “bullshit.” I’ve seen him use it in the context of a quiz show, like, “That was some malarkey.”      Yeah, but he’s not wrong. I’ve heard it used in the UK, too. Though I think it’s more common in the Midlands or up North. You know, like, “That’s all malarkey” — meaning nonsense.      I think he just thought it was an exotic word. And now he’s been getting called out for it. He’s got a message saying, “Malarkey isn’t a word — it’s slang.”      That’s what I told him. But he’s not taking it lightly. He’s written back saying, “I’m from Manchester, and I’ve used it my whole life. It’s not slang, it’s a word.”      Mate, you can’t argue with a Manc. You just have to accept that some of their words are just… different. You know what I mean?      Yeah, I’ve heard that one. I think it’s from the old days when people used to talk about “malarkey” as a word for nonsense, like in the army or something.      Exactly! And I think it’s starting to creep into the mainstream. I saw it used in a blog post the other day.      Speaking of words — did you hear about the supper club we’re going to? It’s at this tiny café in Shoreditch. The owner’s a friend of mine, and she’s got this crazy menu.      Oh, I know her! She’s the café owner down the road. She told me she’s been experimenting with fusion dishes — like, Korean tacos and something with truffle.      Sounds like a night out. I’ve been thinking of trying to move up from barista to something more stable. Maybe I could start working in a restaurant or café?      You should! I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve got my degree, but I’m stuck in a dead-end job. Maybe I can start a food blog or something.      That’s a good idea. You could even write about supper clubs, or how to cook things properly.

So, what’s the deal with the new café down by the library? I’ve been meaning to try it, but I’m not sure if it’s worth the walk.      Oh, it’s great! The food’s pretty good—especially the fish and chips. It’s actually pretty decent for a place that’s only been around a few months.      I love fish and chips. I used to go to one in Aylesbury when I was younger. But, of course, those places are getting fewer and fewer these days. It’s so rare to find someone who knows how to cook it properly.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I think the key is the batter—it has to be light and crispy, not that thick, heavy mess that some places serve. I’ve been trying to find a good one for a while now.      I’m always on the lookout for a good meal. It’s one of the few things I still enjoy doing. Though I have to say, I’ve been so busy with work lately that I’ve barely had time to cook anything.      I can relate. I’m often just grabbing a sandwich or something on the go. Although, I’ve been trying to get back into cooking. I even signed up for a few online classes. It’s kind of a hobby now.      Oh, really? What are you cooking?      Beginners stuff—like soups, salads, and even some simple pasta dishes. I’m not the best, but it’s fun to experiment. I think cooking is a good way to unwind.      I used to do that too. When I was younger, I’d make proper meals for my kids. Now, they’re older and have their own tastes. I don’t cook much these days, but I miss the routine.      Kids do change a lot. I remember when mine were little, I’d make them everything. Now they’re more into fast food and takeaways. But I still try to cook for them when I can—it makes me feel like I’m still part of their lives.      It’s a big part of being a parent, isn’t it? Even if you’re not cooking, just being there and sharing a meal can be so meaningful.      Definitely. I think that’s why I still try to make time for it, even if it’s just a quick dish.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time when we were in university and we got lost trying to find the library? I swear we ended up in the art faculty by accident.      Oh, you were  so  excited about the art department. You kept saying it was the 'most creative place on campus'. But then you got a bit nervous when you saw all those abstract sculptures.      Yeah, I said to myself, “This is where the real magic happens!” But then the professor came up and asked me to critique a piece, and I just froze.      I remember that. You were so nervous you couldn’t even look at the sculpture. I had to rescue you.      Yeah, and then I ended up writing a five-page essay about it the next day.      That was one of the best days of your life, wasn’t it?      Absolutely. Though I still don’t know what that piece was even supposed to represent.      That’s the thing about art. It’s all about interpretation.      Speaking of interpretation, have you seen the new shop in Preston? I went in yesterday and they had these amazing baby blankets.      Oh, really? I was just thinking about buying a new blanket for my mum. She’s been having trouble with the cold lately.      I hear you. I’m thinking about getting a new one for my place too. Maybe some kind of wool one.      Yeah, I found one that’s super warm and it’s got a little pattern on it. It’s like a modern version of the ones my gran used to have.      That sounds nice. I’ll have to check it out. Do you think they have them in different sizes?      They do. I think they even have ones for babies. But I’m more of a grown-up blanket person.      You’re not getting any younger, Mike. You need to invest in some baby blankets.      Oh, I’ve got a few in the car already. I bought them at the last shop we went to.      I can’t wait to see them. I think I need to get one for my mum, and maybe one for my baby sister when she comes.      That’s sweet. I think that’s what makes life special – small things like that.      Yeah. It’s funny how the things you buy in a shop can change your life.

So, I just got back from that game night with my mates, and it was  so  intense. I mean, I’m not even that good at these games, but we were playing this new internet game—like, the one where you’re a scientist trying to save the world from a virus. It’s like  The Sims  but with lab coats and panic buttons.      Sounds like one of those social experiments where you're stuck with a group of strangers. I tried one once, and I ended up teaming up with someone who kept trying to build a bunker instead of a vaccine. It made me question my entire life choices.      Yeah, I remember that. The one where you could spend hours building a simulation and then realize the game had a glitch that made everyone forget how to use the defibrillator. It was unreal. I still haven’t recovered from that.      Exactly! It was so stressful, but in a fun way. I think I got more out of it than a night out. Plus, I ended up learning about some actual psychology stuff—like how group dynamics affect decision-making. It was weird, but kinda cool.      I remember reading about something like that. I think it's called  social psychology  or  cognitive bias . It's all about how people’s moods and environments can influence their choices. Like, if you're in a bad mood, you're more likely to make a rush decision, right?      Or if you're stressed, you might not even notice the obvious. I've seen people do that at work. They’re so focused on the problem that they miss the solution right in front of them.      Yeah, I guess that's kind of what happened in the game. We were all so caught up in trying to save the world that we didn’t realize the virus was actually a hoax. I mean, it was a game, but it felt real for a while. It’s weird how our moods and environments can affect how we process things.      You’re not the first person to say that. I remember reading about how stress can make people more susceptible to anxiety or even depression. It’s interesting, really. I think it’s one of the reasons why people need to take breaks, like Christmas or holidays. To reset their mind and mood.      And it’s not just about holidays.

So, I was just telling the boys about the different metals and fabrics we can find in Minecraft, and they were all so excited. It’s like they’ve discovered a whole new world!      Yeah! I found this really cool item called “Gold Ingot” and I used it to make a really fancy sword! But I had to fight a bunch of zombies to get it.      I tried to make a shirt with fabric, but it was so hard to get the right material. I think I used some wool, but it looked really plain.      That’s normal for a beginner. My son, Tom, started with just wool and basic tools, and now he’s making all sorts of fancy armor and weapons. It’s amazing how quickly they pick it up.      I think I’ve even invented a new legend in the game. I found a hidden temple, and there’s this strange creature that only appears at night. I named it the “Shadow Warden” and it’s really scary!      That sounds like something out of a storybook! I made up a legend too. I think there’s a magical flower that grows in the desert and gives you superpowers if you drink its nectar. It’s not real, but I like to imagine it.      That sounds like a great story! I read once about a child who invented a legend about a rainbow that leads to a hidden treasure. It helped her feel more curious and creative.      I wonder if the gold and the fabrics we found in the game are really valuable. Maybe they could be used to build something special.      That’s a good point. In Minecraft, every material has its own purpose. Gold is used for making tools and jewelry, while wool is used for clothing and blankets. You can even use it to make carpets and banners.      I heard that some people take vitamins to be healthier. Is that like a legend too?      Not exactly, but it’s a kind of real legend in the real world. Vitamins are important for our bodies, just like different materials are important in Minecraft. You need the right ones to stay healthy and strong.      So, like, we need to take vitamins to make our characters stronger in the game too?      Not exactly, but the idea is similar. In the real world, we take vitamins to help our bodies function properly, just like we use different materials in the game to build and create.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to play  The Smiths  at the gig in Hebden Bridge? I think we sounded like a bunch of confused ducks with a guitar.      Oh, you were terrible. I remember you tripping over the cord and almost knocking over the amp. You were so focused on not looking like a complete idiot that you forgot to actually play the song.      Yeah, it was a disaster. But I still love that band. I mean,  The Smiths —they’re like the sound of a rainy day in Doncaster. You know, the kind of day where you just want to curl up with a guitar and a mug of tea.      I get it. There’s something about playing music that just feels like home. Though I’ve been thinking—do you ever wonder if all those bands we used to listen to, like the ones we used to follow in school, are still around? I mean, some of them have been around for decades.      Yeah, it’s weird, isn’t it? You think you know a band, and then you find out they’re gone—or worse, they’ve gone off the rails. I heard about some of them getting into all sorts of trouble. You know, paedophiles and stuff. It’s like, how could they ever be the same?      Yeah, it’s a real shame. Music’s supposed to be about expression, about connection. But when people misuse that… it’s just heartbreaking. I mean, I’ve seen some of those stories online. It’s not just about the music anymore, is it?      No, it’s not. It’s like the whole thing gets tainted. I just hope that the music we’re making now stays pure. You know, the real kind of music. Not the kind that’s all about money or fame or stuff like that.      Well, I think we’re doing it right. We’re just playing for the love of it. That’s what it’s always been about, isn’t it? Yeah, go out there and make some noise. Just like we did at that gig in Hebden Bridge.      Yeah, and we’ll be playing again soon. Maybe even with a proper setup. I’m thinking of getting a new guitar. Something that’s got a bit more sound.      Sounds like a plan. I’ll chip in for the strings.

So, I just got an email about the Montenegro trip. Are we still on for next month? I’d love to go, but I’ve got this EPQ thing to finish. It’s about renewable energy, which is kind of related to what we’re talking about in geography class.      Yeah, we’re still on. I was actually thinking about that last night. I’ve been looking up some info on Dubrovnik and the beaches. I heard it’s really beautiful this time of year. But I do feel bad about the EPQ. It’s taking up so much time. I mean, I’ve got to do research, write a report, and present it at the end of term. It’s like a full-time job.      I know, right? I’m doing mine on vegetarianism and how it affects the environment. It’s super interesting, but honestly, I’m exhausted. I’ve been trying to find stats on meat production and carbon footprints. It’s not easy.      I can’t even imagine doing that. I mean, I’m doing something related to my A-levels, but I don’t think I’ve ever had to spend this much time on one project. I was thinking—what if we all do a little project together? Like, maybe a cooking challenge or something related to food and sustainability?      That sounds fun. I’ve been meaning to try some new recipes. Last week, I made a vegetarian stir-fry, and it was actually really good. I used a lot of vegetables and some tofu. I think it’s getting easier to find vegetarian options now.      Yeah, I’ve been vegetarian for a year now. I used to eat meat, but the more I learned about animal welfare and the environment, the more I decided to change. It’s not always easy, but it’s worth it. My mum’s not too happy about it, though. She insists on giving me meat at meals.      That’s tough. I tried being vegetarian for a week once, and I missed meat so much. Maybe I’ll give it another try next term. I mean, with the EPQ, maybe it’ll be easier to focus on sustainable eating habits.      That’s a good idea. We could even plan a vegetarian picnic next time we meet. I’ve got a few recipes I can share. And what about the Montenegro trip?

So, I just got a text from my sister saying her new flatmate’s like... got a cow in the garden. Like, a  real  cow. You know, with a bell and everything. She’s like, “I can’t even open the window without it mooing at me.”      Oh no, that's  so  not a cow. That's a  teapot . Or maybe a parrot with a broken beak. She's just trying to blame the cow for the mess.      Yeah, I mean, who  would  keep a cow in the garden? That’s like,  unreal . I mean, I’ve got a roommate who’s got a cat that’s basically a gremlin. It climbs the fridge and eats my snacks.      Yeah, but that’s just a  cat . You can’t even blame a cow for the milk in the fridge, right? I mean, I’ve got a roommate who’s like, “You can’t get a job without a degree.” I’m like, “I’ve got a degree, and I’m still stuck in this flat.”      You’re telling me. I swear, university accommodation is like a  disaster zone . Last week, my flatmate tried to cook something and it smelled like a landfill site. I don’t even know what she put in the pan.      Oh yeah, I had a similar thing. My roommate tried to make a curry and ended up burning the whole kitchen down. We had to call the fire department. They said it was a type of “indian fire.”      Oh that’s  so  not a real thing. Maybe it’s just the smell of burning garam masala.      Yeah, it’s just the smell of  failure . I tried to make a pizza once, and it looked like a  tomato-based weapon of mass destruction .      Oh no, I  knew  something was wrong when the smell started getting stronger. I thought it was just my flatmate’s  natural perfume .      You’re telling me. I’ve had to move out of my flat three times. First time, the landlord said I was “being too loud.” Second time, I was “being too quiet.” Third time, the flatmate said I was “trying to steal her soap.”      That’s like,  classic . I’ve got a roommate who’s like, “You can’t even pay your rent on time.” And I’m like, “I  can’t  pay it on time. You’ve got the most expensive groceries in the flat.”

So, I was just telling my cousin about the time my mum tried to cook Christmas dinner and ended up setting the oven on fire. It was  absolutely  chaos. She had a roast chicken in there, and then she went to make some stuffing and forgot about the oven. By the time she noticed, the smoke alarm had gone off, and the whole kitchen was full of smoke. I had to call the fire brigade.      Oh, I know that story. You told me about it last year. Didn’t your dad come rushing in with a fire extinguisher, only to find out it was just the chicken?      Exactly! He looked like he’d been in a war. He tried to put it out, but it was already too late. The chicken was basically a blackened mess. We had to eat it with a fork, it was so hard. And then we had to go to the pub afterwards, and the barman said, “I’ve seen more drama in a pub than that.”      Oh yes, I remember. You were so embarrassed. But honestly, that’s the kind of thing that makes Christmas memorable, isn’t it? You know, the little mishaps.      Exactly. I think the real joy of Christmas is the  people  – the family, the friends, the traditions. Even if the turkey burns or the tree falls over, you still have the laughter and the love.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? I was just talking to my sister yesterday about how we used to travel around the UK for Christmas when we were younger. We’d do a different place every year – Manchester, York, even as far as Edinburgh. It was like an adventure.      I love that. I think I’d like to do that with my kids one day. Take them on a road trip for Christmas. Maybe even to the Lake District or something. Do you think they’d like that?      Oh, they’d  love  it. I mean, you’d have to keep the car warm, and you’d have to plan the route, but it’s all part of the fun. I still go back to my hometown every Christmas, even though I live in London now. It’s just nice to be with family, you know?      Definitely. It’s about the connection, isn’t it? Even if we’re miles away from where we started, the traditions and the people keep us grounded.

So, Dad, I’ve been meaning to ask you—why do you still use that old Nokia you got back in the early 2000s? It’s like a relic from the Stone Age. You can’t even take photos with it.      Oh, I like the simplicity, laddie. No notifications, no distractions. It’s like a digital detox. Plus, I got this one from a friend who said it was “unhackable.”      Unhackable? That’s a joke, Dad. You’ve been living under a rock. I’ve seen smartphones that can do more than a whole computer.      I know, I know. But I like the way it feels in my hand. And the battery lasts all day. No need for charging. You know, when I was your age, we had to wait for the phone to ring, not five times a minute.      Yeah, that’s true. But tell me—why haven’t you moved to Brighton like you said you would? I thought you were serious about that.      Well, it’s not that I don’t want to. It’s just, I’ve got this old flat here, and my daughter’s staying with me for a bit. Plus, the kids are back at school, and I’ve got this new work contract in Crawley. It’s not the same as Brighton, but it’s a start.      But you’ve been talking about moving for years. This is your third time saying you’re finally going.      I know, laddie. I know. I just keep getting tied up with things. And honestly, I’m not sure if I’m ready for the pace of Brighton. It’s too fast for me.      I get it, Dad. We all have our pace. But if you ever decide to move, I’d love to visit. I hear the beaches are amazing.      You’ll have to come visit me then. I’ll show you the best views in the area.      Deal. But only if you promise to upgrade your phone first.      You’re on. Just don’t expect me to start using Instagram or anything.      I wouldn’t expect that. You’re too old for that.      Hey, I’m not that old. I’m just... traditional.      Yeah, I guess that’s a fair point. You’ve always been the traditional type.      Yeah, well. I’ve got a good reason to be. And besides, if I start changing too much, I’ll end up like you—always on your phone, never looking up.

So, I just got back from the weekend market in Norwich. It was a bit of a madhouse, honestly. I thought I’d grab a few things for the house, but by the time I got there, it was like a proper fair. People were everywhere, and the stalls were all over the place. I ended up buying a few things I didn’t really need, but it was fun all the same.      Sounds like you got more than just a few items. I remember you talking about that place last week. Did you manage to find anything useful?      Oh, I did! I got a couple of nice candles and some local honey. The honey was amazing—this amber colour and this rich taste. I think it’s from a local beekeeper. I brought some back for the flat, and I’m planning to share some with the neighbors. It’s a bit of a small gesture, but I think it helps build good relations.      That’s a lovely idea. I remember you mentioned you were thinking about improving the community vibe. I reckon those little gestures can go a long way. Speaking of which, did you hear about the PR event happening next month? It’s a local initiative for the town’s image.      Yeah, I heard. It’s a bit of a big deal, actually. They’re aiming to promote Norwich as a cultural hub. I’m not sure if I’ll be involved, but I might check in with the council about volunteering.
