Oh, and I saw a new album by that indie band you like the other day. It’s called  Echoes in the Static . I think it’s got some really interesting sounds. You should check it out.      Oh, really? I’ve been meaning to. I’ve been pretty swamped with work and the house, so I’ve not had much time for music. I hope it’s good. I’ve been listening to a lot of folk lately, but I do miss some of the more experimental stuff.      I think you’ll like it. The guy has a unique style. I think it’s got some soul, you know? Anyway, I’ll let you know if I get a copy.

So, I was just thinking about the bean bag I’m knitting. I know it’s supposed to be a comfort item, but I’m starting to wonder if it’s going to be more like a giant, fluffy stress ball. You know, the kind that makes you want to throw it across the room when you’re having a bad day?      Oh, come on, you’ve got to be kidding. You’re not going to knit a stress ball, are you? You’re making a bean bag, not a weapon. Although, honestly, I can see you tossing it around if the washing machine won’t stop spinning.      Exactly! I keep thinking about the way the shower curtain is peeling at the corners. It’s like it’s fighting back against the humidity. I was just wondering if we should replace it with something sturdier. Maybe a waterproof one with some pattern on it? You know, something that actually looks nice in the bathroom.      I’d say go for it, but I’m not sure about the pattern. I mean, I like the simplicity of the plain white one we have. It doesn’t distract from the tiles or anything. But maybe we could do something with a subtle geometric design? You know, to match the new bath mat we got last week.      I was thinking about that too. The mat’s got this sort of modern black and white stripe thing going on. It looks really clean. I’d love to have a curtain that complements that. But also, maybe not too bold? It’s a bathroom, not an art gallery.      Fair point. Still, I think a bit of personality is good. Especially if we’re going to be spending more time in the bathroom now that we’ve got that new shower. Speaking of which, are we going to be cooking supper while it’s running? I mean, I know you’re trying to keep things low-key, but I feel like we’re getting into a bit of a domestic rut.      Oh, I was just getting to that. I was wondering if we should try something different tonight. Maybe a proper meal instead of just leftovers? I’ve been meaning to try that new recipe for spiced lentil stew I found online. It’s supposed to be really hearty, and it’d be nice to have something that actually tastes like it’s been cooked with care.

Well, I’ve been thinking, lass, about the old days when we first met. You were always one of the liveliest people I knew. Still are, I suppose.      Oh, don’t start that again, Tom. You know I’ve had my share of ups and downs. But I’ll have you know I’ve never been one to sit around and do nothing. Not since I was a child.      Aye, and you weren’t. You always had that fire in your belly. Remember when you used to take the kids out and teach them how to bake? That was a sight. Still is, in a way.      Oh, I remember that well. I used to watch from the kitchen, thinking, “What’s she doing with those little ones?” But it was a good thing. You always knew how to keep the kids entertained.      It wasn’t just the kids. It was the community, you know. We used to have these little gatherings—tea, cake, and stories. It was like a little family.      Aye, and it was all because of you, Brenda. You had that knack for bringing people together. Even when times were hard, you knew how to make the best of them.      And you, Tom, you were always the one who could fix anything. That old shed? It was a mess, but you turned it into something useful. Still is, I reckon.      And you still have that same old stubbornness. You won’t admit it, but you’re still the same man you were back then.      Aye, and I suppose I am. Though I’ve got less hair now. And more tea. And more time to sit and chat.      That’s the price of retirement, isn’t it? More time to sit and chat, more time to catch up on the things you used to have to do when you were working.      Yeah, I suppose it is. But I wouldn’t change it for the world. We’ve got each other, and that’s enough.      Aye, that’s the thing. We’ve got each other. And that’s more than most people have.      And we’ve got the memories. That’s what keeps us going, isn’t it?      Yeah, and the house. It’s a good house, isn’t it? Still standing after all these years.      Aye, and it’ll be standing for many more. As long as we’ve got the strength to keep it going.

So, I was just telling my sister about the time I tried to cook a Christmas dinner and ended up with a burnt turkey and a very confused cat. You know, the one that kept sneaking into the kitchen to see what the fuss was about.      Oh, I remember that. You were so sure you could do it, and then you ended up with a plate of undercooked meat and a very confused cat. I swear, that cat was trying to help you. What did you do with the turkey?      I think the cat ended up eating the stuffing. I don't know how it got in there, but it was like a mystery movie. I was so distracted by the cooking that I didn't notice it until I came out of the kitchen and saw the cat sitting on the table with a piece of bread in its mouth.      That sounds a bit like my experience when I tried to make a lasagna for the first time. I followed the recipe, but somehow ended up with a dish that looked more like a blob than a lasagna. My mum came over and said it looked like something from a science experiment.      Oh, I can imagine. My brother-in-law once tried to make a Christmas cake and ended up with something that looked like a rock. He said he was trying to use a special ingredient he found in the cupboard, which turned out to be someone’s old spice jar.      I can definitely see that. We all have our moments. I think the key is to just enjoy the process, not the outcome. Especially when it comes to Christmas. I mean, the real magic is the time spent with family and friends, not the food.      Absolutely. I think that’s what makes it special. I’ve been thinking about my plans for Christmas. I want to do something a bit different this year. Maybe take a short trip to Brighton? I’ve heard the Christmas markets there are amazing.      That sounds great. I’ve always wanted to go to Brighton. I think it’s a bit of a cultural difference for me, growing up in Kent. But I think it would be a nice change of scenery.      I think that’s a great idea. Maybe we could all go together. It’s been a while since we’ve all hung out.

So, I heard you've been living in Northern Cyprus for a while now? How's it going? I mean, I've only been here a few weeks, and I'm already struggling with the heat and the language.      Oh, I've been here for over ten years now, actually. I retired and moved here with my wife. We thought it would be a quiet place to relax, but let me tell you, it's not exactly what we expected.      No way? I mean, I thought it might be peaceful, but I never imagined it would be so… different. I can barely understand half of what people say, and the food is completely foreign to me.      It's a bit of a culture shock, to be honest. But you get used to it. You just have to pick up the local dialect. I speak English pretty well, but the way they talk here is so different from back home. It’s like a whole new language.      I can tell you that. I tried to ask for a coffee the other day, and I said "I want a cup of coffee," and the barista just stared at me like I was from Mars.      Oh, you should’ve said "I want a coffee" – no "cup of." They don't use that phrase here. It's all about the word "coffee" on its own. And the way you order is different too. You don't say "one coffee," you just say "coffee."      That's a bit of a language hurdle. I was so confused the first few days. I even thought they didn't have coffee at all. I asked for tea and got about five cups of something that tasted like burnt beans.      Oh, I remember that. You're not the first to make that mistake. The locals think it's funny. They laugh and say, "Ah, you’re from the UK, aren't you? You'll get it soon."      I don't know if I'll ever get it. I mean, I'm a teacher, so I'm used to explaining things, but this is different. It's not just about words—it's about how people live.      Yeah, it's really about lifestyle. I've learned a lot here. The pace of life is slower, and people are more community-oriented. But it’s not for everyone. It took me a while to settle in.

You know, I still can’t get used to the air here. It’s like walking through a cloud all the time. I mean, sure, it’s a busy city, but I feel like we’re all breathing in something that’s not exactly clean.      I know, right? I’ve been trying to get a mask for weeks, but they’re all sold out. I’ve even seen people using scarves as filters. It’s just… strange. I mean, when I was in London, the air was smoggy too, but it had a different kind of smell. This is like a different kind of pollution altogether.      Yeah, I remember when I was studying in Norwich, the air was pretty clear. I mean, the countryside’s got its own kind of pollution—like agricultural fumes, but nothing like this. I guess it’s the combination of industrial activity, traffic, and the weather here, the way it traps the smog. It’s really worrying.      It’s not just the air. The noise, the heat, everything feels more intense here. I sometimes wonder how people manage to live like this. I mean, I know it’s a big city, but still, it feels like there’s a constant pressure to move faster, to be more efficient, to not complain. And yet, every time we step outside, it feels like we’re in a pressure cooker.      You know, I think that’s why I love being back in England. Even when it’s cold or damp, there’s something comforting about the air. I can smell the sea from the coast, or the earth after rain. It’s not perfect, but it feels… natural. I miss that.      Yeah, I do too. I mean, it’s not like we don’t have our own issues, but there’s a rhythm to it. There’s a kind of simplicity to the way people move through the streets, the way the seasons change. It feels… more…  human  in a way.      Exactly. I think that’s part of what makes us friends, you know? We both came from places where the air was different, and we both miss it. Even though we’re lecturers and we live in a different country, we still find ourselves talking about the same things—like how the air feels, or how the weather affects our mood. It’s like we’re part of the same conversation, just in different parts of the world.

Right, I’ve got the veg sorted. I think I’ll make a chilli with the beans and tomatoes. I’ve got some leftover rice from last night, so that’ll be nice and filling.      That sounds good. I brought some fresh parsley and basil from the garden. Might be a nice touch to add some freshness to the chilli. You know, I used to make it all the time when I was in the south. It’s one of those things that feels like home.      Oh, I just got a text from my sister. She said she’s going to be late for lunch, but she’ll bring some homemade bread. I can’t wait. I think I’ll make a green salad with some cottage cheese and olives. It’s light and goes well with chilli.      Great plan. I always say that green salad is a perfect match for anything. It’s like the hero of the table. Speaking of which, I’ve been meaning to ask—did you see the latest episode of  Doctor Who ? I think it was the one with the Time Lord and the alien market. It was wild.      Yeah, I watched that. I thought the twist with the main character was really clever. I mean, you never see that coming, do you? It kept me on my toes. I’ve been meaning to catch up on some episodes I missed, but work has been a bit hectic.      I’ve been trying to catch up too. I even watched the entire series on Netflix last weekend. I had so much popcorn I thought I’d start a business. But I have to say, the sound effects are just so immersive. You can almost smell the TARDIS.      You’re absolutely right. I think it’s one of those shows that just gets better with time. Speaking of time, have you seen the photos I took of the countryside recently? I think I’m going to frame a few of them and put them on the wall.      Oh, I saw some of them on your Instagram. The one of the old church with the autumn leaves was amazing. You’ve got a real eye for composition. I’ve been meaning to take up photography again, but I’m not sure where to start.      Yeah, you’ve got a natural talent for it. I think if you start with a basic camera, you’ll be fine.

So, I was just thinking about that new bus route they announced last week. I mean, it’s supposed to go from the city centre to the Cambridge University Press bookshop, right? But I don’t think it’s actually going to help anyone. You know how the buses are in Cambridge? They’re always delayed, and the stops are all over the place.      Yeah, I remember hearing about that. I mean, it’s a good idea in theory, but it’s one of those things that sounds great on paper. I was actually talking to a friend of mine the other day who works in the city. He said the route’s going to pass by the bookshop, but the timing is all wrong for students. And the protests last week about the university budget – I still can’t believe how much noise they made. Some of them were even blocking the main road.      Oh, I saw that. It was like a small revolution! I mean, the university’s got a budget, but I guess some students feel like they’re being taken for granted. I can’t really blame them, honestly. I mean, I studied at a different university, and I’ve seen how things can get cut. Cambridge’s got a good reputation, but I don’t know if it’s as well-funded as it used to be.      You studied at a different university? You don’t say. Where? I mean, someone who works in a bookshop and gets to know the ins and outs of university life – what’s the story?      I did my degree at Manchester, actually. Not as fancy as Cambridge, but I liked it. The vibe was different. You had more of a student culture there. Anyway, that’s why I find it weird that Cambridge students are getting so worked up over budgets. I mean, if you’re going to protest, you’ve got to have a solid argument. I was at the bookshop last week, and I saw some of them hanging around. It was a bit of a mess.      Yeah, I saw some of them. I think they’re a bit overdoing it. I mean, the university has to balance things. But if you’re going to fight for your rights, you’ve got to do it properly. I’ve got a friend who’s a lecturer here, and he said the protests are starting to get a bit out of hand.

So, I was just telling my niece about the time her dad tried to cook spaghetti and ended up with a soup-like mess. It was  so  funny, and I think it's probably going to be a family legend by the time she's thirty.      That sounds like the kind of story that gets told at every family gathering. I remember my own dad tried to make a lasagna once and ended up with a layer of cheese on the bottom, a layer of tomato sauce in the middle, and then just... nothing on top. He claimed it was "a frozen lasagna, but with  more  layers," which is the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever heard.      I think I’ve been there too, but I’d say my dad’s attempt at a cake was the real disaster. It was like a cake with no frosting, no filling—just a flat, dry pile of flour and eggs. He was so proud of it, though, and even showed it off to the neighbors. I still don’t know how he managed to get a cake out of that.      Oh, I can  just  picture it. You know, I've always wondered about the whole "boyfriend visit" thing. I mean, I'm not saying I don’t have any, but the idea of someone coming over and making a mess in my kitchen? I could foresee a situation where the toilets overflow and the food is inedible. Although, maybe not. Maybe I'm just being dramatic.      Or maybe you’re being overly cautious. I mean, your kitchen is spotless, right? I've always admired how you manage to keep it so clean, even after all those cooking disasters.      Well, I  do  have a system, I suppose. I keep things separate. All the ingredients in their own designated spots, and the cleaning is a ritual. But I think I’d rather have someone else in the kitchen. I mean, if you’re going to have a boyfriend visit, you’d want to keep the food decent, wouldn’t you?      Exactly. I think it's important to have someone who actually knows how to cook. I mean, I could handle a few burnt meals, but I’d rather not have the entire house smell like something that’s supposed to be dinner but isn’t.      And then there's the language thing. I’ve noticed over the years how the English language can be so confusing.

So, I was just thinking about how we used to walk along the Thames like this when we first moved to London. You remember, back when we were just starting out, and we had that tiny flat in Southwark. I used to love stopping by the O2 Arena — you know, that massive structure that’s like a floating palace of culture?      Oh, I remember all too well. I used to take you there for your birthday every year. You always said you’d rather go to a concert than go to a restaurant. And I mean, what’s not to love about the O2? It’s like the whole city comes together there.      Exactly, but now I find myself wondering why we don’t go there as much anymore. Life got busy, you know? I’m constantly on the move with work, and I think I’ve managed to forget how to just  enjoy  the city. I feel like I need to have a car to get anywhere these days. It’s so inconvenient not having one, even though I told myself I’d never own one.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I still don’t have a car, and I’ve tried. It’s just the way things are now. You can’t really get around London without one. I mean, the buses are okay, but they’re not reliable, and the Tube is a minefield. Still, I somehow manage. I just use the bike more and try to plan everything around public transport.      That’s admirable. I wish I had your sense of adventure. I mean, what about holidays? I feel like we’re always looking at holidays as something we  have to  do, not something we  want  to do. I used to love going on holiday with the family. It used to be so much fun. But now, I’m worrying about how long we’ll be away, how much it’ll cost, and if it’s even worth it.      I know. It’s funny how the philosophical questions come up when you’re just walking along the Thames. Like, what’s the point of all of this? What’s the meaning of life? Or why are we even here?      I know, right? Sometimes I wonder if we’re just wasting our time chasing things that don’t really matter. But then again, isn’t that what life’s about?

Oh, I can't believe it's raining again! I was just about to go for a walk in the garden with the kids.      I know, it's been a right sodden week. But at least the kids are getting used to it. My nephew’s been playing outside every day, and he’s got this little bucket and spade, like he’s building a castle.      Yeah, I saw that. He’s obsessed with the beach, even though we’re in Kent. He’s got this little toy bucket from Build-a-Bear, isn’t he? I think he’s been asking for one for ages.      Oh, he’s got the whole set! I bought it for him for his birthday. He absolutely loves it. It’s like he’s building his own little village.      He’s got that cute little bear from Build-a-Bear too, isn’t he? I saw it on the sofa the other day. He’s got it in a little patchwork blanket, like it’s his very own teddy.      Yep, and he’s got this little book that goes with it. I tried reading it to him, but he just wants to hug the bear and say, “I love you, Bear.” It’s so sweet.      I can imagine. When I was little, I had this teddy too. It was a bit grubby, but I still loved it. I think I outgrew it, though.      I had a similar one. My mum used to say I was like a little bear myself. I remember the day I had to give it up for a new one. It was heartbreaking.      I know! I had to do the same with my little boy. He was so sad when I gave him a new one. But he’s got this new one now, and it’s got a little stick on it, like he can’t wait to go swimming.      Oh, swimming! I remember the first time I went in a pool. I was like a fish out of water. But now I can do it. It’s just so much easier with a little bit of practice.      I tried to teach my nephew to swim. It was a disaster. He kept screaming and wanted to get out. I think he’s not ready yet.      I think he’s still in the potty training stage. I’ve got this little potty chair in the kitchen, and he’s been using it for weeks now.

So, I’ve been thinking a lot lately about what I want to do with my life, you know? I mean, I’ve had this dream of starting my own coaching business for a while now, but I’ve been putting it off because of the uncertainty. I’ve got the skills, the experience, but it’s all about taking that first step. Do you ever feel like that? Like you know what you want but you’re just not sure if you’re ready?      Honestly, I can relate. I’ve been wanting to move into a role that’s more creative or educational, but I keep telling myself I need to stick with what I know. I mean, I love teaching, but I feel like I’m not doing what I really want to do. It’s like I’m stuck between two worlds—my current job and my dream of working with kids in a more hands-on way.      Yeah, I get that. But I think it’s important to take the leap at some point. I mean, we’re both in our early forties, and time is passing. I’ve been talking to a few friends about maybe starting a business together. I know you’re not in the same industry, but do you think collaborating might be a good idea? I mean, it could be a way to test the waters without going it completely alone.      That’s an interesting idea. I’ve been thinking about moving to a different area for a while—maybe somewhere with more opportunities for education and personal growth. If we could combine our skills, maybe we could create a program or something that supports people in their personal and professional development. It might be a way to bring in more income while doing something we’re passionate about.      That sounds like a win-win. I mean, we’re both driven, and we’ve got good networks. I think if we set up a small initiative, we could start with a pilot program. Maybe something local here in Australia. I know you’ve been wanting to move, and if this works, it could be a stepping stone. What do you think about making it a real thing?      I’d love that. It’s a little scary, but I think if we do it together, we’ll be more likely to stick with it.

So, I was at the shop earlier, and this bloke comes in with a Fitbit and a face like he’s seen a ghost. I said, “Oi, you alright?” and he goes, “I’m fine, I just—” and then he starts talking about how his heart rate went up  again  while he was waiting in line. I thought,  I’ve seen a man’s heart rate go up from just looking at a Fitbit.       Yeah, I remember the time my cousin tried to run a marathon in the North West. He had a Fitbit, and it kept beeping like it was trying to tell him he was dying. He ended up falling over in the middle of the street and got a wedgie from a bin bag.      Oh, I had an aunt once who thought Fitbits were for breakfast. She tried to put hers in the toaster. I had to explain to her that it’s not a toaster, it’s a  fitness tracker .      Honestly, I think some people take these devices too seriously. I’ve got one, and I use it to remind myself to move when I’m watching Netflix. That’s it. No “battle of the bulge” or whatever. I’m not into that kind of nonsense.      Yeah, I think the Fitbit is just a way to make people feel like they’re doing something. Like, “I’ve walked 5,000 steps, so I’m a healthy person now.” But in reality, I’ve just been walking to the shop, then back, and then to the Costa. I walk a lot, but the Fitbit’s like, “Not enough!”      I think the real issue is that people are trying to be  perfect  in every little thing. Like, I saw a friend of mine at the pub the other day, and he was  worried  about his posture. He said he’s been told to “stand up straight.” I asked him, “Have you been told by the Fitbit or the boss?” He said, “Both.”      That’s classic. You know, I’ve had more advice from my dog than from my Fitbit. He just stares at me like he knows I’m wasting my life.      I think there’s a fine line between being healthy and being  obsessed . I had a friend who went overboard with the Fitbit and started tracking  everything —sleep, heart rate, calories, even the number of times he flushed the toilet.

Well, I’ve been thinking about that garden party we had last summer. You remember when we tried to serve homemade lemonade and it turned out like it had been left in the sun for three days?      Oh, yes! And then you tried to pass it off as  sparkling  lemonade, thinking it was some sort of sophisticated drink. I nearly choked on it!      Oh, don’t forget the time you tried to make a  proper  soufflé. It looked like a lump of wet cement when it came out of the oven.      I still remember how you managed to set the table with all the plates upside down. It looked like a post-apocalyptic dinner.      Well, I did say it was a  family  dinner! And I still say that if you want a proper meal, you need to have a cook. I mean, we’ve all got our skills, but I’m not one for the kitchen.      True enough. I mean, I did spend years childcare, so I know how to handle kids, but if it comes to cooking, I’m a little lost. Though I do know how to make a decent Sunday roast, and I’ve had a few years to perfect it.      I think the real secret to a good meal is the people you’re with. I mean, I’ve cooked fancy dinners in my own kitchen, but nothing beats sitting around a table with friends and family, even if it’s just baked beans and chips.      Ah, yes. I remember the time we all had a takeaway and just ate on the floor. It was chaos, but it was the best kind of chaos. You know, the kind where you laugh so much you forget about the mess.      And the time you tried to play football in the garden and ended up getting your trousers stained with grass and mud. You looked like a raggedy clown.      Wasn’t that you who tried to run with the ball and ended up falling into the pond? You were soaked from head to toe, and you still refused to admit it.      Oh, I can still remember that. I said it was just a small puddle, and then I saw the water was actually  moving !      That was the day you swore off playing football for good. You said you’d never do it again, but you’re always trying to get us to go out for a match.

So, I was just thinking, do you ever miss those days when we’d get up at like 8 in the morning, and the first thing we’d do was kick off our shoes and just collapse on the floor? No, not the floor—we’d collapse on the carpet, or whatever it was.      Yeah, I remember that. You know, those mornings when we’d wake up before the sun even got up, and we’d just lie there, like, “I don’t wanna get up,” but then we’d get up anyway because we had to.      Exactly. And the worst part? Our shoes were always like that—so muddy, and we’d just leave them by the door. I swear, if I had a cent for every time I walked into the living room and saw someone’s shoes still covered in mud, I’d be rich.      Oh, you’re not telling me you didn’t do that? I thought we were both guilty. I mean, do you remember when we used to just—      —Drop everything and run to the bathroom to scrub our shoes? Yeah, we were both guilty. I swear, we were like two little kids with dirt on our feet, and we were trying to be cool.      I think we were just trying to survive university. Honestly, I can’t even remember how we got through the first year. It felt like we were always on the edge of dropping out.      I know, right? I mean, I still don’t know if I’m going to stay. It’s just—everything feels so heavy lately. Like, I don’t know if I’m even cut out for this.      I get it. I’ve been thinking about that too. But you know, think back to when we were kids. Remember when we used to stick our feet in puddles just to see how muddy we could get?      Oh, I remember you trying to get me to do that! I was like, “No way, I’m not getting my shoes dirty again.” But you just kept on, like, “Come on, it’s fun!”      Yeah, and you still won’t do it. I think that’s why your name is still “Sam,” and mine’s “Sophie.” Or maybe that’s just a coincidence.      I think it’s fate. You know, sometimes I think we were named for the way our parents used to argue about what to call us.

So, I can't believe it's been almost a year since we last caught up! I've been dying to see you, but work just keeps getting in the way. How have you been?      Honestly, I feel like I've been in a haze for the past few months. Between work and trying to figure out what I want to do next, I haven’t had much time to breathe. But I’ve been thinking about you a lot. How’s your life?      It’s been pretty busy too. I was promoted to project co-ordinator last month, which is a big step up. It’s been hectic, but I’m enjoying it. I’ve been trying to balance work with my personal life more, though. I’ve even started going to the gym again. You know how I used to love going, but then I just lost the motivation.      Oh, I know! I still miss that. I’ve been trying to get back into running, but I keep getting distracted by work. Actually, I’ve been thinking about taking a break from marketing for a while now. I feel like I need a change, maybe something more creative or even a different industry. Did you ever think about changing careers?      Honestly, I’ve been considering it. I love what I do, but I often feel like I’m not making the impact I want to. Aye, it's a real shame what's happening to the city, innit? I mean, I've lived in London all my life, and I've seen it change more in the last twenty years than in the whole of the twentieth. Right, so I was thinking, we need to figure out how we’re gonna get back from the airport on Christmas Day. I’ve got my flight at 7 a.m., and I don’t fancy driving home with a hangover. So, I was just telling the boys about balanceability. You know, that thing when you’re on a tightrope or a swing and you have to keep your balance? That’s scary.      Definitely. It’s all about knowing your limits. And speaking of limits, have you heard about National Cat Day in Japan?      I think I saw a cat poster at school.      Yeah, and we saw a cat at the bakery yesterday. It was so cute!      That’s the spirit. And don’t forget, food is a big part of life too.

So, I was just telling my nan about the gym again, and she said, “You don’t need a gym, you just need to go outside and walk like a proper human being.” I don’t know, I’ve tried, but I’m just not into it. So, I was just thinking about that pub we went to in Chester last week. You remember the one with the giant dartboard and the weird mural of a stag?      Oh yeah, the one where the barman accidentally poured me a shot of rum instead of a pint? I still haven’t forgotten that.      That was  the  night! Oh, is that the one with the strange name? Like,  The Green Garlic ?      No, that’s the one with the weird vibes. I’m talking about  The Rooted Spoon . Well, I guess I can’t argue with your taste buds. But I still think I’d rather have a proper steak than some weird vegan dish, even if it  does  taste good.      Yeah, but you know what they say— vegetables are the new meat . And if you’re gonna go meat-free, you might as well go all the way.      You’re right. But I still think I’d rather have a bit of meat. And, honestly, I’d rather be in a pub than some strange vegan restaurant.

So, I was walking down the High Street the other day, and I seen this bloke on a bike, lookin’ like he’d been through a war.      Did he fall off? So, I heard you mentioned you're from Lincoln? That’s not too far from where I grew up—Aylesbury in Buckinghamshire. I’ve visited Lincoln once, actually. It’s a lovely place, but I always thought it felt a bit… I don’t know, quieter than the big cities.      Yeah, it’s very much a small town, isn’t it? I’ve actually taught a module on the Welsh language at the university. It’s fascinating how much of a cultural identity that holds. It’s cool how much variation there is in how people speak—even within the same area.      Absolutely. It made me realize how much of the language is rooted in the people and the places.      That’s what I mean. I’m currently working on a project about regional dialects in England. I’ve been trying to map out different phonetic variations. It’s quite a challenge, but it’s also really rewarding.      I’d love to hear more about that. I’ve always been fascinated by how language can tell you so much about a place. I was in Spain once, and I tried to speak a little bit of Spanish. It was such a different way of communicating.      Spain is a great place to study language, but the Basque Country is even more interesting. They have their own language, Euskara, which is completely unrelated to any other language in Europe. That’s pretty unique.      That’s incredible. I’ve never been to the Basque Country, but I’ve read a bit about it.

So, I just saw this post on Facebook from my cousin Sarah.
