It’s like, what even is that now?      Oh, I remember that. It was one of those viral things, wasn’t it? You know, that whole ALS thing. People would dump ice water over themselves to raise money. I think it was a bit of a fad, but it did raise a lot for charity, didn’t it?      Yeah, it was  everywhere . I remember my cousin Tom doing it at his office. He got so cold, he nearly froze! But it was good for awareness. Although, I have to say, I feel like it’s been a while since we had an ice bucket challenge. I’m not sure if it’s even trending anymore.      I think it faded out pretty quick. There was a lot of backlash about it being a bit too over-the-top, like, why do we have to suffer for a cause? But I can see the point. Still, I feel like the real challenge is still out there. Speaking of challenges, have any of you seen the new “stair challenge”?      No, not that one. But I’ve seen a lot of stuff on Facebook lately about people getting into fitness again. There’s this guy who started a challenge where he does a push-up every day and posts it. He’s like, “I want to do this for my son,” and it’s gone viral. It’s kind of inspiring, actually.      That’s about the same time as the whole "500 days of coffee" thing. I think that was a failsafe for people who wanted to be productive but weren’t really productive. I do think, though, that the whole ice bucket challenge was more of a fun way to raise money. You know, a bit of a lighthearted way to support something serious.      Exactly. I mean, it’s not like we were asking people to do anything that would cause them harm. And it was a good cause. I think it was a reminder that even small actions can make a difference. Speaking of actions, I was just thinking—do you think we should do something for charity this year?

I just can’t get over this coffee machine we got. It’s been causing more trouble than it’s worth. I've been trying to figure out how to use it for weeks. I mean, what's the point of having a coffee machine if it takes longer to make a cup of coffee than it does to brew it on the stove?      Oh, I know, I know. I’ve had the same machine for years and I still can’t get it to work properly. It’s like it has a mind of its own. But I guess it’s a bit of a novelty. I mean, you can make a proper cappuccino, which is something you can’t really do on the stove.      Yeah, but I still don’t get it. Why spend all that money when you can just make a proper cup of tea? I mean, I don’t even know if I can afford to keep buying coffee. Between the coffee machine and the removal and storage costs for the rest of the stuff we’re getting rid of, I’m already out of pocket.      Oh, I know, I know. The removal costs are ridiculous. I remember when we were talking about moving out, and I said, “We’ll just sell everything and move in with the kids.” But now, even that seems impossible. And the storage—do you know how much that costs? It’s like paying rent for a warehouse.      Exactly. And now with the Labour leadership thing going on, I’m not sure if there’s even a government to make sense of any of this. I mean, what’s the point of having a Labour party if they can’t even agree on who should lead it?      Idealism. That’s what they call it, isn’t it? All that talk about change and fairness, but when it comes down to it, they can’t even agree on the basics. I remember when I was in the oil industry, we had to keep things running, no matter what. Now, it's like everything’s on hold.      It’s like we're all stuck in this limbo. I was a maths teacher for thirty years, and now I’m unemployed, and I can’t even find a job that pays the bills. I mean, where do you start when you’re over fifty and you’ve been out of work for years?

You know, I’ve been thinking about Christmas a lot lately. I just can’t believe it’s already mid-December. It feels like only yesterday we were planning the tree and the cards.      Oh, I remember that perfectly. You were so excited about the lights and the scent of the tree. I think you even got a bit teary-eyed when we brought it in. Still do, every year.      Yeah, I guess it was the same for me. But this year, I’ve been trying to get the kids involved more. I mean, they’re older now—eight and ten—so they can help with the wrapping and the baking. It’s a bit of a hassle, but I think they’re starting to enjoy it.      That’s wonderful. I remember when I was a kid, I used to watch you and Dad wrap presents in silence, just looking at the shiny paper and the ribbons. I never thought I’d be the one doing that with my own kids.      I know, it’s a full circle. And I’ve been trying to make more time for them, even with work. I’ve been thinking about taking a break for Christmas. Maybe a short trip, like to the coast somewhere? I’ve had enough of the same old routine.      You? Taking a break? I thought you’d be too busy with your TEFL students and your own family. But I do understand—everyone needs a little break. What about your parents? Are they coming over?      Yeah, they’ll be here. It’s always a bit chaotic, but they love being around the kids. I think they enjoy the chaos more than the peace and quiet.      That’s the spirit. And what about your career? You’ve been talking about moving to a different country for a while now. Still considering it?      Yeah, I’ve had a few offers, but I keep hesitating. I love teaching, but I want something more… stable. I’m not sure if I’m ready to go back to the UK life if I move abroad.      I understand. It’s a big decision. But what’s important is that you do what makes you happy. You’ve always been so passionate about your work, and I’m proud of you for that.      Thanks, Mum. I just hope I make the right choice. I don’t want to regret it later.

So, I was up at 3 this morning trying to get some sleep, and I got this massive snore from the other side of the room! It was like a chainsaw in a bakery— thump thump thump —and I thought, “Is someone trying to build a new house in here?”      Classic. You know how everyone’s got a different snoring style. Some just squeak like a mouse, others sound like a foghorn. I’ve had mates who snore so loud, it’s like they’ve got a whole orchestra in their head.      Yeah, I still remember that one time at Waterfields when Dave started snoring mid-song. The whole room just froze. I swear, the bass player looked at him and said, “Are you trying to take over the band?”      Oh, that’s not even the worst. Remember when we went to the bakers on Monday? That guy next to me, he was like a walking thunderstorm. I had to cover my ears with a handkerchief just to keep my sanity. I still have it, actually. Stained with something I can’t even remember.      Yeah, I remember that. I think he was actually sleeping on the bench. You could hear him snoring from the other side of the street. I was like, “Are we in a pub or a sleepover?”      It’s not just snoring, though. I’d say half the people in Warrington snore like they’ve had a week of heavy metal. I’ve even heard Steve from Richmond sausages do it once. He was on the phone with his mum and started snoring so loud, she asked him if he was  trying  to wake her up.      Oh no,  Steve ? That’s a new level. I can only imagine what that sounds like. You know, I once had to leave a party early just to avoid a snoring marathon with my cousin. It was like being in a sleep clinic with no medical equipment.      Yeah, I bet he’s got a medal for that. I think he’s been nominated for the  World’s Loudest Snorer  award by now.      Maybe he should start a band.  The Snoretones —covers of all your favorite songs, just with sound effects.      You know what’s funny? I think they’re all in the same podcast group. They always talk about sleeping and snoring like it’s the most important thing ever.      I know, right?

So, I just wanted to check – are you going to be at the family gathering this weekend? I know it’s on Saturday, but I’m not sure if you’ve got anything else planned.      Oh, I’m pretty much free. I’ve got a few things to sort out at the farm, but nothing that can’t wait. I’ll be there, definitely. It’s been ages since we’ve all got together.      That’s good to hear. I’ve been meaning to ask – how’s the crop season going? I know it’s been a bit tricky with the weather.      Yeah, it’s been a tough one, no doubt. We had a few days of heavy rain, and then the sun came out just when we needed it to dry things off. It’s all good now, though. The fields are looking decent, and the wheat is coming on strong.      That’s great to hear. I was worried you’d have some major issues, given the weather. I mean, I know you’ve had a few problems with the machinery before, haven’t you?      Oh, definitely. We had a few breakdowns, but we got through it. I’ve got a new mechanic now who’s been really helpful – saves me a lot of hassle. I think he’s from the same area as you, actually.      Oh, is he? I might have heard his name somewhere. Anyway, that’s good news. I’m glad you’re managing. It’s amazing how much you manage on your own, honestly.      Well, it’s not all on my shoulders. I’ve got a good team, and I’ve had a few years of experience. I mean, I didn’t start off as a manager, but I learned the ropes over time.      That’s for sure. I always admire how you’ve built up the business. I remember when you first started out, you were just working with your dad, right?      Yeah, and it’s still a family business in a way. I’ve taken over the management, but I still work with the same people. It’s a nice balance.      That’s fantastic. I’m really glad you’re still involved. You’re one of the few people I know who’s managed to stay grounded and still run a successful business. It’s not easy, especially with the way things are now.

So, I heard you mentioned you're thinking about going back to teaching? That's interesting, especially with the baby coming. I mean, I can't imagine how you'd manage it all, but I suppose with support, it could work.      It's not exactly a sudden decision, though. I've been thinking about it for a while now. Teaching has always been my passion, even if it's not the same as when I first started. Plus, I’ve been working part-time in a local library, and it just feels like the right time to get back into the classroom. But honestly, I'm a bit nervous about juggling it with the baby. I don't want to feel overwhelmed.      My feelings are exactly the same! I've got this new language course I’m planning to start, and I’m already feeling the pressure. But I know it's important for my career. I think it's about finding the right balance, though. Maybe you could start part-time again, like you did before?      Yeah, that’s actually something I’ve thought about. I could do some evening classes or weekends. I’ve got a few contacts from my old school, and they’re willing to help. Plus, I’ve been reading a lot about flexible teaching roles. It’s a bit of a shift, but I’m excited, honestly. It just feels like the right step.      That’s great! You know, I’ve been looking at similar opportunities, and I’m thinking about taking a language teaching course in Spain. It’s a bit of a big move, but I’ve had this dream about teaching in a different country for a while now. I mean, it’s not like I have a baby to worry about yet, but I know it’s something I need to do for my own growth.      That sounds amazing. I admire your courage. I mean, I’ve always thought about doing something like that. Maybe one day, when the baby’s a bit older. But I can see how it would be a huge step for you.      It would be. I know it’s a lot to take on, but I think it’s worth it. I’ve also been thinking about how important it is to keep learning, especially with the way the job market is changing. I mean, I’m a language teacher, but if I don’t continue to develop my skills, I might get left behind.

Aye, I’ve been watching these birds all morning. They’re like little chefs, flitting from one feeder to another, and I’ve got this one little seed bag that's just thrown out. You’d think they’d be more clever than that.      I know, I reckon they just like the taste of the seed. I’ve had a few birds come in this morning, even a few blue tits. I put out some suet and some oats, and they were like little greasers, zooming in and out.      That’s lovely, isn’t it? I’ve made some raspberry cake for us. I thought you might like some. I’ve got a few left, and I’ve made some little cupcakes too.      That’s kind of you, love. I’d be ever so grateful. You know, I always say the best thing about retirement is the cake—especially when it’s made by someone like you.      Aye, and the birds as well. I’ve been reading that birds have a sort of memory. They come back every year to the same place. I suppose they think it’s the best bit of the garden.      I don’t know about memory, but I do know that when I put out the cake, they come like clockwork. I’ve even got a few little ones that have been coming over for weeks now. I think they’ve got a bit of a taste for it.      That’s right. I’ve seen a few of them. I was thinking the other day, I’ve got a few bobbin things around the house. I thought about making some little puppets. I’ve got that old sewing machine in the attic.      Oh, really? I always thought you had a good eye for that sort of thing. I always used to do a bit of sewing when I was younger, but I never got too good at it.      That’s a shame, but I’m sure you’d have made some beautiful puppets. I’ve always thought that puppets can be a bit of a therapy. You know, it’s like talking to someone else, but it’s also fun.      I’ve been thinking about it. Maybe I could make a few for the garden. The birds could have a puppet show. I wonder what they’d think.      I think they’d find it fascinating, though I doubt they’d understand the plot.

So, I was sitting at the table next to this couple—the man kept asking his wife, "Do you want the salad or the kebabs?" and she kept saying, "I'll have the salad, dear," and he’d say, "But you hate the salad!" and she’d say, "I do  not  hate the salad!" and then she’d actually order the kebabs. It was so funny. I couldn’t help but smile.      Classic. You know me, I’ve had the same thing with my wife. She says she’s not a fan of fish, but every time I order the grilled fish, she ends up eating half of it. I think she’s just being polite.      Yeah, maybe that's it. But you know what’s even more amusing? The old man who’s been coming here every week for years. He always orders the same thing—grilled chicken and a side of feta salad. I asked him once, “Why don’t you try something new?” and he said, “I’ve had the same meal since I came here in ’85. It’s like a ritual.”      Rituals are good. Though I suppose that’s one way to deal with the loneliness of being in a new place. You know, I’ve been here for the summer, and I’ve already lost touch with my sister, who’s in London. She sent me a message the other day asking if I wanted to meet up, and I said, “I’d love to, but I’m here for the solstice.”      Solstice? You’re into that kind of thing?      A little. I used to be into dowsing, you know—finding water, like the old shamans. It’s not quite the same here, but I still feel like the earth has something to say. I’ve been trying to learn a little Turkish, too. It’s hard, but I’m getting there.      That’s impressive. I’ve been trying to count in Turkish, but I can’t get past “bir, iki, üç…” and then I get stuck. I think I just give up and say “one, two, three…” in English.      You’re not the only one. My son tried to teach me, but I kept confusing “beş” with “beef.”      I can imagine. You know, I still miss my mother, who passed away last year. She used to tell me stories about the stars and the constellations.

So, I’ve been thinking about what we’re going to do with the house. I mean, the roof’s been leaking for months, and I can’t even remember the last time we had a proper meal in the kitchen. It’s like we’re living in a museum!      I know, I know. I reckon it’s about time we started planning a bit. I’ve been talking to the local builder about getting a quote for a few things. Maybe a new roof, some fresh paint, even a bit of new flooring in the living room. You know how much the kids love that room.      Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that too. With the weather getting colder, it’s starting to feel more like a liability than a home. I’ve even thought about knocking through the living room and the dining area to make it one big space. More room for the kids to run around, and for us to all gather.      Knocking through? That sounds like a big project. You sure you want to do that? I mean, it would be great if we could all be in the same space, but what about the plumbing and wiring? You’d have to run new pipes, right?      I’ve done a bit of renovations before, you know. I’ve got a soft spot for restoring old buildings. If we do it right, it could look amazing. Plus, it’s not like we're doing it for the money—this is our home.      It does seem like a good idea. But I’m not sure about the cost. I mean, I’ve been working hard all these years, and the last thing I want is to take on more debt. Maybe we should wait until after the holidays? The kids will be back soon, and we can all pitch in.      Yeah, maybe. I mean, Christmas is coming up, and we still need to figure out what to get the kids. I was thinking of getting them some rugby gear—there’s a local team they’ve been talking about joining.      Rugby gear? I told you, you go to a game, and you’ll end up with a black eye. I remember when I played, I was always the one getting tackled.      I think it’s safe to say we’ll miss those days, though. But as long as we can get them into a team, it’s worth it.

So, I was just watching Jeremy Kyle the other day, and it was  so  ridiculous. I mean, I don't even know why people still watch that show. It's like, what's the point?      Yeah, it’s like watching a reality show where everyone’s just arguing about the most trivial things. I mean, I get that it’s popular, but honestly, I just can’t stand the way they play up every little conflict. It’s like they’re paid to make drama.      I know, right? I watched one episode where they were arguing about catfish, and it was just so over the top. One of the people was saying they had met someone online and it turned out to be a scam, and the host was just  gaslighting  the whole thing. It was ridiculous.      Oh, I remember that one! The guy was so convinced he was being treated like a criminal, even though the other person was clearly just trying to play it off. It was like a soap opera in real life.      Yeah, and then the host just kept saying, “This is what happens when you don’t take people seriously,” like it’s somehow the fault of the person who got scammed. It’s so  biased . I mean, I get that he’s trying to be helpful, but it’s not helpful at all.      And don’t even get me started on the way they talk about catfish. It’s like they think it’s a real thing, but it’s just people being reckless online. I mean, I’ve had a few people try to contact me through social media, and I just block them. No need to be paranoid.      I know, but it’s like the whole world’s obsessed with it now. Everywhere I go, people are talking about catfish. It’s like the new slang or something.      Yeah, I swear, the only thing people talk about now is catfish or Jeremy Kyle. It’s like the two main things that define our generation.      Honestly, I think it’s just the way the media is trying to keep us entertained. It’s not like we have anything  real  to talk about these days. We just have to watch people argue about online scams and courtroom drama.      I guess it’s better than nothing, I suppose. Or at least it’s something to laugh about.

So, I was just telling my mates about the time I got lost in Paris and ended up in a cheese shop. You’d think with all that history and architecture, you’d be able to find your way, but I ended up in a place that looked like it had been there since the 16th century, and the only thing I could do was ask for directions in broken French.      Oh, I remember when I used to travel through Paris like it was my second home. I lived there for a few years, actually. I even taught German there for a while. Still, I’ll never forget the day I got stuck in the Louvre for three hours because I thought the bathroom was in the other wing.      You’re not the only one who’s ever had that problem. It’s like the city doesn’t want you to leave. But then again, I’ve always loved the way Paris smells—like old books and fresh croissants. It’s got this magic that makes you want to stay forever.      Yeah, it’s a city that speaks to you. And I think that’s why I’ve always wanted to live there. But then again, I got my start in Vienna, and I still often find myself dreaming in German. Though I’ve been brushing up on my Italian lately—my nephew’s studying in Rome, and I want to be able to chat with him properly.      That’s cool. I’ve been trying to learn some Italian too. My mate’s from Milan, and he’s been teaching me phrases. I even managed to order a pizza in Italian last week. It felt like I was part of the real deal.      That’s the key—learning the language opens up so many doors. My husband and I used to travel all over Europe, and knowing a few words in each language made the whole experience richer. Speaking of which, have you ever thought about studying Classics? I did, and it opened up so many opportunities.      Not really, but I do love history. Though I’m more of a modern history guy—like the 20th century. But I guess there’s something about the classics that makes you really think.      Exactly. And if you ever feel like you need a break from all this tech stuff, I’d say take a road trip to Italy.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time when we were driving to Cornwall and the car started to drift into the lane next to us? I swear, I thought we were gonna end up in a pile-up!      Oh yeah, I remember that! You were so scared, you didn’t even dare look at the road for five minutes. I’ve never seen anyone so white-knuckled in my life. And don’t even get me started on the guy in the car behind us—he was literally dancing in his seat.      I remember that too. I was in the back, and I could feel the tension like a storm. You two were like two raccoons in a car crash! I mean, I’ve seen some pretty wild driving around here, but that was something else.      I know, right? I mean, I’ve been in cars with people who have no idea what an MOT is, let alone how to drive safely. I think we should all get a refresher course—especially you, Dad. You’ve been driving for decades, but do you even remember the last time you checked your tyres?      I got a new set last week. Or was it two weeks? Honestly, I can’t remember. I just like to pretend I know what I’m doing. You know what I hate more than bad driving? People who don’t know how to use a Sat Nav. I still can’t figure out how to get to Dorset without asking someone.      I still use paper maps. I prefer the old way. I mean, I know where I’m going, and I’m not depending on some app that might crash and leave me stranded. Not that I’ve ever been stranded, but you never know.      You’re like a human GPS. I’m trying to figure out how to use Windows 8 again, and I’m struggling. You’d think after all these years, you’d be able to navigate a phone screen.      I blame the government. They must have decided that teaching people how to use technology is no longer a priority. But enough about that. I was just saying, I think we should take a break when we get to Bournemouth. I need to eat something. I haven’t had a proper meal since breakfast.      Yeah, I’m with you on that.

Well, I’ve been thinking, Bill. I was just down by the old village shop, and I saw old Tom from the mill. He was all dressed up like he’d been to a fancy dinner. I said, “Tom, what’s the occasion?” He said, “Just felt like a bit of a treat, you know.” I thought, “Well, I’ve not been out in a while.”      That’s Tom for you. Always had a bit of a spark. You know, I remember when he used to take his wife to the theatre every Sunday. Right up until she passed away. He still goes, though. Just sits in the front row, and stares at the stage like he’s waiting for her to walk in.      Aye, I suppose it’s a sad thing. But he’s got a good heart, that old Tom. Still doesn’t miss a beat. I mean, he’s got no family left, but he’s always got that little dog of his. Old Paddy. That dog’s been with him since the war.      Oh, he’s a good old dog. I’ve seen him out walking in the early mornings, just the two of them. You can tell they’ve got a real bond. I remember when I was a child, my gran used to say, “A dog is a man’s best friend,” and she was right.      That’s true. I’ve never had a dog, but I’ve always liked ‘em. Used to have a spaniel when I was younger. Named her Fluffy. She’d follow me around like a shadow. I’d take her for walks by the river, and she’d run ahead, then come back and sit by my side. It was a nice time.      That sounds lovely. I used to have a cat when I was a girl. Her name was Marmalade. She was a bit of a diva, but she’d always curl up on my lap when I read. I miss her sometimes. We lost her a few years back.      Aye, pets do bring a bit of joy to life, don’t they? I suppose that’s one of the things that makes us human. We care for them, and they care for us in return.      Exactly. I think we all need that sort of connection. Even if it’s just with an animal. It helps keep the loneliness at bay, don’t you think?

So, I was just thinking about that gig we went to last week with the band from Newcastle. You remember? The one that played at the old warehouse in Norwich?      Oh yeah, I remember—  the one   with that crazy drummer who accidentally set the stage on fire. You told me it was an accident, but I still don’t believe you.      I told you it was an  accidental  fire, not a  deliberate  one. Didn’t even get the insurance claim through. Though I did get a free T-shirt.      That’s the kind of luck you get when you’re out with me. Anyway, I was thinking about the band. I’ve been doing some research on indie music scenes in the North, and it’s fascinating. You know, the grassroots stuff, the DIY ethos... it’s like a whole culture.      Yeah, I think that’s what makes it different from the mainstream stuff. You know, the music doesn’t just come from the cities. It comes from places like Sunderland, like my hometown. It’s raw, it’s real.      Exactly. And I was thinking—what do you think about the role of local music in community life? Like, do you think places like Sunderland could support a proper music scene, even with the economic challenges?      It’s tricky, but I think it’s still possible. Especially with the internet. You don’t need a huge venue anymore. People can stream, share, and even make a living doing it. I mean, look at the guy who started that band in Newcastle—he’s now playing festivals all over Europe.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? It’s not about the size of the crowd, it’s about the passion. I was just talking to my flatmate about that. He’s into gardening, you know. Likes to grow his own veggies.      Oh, he’s got the green thumb, for sure. You know, I told him he should go to a gardening show or something. He said he’d rather just plant a few herbs in pots.      Maybe he’s onto something. I mean, it’s not like we’re in Cambridge where everything’s all manicured and perfect. Sometimes, a little bit of chaos is good.      You’re right. I was thinking about the weather too. It’s been so unpredictable lately. One day it’s sunny, the next it’s pouring.

So, I was just thinking about how we both had this dream of working in the arts, and now I’m managing research projects and you’re doing a PhD, and we’re both still somehow pretending we’re not living off savings from our twenties. It’s wild.      Yeah, it’s like we’re both still in the same boat, just with a slightly different motor. I mean, I got this PhD because I thought it’d be a stepping stone, but it’s just another degree in the pile. And you? You’re the research manager now, which sounds like a real job, but honestly, I still feel like we’re just paying rent and hoping for the best.      Exactly. I mean, I’m working, but I can’t help but think about the people who are unemployed, you know? My cousin is still waiting for a job in London, and he’s been out for over a year. It’s like the job market’s got this weird filter that only lets certain people through.      Yeah, I get that. I’ve been talking to my friend from university who’s been trying to get into the arts sector for years. He’s been rejected from every single job he’s applied for. It’s not just about having the right skills, it’s about the connections, the right connections, and the postcode you were born in.      It’s so frustrating. I mean, my mum always said, “Education is the only way out,” and that’s kind of true, but it’s not the only way  through . You know? I have a postgrad degree and I’m still not guaranteed a job.      I know. I think the system is broken. And then there’s the student debt, too. I took out a loan for my PhD, and even if I do finish, the amount I’ll owe is going to be a huge chunk of my future income. I don’t know how people even  start  to think about getting a PhD with that kind of pressure.      It’s a mess. But hey, at least we’re not in the same boat as those people who are completely out of work. I mean, I’m still working, and you’re still working, even if your work is academic. It’s not like we’ve been totally abandoned by the system.

Hey, look at this book, Mum. It’s got all these pictures of families—some with two mums, some with two dads, some with step-siblings… it’s really cool.      Yeah, I remember when you were little and we tried to read that one. It was a bit confusing for you. You kept asking, “But where’s the baby?” It was adorable.      I remember! Didn’t you get frustrated trying to explain it? I think you ended up drawing a baby on the back cover.      Ah, I heard the chatter. That book, eh? I used to read it to my class. It’s important for children to see all types of families. It makes them feel included.      Yeah, I agree. It helps people understand that families come in all shapes and sizes. Like, my brother’s got a stepson from his ex, and he treats him like his own. It’s not always easy, but it’s still a family.      Exactly. I mean, I’m not working right now, but I still feel like part of a family. I’ve got my daughter, and even though my ex is gone, she’s still part of our lives. It’s just… different.      Difference is the key. I’ve seen so many people struggle with how to talk to their children about relationships and family changes. It’s not just about being ‘right’—it’s about being honest and open.      That makes sense. I think talking about it makes it easier. Like, I don’t hide the fact that my dad and my stepdad are divorced, but they’re still both part of my life. It’s not like they’re fighting or anything. It’s just… different.      Exactly. And I think that’s what the book is trying to show. It’s not about being perfect—it’s about being real.      Real, yes. And it’s also about understanding that family isn’t always blood. Sometimes, it’s the people you choose to love, even if they’re not your birth family.      That’s why I think it’s so important to show kids that. They need to know that they’re not alone, no matter what their family looks like.      And that’s something we should be helping them understand, right? We’re their role models, whether we’re working or not.      Aye, and that’s what makes us family, isn’t it?

So, I’ve been thinking about that thing we talked about last week — you know, the whole shaving thing? I’ve been trying to work up the courage to actually start shaving my legs. I mean, I’ve always grown it out, but now I’m like, “Right, it’s time to sort this out.”      Yeah, I heard you were considering it. What’s holding you back? Is it the pain, or is it just the whole idea of it?      Honestly, it’s the pain. I remember my nan used to tell me how  horrible  it was when she first shaved. She said it felt like a thousand bees were crawling under your skin. And then there’s the whole thing about the razor — you’ve got to be so careful not to nick yourself. I’m not exactly the most careful person when it comes to things like that.      I get you. I tried shaving my legs once, and I ended up with a few red patches that lasted for days. My mum told me I’d be lucky if I didn’t get a facial infection. But honestly, I think it’s just a matter of getting used to it. I mean, I’ve got a relative who shaves every single day, and she’s like, “It’s not that bad once you get the hang of it.”      Yeah, but she’s got a  very  steady hand. I’m more of a “do it once and then forget it” type. Although, I have to say, I do feel a bit self-conscious about my legs when I’m in the gym. I mean, I’m not the only one, but still — it’s like I’m trying to compete with the girls who’ve got that smooth, baby-skin look.      You know, I actually feel the same way. I’ve been thinking about trying a depilatory instead. I heard it’s less painful, although it can be a bit messy. But honestly, I’m just trying to find a way to do this without spending all my money on razors and lotions.      I’ve been looking into that too. I think I might try a depilatory next week. I just need to make sure I read the instructions properly, or I’ll end up with a big rash. Although, I’ve heard that some people say it’s worse than shaving.

So, I was just telling my mates about the time I tried to teach my nephew the alphabet using boxing terms. You know, like “A is for a punch, B is for a blow, C is for a clap…” It didn’t go well. He was like, “Auntie, I don’t wanna punch my alphabet!”      Sounds like you’re mixing up your education and your upbringing. You’re a research manager, not a gym instructor. But I can imagine the look on his face. Still, it’s a creative way to teach kids. Though I’d be more inclined to use football references, given the context of racism in football.      Yeah, I guess you’re right. I’ve been thinking a lot about that lately. I mean, I used to go to the matches down in Sunderland, and I’ve seen how fans can get really aggressive—especially when they’re playing against a team like Manchester United. It’s not just about the game, it’s about identity and pride. And when that pride turns into something toxic, it’s a real problem.      Absolutely. I’ve seen it firsthand. I did my PhD on social dynamics in sports, so I’ve studied a lot of that. It’s not just about the fans; it’s about systemic issues in the sport itself. There’s a lot of historical racism in football, and even though things are better now, it’s still a massive issue. I mean, just last week there was a race row at a local tournament. It got pretty heated.      Yeah, I heard about that. It’s frustrating because you know the right things to say, but sometimes people don’t want to hear it. I remember the time I got into a bit of a debate with a mate at the bar about it. He said, “It’s just a game, man. Why make such a big deal?” I nearly pulled out my phone and showed him some stats on the number of black players being excluded from certain positions.      You’re doing good work, mate. It’s not just about stats—it’s about changing attitudes. I think the key is education. If people understand the history and the impact of racism, it changes how they see the game. Though I’ll be honest, sometimes I think about how much easier it is to drink and forget that stuff.

Well, I’ve been thinking about that old manor house in Wiltshire again. I’ve got a potential client who’s really interested in restoring it, but I’m not sure how to structure the bid properly. I keep running into the same issues with funding and what they’re actually looking for.      I can imagine. I’ve had similar conversations with a few people. You know, they always say they want to preserve the history, but when it comes to details, they’re vague. It’s like they expect you to do all the research for them. Didn’t you have that problem with the one in Oxfordshire?      Oh, that was a nightmare. I spent weeks going through the archives and local records, and when I presented my findings, they were like, “Well, we wanted the main hall restored, but not the servants’ quarters.” I had to revise the entire plan and cut costs almost in half.      Exactly. You have to be careful not to be too ambitious. Clients often don’t realize how much work goes into a project, especially with historic buildings. They’re often more interested in the aesthetics than the structural integrity. You have to walk them through the process step by step.      That’s what I’m trying to do now. I’ve started drafting a business plan that outlines the different phases and what each phase entails. But I’m still worried about the funding part. Do you have any advice on how to approach grant applications?      Definitely. I found that using a combination of local government grants and private funders works best. You need to make sure your plan is realistic and includes clear timelines and milestones. Also, make your case for preservation compelling. Highlight how the building contributes to the local heritage and the community.      That makes sense. I think I’ll include some photos and a brief history of the building in my proposal. Maybe even mention the potential for tourism if it’s restored properly.      That’s a smart move. People are always drawn to stories. Also, you might want to mention the challenges you’ve faced in similar projects. It shows you’re experienced and able to manage unexpected issues.      I hadn’t considered that. I think I’ll make a section on lessons learned from previous work. It might help build trust with the client.      Exactly. And don’t forget to emphasize the long-term benefits.

So, I was just thinking about that paper we had to read for the linguistics module last year. You remember the one about dialects and social class? I was so confused about how they linked pronunciation to socio-economic status.      Yeah, that one was intense. I remember we had to break down the vowel shifts in different regions. It was interesting how they connected the way people speak to their upbringing. I mean, I guess it makes sense—like, if you grow up in Sunderland, you’re more likely to use certain vowel sounds compared to someone from Birmingham.      Exactly, and the study found that people from the North like me tend to use more "r" sounds, right? It’s like a marker of identity. And I can see how that could influence how people perceive you. It’s funny, isn’t it? I mean, I was always proud of my accent, but I never thought it might affect how others see me professionally.      I guess that’s part of the research, isn’t it? Like, how language can be a tool for both communication and exclusion. It’s not just about what you say, but how you say it. And then there’s the whole thing about socio-economic status. I mean, people like you from the North, we’re seen as more working-class, even if we’re now in higher education or professional jobs.      Yeah, it’s a bit of a paradox. I mean, I work as a research manager now, but I still get that look when I speak. People are surprised when I say I’m from Sunderland. They think of it as a rough area, not a place with a rich cultural and linguistic heritage.      That’s kind of what the research tried to highlight. It’s not just about grammar or vocabulary—it’s about how language is intertwined with identity. And I guess that’s why I’m doing my PhD on regional dialects. It’s a bit of a passion of mine.      That’s cool. I wish I’d done that. I mean, I like the idea of looking at how language shapes how we see ourselves and others. But then again, I’m more of a people-person than a linguist. I prefer the practical side of research.      You’re not wrong. But I think there’s value in understanding both sides.

So, I just got a text from Mrs. Taylor about the school tennis tournament. It’s next week, and they’re asking for volunteers to help out at the event. I said I’d be there, but honestly, I’m not sure what I’ll do. Maybe I’ll just sit on a bench and eat a sandwich while the kids play.      You’ll be fine, Mummy! I bet you’ll be the best volunteer ever. You know you’re the one who always makes the best sandwiches.      Yeah, but I think you should bring some clowns too. That’s what you said last week. You said if the kids are bored, you’d bring clowns.      Oh, I said that as a joke. But actually, the school is having a clown at the tennis tournament, just for fun. I think it’s a new thing.      Is it? Can I see the clowns? I love clowns! They’re so funny.      Me too. I think they’re real clowns, not just costumes. I saw one in the park last week. He had a red nose and a big hat, and he did tricks.      It’s actually a local circus group who are doing the event. They’re doing a mini-circus at the tournament. There will be jugglers, acrobats, and even a magic act.      Wow, that sounds amazing! Can we come?      Of course you can! We’ll have to check with the school about the timing, but I think it’s open to all the kids.      What about the school dinners? Mummy, I’m worried about the one tomorrow. I don’t like the meat.      I know, I know. But we can always bring a packed lunch. I’ve already asked the school if we can do that for tomorrow, and they said it’s okay.      I like the sandwiches you make, Mummy. I think I’ll bring a banana and a cookie tomorrow.      That sounds perfect. Oh, and we need to make sure the money for the school trips is sorted. I saw a notice about the next one, and the fee is quite high.      I don’t want to pay too much.      I know, sweetheart. But it’s a once-in-a-lifetime chance to go on a school trip. We’ll talk about it more later.      I think I’m going to eat at Granny’s this week. She makes the best chips.

So, what do you think of that film we saw last night, Martin? Was it worth the money? I mean, I’m still trying to figure out what the point of it was.      Honestly, I thought it was a bit of a mess. I liked the cinematography, but the storyline just didn’t make sense. It felt like they were trying too hard to be serious.      Oh, I thought it was interesting, actually. Especially the part where the main character talks about the national curriculum. That made me think about the debate we had in Cambridge last week—about how history is taught now versus how it was when we were kids.      Yeah, I remember that. I was at the event. It was interesting to hear the different opinions. Some said the current curriculum is too narrow, while others argued it should be more focused on critical thinking.      Exactly. I agree that teaching history should involve more debate and discussion. I mean, I was a teacher for years, and I always found that students were more engaged when we did role-play or analyzed different perspectives. It made them think more deeply about the material.      I remember when I was at school, we just memorized dates and events. There wasn’t much room for interpretation. I did well enough, but I was never really interested in history.      That’s a common experience. I was a bit of a history buff, but even I had to admit that some of the way it was taught in schools felt outdated. It’s a shame because history is about understanding the past to inform the future.      It’s true. And that’s why I think the national curriculum needs to be revised. I mean, I’ve seen how higher education degrees are structured now—there’s more emphasis on practical skills and real-world experience. You can’t just rely on theory anymore.      I suppose that makes sense. Though I’ve never done anything like that. I’ve always been more of a “classroom” person. Still, I can see the value in combining theory with practice.      Exactly. I’m in advertising, and I find that industry experience is vital. It helps you understand how theory applies in the real world. It’s all about linking education to what you want to do in your career.      True. I think the key is to make sure that education isn’t just about exams and grades.

Well, I'll be, old man. I was just telling Sue about the first time I saw a tank in the street. It was 1941, I think it was, and we were all in Costessey, just outside Norwich. The air was thick with smoke and the sky was red as a brick. I was just a kid, about ten, but I remember the noise—like thunder from a hundred miles away.      Oh, I remember those days too. My dad used to talk about the Blitz, how the bombs were falling like rain. We had a shelter under the garden, you know, just a bit of a dug-out. It made me think of the stories my gran used to tell me about her mother, who was a nurse in London during the war. She said the streets were full of people with bandages and empty pockets.      I still remember the war stories my grandfather used to tell. He was a corporal in the Royal Army, and he had a real love for the countryside. He often said that the war made him appreciate the simple things—like a good cup of tea and a dry floor.      I remember when the war broke out, too. I was just a boy, but I remember the queues for bread and the ration books. It was a different time, you know. People were more together back then.      Yes, back then, everyone had a job, even if it was just keeping the house warm and the family fed. I used to look at the men in the village who had gone off to war, and I used to wonder if they’d ever come back. Some did, some didn’t.      It’s strange, isn’t it? All those lives lost for a few square miles of land. I remember when my father passed away, he said something about how he was glad he had lived through the war, even though it was hard.      I always think about how different life is now. I’ve got a grandchild who’s just learning to ride a bike, and I can’t believe how much the world has changed. I sometimes miss the simplicity of those days—no computers, no phones, just people and the land.      I sometimes get lost in the past, but I’d rather be with the people I love than anywhere else. The talk about the war always brings us together, doesn’t it?

So, I just wanted to check – are we going to stop off at the supermarket on the way? I’d like to pick up some chicken for the Sunday dinner. I know it’s the last time we’ll be doing this, and I’d hate for the food to be bad.      Yeah, I was thinking the same thing. It’s funny, isn’t it? We’ve been making these trips for years, and now it’s the last one. I feel like we’re practically old now, pulling up to the same shops and picking up the same stuff.      You’re not old, Dad. You’re just . . . well, you’re still the same guy who used to grill me about my homework when I was a kid. Although, to be fair, back then I didn’t like you much. Still don’t, honestly.      You were a pain in the backside, lad. Remember when you tried to skip school and I had to track you down in the town centre? You were wearing a hoodie and eating a hot dog. I nearly had a heart attack.      Yeah, and you still don’t like me. Still think I should’ve stayed in school. But I’ve got a degree now, and I’m an English teacher. So I’m not the same kid you used to deal with.      Well, you’ve got a good job, and you’ve got a good head on your shoulders. Still, I’d have preferred you to stay in the UK. I mean, you’re in London now, right?      Yeah, I’m in London, but I still come home every weekend. I’ve got a mortgage, and I’ve got a place in Bedford. I’m not going anywhere. I just thought I’d take the opportunity to move out of my parents’ house before I have to.      That’s good. You’ve got your own place now. I just hope that house doesn’t fall apart. You know, I’ve been trying to sell it, but no one’s interested. We’re stuck with it.      I know, Dad. I keep telling you, we could rent it out. That way you don’t have to worry about the mortgage. It’s got good bones, and it’s in a good area.      Yeah, I know, but I just don’t know what to do with it. It’s like I’m planning for the future, and the future keeps changing.

So, I was just thinking about the seating plan again. We’ve got the grandparents, the aunts and uncles, and then the cousins. I’m not sure if we need to split the table or keep it all together. Do you think it would be better to have the older generation on one side and the younger on the other? I don’t want anyone to feel left out.      Honestly, I think keeping it all together would be better. It’s a family gathering, and everyone deserves to feel included. Plus, we’ve got the Great British Bake Off theme—what better way to celebrate than with a big, cozy table full of people? I was just looking at the menu again, and I think we should definitely include the fish. You know how Grandma loves her fish and chips. And I found some really nice candles at the market—maybe we can set the table with those to make it feel more special.      Yes, the candles are a great idea. I thought about that too. I was also thinking about the photographs. Should we have a photo board or something? I mean, it’s her birthday, so it’s not every day we get to celebrate her. We could put up some old photos of her with the family and maybe even some of her baking. It would be a nice touch.      That sounds perfect. I was just thinking about the cupboards too. We need to make sure everything is in order. I’m going to rearrange them so that the plates and cutlery are easy to reach. And I found this new tablecloth—light blue with some floral patterns. It matches the candles and the menu. I think it will tie everything together nicely.      I like that. The table setup is such an important part of the meal. I was also wondering about the menu. Have you thought about the dishes? I know she loves the traditional things, but we can also include some lighter options. Maybe a vegetable tart or something. And I think we should definitely include a dessert—maybe a birthday cake with a candle on it. You know, like the Bake Off queens.      Exactly! And I’ve got a couple of recipes I’ve been thinking about. I even found a recipe for a lemon drizzle cake that’s simple but delicious. I think that would be a hit.

So, I’ve been thinking about wisdom teeth again. You know, they’re like the last thing you ever want to deal with. I mean, I had mine taken out last week, and it was  so  not worth it.      Yeah, I remember when I had mine done. I was so scared, honestly. I thought it’d be a quick thing, but it turned out to be this  massive  ordeal. I was in pain for days, and then there were these holes where they took them out. It’s like your mouth’s got a little crash site in it.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I had to take antibiotics for weeks. My mouth was just  so  sore, and I couldn’t even eat properly. I remember trying to eat a sandwich, and it just felt like I was chewing sand.      I would’ve gone completely mad if I didn’t have a friend who stayed with me. I was so tempted to just tell them I had a  xenomorph  in my mouth or something.      Oh, I would’ve called it a  space alien  too. But seriously – I’m just glad I’m done with that. I don’t know why people even bother with wisdom teeth. It’s like nature’s way of making you suffer.      I think it’s just because they’re a bit of a  rite of passage . Like, “Oh, you’re 18? Let’s just take out your wisdom teeth and make you a real adult.”      That’s probably what my parents said. They were like, “Oh, you’re going back to uni soon, so you need to be  prepared  for the real world.” And I’m like, “Yeah, I’m  prepared  to have holes in my mouth!”      I think they’re just trying to make sure we’re not too  ungrateful . They told me the same thing when I was going back to uni. “Just make sure you don’t end up in the same situation as your brother.”      Oh yeah,  his  situation was  excellent . He moved house twice in two years.      And now he’s living in a flat with three other people. I think he’s trying to become a  hippie .      Yeah, and I think he’s suffering from  serious  social anxiety now.      Well, it’s not all bad. At least we’re all surviving, right?      Yeah. I just hope when I move house next year, it doesn’t involve a  hole  in my mouth too.

So, I was just thinking about that idea we had for the Chinese New Year—what if we made some lactose-free cakes and cookies for the community centre? It would be a nice little gesture, right?      Yeah, that sounds like a good idea! I mean, I don’t mind making some snacks, and it’s not like we have to do it all ourselves. Maybe we can use the chess and draughts pieces we have for money, like you said. We can sell them to raise some funds for the cakes, or just donate them.      Can we really do that? I mean, do people even want that? I don’t know, maybe they’d think it’s weird?      Oh, I think it could be a fun way to get people thinking about giving. You know, small acts of kindness can mean a lot. I remember reading about a guy who used to trade chess pieces for food at the local market. It helped people who were struggling, and it gave him a sense of purpose.      That’s cool! So, maybe we can set up a little stall at the community centre, or even in the park. We can have the cakes and cookies, and the chess pieces. People can either buy something or swap the pieces for a treat.      Exactly! And it could be a way for people to connect with each other. It’s not just about giving, it’s about creating a sense of community. Plus, it’s a great way to spread a bit of joy during Chinese New Year, which is all about family, tradition, and goodwill.      I guess it’s not too bad. I mean, I love playing chess, so it would be fun to see people using the pieces. But do we have enough to go around?      We’ve got a few sets. We could even ask some neighbours to bring their old sets too. And as for the cakes and cookies, we can make some special ones with the chocolate and the lactose-free flour. I’ve been trying a few recipes lately.      I could help! I love baking. Maybe we can make some red bean paste cookies, like they do in China. That would be perfect for the occasion.      Perfect! We could even start planning the setup for next week. And if we get enough support, maybe we can do it again next year.

So, I was just telling my mates about the time I got into a car accident... Well, not  me , but my cousin. She was driving with her friend, and they were both doing 70 on a country road, and then— poof —a sheep darted out in front of them. The car swerved, and the friend got thrown out. She’s got a scar on her forehead now, like a little crescent moon.      A  sheep ? You're telling me that a  sheep  caused a car accident? That’s not just  dramatic , that's  absurd .      I know! But it’s true! The sheep was standing right in the middle of the road, and they didn’t even see it. It was like a scene from  Alice in Wonderland —like, “What happened to the rabbit? Why is there a sheep in the middle of the road?”      I love that you compare it to  Alice . You always say that the world is like a story, and sometimes you’re the only one who can see the clues.      Yeah, I think that’s why I love reading. Sometimes, like, you’re reading a book and you think, “Wait, did they just say that?” And then it clicks, and you’re like, “Oh, this is  Alice in Wonderland ! I’ve read this a million times!”      You’re like a literary detective, aren’t you? I remember when you were little and we were watching  Alice , and you kept trying to point out all the “hidden messages” in the story.      I  still  do. My sister says I’m just being weird, but I think it’s called  analyzing  the text.      Yeah, but when you’re doing it while you’re wearing your yellow dress and doing a ballet move, it’s not  analysis —it’s  performance art .      Oh, you’re  so  cruel. But I  do  think you’re right—there’s something magical about dressing up. Like, when I wear my costume for Halloween, it’s like I’m stepping into another world.      And that’s why I love you. You have this way of seeing the world that’s so different from everyone else. You’re like a collision between  Alice  and the internet. Always wondering, always questioning, always searching for the next story.      Sometimes I wonder if I’ll ever find my own story, you know?      You already have, darling. Every scar, every book you’ve read, every performance you’ve done—it’s all part of yours.

Well, I just had a meeting with the local solar panel group last night, and it’s a bit like a chess game. You’ve got the council, the energy companies, and then the local protest groups, all tangled up. It’s not just about technical stuff—there's a whole political layer to it.      I know. It’s like a battle of ideologies. The council’s trying to keep things moving, but the energy companies are more about profit than community. And the protest groups? They’re like the underdogs, fighting for the village and the environment. But how do you even start? You need research, right?      Exactly. And the research is expensive. I’ve been trying to get the local university to help with some studies on the impact of wind turbines on the landscape and the wildlife. But they say they’ve got more money for renewable projects than for research. It’s frustrating. You need the science to back up your arguments, but the funding’s not there.      That’s the crux of it. I told them last night that without solid data, it’s like trying to fight a war with a tin pot. You have to know the facts. And the real issue is the storage of energy. You can't just have wind or solar without a way to store the power when it's not sunny or windy. That’s the missing piece, isn’t it?      And the government’s subsidizing the big energy firms with billions, while they’re skimping on the research. It’s a shame. I remember reading that the UK gives more money to the fossil fuel industry than to the renewable sector. It’s a bit of a paradox, really. They’re trying to be green, but they’re not funding the tools to make it work.      There’s also the politics of it. The local planners have their own agenda, and sometimes they’re not aligned with the community. I was told that one of the planners on the committee has a side job with a renewable energy company. That’s not good. You can’t trust them when they’re playing both sides.      That’s why the protest groups need to be well-organized. They need a strategy, not just a rant. You’ve got to know the law, go to the right meetings, build alliances.

So, I’ve been thinking, do you really think you’re ready to start learning to drive, Claire? I mean, I remember when I first got my license, I thought I was a pro, but it turned out I was just a bit of a disaster.      Dad, I’ve been doing the theory for ages now, and I’ve got a clean slate. I’m not going to mess this up. Plus, I’ve got the support of the whole family. You can even come with me for the first few lessons, right?      I’d be happy to, love. But I’ve got to say, I’m still amazed you’re doing this at your age. When I was your age, I was still obsessed with the idea of getting a car, but I never actually got one. Worked too hard, kept it all on the back burner.      I know, it’s amazing, isn’t it? I think I’ve got the motivation now that I’ve got the time, and I don’t want to be reliant on the bus anymore. Plus, I’ve got the holidays coming up, and I was thinking—what if I could take a little road trip? Maybe to the seaside?      That’s a good idea. You know, I used to love taking the family down to the coast in the summer. It was a real treat. But these days, it’s more about convenience. Still, a road trip sounds like a great way to get some experience.      You’d better make sure you’re insured, love. I mean, I know you’re the one who’s paying for it, but if you’re going to be out there driving, you need the right cover.      Oh, right, I was going to call the insurance company today. I’ve been meaning to. I’ve got a few questions about the process. Do you think you could help me sort it out?      If I can help, I’ll be glad to. But I’ve got to say, the insurance game can be a bit of a nightmare. You end up paying for things you never even think about, but that’s just how it is.      Yeah, I remember when I first got my insurance, I thought I was getting a bargain, but it turned out I was paying for stuff I didn’t need. Still, it’s a necessary evil.

So, Dad, I was just thinking—when you were younger, you used to bet on the horses like it was nothing, right? I remember you telling me about the time you bet on a horse called “Rocket” and it won the Grand National. You were so proud, you even bought me a new jumper with the winnings.      Oh, aye, that was a good one. I was just a young man then, nae money, nae worries. We used to go down to the track every Saturday, get a cup of tea and a slice of cake, and just talk about the horses. Now, I’m just a retired bloke with a mobile that buzzes like a bee every time someone sends me a message.      I know, I know. You’re always getting notifications about Facebook and the weather. It’s like you’ve been turned into a robot. But I get it—your old phone didn’t have all that, right?      Aye, I used to have a clunky old thing, just for calls and texts. Now, it’s got apps for everything—Facebook, WhatsApp, even a weather app that tells me if it’s going to rain in the next hour. Sometimes I wonder if I should just throw it away and go back to the old ways.      You could, but I’d miss your stories. Like the time you tried to feed the kids with a leftover meat pie and ended up with a fridge full of moldy cheese.      That was a classic. I thought I was being clever, saving money by reusing leftovers, but the kids ended up with tummy aches and I had to go to the shop and buy fresh stuff.      And then you started arguing with the shopkeeper because he said his prices were too high. I remember you saying, “I won’t pay more than I have to, even if it means my kid’s sick.”      Aye, I was fiesty then. Now, I’m more of a quiet bloke. Still, I reckon the government should do something about food banks. If you can’t afford groceries, you shouldn’t have to go without.      I agree. I’ve seen it all—people struggling, kids going hungry. It’s not right. But I suppose we can talk about that another time. For now, let’s just enjoy our tea and biscuits and remember the good old days.      Aye, let’s do that.

So, I was just telling my mate about that time I tried to play golf for the first time. You know, the one where I thought I was going to be the next Tiger Woods.      Oh man, I remember that! I bet you hit the ball so far it landed in a tree, and then you had to climb up to get it back.      No, worse. I hit it straight into the pond. I was so proud, like, “Look at me, I’m a golfer now!” But then I saw the guy in the next tee and he was just like, “You’re not  playing  golf, you’re  accidentally  throwing a ball into a lake.”      That’s rich. You know what’s even worse? I once tried to play a round of golf with my granddad. He used to say, “You’re not learning the game, you’re just mastering the art of getting in trouble.”      That’s pretty much the whole thing, isn’t it? You’re a graduate, aren’t you? I thought you were gonna be the one who “wins” at everything.      Oh, I’m not the one who wins. I just think I’m gonna. And honestly, my surname is  Smith , so I definitely need to “win” at something. Or at least get a nickname that’s a bit more interesting than “Smithy.”      You’re not the only one with a boring surname. I’m a  Taylor , and I’ve been called “Tay” for as long as I can remember. My sister’s got the nickname “Taz.”      That’s worse. You’re like a nickname from a video game. I tried to change my nickname once—called myself “The Professor.” My mates just laughed.      You need to be more dramatic. What if you called yourself “The Bard” after Shakespeare? You’re a student, you’ve got the vibe.      That’s not a bad idea. I mean, I  have  been studying English literature. Maybe I can start writing plays. I’ve got the sarcasm down, and I’ve got the knowledge to back it up.      You’re on fire. Just don’t forget to bring the sarcasm to the golf course.

So, what’s the deal with you lot? You’re always moaning about work, but I’m working my arse off coordinating conferences and events, and I’m still getting paid less than you, Mark. Oh, come on, you don’t even know how to cook. I’ve seen you try. You burnt the toast and then tried to eat it with a knife.      That was  one  time. I’ve been trying to get back into cooking. But for now, I’m just trying to stay healthy.

Well, I’ve been trying to get that thing on my phone to work properly. It’s like trying to teach a cat to do tricks. I’ve had it for months, and I still can’t figure out how to download the latest update.      I know, I’ve been told the same thing. My grand-daughter said it’s simple. I asked my daughter how to do it, and she said, “Just tap the little circle with the ‘A’ in it.” I did that, and the screen flashed, and then everything went black. I thought I’d broken it.      Aye, I had that happen too. I thought I’d been cursed, really. But then I found out it was just a crash.      You’d think the people who made it would at least tell you when it’s crashed. I mean, it’s not like it’s a landmine or something.      You’d think. But I suppose when you’re putting so much effort into making it look sleek and modern, they don’t want to bother with the old-fashioned stuff like telling you when it’s broken.      Anyway, I was just saying, I’ve been looking at the sky a lot lately. That eclipse came through, and it was something else. I thought I’d seen a lot of things in my time, but that was special.      Aye, I remember watching it from our garden. We had a good view. I was trying to take a photo, but the light was too bright. I ended up with just a black square.      I did better. I managed to get a picture of the sun just before it went dark. My daughter said it was brilliant. I think she’s got it on her computer somewhere.      That’s a good idea. I should try that. I’ve been meaning to get back into photography. It’s been ages since I took a decent picture of anything.      Aye, you could do worse than get a camera. I’ve been thinking about starting a garden, too. You know, to keep me busy.      I’m not sure you’ve got the patience for that. But I’m sure you’ll manage. You’ve got the patience of a tortoise.      Yeah, I suppose I do.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that restaurant in Chester that we tried last year? The one with the weirdly shaped pizzas?      Oh, yeah, that place with the ‘mystery toppings’? The old Italian place near the cathedral. Still there?      I think so. I haven’t been there in a while, though. I remember it was always packed with students and locals. You’d have to wait for a table, but the food was solid. I think they still have that famous lasagna that’s been around since the 80s.      Yeah, that’s the one! I swear it’s like the same recipe.
