Anyway, speaking of places, did you ever get that new house on the edge of Tyne and Wear? The one with the green roof?      Oh, you mean the one that’s  still  under construction? I’ve tried to visit it twice, but every time they’ve got a sign saying “Under Development – No Entry.” I think it’s been like that for three years now. I’m starting to think it’s just a land developer’s joke.      I know, it’s like a ghost town. But I heard they’re going to open a co-working space there. I might check it out next time I’m in the area. Anyway, I’m just saying, we should maybe plan a road trip. Pass through Durham, stop at the cathedral, grab a pizza, and maybe check out that new house.      Sounds like a plan. I’ll start researching the best places to stop. I’ve been meaning to drive through the north-east more.

Aye, it's such a treat listening to the birds out there this morning. I’m more of a gardener than a birdwatcher, but I’ve started to notice the difference in the songs as the seasons change. You know, the robins are still singing, but I think I’ve heard a bit of a chaffinch lately. Though I’m not sure if it’s a chaffinch or a greenfinch. Sometimes they sound alike to me.      I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to get my head around bird calls for years. My gran used to say that if you listen carefully, you can tell the difference between a thrush and a blackbird by the way they sing. But I’m not sure I’ve ever managed it. Although, I do remember once mistaking a sparrow for a wren and getting a bit flustered in front of a group of tourists at the local reserve.      That’s the thing with birds, isn’t it? You think you’ve got it figured out, and then they throw you a curveball. I still get confused with the blackbirds and the crows. Though I do love the sound of the magpies. They’re such a cheery bunch, even if they are a bit of a nuisance with their “paa-paa” calls.      Oh, I know. I’ve also started feeding the birds in the garden, which is a bit of a challenge. I’ve got a couple of feeders up, but the squirrels are always trying to take over. I’ve even had to get a bell on the door so I can warn them off. Though I suppose it’s not all bad—I love watching the birds come and go, especially in the mornings. My sister-in-law says I’ve got a “fairy tale garden” now.      Sounds like you’ve got a bit of a garden adventure going on. I’ve been meaning to start feeding the birds too, but I’ve been too busy with work and the dentist. I’ve had this annoying nosebleed lately, and I think the dentist might have something to do with it. I’ve been told it could be a sign of something more serious, like throat cancer. I’m not sure I want to hear that.      Oh, that does sound worrying. I hope it’s nothing serious. I had a friend who had throat cancer, and it was quite a shock.

So, I heard you've been through IVF again, Sarah. How's it going? I know it's been a tough road for you.      Honestly, it's been a rollercoaster. I tried once before, and it didn't work out. But I'm not giving up. I'm just trying to stay positive. It's hard, though. You know how stressful it gets with the appointments and the waiting.      I can only imagine. I used to think I'd never go through that, but now I'm single parenting my daughter, and I'm starting to think about it too. It's not something you really plan for, is it?      No, not really. It just kind of happens. I've got my daughter, and I love her to bits, but I feel like I'm not whole. I mean, I'm not saying I want to have another child, but I do feel like there’s something missing.      I get that. I used to think I’d be the kind of person who would have a family, but life doesn't always work out that way. I guess I’m also thinking about writing a book. I’ve been meaning to for ages, but I keep procrastinating.      That’s so brave of you. I’ve always wanted to write, but I just don’t know where to start. Have you thought about what kind of book you want to write?      It’s kind of a memoir, but not just about me. It's about the experience of being a single parent, the struggles, the ups and downs. I think it could help others feel less alone.      That sounds amazing. I’d love to read it. Have you thought about how you’re going to handle social media? I mean, that’s such a big part of how people share their lives these days.      I’ve been thinking about it. I want to use it as a platform to share my story, but I also want to be careful about how much I reveal. It's such a double-edged sword. On one hand, it can be empowering, on the other, it can be overwhelming.      I know. I’ve been on and off social media for years. It's like you’re always being judged. But I also think it’s important to stay connected with people, especially when you're in your 40s and you're navigating such big life changes.

You know, I’ve been thinking a lot about education lately. It’s such a big part of people’s lives, isn’t it? Especially for someone like me, teaching languages is all I’ve ever known. But I can’t help but wonder—what do you think about the state of education these days? It feels like it’s changed so much since I was in school.      Oh, I’ve seen quite a few changes over the years. I used to teach in the sixties and seventies, when things were pretty different. You had to work your way up from scratch. No computers, no internet—just pen and paper. But I have to say, the system back then had its own sort of rigidity. You had to be good at memorizing, and that was about it.      That sounds quite different from now. I teach at a college, and I find that students these days are more tech-savvy, but often struggle with the basics—like grammar and spelling. It’s a bit of a contradiction, isn’t it? They can write emails and text messages flawlessly, but when it comes to formal writing, they’re lost.      You’re not wrong. I remember one time I had a student who could type a whole essay in ten minutes, but it was full of spelling mistakes and grammatical errors. It was a real eye-opener. I suppose the pressure to perform in a digital world has made students careless with the basics.      Exactly. It’s a bit frustrating, but I suppose that’s part of the world we live in. I guess I’m just lucky I had the right teachers when I was growing up. My father was a school inspector, so I had some pretty strict rules. He always said, “If you want to succeed, you have to put in the work.”      Sounds like a solid philosophy. I used to tell my students the same thing. “If you want to move up in life, you have to be willing to work for it.” And that’s the thing—people like you, who are in education, are the ones who can really make a difference. It’s not just about teaching subjects; it’s about shaping minds.      That’s the beauty of what we do. It’s not just about knowledge—it’s about inspiring and enabling others to reach their potential.

So, I was just tellin’ me nan about this new album I got. It’s this indie band from Leeds, y’know? Proper gritty, real raw stuff. She said she’d rather listen to the radio, but I told her it’s like the sound of the town when it’s raining and the lights are out. Proper down-to-earth.      I can imagine. I’ve been listenin’ to a lot of that kind of music lately. Actually, I just downloaded this new album by a band from Sunderland. It’s got that real northern edge to it, y’know? Not like the poppy stuff you hear on the radio. Proper raw and real.      Yeah, I’ve been hearin’ about that too. But I’m more of a classic rock guy. Though I’ll admit, there’s something about that British indie scene that’s just...  different . I mean, it’s got that grit, that roughness, like the kind of music you’d hear in a pub in Manchester or Newcastle.      I’m with you on that. I’ve been listenin’ to some of that stuff on my commute. Though I’m still partial to the classics. I mean, I’ll never forget the first time I heard The Rolling Stones. It was like a thunderclap in my ears. Real raw, real powerful. But I’ve been keepin’ up with the new stuff too. There’s some real talent out there.      Yeah, and don’t get me wrong, I still love a good rock band. But I’ve been tryin’ to branch out more. I mean, I watched this film the other day called  The Death of Stalin . It was proper dark, but I couldn’t stop laughin’. It’s like the kind of comedy that makes you question your own sanity.      Oh, I saw that too! It was intense. I was so nervous I’d be offended, but it was so funny. I think it’s the kind of film that makes you wonder what the director was thinking the whole time.      I’ve been meaning to see that. But I’m more of a romantic comedy guy. Though I do love a good drama. I mean,  The Time Traveler’s Wife  was a real tear-jerker. Made me think about time in a whole new way.      I’ve seen that one. I think I cried more than I should have. But I love that kind of emotional depth.

So, I was at the gym this morning, and this guy was doing this like...  dramatic  pose after his workout, like he'd just stared down a mountain or something. I was thinking, “Mate, you’re in a gym, not a movie set.”      Yeah, I saw that on Instagram the other day—some gym bro doing a whole routine in a mirror, like he's got a personal trainer in there. It was so over the top. I almost fell off my chair.      Honestly, I think people take gyms too seriously these days. I mean, the last time I went, I just did a few squats and called it a day. I’m not trying to flex or anything. I’m just trying to stay healthy.      Yeah, but if you’re going to do it, you might as well do it right. I mean, I play games for a living, and even I have to stay in shape. I’ve got this new game coming out, and I need to be able to run around in the game without collapsing from exhaustion. I’ve started going to the gym a few times a week.      You? A game developer? I thought you were more of a couch potato type. You know, the guy who spends all his time in front of a screen, eating snacks and watching cat videos.      Hey, I’ve got a degree, not a hoodie. I’m not a kid anymore. I have responsibilities. Plus, I’ve been trying to get into shape so I can actually run around without getting winded during the game’s multiplayer mode.      That’s noble. I think I’d rather just ride a bike. I mean, I’m a teacher, not a game developer. I can’t even run a mile without stopping to catch my breath. But I do love the idea of being active. I’ve been planning a trip to France this summer. I wanted to take a short hiking trip with some friends. It’s just been the wrong time, you know? Work’s been hectic.      I totally get that. I’ve been wanting to go to Spain for a while. I’m thinking of taking a kids’ camp group there. I mean, it’s not exactly a beach, but it’s got good weather, and the kids seem to like it. It’s a chance to get out of the office for a while.

You’ve got to be kidding me. That ref just missed the clearest penalty of the season. I don’t care if it’s a friendly, you can’t just let that go. It’s not like we’re playing for the cup or anything.      Yeah, yeah, I know. But you know what? If it wasn’t for that miss, we’d probably be down by two or three. Maybe even out of the game. Sometimes you’ve got to be lucky. Especially when you’re playing against a team that’s got more experience.      Experience? They’ve been playing for years and still can’t get a decent block. I mean, look at that centre-back. He’s like a brick wall – if he was made of bricks. But he’s just standing there like he’s got a cricket bat instead of a foot.      Yeah, I saw that. And the keeper? He looked like he was trying to juggle the ball instead of catching it. It’s like he’s been watching a tutorial on YouTube. “Oh, I should keep my legs wide, and my arms up, and everything will be fine.”      Yeah, and it worked too – till the last second. I swear, sometimes these players act like they’ve never seen a goal before. You’d think after playing for so long, they’d have at least one decent save in them.      I know, right? But I guess it’s all part of the game. You can’t control everything. Even if you’re playing for your hometown team, you still have to accept that sometimes the ref’s not on your side.      Yeah, but that was just one game. I still think we should have won. I mean, we’ve got the best players in the league. We should be up there with the top teams.      Well, maybe next week. We’ve got a few more games to play. And if we keep this up, I think we might just make it to the next round. Still, I’m not sure how we’ll manage Easter. I’ve got a few cousins coming over, and I’m not sure if I can even watch a full game without someone asking me about the egg hunt.      Yeah, I remember that. You were trying to explain the rules of football to my aunt last year. She thought it was a type of egg dyeing.

Ah, look at those two — they were barely standing on their feet when we took this photo. I can still remember the day, lads were running around like mad, shouting at the carousel like it was going to take them to Iceland or something.      Yeah, I remember that. Dad kept trying to get us to ride the Ferris wheel, but we were too scared. I mean, what if it broke?      Didn’t it? You were so scared you wouldn’t even sit down. Still, it’s funny how much they’ve grown. I still can’t believe they’re older than me now.      They’ve come a long way, haven’t they? I remember the first time they ran the London Marathon — both of them. It was such a proud moment. I mean, running 26 miles at their age, it’s not easy, but they showed so much determination.      Yeah, it was incredible. They both finished, and the way they did it made me want to sign up for one too.      Be careful, love. You might end up with a sore leg and no medals.      It’s not too late for you to join them. Besides, you’ve got the same stubbornness as your grandfather — just in a different way.      Yeah, I’d say I’ve got the same stubbornness as you, Dad. I mean, I’ve been trying to get you to take me to the cinema for weeks now.      You know I love the cinema, but it’s not every day I go. My wife’s got the toddler to look after, and I’ve got work. But I’ll tell you what — if you ever get me to go, I’ll take you to see that new one about Iceland.      Iceland? You mean the one with the Northern Lights? I thought you were going to take us there for our birthday.      That was the plan, love. But with the toddler and the work, it’s harder than it looks. But we’ll get there.      Yeah, I think it’s worth waiting for. Just like the London Marathon.      It’s amazing how time flies. I remember when they were little, and now they’re both running their own marathons.      It’s a beautiful thing. Yeah, we’ve got a lot to be proud of.      And we’ve got a lot more to look forward to.      Including a trip to Iceland.

So, I just made this really nice vegetable quiche for lunch. I thought it would be a nice change from the usual. I’ve been trying to get more creative with my cooking lately.      That sounds lovely. I love quiche. It’s one of those classic comfort foods. I always make mine with spinach and mushrooms. It’s like a little breakfast in the middle of the day.      Yeah, I tried adding some leeks and some goat cheese. It gave it a nice tang. I remember when I was a kid, my mum used to make quiche every Sunday. She called it “Sunday glory.”      Oh, I still remember that! You used to have to wait all week for that. I think it was one of the few times you could have something a bit special. I used to help her make it, even though I was just a kid. I’d stand at the counter and just watch, pretending I knew what I was doing.      You were always the one who wanted to help, weren’t you? I remember you used to try to whisk the eggs and make a mess with the flour.      That’s right. You were always so enthusiastic, even if it didn’t always work out. I remember one time you spilled the whole bowl of flour on the floor and had to clean it up with the broom. It was a disaster.      Oh, yes, and then you had to make the quiche again. I think it was a Tuesday. That was a Monday. Never mind. Anyway, it was a mess, but it was fun.      It was a lesson about patience. I think I learned that early on. But speaking of childhood, I’ve been reminiscing about some of the games we used to play. Remember those little wooden toys we had? The ones with the little animals and the little cars?      Oh, those were the best. I still have one of those wooden farm sets. I remember we used to set up the whole thing and pretend we were running a farm. You were always the farmer, and I was the cow.      I was the cow, and you were the farmer. I remember you used to try to milk me with a rubber tube. You were so serious about it. I don’t know how you ever got anything out of me.      I was really into it, though.

Aye, it's a real shame what's happened to the village, isn't it? I've been knocking around these parts all my life, and it's like a different place now.      I know, love. I remember when the market was still going on every Saturday, and everyone knew each other by name. Now it's just a few shops, and even those are closing down.      You know, I was talking to the old chap from the pub the other day. He said he's been getting the same letters from the council about the town hall. They want to knock it down and build a car park or something. I said, "What, the old town hall? That’s the only place we had for meetings when we were kids."      Oh, I remember that. It was the only place we could get a drink before the pub closed. And the council used to bring in the odd statue, didn’t they? That one of the old war hero, it was so big, it scared the horses.      Aye, and the way it looked at the top of the hill, you could see it from miles away. It was the pride of the village. Now they want to turn it into a shopping centre? I don’t know, it all feels a bit strange.      I think it’s just the way things go, love. You know, the world changes, and we just have to make do with what we’ve got. I mean, I’ve been here all my life, and I can’t say I’ve ever been anywhere else.      I suppose that’s true. I’ve always thought that if you’re born in a place, you’re tied to it somehow. Even when times are hard, you still feel a connection. I don’t know if I’d ever feel comfortable being anywhere else.      I know what you mean. I’ve lost a few friends over the years, and the ones I’ve kept, we still get together if we can. Life’s too short, isn’t it? We might not be able to do much, but we can still enjoy what’s left.      To the village, then. May it stand tall, even if it’s changed.      To the village, love. May it stand tall. And may we all be able to keep a bit of it in our hearts, even when it’s not there anymore.

So, I was just telling my mum about the cat I got for Christmas. Oh, I’ve been there. I once walked into a lesson thinking it was the wrong class and almost got stuck in a circle of year fives. I think the kids still go off me.      I think we’ve all had our moments. Speaking of work, how’s your holiday planning going? I’m trying to get my head around when to take my next trip. Well, I suppose we've got to think about how to stop the strings breaking again. They've been a real pain, haven't they? I tried using more adhesive, but it just didn't hold.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I've had the same problem. I tried using cable ties, but they don't look very good and they're not very secure. Maybe we could use something more durable? Like maybe a stronger type of thread or even some sort of elastic?      Hmm, elastic might work, but it could stretch over time. I remember when I used to teach, we had these little plastic clips that kept the strings in place. But they’re not really made for this kind of use anymore.      Right, and I think I read somewhere about using special strings designed for badminton rackets. They’re heavier and more resistant to breaking. I could check the dimensions and see if they fit the rackets we have.      That’s a good idea. Also, the positioning of the strings matters—too tight and they snap, too loose and they don’t last. People might be willing to pay more for longer-lasting rackets.      I like that. We could even call it “Fleet Racket Repairs.” Wait, did you just say  fleet ?      Yes, I did. Fleet could mean a group of rackets, or maybe it’s a play on the word  fleet  as in quickly moving.      Oh, that’s clever. I think it works. That’s a great idea. And I’ve got an idea for the haircut. I was just about to cut my ear lobe and the stripe in my hair, but I think I might have messed it up a bit.

Well, I’ve been thinking about that picture on the wall again, you know. That one with the blue and green tones. It’s got a real feel to it, don’t you think? Like it’s capturing the Norfolk sky on a misty morning.      I couldn’t agree more. Aye, it’s got that kind of quiet, reflective mood. I’ve always found that kind of art calming. It’s like the world slows down when you look at it. You know, I used to take my grandkids to the gallery in Norwich, and the way they’d sit and stare at the paintings… it was like they were trying to talk to the artist.      That’s actually really interesting, Mums. I mean, I’ve always thought about art in terms of technique and form, but I never really considered the emotional connection people have with it. It’s like a bridge, isn’t it? Between the creator and the observer?      Exactly. And the more you study art, the more you realize how much it can mean to different people. You can have one piece that’s completely different to another, and yet both evoke something deep. I remember once seeing a painting in London that was all about isolation, and it just struck a chord with me, even though I didn’t fully understand it at first.      Aye, and that’s the thing, isn’t it? Even if you don’t get it at first, there’s something about art that makes you want to. I mean, I’m not one for galleries, but I can’t help but look at that painting and think, “This person must have seen something special in that moment.”      It’s true. I used to work with children, and one of the things I tried to teach them was how to look closely. You know, not just see the shapes, but feel the story behind it. It’s a skill, like reading, almost. You learn to read the world through different eyes.      And that’s what makes art so powerful. It doesn’t just sit there—it invites you in, challenges you, and sometimes changes you. It’s not just about what you see, but what you feel when you see it.      And that’s what I love about it. It’s a conversation that never ends. A dialogue between past and present, creator and viewer.

So, I just wanted to say, I am  so  over the whole “girls are always so hard to please” thing. I mean, if you think about it, it’s not even that girls are difficult — it’s that  we  are so used to being the ones who are supposed to be nice and understanding. I mean, when you're a guy, you can just walk into a room, say “Hey, wanna go out?” and it’s like, “Sure, cool.” But if you’re a girl, it’s like you have to go through this whole litany of “Are you sure? I’m not sure if I’m ready. I need to think about it.”      Exactly! I mean, I’m not saying I don’t have any of that, but it’s like the minute you say “I want to go out,” it’s like you’re being super dramatic or something.      Oh, I know. Ugh, that’s just  so  frustrating. I mean, why does it have to be so complicated? I’m not saying it’s not hard, but sometimes I feel like we’re all just  overthinking  it.      Yeah, but then again, it’s different for everyone. I mean, I’m a mental health nurse, so I see a lot of people who are dealing with anxiety, and a lot of them just…  overthink  everything. So maybe that’s just me.      Wait, are you saying that girls are just naturally more anxious?      No, no, no. I’m just saying that sometimes the whole dating thing is like,  way  more complicated than it needs to be. And I think part of it is that we’re all so used to being  the  one who has to be in control. Like, we always have to be the ones who are  proactive  in relationships.      Yeah, I get that. I mean, I’m not exactly a pro at it myself, but I think part of it is just that we’re all so busy with work and everything.

You know, I’ve been thinking about our routines lately. I mean, I’m a PA to a director, so my days are pretty structured, but I think I’ve been doing a lot of the same things for years. It’s like a habit now. Do you ever feel like you’re just going through the motions?      Yeah, I can relate. I’m an IT consultant, so I’m always on the move, but even I have my routines. I’ve been trying to break the habit of smoking when I get stressed. You know, I used to light up every time I felt overwhelmed. Now, I just take a walk or do some push-ups. I think we’re all just trying to survive this life. But sometimes I wonder if people overestimate their intelligence. I’ve got a friend who insists that women aren’t as capable as men in tech. He says it’s just a matter of intelligence, but I don’t know. Maybe he’s just not looking hard enough. I mean, I work in a field where women are making a big impact. It’s not about being smarter—it’s about opportunity and support.      Exactly. I think feminism isn’t about being better than men, it’s about equal opportunities. And I’ve seen how different cultures shape people’s views on gender roles. Growing up in Kettering, I always felt like women were expected to be more nurturing, but now, I see so many women excelling in every area. It’s a shift, but I think it’s for the better.      I agree. I think we’ve come a long way, but there’s still a lot to do. And I always say, it’s not about changing the world—it’s about changing our own attitudes. Like, I used to think drinking was the only way to unwind, but now I just enjoy a glass of wine or a nice walk. It’s not about giving up everything, it’s about choosing better habits.      I think that’s the key.

So, I think we’ve decided on the farm visit for today, then? I’ve got the tickets sorted and the car all ready to go. Just need to make sure the kids are buckled up and don’t start a food fight in the back.      You mean like last time when we went to the zoo? Though I’m still worried about the sandwiches.      You know what they say—every child needs a snack, especially after the school bus.      Exactly. Just pick one and we’ll watch it on the way.      I want the one with the cows!      Alright, the cows it is. Now, just make sure you don’t start a food fight in the car.      I won’t.      I’m just glad we’re going to the farm today. School was so boring.      I know, I know. You two were both so distracted in class today.      It’s just so hard to concentrate when the teacher keeps asking questions and I don’t know the answers.      That’s okay, it happens. But today’s going to be different. The bus is leaving in thirty minutes.      Okay! I’ll get my sandwich.

So, I was just thinking about that video I saw of the Olympic opening ceremony—what a spectacle! I mean, it was like a whole festival of lights and music, right?      Yeah, it was amazing. I watched it live, actually. My friend was over, and we got the whole thing on the big screen. It was like a whole nation coming together, wasn’t it?      Oh, totally. Speaking of which, have you seen the new British celebrity that’s been everywhere lately?      You mean that guy who’s always on the news? The one with the weird hair? I tried to watch a clip of him the other day, but it was so surreal. I still don’t get why he’s such a big deal.      I know, right? It’s like he’s got a whole personality just for being in the media. But seriously, I did hear he’s been working on some art projects lately. I think he’s doing some installations at a gallery in London.      Oh? That’s something, I guess. I’ve been meaning to look into more art stuff. I’ve been knitting a lot lately, actually. My mum sent me some wool from her stash, and I’ve been making a scarf for my sister.      That’s cool. I do a bit of knitting too—just basic stuff. I’ve been making some socks. It’s a bit of a meditative process, isn’t it?      Definitely. It’s like a little escape. I always feel more focused when I’m actually doing it. I guess it’s the same way people get into meditation or something.      Yeah, I suppose it’s a form of mindfulness. Though I’ll admit, I’m not the best at it. I’ve messed up a few rows and had to rip it all out.      It’s all part of the learning curve. You know, when I was younger, I used to think I was pretty good at it, but now I’ve kind of realized that it’s more about patience than skill.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to get into that IMAX in Manchester? You were so excited about the 3D effect, and you kept shouting “Look at this!” every time something popped out of the screen. I nearly had a heart attack when the dinosaur came out of the corner!      Oh come on, you were the one who insisted we go in the first place. You said it was “a must-see for any true movie buff.” And don’t forget the smell of that popcorn—it was like walking through a candy shop!      Well, I had to live up to my reputation as the movie expert, didn’t I? Though I must say, the 3D was a bit of a letdown. I mean, the effects were fine, but it felt like we were just paying extra for the same old film. Still, it was fun in a way. I think the real highlight was when we got stuck in the queue outside the cinema for over an hour—after the previews, of course!      Oh, that was a classic. You were so impatient, you kept checking the time every five minutes. I was just hoping you’d give up and take us to the local cinema, but no, you had to prove a point.      You know what I love about London? The mix of old and new. You can have an ancient museum next to a modern IMAX. It’s like the city itself is a living museum. I was telling my students the other day that museums are the perfect place to learn about history without feeling like you’re in a classroom. You can just wander around and take it all in.      I suppose you’re right. But I still think the real treat is the public transport. I mean, you can get from one end of London to the other in a matter of minutes. I never thought I’d say this, but I’ve started getting out of the house more now. Just to see the sights and not have to rely on a car.      That’s a huge step forward, mate. I remember when you said you’d never get back on a bus or train after that time in the rain. But here we are, talking about museums and IMAX films, and all because you decided to take the Tube.

So, mate, I’ve been thinking—what’s the plan for Christmas? We’ve got the kids coming over, and I’m feeling like we need to do something decent. Maybe a proper dinner?      Yeah, I was just thinking the same. I’ve got the turkey in the fridge, and the vegetables are all prepped. But I think we should do something different this year. Not just the usual stuff. Maybe bring in a few of the old mates from uni?      That sounds good. You know, I was just telling my sister about how we used to have these mad Christmas parties at the student union. Remember when we had that one with the Christmas lights and the karaoke machine?      Oh, don’t even get me started. I still have the DVD of that night. It’s a bit of a mess, but it’s a good memory. I reckon we should do something like that. Rent a hall, get some lights, maybe even hire a few of those Christmas trees that you can plug in.      That’s a solid plan. I’ve got a few old friends in the area—those blokes from the postgrad course. We could all meet up. Mate, I’ve been meaning to ask, have you seen that new film about the Christmas spirit? The one with the dad and the kid?      Yeah, I saw it. It’s a bit cliché, but it’s got that warm, fuzzy feeling. I think it’s got a scene where the dad comes home early and finds the kid baking cookies. It’s a bit sentimental, but I think it’ll be a good watch before Christmas.      Definitely. I think it’ll help set the mood. Maybe we could have a little ‘movie night’ after the dinner. I’ve got a few classics I could bring— Home Alone ,  National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation , and even that cult classic with the reindeer.      Oh, I’d love that. I’ve been meaning to rewatch  National Lampoon’s  for ages. It’s the kind of thing that brings people together. And if we’re going to have a movie night, we might as well make it a proper event.      To Christmas, then. To friends, and to not falling into the same old traps every year.      To not falling into the same old traps. And to a Christmas that’s a bit more memorable than last year’s.

So, I just saw this post on Twitter about this new restaurant in Margate. It’s got some kind of “art deco” vibe, but the photos look like they were taken in a flat in Islington. I don’t even know what they’re  serving .      Yeah, I saw that too. The review said the food was “experiential” and “modern,” but the actual photo of the steak looked like it was from a takeaway. And then there was this comment saying, “If you want to be confused, go there.”      That’s the problem with internet reviews these days. You can’t tell if it’s real or just someone trying to make a joke. I mean, I had this customer last week who left a five-star review for my café saying, “The coffee was amazing, and I even got a free croissant.” But I didn’t give away any croissants.      That’s not even funny. I’ve had worse. My mate’s uncle used to run a sandwich shop in London, and one of his customers left a review saying, “The sandwiches were so good, I considered buying the whole shop.” Then he left a photo of a sandwich with a skull and crossbones.      That’s dark. I mean, I get it—some people just want to make a point, but it’s not helpful. I read this one review for a place in Margate that said, “I came for the lobster, I left with a headache.” It was basically saying the food was terrible, but it sounded like a conspiracy about the government.      It’s like people think reviews are some kind of art form now. I mean, if you’re going to leave a review, at least be honest. I got a review once that said, “The service was slow, but the cakes were fresh.” I had to check if they even knew what a cake was.      That’s probably the best one I’ve heard. I’ve had some weird ones too. One said, “I had a bad time, but the Wi-Fi was really good.” Like, what even  is  this?      Yeah, I can see that. It’s like people don’t know what to say, so they just mix it up.      I just want to know if the place is worth going to. I’m thinking of opening up a little café in Margate. I mean, the location’s good, and I’ve got a decent idea.

So, Oisin, what did you do today? I saw you came in like you'd been chased by a giant dog.      I just chased a squirrel, Mummy. It ran up the tree, and I couldn’t get it down. I tried to climb the tree, but it was too high.      You should’ve brought a ladder, Oisin. Or maybe a net. I saw some in the garden. We could’ve caught it for dinner.      Oh, you're already planning your next meal. I love that. But I think the squirrel will be fine. It’s not like it’s going to stay up there forever. Though I do wonder if it’s the same one every day. I think it’s been around since you started school.      I found some bird eggs in the garden this morning, you know. Just sitting there, perfectly still. I was so tempted to take them, but I thought maybe they’re not ready yet. I mean, they looked like they were just hatching.      That’s a tough call. I remember when I was a kid, I used to collect bird eggs all the time. My mother would get really upset and tell me it was wrong. But I did it anyway. Silly me.      I think it’s not just about collecting eggs. I think it’s more about the experience. Like, when I was younger, I used to feed the gerbils in the classroom. They’d come running when they heard the sound of the door opening. It was so cute.      Can we get gerbils? I want a pet! I want to feed them too. My friend Lucy has a hamster, and it’s so fluffy.      You know, I think it’s a good idea. But we need to be responsible. Maybe we can start with a small animal, like a hamster or a gerbil. But we have to make sure we can look after it properly.      I remember when I was your age, I had a goldfish. I named it Goldy. I used to feed it every day, and it would come to the top of the bowl. I still remember that.      You know, I think we should start a little garden this summer. We can grow some raspberries and vegetables. You know, like the ones we had last week. I think Oisin would like that.      Yeah! I can help with that! I can plant the seeds, and then we can eat the vegetables.

I was just thinking, I need to get some fresh veggies for the week. I got the list from the fridge, but I wonder if I should stop by the local market or just go to the supermarket. You know, the one near the station?      I think the market’s better, if you can manage it. You know how fresh the produce is there. Plus, I’ve seen some of the locals doing their own thing, like bartering or just chatting. It’s more of a community vibe. Although, I suppose if you’re short on time, the supermarket’s more efficient.      I’d say the supermarket’s more efficient, but I’ve never been to a market. I just shop online these days. It’s easier, especially with the arthritis in my hands. But I suppose if you like to talk to people, the market’s the way to go.      I like the idea of chatting, but I’m always worried about running out of time. I have to pick up my cousin from the station later, and then I have to drive her home. It’s a bit of a tight schedule.      That’s a lot. I get that. I’ve been meaning to ask you—do you mind if I help you with the shopping sometime? I don’t get out much, but I’d rather do it with someone than be by myself.      Of course not! I’d welcome the company. It’s good to have someone to chat with. You know, it’s not just about the shopping; it’s about the conversation.      Oh, I know what you mean. I used to go to the local café with my late husband. We’d talk about everything—politics, food, even the weather. It’s nice to have that connection.      I miss that. I used to go to a little café when I was working, but now I just stay home. I’ve started getting my hair cut by the local barber. He’s been doing it for years, and he’s pretty good.      That’s a good idea. I’ve been meaning to get my eyebrows done. I’ve been trying to do it myself with镊子, but it’s not working out. I’m starting to look like a raccoon.      Oh, I know the feeling! I tried doing mine when I was younger, and I ended up with something like a little moustache.

Well, I think it’s time we start weening the baby. I’ve been reading up on it, and it seems like the right time. You know, they’re getting more mobile, and it’s just easier for us all.      Yeah, I agree. It’s been a bit of a challenge, but I think we’re ready. Have you decided on how you want to approach it? Gradually or more abruptly?      I think gradually is better. It gives the baby time to adjust. I’ve seen some examples online, and they do it by slowly reducing the number of feeds each day. But I also heard that every baby is different, so we’ll have to watch how they react.      Yeah, I think that makes sense. I mean, we’ve noticed that she’s more interested in exploring now, so maybe she’ll be more willing to try solids. Have you thought about when you want to start the weaning process?      I was thinking maybe early next week, after the weekend. That way, we can have a little buffer if things don’t go as planned. I’ll make sure to prepare some purees and keep track of what she likes and dislikes.      That sounds like a good plan. And I can help you out with the cooking. I’ve been making some baby-friendly meals lately, and I’d love to share some recipes with you. It’s been fun experimenting with different textures and flavors.      That would be great. I’ve been a bit stuck on what to prepare. I think I need some more variety. Also, I’ve been thinking about the sign language classes we’re both going to. How’s that going for you?      Honestly, it’s been a bit tough. I feel like I’m not grasping the basics yet. But I’m determined. I think it’s going to help with communication, especially once the baby starts to understand more.      You’ll get the hang of it. It’s just like learning anything new. And it’ll be so useful when the baby starts to show more interest in interacting with us. I can’t wait to see you both at the classes.      I can’t wait either. It’s been a great way to connect with other parents, and I’ve made a few friends. I think we’ll be ready for the next step in the baby’s development, whether it’s weaning or learning to sign.

You know, I still can't get over how different it is out here compared to London. I mean, I’ve walked through so many villages, but none of them feel quite like this. It's like the air is… cleaner, or something.      Yeah, I feel the same. It’s not just the air—it’s the rhythm of it all. The way the hills roll on forever, and the way the light hits the fields at this time of day. It’s almost like the landscape has a heartbeat.      It does, doesn’t it? I think I’ve always felt that way about the countryside. Even as a kid, when I’d come up here with my parents to visit my aunt, I’d just stand on the hill and feel this strange sense of peace. It’s like the world doesn’t rush here.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? No rush. No traffic, no deadlines, just the wind in the trees and the occasional farm animal. I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. I’ve been working long hours in London, and I’ve been… stressed.      I know. I can see it in you. You’ve been more quiet than usual. You need this. It’s good for you.      I just… miss it. The simplicity of it. I mean, not that I don’t love London, but it’s so different. You can’t really ‘feel’ the countryside in a city, can you?      No, you can’t. It’s like it’s all around you, but you don’t notice it until you step away from the noise. I think that’s why I chose to come here. To live here, actually. I wanted to be part of this.      That’s good. I like that. I think we’re both trying to find our way back to that place. Not just physically, but… emotionally.      Yeah. It’s not just about the view or the hills. It’s about the space to breathe. To think. To be.      I think that’s why we’re here, together. In the countryside. Just like we were when we first met.      I’ll take that as a compliment.      It’s a compliment. And I think we’re both better for it.      Yeah. I think we are.      So, what’s next? Another hill? Or should we head back to the village?

So, I was just thinking about that film we watched last night,  The Banshees of Inisherin —it was so bleak, wasn’t it? I mean, I get it, it’s about friendship and the way it can unravel, but I just couldn’t stop thinking about how the whole thing felt like a bad breakup.      Yeah, I felt the same. I mean, it’s got that raw, emotional weight, right? But you know what? It’s not like the films we used to watch, the ones with all the explosions and everything. This one just . . . breaks you down.      Totally. I mean, I’ve been thinking about it all week. I can’t stop wondering how the characters even ended up in that situation. You know what’s weird? It’s like the kind of thing that could happen in real life. Like, with a friend—just slowly pulling away, and you don’t even notice it until it’s too late.      Yeah, I guess. I’ve been thinking about that too. It reminded me of when Tom started working with that agency in London. You remember how it was? Suddenly, he was gone for weeks at a time, and then he’d just drop by for a coffee and act like everything was fine. It was so weird.      Yeah, I remember. And I get it, he’s a consultant engineer, so it’s all about meetings and deadlines. But still, it felt like he was cutting off from the people he used to hang out with. I mean, even your mum said she felt left out.      I know. But you know what? I think that’s just the way it is now. Everyone’s so busy with their ‘career’ and all that. It’s like, if you’re not working 80 hours a week, you’re not trying hard enough.      Ugh, I hate that attitude. It’s like people think life is just about climbing the ladder, not about actually  living . But I guess with the way things are, you can’t really blame them.      I guess not. It’s just weird how the more successful you get, the more you lose touch with people.      Wait, so what about you? You said you’ve been working on that bike project, right?      Yeah, it’s going okay. I mean, I’ve got the design sorted, and I’ve got a few investors on board.

You know, I’ve always loved the way the countryside feels when it’s just you and the open space. It’s like everything slows down here, isn’t it?      No doubt about it. It’s a far cry from the chaos of London, isn’t it? I still remember the first time I came out here with you. You were walking with that bunch of tulips in your hand, like you were about to plant them in the middle of the road.      Oh, that was the day we got stuck in the middle of a field! I thought I was just taking a shortcut, but the path had been washed away by the rain. We ended up walking for nearly an hour just to get back to the main road.      And then you insisted we’d found a ‘hidden garden’ because of the wildflowers. I almost believed you for a second.      Well, it was a pretty rare sight, wasn’t it? I do love the way the flowers bloom here—especially in spring. It’s a different kind of beauty than the city, don’t you think?      Absolutely. But it got me thinking about cash crops and economics. You know, I read this article the other day about how the countryside is struggling because of the decline in traditional farming. It’s not just about aesthetics anymore—it’s about livelihoods.      Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. I mean, you can’t just have a field of flowers and expect people to make a living from it. There’s a lot more to it than just beauty.      Exactly. I was thinking about a language study I did once—how people in rural areas are becoming more isolated because of the economic shift. It’s like they’re being pushed out of their own communities.      That’s a heavy thought. But I guess that’s part of what makes the countryside such a deep place to live—there’s a lot of history and meaning in the land.      You know, I still think the best thing about being out here is the quiet. It’s not about work or deadlines or even football. It’s just being.      And that’s why I never want to leave. Even though I live in London, I always come back here. It’s like a reset button for the soul.      I couldn’t agree more.

So, I was just thinking about that flat we saw in Newcastle. You know, the one with the huge garden and the view of the Angel of the North? It’s got that classic “city living” vibe, but also the space to actually live.      Yeah, I remember that one. It was a bit pricey, though. I mean, I’ve got a postgrad degree and all, but I’m not exactly rolling in cash. Plus, I still need to pay off that loan from my engineering courses.      I know, I know. But think about it—living in the city, close to the station, and that view of the Angel? It’s like a dream. And you’d be closer to the football matches, too. I mean, Sunderland’s got that new stadium, right?      Yeah, I mean, I’ve been to a couple of games. The atmosphere’s amazing, even if the team’s not exactly flying. I reckon we’d both be able to tell you a story or two about that.      Oh, you’d love that. I remember watching a match with my cousin in the north-east. We ended up getting stuck in a queue for ages, and then we had to park three miles away. But the game was worth it.      I can imagine. I once had someone park in a restricted area and got a ticket. I had to pay it, and then I had to explain to my boss why I was late. Still, it was worth it for the game.      That’s the spirit. We’re talking about moving in, though. I mean, I’m not sure if I’m ready to uproot my life. My flat’s got a nice little garden, even if it’s just a few plants.      You’re still living in a little flat with a garden? I thought you were more of a city person.      I’m not a city person—I’m a  Northeastern  person. That’s different. I mean, I love the city, but I still miss the open space.      Well, if you ever decide to make the move, I’m there to help. We can even take the car to look at flats together. I’ve got a spare key, and I know a few good places to park near the Angel.      That’d be nice. I think I’d like that. And we could even go to that new tennis club in the area.

You know, I was watching the news the other day, and they were talking about that celebrity trial—some actor accused of assault. It was all over the headlines. It’s a shame, really. I mean, they’re supposed to be role models, aren’t they?      Yeah, it’s really hard to believe. I mean, they’re on TV every day, doing all sorts of things, and then something like that happens. It’s like, you never know what’s going to happen. But I guess people are just human.      Absolutely. I remember when that one pop star was in the news for some kind of scandal. It was all over the papers. I think it was about drugs or something. It was crazy how fast it all unfolded.      I don’t watch much of that stuff. I prefer to read about nature or animals. Though I do like to hear stories about wildlife, you know? I’ve always been fascinated by birds, especially the geese.      Yeah, I love that too. I’ve seen those geese on the lake near my house. They come in the spring and fly south when it gets too cold. It’s amazing how they know the route, isn’t it?      It really is. I think they’ve been migrating for generations. I’ve been told they follow the same paths year after year. It’s like a big family trip, just without the kids arguing over what to pack.      That’s true! I’ve watched them for years. I even used to walk by the lake every morning. They’d take off in the early hours, all together, like a big convoy. It was so peaceful. I miss that now that I’m retired and don’t go out much.      I used to go there too. Before all the changes with the park, you know. I remember when it was just a quiet spot. Now it’s more crowded, but the geese are still there. I guess they’re the only constant.      Maybe that’s the beauty of wildlife. They don’t change with the times. They just keep doing what they’ve always done. It’s a bit comforting, isn’t it?      Yes, it is. I think that’s why I like to hear stories about them. They remind me of simpler times, when the world wasn’t so fast-paced. You know, when you could just sit and watch the sky and not worry about anything else.

So, I just wanted to say, I am  so  sorry I missed your baby shower last week. I got caught up with a job interview for that teaching position in Manchester. I know it’s not a big deal, but I feel awful I couldn’t make it.      Oh, don’t worry about it, really! I understand completely. I know how busy you’ve been lately. Plus, you’ve been through so much with your own baby stuff, right? You had that miscarriage, and then the adoption process—must have taken a toll on your schedule.      Yeah, it’s been a rollercoaster. I’m still not over it, honestly. But I’ve been trying to focus on the positives. I’ve actually got a job offer now—part-time, teaching English at a local college. I’m so excited, but I’m also a bit nervous about the transition.      That’s amazing! I remember when you were in your first teaching job, you were so passionate about it. You always said you wanted to inspire others, and that’s exactly what you’re doing now. You’re going to be great.      Thanks, you’re so kind. I still miss the classroom sometimes—it’s just so different now. But I think I’ll settle in. I’ve been looking into some food places near the college, though. I thought maybe we could go out to lunch next week?      That sounds lovely. I’d love that. I’ve been meaning to try that new café in the city centre. They have these amazing brunch dishes—like avocado toast with a side of roasted mushrooms and a proper egg. I’ve heard it’s a hit with the locals.      Oh, I’ve heard of it too! I think they do a special weekend menu. Maybe we can try it on Saturday? It’s been ages since we’ve just grabbed a bite together. I miss our lunch dates.      I know, it’s been too long. I’ve been so busy with my own work—teaching English at the high school. I’ve been preparing for a job interview myself next month, actually. They’re offering me a promotion to head of department.      No way! That’s incredible! I remember when you were just starting out, you were so humble and dedicated. You’ve come a long way. I’m so proud of you.

So, I was just thinking about what we're going to do next. Like, where do we go from here? I mean, we've both got these postgrads, and now we're kind of stuck in this limbo between work and… well, not quite work. You know?      Yeah, I feel that. It’s like we’re both at this crossroads. I mean, I’ve been working in admin for a while now, and I’m kind of settled, but I don’t know if it’s the right path long-term. I keep thinking about getting into something more creative or maybe even starting my own thing. But how do you even start?      That’s the thing, isn’t it? I mean, I’m in production control, which is more of a managerial role, but it’s not exactly what I dreamed of doing. I used to think about going into something more technical, but now I’m just trying to make ends meet and figure out what the next step is. I keep telling myself I’ll take a break, but I’m not sure how to even begin.      I hear you. I mean, we’re both in the same boat, in a way. I think the hardest part is not knowing what we want. It’s like we’re waiting for some sign or a new opportunity to come along, but it’s not really happening. I’ve been thinking about moving back to London, but I’m not sure if that’s the right move. I mean, someone like me, who grew up in West Sussex, it’s just different.      Yeah, I know. I was born and raised in Lewisham, so I’ve got that city lifestyle in my blood. But even though I love living in London, sometimes it feels like I’m just going through the motions. I mean, you’re surrounded by people, but it’s not always the most supportive environment for someone trying to figure out their next step.      Exactly. I think we’re both stuck in this cycle of comfort and uncertainty. I mean, we could stick with what we know and be safe, or we could take a risk and go for something we really want. But risks are scary, especially when you’re not sure what the outcome will be.      I know. I think we need to start talking about what we really want, not just what we think we’re supposed to do.

So, I was just telling my cousin about the absolute disaster that was my last flatmate. You know, the one who thought he was dating my best friend? It was  so  awkward, like, I don’t even know how to explain it.      Oh, I  know  that feeling. I had this bloke in my flat who thought he was ‘the one’ for my best mate. I swear, he even used the phrase “I’m gonna ask her out” in front of me. Didn’t even blink.      Oh, I’ve been there too. I mean, not with my best mate, but with my sister. I was 19 and I thought I was in love with this guy who was into her. Made me so jealous. I didn’t even know what jealousy was until then.      Yeah, I remember when my friend’s boyfriend started getting really close to me. It’s like he was trying to replace my friend, or something. I just wanted to scream, “You’re not her boyfriend!”      Oh, I’ve been there too. My friend’s ex was always trying to get back with her – even though she was dating someone else. And it was  so  annoying. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like her, but it’s just so  weird  when people try to play the ‘I’m in love’ card just to get back at someone.      It’s funny, being jealous is one thing, but when people are  trying  to be jealous for you? That’s another story. I had a friend who used to get so jealous of my dates, even though she was barely even dating anyone. It was like she was living in a  soap opera  or something.      You know what’s the worst? When the jealousy is  mutual . Like, when two people are both trying to get back at each other. It’s like a weird game of ‘who can be more annoying’.      Oh, I’ve been in that situation too. My friend had a guy who thought he was in love with me, and I had a guy who thought he was in love with her. It was like we were both in a  rom-com  and we didn’t know it.      I think jealousy is just part of being young and trying to figure out love. You know, like, you get so caught up in it, you forget it’s just a phase.

So, I’ve been thinking about that hockey match we were talking about last week. I got the tickets, by the way—just paid for both of them. You two are going to regret it, I can tell you.      Oh, seriously? That’s awesome, Mum! I told you I’d be there. But I’ve got to ask—what’s the team playing? I think they’re playing against Manchester?      Yeah, that’s right. It’s the Midlands vs. the North. You know how these games get. It’s mostly about the atmosphere. I remember when I was at university, we had a game that turned into a full-blown festival.      Wait, what do you mean? I mean, I’ve never even watched hockey before. Is it like rugby?      No, no, it’s not like rugby. It’s faster, more precise. You’ve got the players skating, passing the ball, and trying to score goals. It’s a real spectacle. I think we’re going to have a great time.      I’m so excited. I’ve been practising my skating for weeks! I’ve even got a new pair of skates.      You know what you’re doing, then? I’d say you’re ready. But don’t get too confident—your brother’s a bit of a powerhouse on the ice.      Yeah, he’s like a tank. I’ve seen him try to do a backhand pass once. It looked like it was going to hit the ceiling.      Oh, it did. It went straight up. My sister had to chase it down.      Well, I’m going to have to be the one to catch it next time. You know, just in case.      That’s the spirit. And speaking of spirit, have you two thought about any travel plans for the holidays?      Yeah! I was thinking about going to Cornwall. I’ve heard it’s beautiful, and there’s a lot of hiking there.      That sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to go. I think I’ll take you both. It’ll be a family trip.      You’d do that? That’d be epic!      I think I’ll come too. I could use a break from the office.      Yeah, I think that’d be cool. We could all go together.      Alright, that’s settled. We’ll plan it out when we get back from the hockey match. And don’t worry, I’ll make sure the tickets are sorted.

So, I just got this really weird message from my cousin Sarah. She said her dog, Biscuit, got into the compost bin and ate the whole thing. I mean, what even  is  a compost bin? Is it like a big bin where you put your food scraps?      Oh, I know, I’ve seen one of those. It’s like that thing in the garden where you put your banana peels and eggshells and stuff. You leave it out and then after a while, it turns into soil or something? I don’t know, it’s a bit gross. But I can’t imagine a dog even  wanting  to eat that. What did she do? Did she have to take him to the vet?      She said the vet said it wasn’t too bad, but they had to give him some sort of stomach medicine. She was panicking the whole time. I mean, I’ve seen dogs eat things they shouldn’t, like socks or paper, but this is like,  compost . It’s got worms and stuff, right?      Oh yeah, and it’s got the occasional bit of rotting leaves or something. I mean, it  is  supposed to be decomposing, but it’s not exactly appetizing. I can’t believe a dog would go for that. I mean, I’ve had a few dogs in my life, and they’re all like, “let’s run through the garden and sniff everything.” But this is just… someone’s food scraps. It’s not even like a normal treat.      I think it’s more about the mystery than the actual food. Like, if you hear your dog knocking over a bin and then you find them with a face full of compost, you’re just like, “what in the world did you do?” I mean, I’d be like, “why are you eating the bin, Biscuit? That’s not your job.”      I can’t believe it. I mean, I’m sure there’s a way to stop that. Maybe you stick the bin in a place that’s hard to get to? Or put a lid on it? I mean, I’ve seen some really weird things happen with dogs around the house. Last week, my neighbor’s cat got into the trash can and swallowed a whole roll of toilet paper. She was hoovering it up like it was a snack.      Oh no!

So, I'm telling you, I've been trying to get those chicken kievs to cook right for weeks. You know how they are—flip them, they stick; don't flip them, they burn. I swear, I've tried everything. Maybe I should just order takeaway again.      You know, Dad, I actually helped you with the chicken kievs last week. You just need to use a little oil and let them cook on both sides. Plus, you forgot to put the breadcrumbs on the outside when you mixed them up. That’s why they kept falling apart.      Oh, don’t be too harsh on him, love. I remember when I was your age, I tried to make a soufflé once and it collapsed like a deflated balloon. You were in hysterics, and I was in tears.      Yeah, and I still have the soufflé pan, stuck in the cupboard. I swear, I could still hear the sound of it collapsing, like a heartbeat gone wrong.      I think it's time we went to visit Granny. She's been asking about you, Dad. You know, she’s been watching that Rugby match every Sunday and wants to know who’s winning.      Oh, I'm not going to let a bunch of Wallies out in the North scare me. I’ll be there, even if it means dragging my biscuits with me.      Hey, you know what I just thought? If you take the biscuits, I’ll take the chicken kievs. You know, to make it fair.      Deal. But if they're not good, I'm blaming you.      And if they are good, I’m blaming you for not being able to cook. You know, you’ve been on Dropbox and Flickr too long, and your brain’s going to mush.      Oh, come on, I’ve got a brain, mate. I just don’t have the time to cook. I’ve got a toddler to look after and a job to manage.      I know, love. And I’m sorry I’m not working. I just… I don’t know where I’m going with this. It’s hard to find work when you’re over thirty and you’ve got a baby.      I know. But you’re doing the right thing. You're taking care of the kids. That’s what matters.      Yeah, and we’ll go visit Granny. We’ll bring the biscuits, the chicken kievs, and maybe even a hedgehog.

So, I just got an email from the seller about the vintage cups and saucers I bid on. They said they’re sending them out today, and I should expect them in the post by Friday. I was hoping we could have them set up on the sideboard by the weekend. It would make such a nice addition to the dining area.      That sounds great. I’ve been thinking about how much I miss having proper china on the table. I mean, I know it’s not like we’re having fancy dinners every night, but having a set like that makes the whole meal feel more special. Did you get the ones with the floral patterns or the ones with the more modern design?      Oh, the ones with the floral patterns — you know, the ones that look like they came from the 1950s. The seller said they were from an antique shop in the north of England. I could almost imagine someone using them every day back in the day. It’s like you can almost hear the clink of the cups and the smell of freshly brewed tea.      That’s exactly the feeling I get when I see them. I remember when we used to go to the local community market and pick up some local produce. I think we should go again soon. It’s a lovely way to start the weekend. I’ve been meaning to ask you — do you want to try the buckwheat bread from the market? I heard it’s really good with some homemade jam.      Oh, I’d love that. I’ve been meaning to try buckwheat bread for a while now. I think it’s a healthier alternative to regular white bread, and it’s got that nutty flavor I really enjoy. Plus, the market’s having a little stall with homemade jams and chutneys this weekend. I was thinking we could make a proper supper out of it — maybe some roasted vegetables, some bread, and a glass of wine.      That sounds perfect. I’ve been working on a work leaving do for the office, and I was wondering if you wanted to help me put together the guest list. It’s not too big — just a couple of colleagues and some friends from the office. I think it would be a nice way to say goodbye to the team before the new year.

So, I was just tellin’ my nan about this new ‘app that let’s you invest in property from your phone, and she’s like, “You sure that’s not a scam?” Honestly, I don’t know, but it’s got a  lot  of reviews.      Yeah, I’ve heard about that one too. Bit of a minefield, though. I had a mate who tried to set up a business through a shell company, and it ended up with him getting hit with some pretty hefty fines. He said the bloke who helped him was a real smooth talker, but apparently, it was all a bit of a money laundering scheme.      Wait, so is that like, if you’re not actually running the business, and you’re just funneling money through different accounts? I’ve heard stories about that. My cousin was involved in something like that, and it went south pretty quick.      Yeah, it’s like that. The moment you start getting suspicious, the authorities come knocking. I’ve got a friend who’s a self-employed guy, and he got caught with some dodgy transactions. You’d think he’d be careful, but he said he was just trying to make ends meet.      Yeah, but it’s not just about making ends meet. If you’re not careful, you could end up in real trouble. I mean, I’ve got a cousin who got fined a fortune just for not declaring some expenses. And now he’s got a kid, so the fines are gonna stick with him for years.      Right, the problem is that people don’t think about the long-term consequences. You know, I used to work in banking, and we saw all sorts of shady stuff. Some of the guys were just trying to make a quick buck, and they didn’t think about the risks.      You know, I’ve been thinkin’ about that. I’ve got a bit of savings, and I’m tryin’ to figure out the best way to invest. But I don’t wanna get into the same mess as my cousin. I mean, if you’re not careful, you could end up with more than you started with.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I had a bloke come to me once, said he wanted to invest in some kind of ‘legal’ money scheme. Turns out, he was just stringing me along.

So, what do you think about the weather today? I mean, it’s like it’s trying to decide whether it’s going to be spring or winter. I've been out this morning and it was sun, then it started raining like a bucket!      Yeah, I saw that on the news. They said it’s all about the jet stream shifting. I’ve been trying to get my garden sorted, but it’s like the earth is holding its breath.      I know, it’s been so unpredictable. I was just outside with the kids this morning, and I had to put the sunhat on before I even left the house. My little one was so excited about the sun, but then it just rained on us like a waterfall.      Sounds like a day at the park. I was just thinking about that this morning. I’ve been trying to plan a family picnic, but I keep getting caught in the weather. I was going to take the kids to the park today, but if it keeps raining, I guess I’ll have to keep it for another day.      Yeah, it’s tricky. I was out buying groceries earlier and the shop was all wet from the rain. I had to take my umbrella everywhere. I think I’ve got more umbrellas than clothes now.      I can relate. I had to put an umbrella in the car because my wife insists on having one. I think she’s just being cautious, but I can’t fault her logic.      I think it’s just the way the season is changing. I mean, I had to teach a lesson outside this morning, and the kids were barely able to handle the weather. Maybe I should have brought a tent for the class.      I could see that. It’s not just the weather, though. I’ve been working overtime at the store this week, and I’m trying to get things under control. There’s a big sale coming up, and I need to make sure everything’s set.      I know, I remember you mentioned that. You must be exhausted. You’re always so busy. How’s the baby doing?      She’s fine, thank you. She’s been sleeping a lot lately, which I guess is normal. But I can’t complain, she’s healthy and happy.      I remember when I was pregnant, I used to get so tired, but it was worth it.

So, I heard you're from Malaysia. That's interesting, I mean, I know you're British, but growing up in KL, how does that shape your accent? I mean, I've heard some funny things about British people in the East.      Oh, it's a bit of a mix, really. My parents are both British, but I was born in KL. I think I picked up a lot of Malaysian slang and pronunciation, but I still sound like a Brit in terms of intonation. It's fascinating, though—you get the best of both worlds, like, I guess, you can blend into both cultures pretty easily.      My accent is pretty neutral, I think. I grew up in England, but I was always around people from all over. I think it's because of my job in publishing—so many people from different places, different accents. It's kind of like a microcosm of the UK, maybe?      Yeah, I feel that. I grew up in Sweden, but I've been in the UK for years now. I’ve picked up a lot of British slang, even though my accent is still pretty Swedish. I remember when I first arrived, I tried to speak like a local, but I kept getting confused. It's like trying to fit into a new culture without really knowing the rules.      That must be tough. I mean, I'm from Aylesbury—small town, so the accent is pretty standard. But I've worked in publishing for a while now, and it's surprising how much variety there is in accents here. I mean, even within Cambridge, there's so much variation. I think it's because of the universities and the international students.      Exactly. I work as an assistant editor here, and every day I hear different accents. Sometimes it's hard to understand people from Scotland or Wales, but it's also fun. I love the diversity.      I think it’s the same for me. I work as a temporary publishing assistant, and I get to meet so many people. It’s like a huge melting pot. I think that’s why I like the job so much. You get to learn so much from different people.      Yeah, I think that’s what makes the publishing industry so interesting. You're always learning, not just about books, but about people and cultures. I mean, even with all the diversity, there's a kind of shared language here.

So, mate, I’ve been thinking—what’s the plan for the visa application? I mean, I’ve got the forms, but I’m not sure what exactly we need to do next. I’ve heard of people needing proof of funds, but I don’t know how much we actually need to show.      Yeah, I know—this is a bit of a nightmare. I’ve got the forms too, but honestly, I’m not sure what to do with them. Should we just send them off and wait? Or is there something else we need to do?      I think we need to check with the embassy first. I remember someone saying they had to book an appointment for an interview. I’m not sure if we need that, but better safe than sorry. I’ll check the website later tonight.      Yeah, that makes sense. And don’t forget about the passport photos. I’ve got the camera, but I’m not sure if the photos need to be in color or black and white. Also, what size?      You’re right—those are the real headaches. I think they need to be 3.5 cm by 4.5 cm. Yeah, that’s what I saw on the website. And they have to be in color, no glasses, no hats, and the background has to be white. You know, the whole nine yards.      God, I hope they don’t want us to pose with a mountain in the background. That’d be a nightmare. I mean, where would we get a mountain? We’re about to go to Mongolia, not climb it.      True. But seriously, I’m thinking of just taking them to the local photo booth place. I heard they do passport photos. It’s cheaper than going to a professional. Plus, they’ll know what they’re doing.      Yeah, that could work. I’ll call them later. Also, we need to start putting up the ads on Gumtree. I’ve got the flyers ready, but I’m not sure where to post them. Should we focus on Warrington or spread out more?      I think we should start with Warrington first. It’s where we’re based, and people here might be more likely to donate. But I’m also thinking of maybe doing some social media posts. Facebook and Instagram, you know?      Yeah, that’s a good idea. We could use some kind of hashtag, like #RallyForMongolia or something.

So, what the hell happened last night? I was up at 3 a.m. trying to wake you up because you were like, “I’m not moving, I’m not getting out of bed!”      Oh, come on, it wasn’t that bad. I was just tired. I mean, we were out all night, and then I came back and my arm was like,  crack .      Oh, yeah, I was there. You were literally dancing like a maniac with that guy from the bar, and then you just  cracked  your arm. What even happened?      I don’t know, I just tried to lift this dumb beer bottle and, boom, arm gone. I was like, “Ow, oh my god,” and then I was on the floor. I thought I’d broken it.      Yeah, I thought I had. I was in so much pain, I nearly cried. Then, like, half an hour later, I managed to get out of the flat and walk to the hospital.      Oh, that sounds brutal. How did they even know what was wrong?      They took an x-ray and said it was just a sprain. But I’ve been so tired since then. Like, I haven’t been able to sleep properly. I just lay there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about how stupid I was.      I get it. I’ve been feeling about the same. I think the whole week has been insane. Between classes, trying to keep up with work, and then that night out... I’m just so knackered.      I can’t even imagine. I’ve been trying to stay up late to study, and then I fell asleep mid-lecture. I think I’m just not used to this pace.      Yeah, I know. It’s like, you think you’re ready for uni, but it’s all so different. And then on top of that, you’ve got these stupid little mishaps like that arm thing.      Yeah, but at least it wasn’t anything serious. I mean, it was annoying, but I’m not like,  dead  or anything.      True. But still, I feel like I’ve done so much this week. I mean, boys, exams, friends, everything. It’s just a lot.      Yeah, I feel the same. I don’t know how people do this. I mean, it’s all so much, but I guess that’s just how it is.      I guess. But hey, we’re in this together.

So, I was just telling my cousin Ann about that time we tried to cook Sunday roast for the family, and it went off like a rocket. You remember, the one where we used the wrong side of the lamb?      Oh yeah, that was a disaster! I swear, we ended up eating it cold with some spare ribs and a side of mashed potatoes that looked like it belonged in a museum.      Exactly! And you were the one who said, “It’s just a bit of roast, it’s not like it’s the Queen’s birthday or something.” And then it turned out to be the Queen’s birthday the very next day!      I think I still have the photo of the lamb on the floor with the sauce and everything. It was like a piece of art, albeit a very sad one.      Yeah, and in the end, we ended up getting takeaways, which was the smart move. But the memories? They’re priceless. Anyway, do you remember what we were doing at the anniversary party last week? Was it that time you tried to tell a joke and ended up making everyone cry?      Oh yeah, I tried to tell that joke about the sheep and the farmer, and somehow it turned into a sombre tale about loneliness and loss. Silly me.      You were just trying to be funny, but you got carried away. It was one of those moments where everyone was laughing, but it felt like we were all being told a story about our lives.      I know, it was weird. And the fact that we had our Uncle Bob doing the karaoke again—what was that song? “Imagine”?      Oh yeah, and he was wearing that ridiculous hat again. You know, the one with the feathers and everything. He said it was a tribute to his youth.      I think he’s still young at heart, even if his hair is gone.      That’s the thing about family gatherings, isn’t it? You get all the chaos, the laughter, and the stories that stick with you for years. I think we all need them, especially after a long week of exams and marking.      Yeah, and those moments are what make the hard times bearable. I couldn’t have asked for a better family to be part of.      That’s the spirit. Now, let’s go and see if the others are still alive.

Dad, I just put my water bottle in the fridge again. I think it’s gone off. I’ll have to check when I get to Cornwall.      You can’t leave a water bottle in the fridge for more than five minutes, lass. That’s when they go off. You need to drink it fast or it's all gone.      Yeah, yeah, I know. But it’s been in there since you started the journey. It was like a cold drink when we left, but now it's just hot and frozen. I think it's  trying  to kill me.      It’s not trying to kill you, it’s just being a bit of a drama queen. I remember when I was your age, I used to do the same thing with my pen. I’d leave it in my pocket for hours and then complain it was “corrupted.”      You didn’t have a laptop back then, did you?      No, I had a typewriter. Or a pen. Either way, I'd get lost in my own writing.      Speaking of writing, remember when we were talking about the move? I think I need to get a new washing machine. The one we got last year broke down again. It’s like it’s trying to tell us something.      Yeah, it’s a bit of a pain. I told your mum we’d need a new one before we even got here. But she said “no, it’s fine,” and now we’re stuck with a machine that can’t even spin properly.      I don’t know. I’m thinking of getting a decent one from Amazon. Maybe one that can do both washing and drying? I heard they’ve got some good ones.      You could, but you’ll have to sort out the delivery. I heard the post office’s doing a bit of a thing with Amazon right now. If you do it right, you might even get it before the holidays.      That would be amazing! I’d rather get a new washing machine than have to wash all my clothes by hand.      You’d have to get used to it, though. I’d say you’d be better off with a washing machine than a cat flap, though.      You’d  never  say that! We’ve got a cat and a cat flap, and it’s the best thing since sliced bread.

So, I was sorting through old boxes in the attic this morning, and I found this letter from my grandmother—written in the 1950s, mind you. It's all in that lovely, cursive script, and it’s about her days as a headmistress in a small Scottish school. I mean, it was fascinating. I think she must have had a real passion for education.      That sounds like something she’d do. She always said she had a real soft spot for children. Didn’t she once tell me how she used to take the pupils on picnics in the countryside? I remember her mentioning it once when we were having tea. It was a bit of a long story, though.      Oh, I know exactly what you mean. I used to take the girls out every Friday for a walk. We’d visit the village museum, or sometimes just drive out to the hills. It was a way to keep the kids engaged and give them a sense of community. I still remember the one time we got lost on the way back—had to ask a farmer for directions.      Sounds like a tale worth telling.
