I know what you mean. But I’ve been making my own coffee, which is a bit of a ritual now.      That’s a lot of effort for a cup of tea, isn’t it?      I know, but I like the smell of it brewing. It's like a welcome home.      I remember when we used to sit out here in the garden with a cup of tea, and the birds would come to the feeders. You used to tell me about them all the time.      Yes, I do miss those days. Although I’ve been trying to get the garden back to how it was.      You’ve done a decent job, really. The flower beds look lovely, and the roses are blooming again.      I’ve been using some old seeds from the shed. It’s not the same as the ones from the market, but they’ve grown well.      Speaking of gardening, have you seen those spiders in the shed? I found one on the wall the other day, and it was huge.      Oh, I’ve seen them. I think they’re harmless, but I still get a bit spooked.      I know what you mean. I’ve also had a power cut a couple of times this week. It was so dark in the house, I felt like I was in a cave.      I can only imagine. I’ve been trying to keep the lights on, even if it’s just a single bulb.      And don’t get me started on the local festival. I was hoping to go this year, but I think I’m too old for that kind of thing.      You’re not too old, you’re just too stubborn. I remember that time you fell over in the kitchen while trying to reach the biscuits.

So, what do you think about going to the coast for our holiday? I mean, we haven’t been to the beach since I was a kid, and I've been dying to go back to Hastings. It's like, the place where my memories started.      Oh, I’d love that. It’s been ages since I’ve been back. Though I remember it being a bit different back in the day. I think there were more people on the beach, and the shops were smaller. But I also remember the sea being just as blue.      Yeah, I still remember the days when we used to go there every summer. It’s funny how time flies. I’ve been playing gigs around the North for most of my life, but Hastings always felt special. It’s like the place where I started making music, you know? Those old pubs and clubs—still got that vibe.      That’s so cool, Grandpa! I never get to hear about those days. It’s like you’re telling me a story from a different time. I wish I could have been there with you. Do you think we’ll still be able to find those places?      Hmm, maybe not exactly the same, but I’m sure there are still some spots that are the same. We could check out the old town, maybe even the pier. I’ve heard it’s been renovated a bit, but it still has that charm. And the seaside walks are amazing.      Exactly. And the fish and chips! Still the best in the country, in my opinion. Though I do miss the old seaside candy stalls. I can still taste that saltwater lolly from when I was a kid.      Oh, I bet those were the best! I wish I could still buy one. I think I’ve only ever had a lollipop in a shop, not one that you could just pick up from a passing stall. We should make sure to try that on our trip.      I’ll do some research online. Maybe there are still a few around. Plus, I can’t wait to go back to the pond. I used to go there with my brother when I was younger, and we’d try to catch fish with old bait.      The pond, huh? You were always the adventurous one. I think even now, I can still picture you in that little overalls, running around with a bucket.

So, I just watched  10 Things I Hate About You  again, and it’s like,  what a classic ! I mean, the whole thing is so cheesy, but in a good way. It’s like, who doesn’t love a film where Shakespeare is literally recreated with a modern twist?      I know, right? It’s just so ridiculous, but in the best way. I mean, the dialogue is so over-the-top, but it somehow works. I watched it with my mum last night and we were both laughing so hard. Didn’t you find the scene with Heath Ledger as Patrick totally hilarious?      Oh,  definitely ! That scene where he’s like, “I’m not a creep, I’m not a weirdo” – I mean, who  is  a weirdo? That’s the whole point! It’s like, the entire movie is about being misunderstood, and then suddenly you’re everyone’s favourite. It’s kind of meta, isn’t it?      Yeah, it’s like,  so  much fun to watch, especially when you’re in a really bad mood. Like, if you’ve had a terrible day at school, you can just watch that film and feel better.      Exactly! I mean, it’s got all the drama and the romance, but it’s also totally unrealistic. Like, how did Kat even get involved with Patrick? She’s supposed to be this tough, sarcastic girl, and then she just falls for this guy because he’s a bit of a weirdo.      I know, and then the whole “I hate you” thing – it’s so romantic. I mean, who doesn’t want someone who’s just  so  confident in their feelings? I guess that’s why it’s such a cult film. It’s got that classic teen drama vibe.      Oh, and I can’t wait for our London trip next month. I’ve been dying to go there since I was like, seven. I’ve heard so many stories about it, and I’m just  so  excited to see the actual places.      Me too! I’ve heard it’s  so  different from Cambridge. Like, it’s so much bigger and more chaotic. I guess it’ll be a bit of an adventure, but I can’t wait to see all the stuff we’ve been talking about.      Yeah, and we’re going to try and visit all the places from  Harry Potter  too. I mean, we’ve got the whole Hogwarts thing on our bucket list.

Aye, it's been a bit of a strange few days, hasn't it? So, I was just telling my niece about the time I tried to teach my mum to use a mobile phone. She thought it was a remote control for the TV.      That’s classic. I’ve got enough magic in this house.”      I remember my mum once mistook my brother’s iPhone for a toy. She kept trying to make it sing. That sounds like a story that could be in a book. I remember when I first went to Germany. I asked for directions and they all started speaking in German. I thought I was in a movie. Oh, you're such a clever young man. Now, where's your head at? The sun's shining, the beer’s on tap, and the festival’s coming. So, I just got this recording equipment from the university, and I’m trying to do some linguistics stuff... got to pick up some accents and colloquialisms for my course. So, I just got a call from the doctor, and it’s not good news. They think my mum’s got cancer again. I mean, she’s had it before, and we were all hoping it was in remission. We don’t know if she’ll be able to see Christmas this year, or if she’ll be here to walk us to school next spring.      That’s the hardest part, isn’t it? The uncertainty. But you have to hold on to the moments you have. I know it’s not easy, but try to make sure you’re there for her. She deserves that.      You’re right. So, lads, what have you been up to this week? I know you were both talking about school stuff earlier.      Yeah, we were discussing the new physics project. So, I just got the confirmation that our trip to Lancaster is all set. I can’t believe it’s finally happening. So, I was just telling my mates about the gig we saw last week with that band from Leeds. You know, the one with the lead singer who looks like he’s been through a war?      Yeah, I remember that. Mate, I don’t need a band to make me feel alive. I’ve got you, don’t I? Speaking of which, have you heard that new album from the band you always talk about? So, I think I’ve just lost the game again. How do you even win when you’re the one who’s been stuck with the virus for the last three turns?      No, no, no! Yeah, I think you're just being too cautious. I mean, I got the virus, then the quarantine, then the emergency, and now I’m out of the game. That’s like a full turkey dinner.      Oh, I hear you. So, I was just thinking about how we’re going to manage the birthday bash for the twins next month. I mean, it’s not just any birthday— it’s  their  summer  birthday. So, I’ve been thinking about moving again. You know how I’ve been working in Manchester for the last few years, and it’s starting to feel like I’m just going in circles. So, I was just thinking about how we used to have these giant sticks of chalk in the garden when we were kids. Who’s going?      Just me and a few friends. I think it’s going to be a real treat. You should come.      I might. I’ve been meaning to get out more. Maybe I can bring the French press and we can all have proper coffee while we watch the films.      That sounds perfect. You know, I think we’ve all been too focused on the latest gadgets and not enough on the simple things.

So, Reg, you’re really going to be away for a while?      Yeah, mate, I’m heading out to Saudi Arabia for six months. Got this job with a consultancy firm, doing some infrastructure projects. They said the pay’s good, and the opportunities are there.      That’s cool, but you’re not going to miss the lads, are you? I mean, it’s not like you can just call or text every day.      Oh, I know, lads. But when you're in a place like Saudi, you gotta get used to the time difference. And the language’s a bit of a barrier, too. You know, they speak Arabic, and even the English you get there is pretty basic.      That sounds tough, but I suppose it’s the same for anyone who goes abroad. I mean, I’ve done some work in Germany before, and it was a bit of a culture shock, even though I speak the language pretty well.      Yeah, I’ve heard about that. My mum’s got a cousin who lived in Berlin for two years, and he said it was like living in a different country. Although, I’ve got a friend who’s been there a few months now, and he says it’s actually pretty cool, and the food is amazing.      It’s not just the food, though. I mean, the work’s not exactly easy. I’ve got someone in my family who’s a construction worker, and he’s always talking about how the jobs out there are tough, and the hours are long.      I heard that too. You know, about the working conditions. But the money’s good, so it’s a job you can’t say no to. Although, I’d rather be back in Liverpool, doing what I do.      I can see that. I mean, I’ve always preferred working in a place I know. But I guess it’s about the opportunities, you know? I mean, I’m not exactly looking to stay in the same job forever.      That’s true. I’ve been thinking about moving up, and this job might be the push I need. Plus, the chance to travel and see new places.      Yeah, but don’t forget about your mates, bloke. You’ve got to make sure you stay in touch.      That’s the plan, lads. I’ll be making sure to call you all every week, and we’ll be having a proper catch-up when I get back.

You know, I've been meaning to ask you both—what do you think about using native plants in urban gardens? I’ve been reading up on it, and it seems like they’re way more sustainable.      I think it’s brilliant. I’ve been experimenting with some native plants in my own garden. They don’t need as much water, and they support local wildlife. Plus, they’re more resilient to the local climate. I’ve got a patch of meadow grass that’s been thriving for years.      I agree, but I also think there’s a balance. You don’t want to go overboard with wild plants—they can take over if you’re not careful. I’ve had to pull out a few invasive species that came in with the natives. It’s a bit of a balancing act.      Sounds like a full-time job! I’ve been thinking about starting a small garden at home. I’ve got a terraced plot, but I’m not sure where to start. I’m not exactly a gardener, but I love the idea of having fresh herbs and vegetables on hand.      Start small. Maybe with herbs like rosemary, thyme, or parsley. They’re easy to grow and don’t take much space. I use a few pots on my balcony. And if you want to get more serious, there are community gardens in the area that offer workshops. Maybe you could check those out?      Yeah, community gardens are a great resource. I’ve been part of one for a few years now. It’s not just about the plants—it’s about the people. You meet all sorts of interesting people, and you learn so much. Plus, it’s a great way to stay active and connected.      That does sound appealing. I’ve been a bit removed from the outdoors lately, working long hours. Maybe it’s time I started to make a bit more space for myself. I’ve been feeling a bit run down lately, and I think being closer to nature might help.      That’s understandable. I’ve been there too. If you’re feeling run down, it’s important to take care of yourself. Maybe you could start with something simple, like a morning walk or a few minutes of stretching. Your health comes first.      And don’t forget about your skin and hygiene. I’ve been using natural skincare products lately—things like aloe vera and honey.

So, I was just thinking about how we all sound different, even when we’re from the same area. I mean, I’m from Gillingham, and I can tell a difference between me and my cousin who lives in Canterbury. It’s like our accents are totally different, even though we’re both from Kent.      Yeah, I agree. I grew up in London, so I can tell when someone’s from South East England. Sometimes it’s just the way they say "chips" instead of "fries" or "biscuits" instead of "cookies." It’s funny how that affects how we communicate with people from other parts of the country.      Oh, I know what you mean. I’m from Harlow, and I pick up on accents almost instantly. I can tell if someone’s from South London or North London, or even if they’ve been to university or not. It’s like, you can just tell from how they speak if they’ve ever been to a posh school or not.      Yeah, I think that’s a big part of it. I mean, I’ve been around so many different people, and I’ve noticed that people who’ve had a good education sound different from those who haven’t. It’s like the way you speak is a reflection of your life experience.      And it’s not just about the accent. It’s also about how you use your voice. Like, some people have a really deep voice, others are very high-pitched. I think it comes down to how you speak as a child, how you’re raised, and even what kind of music you listen to.      True. I remember when I was younger, I used to try to sound like my dad. He had this really slow, deliberate way of speaking. I used to mimic him all the time. But it never quite worked out. I think I still sound more like my mum, who was always pretty fast-talking.      That’s the thing with family. You’re always trying to sound like someone else, even if it doesn’t work. I can go back to my parents’ house and hear my brother trying to sound like my dad, and it’s so funny. He just ends up sounding like a robot.      I think that’s where some of those voice recognition apps come in handy. I’ve been trying to use them more, but they just keep mishearing me.

So, I was just thinking about that Halloween party we had last year. You remember, the one when we tried to make a baked Alaska? It was a disaster. I think I used the wrong kind of ice cream, and the meringue just collapsed like a bubble.      Oh yeah! I still remember that. I was so excited to try it out, but then it all went wrong. I mean, I had to use a grater to get the cheese out for the topping, and it took forever. You were trying to teach me how to grate cheese properly, weren’t you?      Yes, I was! I thought it was a basic skill, but I guess you needed some training. It’s not just about holding the grater the right way, you’ve got to know the texture of the cheese too. I remember you kept slipping and making a mess of the kitchen. But it was funny, really.      I still feel embarrassed about it. And then there was the part where I accidentally put the ice cream in the wrong bowl. I thought it was the meringue, but it was just a regular bowl. I nearly ruined the whole thing.      That’s the spirit though. You were trying, and that’s what matters. I mean, we all have those moments when we’re learning, and sometimes it just goes wrong. I remember when I was your age, I tried to recruit people for the school newspaper and ended up getting rejected by half the class. It was a big deal at the time.      That’s not fair! You were just trying to do your best. I guess being a programme director means you’ve had to deal with a lot of people and different opinions. I sometimes wonder if the way people treat you is because of your age or your position.      That’s a good question. I think both come into play, but I’ve learned to be more confident in my role. It’s not always about being the most senior person, but about knowing what you’re doing and being able to explain it clearly. I think that’s what I’m trying to pass on to you.      Yeah, I get that. I mean, you’re a role model. Even if I sometimes mess up, I know I can always come to you for advice. Just don’t expect me to make a baked Alaska anytime soon.

Well, it's a real treat to see you again, lass. You know, I still remember the first time we met in Japan – you were in that tiny flat in Tokyo, and I was just a bit lost in the city. Got a bit of a  bump  with the local bus, if I recall.      Oh, don’t even start! I was so nervous, and you were the one who helped me find the way back to the flat. You remember that guy with the giant scarf who kept trying to talk to me in broken English?      Oh yes, he was a bit of a character. I told him I was a lecturer, and he thought I was a tourist. But then he actually gave me a map – better than the one I had. I still have it, tucked away in my desk drawer, you know.      That map’s probably more valuable than any of your lecture notes, I’d say. Although, I have to say, your lectures were way more interesting. I still remember that whole thing about the Japanese tea ceremony – it was like a little performance.      And you, my dear, were the one who brought the  real  tea. You know, the one with the beautiful pot and the leaves that made the whole room smell like a forest. Spent hours trying to teach me how to make it properly.      And you spent hours trying to be quiet while I did it! Remember when you accidentally knocked over the pot and we had to rush to the shops to get more?      Oh, that was a  moment . But it’s all part of the cultural exchange, isn’t it? You know, I was just telling ANON that I’m thinking of taking flying lessons – something I’ve always wanted to do but never had the time. I could see the skies from my office window, but I never thought I’d take off.      Flying lessons? That sounds exciting. You know, I was in the air force once. Though I didn’t get to fly a plane, just did some air traffic control. But I’d love to see you up there.      Well, I’ll let you know when I’ve got my first lesson booked. And don’t forget to tell ANON about that time you tried to meet someone in New York and ended up in a taxi with a guy who thought you were a model.

So, I'm telling you, I was late to the Chelsea Flower Show last week—like,  so  late. I thought I had a ten-minute walk, but I got stuck in traffic because of that ridiculous car park that's like a war zone.      You were meant to be the one who planned the trip, not the one who got lost in the car park. I would’ve known exactly where to park.      Oh, please. I got there just in time to see the entire garden being dismantled because the organizers thought it was a  test . I was like, “This isn’t a test, it’s a flower show!”      You’re not the only one who got lost, mate. I once tried to find a café in Exeter and ended up at a car wash. I thought it was a themed coffee shop.      Yeah, I remember that. You told us it was a  résumé  of the city, and we all thought it was a spelling mistake. You’ve been meaning to explain that one for ages.      Well, it’s a common confusion. “Résumé” is French, right? I think it’s because the French spell it “CV” and the British just did their thing and started spelling it “résumé” with that weird accent. Honestly, I think it’s just a case of linguistic colonialism.      So, is it a word or not? I mean, I’ve seen it used in articles, but it feels so wrong. I think I’ll stick with the English spelling.      Yeah, that’s the thing. It’s not just about spelling—it’s about how words evolve. I mean, look at “program” versus “programme.” It’s all about where you’re from.      You know, I remember being confused about that when I first came to uni. I thought “programme” was the official spelling. Now I just go with what sounds right.      I bet you’re the only one who’s ever used “programme” in a Scrabble game. You know, the one where you’re trying to get all those high-value letters.      Oh, I did that! I spelled “programme” with the ‘e’ and got a triple word score. It destroyed the game.      I still remember that. You were like a Scrabble wizard that day.      And you were so proud. I still have the photo of you holding up the board like you had won the World Championship.      That was  not  the World Championship—just a group of friends with too much caffeine and a serious case of ego.

Well, I’ve been thinking, Bill. I was just down by the old village shop, and I saw old Tom from the mill. He was all dressed up like he’d been to a fancy dinner. I said, “Tom, what’s the occasion?” He just laughed and said, “Just passing the time of day, old man.” I reckon he’s got more time these days than he used to.      Oh, I know. It’s funny, isn’t it? You’d think with the weather like it is, he’d be staying in. But no, he’s out and about like he’s still got a job. I heard he got a bit of a pension boost last year. I suppose that helps.      Yes, well, I’m not getting anything like that. The pension’s just about keeping the lights on. And the council won’t even give you a grant unless you’re in real trouble. I’ve been writing to them ever since last year, you know. I told them I’m not able to work, but they just say, “Please try again.” Like I’ve got the energy to do anything.      I know, love. I’ve tried too. I was a childminder, remember? I used to have five kids in the house at once. Now I’ve got nothing but time and a few old photos. I still get the odd letter from the old ones, though. They’re all starting to get older, too. I suppose that’s life.      It is, isn’t it? I’m not sure I’ve ever felt so... unimportant. I used to be useful. I used to be the one who fixed the roof, or mended the fence. Now I just sit and watch the birds. I suppose the birds are more useful than me.      You’re not useless, love. You’re a man of the land, through and through. You’ve got that quiet strength. I just wish the world had more people like you. Not that I’m trying to sound sentimental or nothing.      You’re not, love. You’re just being honest. I reckon the world’s changed a lot since I was a boy. Not for the better, in some ways. You don’t go out and get a job, you just sit and wait for the handouts. And even then, it’s not enough.      I know. But I’m still here, aren’t I?

So, I tried this new app called  FitTrack  last week. It’s supposed to help you lose weight by tracking everything you eat and do. Honestly, it’s a bit much, but I thought I’d give it a go.      I saw that on Facebook. I’m not sure I’d trust an app that tells you what to eat. I’ve always cooked from scratch, you know? I mean, I love food, but I don’t think I’d want to rely on an app for that.      I’ve been using it for a while. It’s pretty good. It gives you a daily calorie target and even suggests recipes. I’m not a big fan of the strictness, but I do like the variety of meals it suggests. I think it’s helped me eat more healthily without feeling like I’m on a diet.      I don’t know, I feel like I’m being watched. I mean, I’m not one of those people who need to count calories, but it’s like it’s judging me every time I open it.      Sounds like it’s got a bit of a personality. I’d rather just cook – it’s more satisfying. I mean, I’ve been making this huge pot of chilli this week. It’s been a real hit with the kids.      That sounds good. I’ve been making a lot of one-pot meals lately. It saves time and it’s easy to clean up. I even tried adding some frozen vegetables to make it cheaper.      Frozen vegetables? I still think fresh is better. Though I suppose if you’re short on money, you’ve got to do what you can. I’ve been trying to get back into the kitchen more since I retired. I used to be a manager, so I never really cooked for myself.      I can imagine. It’s funny how things change. I used to always think I’d be a chef or something, but I ended up teaching. Still, cooking is something I love. I think the kids appreciate it.      Yeah, it’s a great way to spend time together. I think the new train station’s going to make things easier for people like us. I’ve been waiting for it to open for ages. It’ll cut down the time to get into town.      It’s a relief, honestly.

So, I just saw this documentary on Shakespeare on TV last night. It was supposed to be a new series, but honestly, it felt like it was made in the 80s. I mean, the acting was so… stiff. Like they were reading from a script instead of actually performing. I don’t get it. I thought the BBC would do better with something like that.      Yeah, I remember that. I think they tried to make it more educational, but it just felt like it was aimed at school kids. I was watching it with my mates, and one of them kept saying “this is like a history lesson, not a play.” I nearly laughed out loud.      You’re not the only one. I’ve been telling my course mates about it. They’re all like, “Oh, you watched that?” And then they start explaining how much they  don’t  like it. I mean, I love Shakespeare, but some of this stuff is just… overkill. Why not just do a proper adaptation?      I think it’s more about trying to appeal to the masses. Europe’s got this idea that Shakespeare is some kind of cultural treasure, and they want to show it as something accessible. But honestly, it’s just not working. I got more out of the old BBC versions. They had real actors and real drama.      Yeah, I don’t know. Maybe it’s just a generational thing. I mean, we’re all students, right? We’ve got to be suspicious of everything. But I can’t help but think that the new series was a bit of a letdown. It’s like they were trying too hard to be modern.      I agree. I think they should’ve just stuck to the classics. There’s a reason why  Macbeth  and  Hamlet  are still popular. No need to reinvent the wheel. Although, I have to say, I did like the part where they compared Shakespeare to the modern media. It was interesting to see how his plays are still relevant today.      Yeah, that part was good. It made me think about how stories have always been told in different ways—whether it’s on stage, in books, or even in films. That’s something I’ve been thinking about a lot lately. I’m taking a seminar on narrative structures in film and literature, and it’s making me see things differently.

So, I heard you were in Oxford last week? How did you end up there? I’ve been meaning to ask you about that.      Oh, it was just a quick trip for a meeting with a client. I had to go and review some of the new campaigns they’re rolling out. I stayed in a hotel near the city centre, and it was nice to just get away for a bit. You should have come too. The weather was perfect—nothing like the drizzle we’ve had here in Cambourne.      Honestly, I’d love to get out of the office for a while. I’ve been stuck in meetings all week, and my boss keeps talking about “synergy” like it’s a real thing. I’m so over the corporate jargon. I was thinking about taking a short break, maybe a weekend away. You know, just to reset.      That sounds like a good idea. I mean, you’ve been working hard on the project co-ordination side, right? Have you had any time to catch up with your family lately? I know your mum mentioned she’s been wanting to see you again.      Yeah, she’s been asking, and I’ve been meaning to. I’ve got a few days off next month, so maybe I can take a trip to see her. I think it’s been a while since we’ve all been together. Speaking of family, have you spoken to your sister lately? I heard she’s been trying to get back into the fitness routine.      Oh, yeah, she’s definitely on a roll. She’s got this new trainer and is being super strict with her diet. I swear, she’s trying to look like a celebrity. I mean, she’s healthy, but it’s like she’s obsessed with the whole thing. Anyway, I think I need to get back to work—I’ve got a meeting in an hour. But I’ll call you later and catch up more. How’s your ex doing? Still holding out for someone?      Oh, bless. He’s still out there, but I’m over it. I mean, we were great, but it just didn’t work out. I’ve been focusing more on my career now. Plus, I’ve met some really cool people at work. I think I’m starting to feel more settled.      That’s great to hear.

So, I was just telling my mum about the one time I tried to grow a vegetable garden and ended up with a bunch of weeds and a few dead tomatoes. She said, “You’re not even from the countryside, lass! What makes you think you can grow a garden?”      Yeah, I can imagine that. My gran used to say the same thing about me trying to bake a cake. I’d end up with something that looked like a rock. But seriously, I was just trying to be helpful.      It’s like we all think we can do it, but the plants have their own minds, don’t they? I mean, I’ve got this basil plant that’s been sitting on the windowsill for months, and it’s just... staring at me.      That must be the old lady trying to tell you something. I’ve got a cactus that’s been in my flat for years, and it’s got more personality than my flatmate. He’s got a face like a grumpy cat.      I tell you, I’ve tried everything. I even got a book on how to grow herbs. It was like a cooking manual for plants. I thought, “Okay, this is easy,” but the first thing I did was water it like it was a thirsty baby. Now it’s in a pot, and I’m just hoping it survives.      I remember when I was in my first flat, I tried to plant a tomato plant in a shoebox. It grew, but it didn’t have enough space. It ended up looking like a twisted tree. My landlord had to dig it out.      Yeah, I remember when my stepdad tried to plant a rose bush. He put it in the middle of the garden and thought it was a show-off. But the thing was, it grew so fast, it blocked the path. We had to clear it out.      I think it’s funny how we all think we can grow things, but the plants have their own rules. They don’t go for the easy way. I think they’re just trying to teach us a lesson.      Maybe that’s why I’ve started learning to cook. You know, I think plants and food are basically the same thing. Both need love, patience, and a bit of time.      I like that. I was just telling my sister that I think cooking is like gardening.

Well, I hope you had a decent weekend, old chap. I confess, I spent it doing absolutely nothing—except for a spot of gardening. I’m afraid the weather was a bit too unpredictable for me to get anything done. Not that I’m complaining, mind you. The rain was a blessing for the garden, if you know what I mean.      Oh, I’m sure it was a blessing for the garden, but not for your muscles! I had a much more exciting weekend. My son’s got a young daughter now, and she’s just starting to run around, which means I’ve been doing a lot of chasing. Still, it’s a joy, isn’t it? Watching them grow up.      Oh, I can only imagine. I’ve got two boys, both in their twenties now, and they’re very much in the world of football. One of them’s a defender for a local team, and the other’s just been signed by a club in the Championship. I’ve been trying to keep up with their careers, but it’s tough. I still remember when they were just little boys, kicking a ball in the park.      That’s the thing, isn’t it? Time flies. I was thinking the other day about how snooker players have such long careers, and how they often start young. I mean, it’s not like football, where you’re out of the game by thirty. But then again, not everyone can be a snooker player. It takes a certain talent and a lot of discipline.      That’s true. I was in the police force for a while, you know. Still, I suppose it’s better than being in the armed forces, which I always thought was a bit more dangerous. But then again, I’m not a fan of violence. I prefer the academic world. Though I have to say, marking students’ work is a bit like policing—just as much detail, and often just as tedious.      You’re not wrong there. I’ve been marking essays for weeks now, and honestly, I’m about as close to a police officer as I’ll ever get. Still, I’ve got to do it, and I suppose that’s part of the job.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve got a few students I’m really excited about. One of them’s writing a thesis on the intersection of sports and politics, which is quite a niche topic.

So, I’ve been thinking, do you remember that time when we tried to plan a family gathering and ended up with half the family in London and half in Leeds?      Oh, don’t even start! I was only five, but I remember being so confused when my aunt turned up with a coat and a scarf, and my cousin had on a tie. It was like a grown-up Christmas party!      Yeah, and then we had to explain to the kids that we were just having a  family dinner  and not a  grown-up gala . I swear, I felt like the host of a rock concert trying to keep everyone calm.      Right, well, we need to make sure this time is different. The Christening is coming up, and the birthday is just around the corner. I’ve been thinking about how to make it a bit more special.      A Christening? Oh, that’s so exciting! I still can’t believe we’re going to be the ones to do that. Are we going to have a little party, like, with cake and everything?      Yeah, and the birthday is next month. I was thinking, maybe we could have something more casual, but still fun. You know, like a garden party or something.      Well, I think the Christening needs to be a bit more formal. I mean, it’s a big event. We shouldn’t underplay it. I was thinking about maybe hiring a caterer, but I don’t want to go overboard.      But what if we just do it at the church? I mean, we can still have a little gathering after. I don’t think it has to be too fancy.      I agree. I don’t want it to be too stressful. We’ve already had a few things going on. I’m just trying to find a balance between being thoughtful and not being too over the top.      That makes sense. I just want to make sure we don’t end up with the same chaos as before. I remember when we tried to send out the invitations and the list got mixed up. It was a disaster!      I think I still have that invitation somewhere. I was going to use it as a coaster!      Don’t even think about it. I’m not letting that happen again. We need to be more organized. Maybe we can use a digital tool this time?

You know, I was just thinking about our holiday to New York. It’s been a while since we went, and I still remember that time we got stuck in a taxi for an hour because of the traffic. Wasn’t that the day after your brother’s wedding?      Oh, that was   the   day. I still have that photo on my phone — me looking like I’d been through a war, and you both were just laughing like it was the best thing ever. I still can’t believe we managed to get to the hotel in time for dinner.      What happened after that? You know I was so tired, I just wanted to go to bed.      You fell asleep on the way to the hotel. I had to carry you in my arms. Remember how you kicked me in the ribs? I swear, you were like a little wildcat that night.      I was just tired, okay? I mean, it was the first time we’d all been together since the wedding, and it was so hectic. I think we all needed a break.      Exactly. And that’s why we’re planning to go back this summer. We could do the same thing — just relax, take it easy, and not rush through everything. Although, I will say, the weather in New York might be a bit of a problem. I heard it’s going to be hotter than usual this time of year.      Yeah, and I don’t want to be stuck in a taxi again. Maybe we can rent a car this time? I mean, if the weather is good, we could even plan a little walk around the city. I love the way the streets look in the fall.      That sounds like a great idea. I can check the weather forecast for the weekend, and if it looks good, we can start planning. I’ve already been thinking about where we could go. Maybe we could visit Central Park again — it’s always so peaceful there.      That would be lovely. I’d love to see the fall colours again. I think it’s one of the best times to visit. And don’t forget, we have to plan our weekend, too. You know we were supposed to go to that concert in Birmingham next Friday. It’s been a while since we’ve all hung out together.      Oh, yes!

Right, I've got this form to fill out for the research grant, but I’m not sure how to go about it. It’s asking for a detailed breakdown of my project objectives and expected outcomes. I mean, I know what the project is about, but putting it into a structured format is another matter.      Yeah, I remember that. You said you're applying for funding to expand your research on urban gentrification in the North West. But when it comes to writing it up, you get all flustered, don’t you?      You could say that. My lectures are fine, but applying for grants is like a different language altogether. I was trying to use some academic jargon I picked up in my seminar, but it just sounds like nonsense to the people reading it.      Exactly. You need to be clear and concise, not too indulgent. People who fund these things want to see that you’ve got a solid plan and that your research is both feasible and impactful.      That’s the thing—impactful. I keep thinking about how this study could help local communities understand the socio-economic shifts happening in their areas, but I don’t know how to frame that without sounding too idealistic.      You don’t have to sound idealistic. You just have to show that your work has a real-world application. Maybe suggest that your findings could inform policy decisions or help local councils in their urban planning initiatives.      Hmm, that might work. I could link the research to specific areas in Salford and Manchester. Maybe even include some case studies from the places I’ve done fieldwork in. But how do I structure the breakdown?      Start with your objectives. List them clearly—like identifying trends in housing prices, analyzing the displacement of long-term residents, and assessing the effect on local services. Then, outline your methodology. Websites, surveys, interviews… you’ve got that covered.      Yeah, I’ve done a lot of interviews already. I just need to make sure I tie them all back to the main questions. And outcomes? I think I need to focus on both qualitative and quantitative data. It’ll make the grant application stronger.      And don’t forget to mention your team. You’ve got some solid collaborators over at the geography department. Showing that you’re not working in isolation will make them feel more confident in funding you.

So, I was just thinking about my dreams last night, and they were so vivid, it felt like I was actually there. I dreamt about this place, like a coastal village, and I was walking along this beach with this dog. It was the most peaceful thing.      Oh, that’s interesting. I had a dream last week about the   Lottery  . I was in a shop, and I won a massive jackpot. I remember thinking, “This is it, I’m going to buy that little house in the country and get a dog.” Didn’t even need to think about it.      That sounds like a dream come true. I’ve always wanted a dog, but I know it’s not just about the dream. There’s the cost, the time, the responsibility.      But Dad, I think it’s just a matter of time before you get one. I’ve been telling you for weeks that you should get a puppy. I’ve got a friend who’s got a golden retriever, and it’s the best thing ever.      Yeah, tell him, Mummy. I want a dog too. I did a bit of research about the costs—food, vet bills, toys, and then there’s the time. But if you really want it, it’s worth it. Still, I dream about it, like that little village with the beach. I dreamt about it so much, I almost believe it might come true.      Then why not take the first step? We could talk to a breeder, or maybe adopt from a shelter. It’s not like we’re not in a position to do it. We’re not broke, are we?      Actually, I think we’re in a pretty good place financially. I’ve been saving a little each month, and we could use that for a deposit. Maybe we could get a small dog, something manageable. You know, a   Bulldog   or a   Poodle  .

So, I was sat in the car park outside the hospital, and this guy comes up to me and says, “Are you waiting for someone?” I said, “No, I’m just waiting for my sister to come out of A&E.” He looked at me like I was crazy. “You’re not waiting for someone to come out of A&E? You’re not in A&E?” I said, “No, I’m just waiting.” He went, “Oh, I thought you were waiting for someone to be discharged.”      That’s not too bad. I mean, I’ve been in A&E myself, and the people in there can be a bit... well, you know, frantic. I remember once I was in there with a broken ankle, and this guy was screaming, “I’m not dying! I’m not dying!” And the nurse just looked at him and said, “You’re not dying, you’re in A&E.”      Yeah, that’s the thing. You go in thinking you’re going to be fine, and then you’re just sitting there with a broken bone, or a sprain, or something that could have been fixed at the GP’s. But it’s too late. You’re already at the hospital.      Totally. I mean, I’m a consultant engineer, so I have a pretty good job, and I’m not exactly a couch potato, but I got in one of those accidents where you just...  crash  into something. I was walking across the road, and a van hit me. The next thing I knew, I was in A&E with a sprained wrist and a bruised ego.      That sounds like me. I was running late for work, and I tripped over my own feet on the pavement. Then I landed on my knee, and it was like,  crack —and then I was sitting there, trying to stand up, and my knee was just...  gone . I had to go to A&E, and the doctor said it wasn’t broken, but it was pretty bad.      That sounds really painful. I bet it was a nightmare.      It was. I was just trying to get to work on time, and then boom. I ended up in A&E, and then I had to wait hours just to get an X-ray. I was so frustrated.      It’s a shame they can’t just fix things quicker. I mean, I’ve heard of some places where they get you in and out in no time, but I guess it’s just how the system is.

Well, I’ve been thinking about this business idea I had for a while now. You know, that little café in the village? Maybe I could turn it into something more, you know, sustainable. I’ve been doing a bit of reading about eco-friendly businesses and things like that.      Oh, that sounds interesting, old chap. I’ve always thought you had the right touch for that sort of thing. You’ve got a real eye for what people want, don’t you? I mean, you know the villagers, and you know what they like. But you’d have to be careful with the costs. You’re not exactly in a position to take huge losses, are you?      That’s true, but I’ve been saving up for a while. I’ve got a bit of a nest egg from the school, and I’ve been thinking of dipping into that. It’s not like I’m going to be taking a big risk. I just want to make sure the place is more than just a café—it could be a community hub. You know, with a few workshops or something like that.      That’s a good idea. And as for the equipment, I’ve got a friend who’s a handyman—he’s been saying he’d be happy to help out with the setup. I think I’ve got it covered.      That’s good to hear. You always had a knack for knowing what to do. I remember when you first moved into the village, you had this vision of turning the old shop into something special. And you did it. I reckon this could be the next step.      Yeah, I’m thinking about it. And you know, I’ve been following some of the international news lately. It’s all about sustainability, isn’t it?

So, I was just thinking, we need to get a proper meal before we head back. I know it’s been a long day, and I’m starving. Have you thought about what you want?      Yeah, honestly, I haven’t given it much thought. I was more focused on catching up with the latest  Happy Valley  episode. That show is absolutely ridiculous, but I can’t help but keep watching. It’s like a guilty pleasure.      Oh, I know, I’ve been binge-watching it too. The way they handle the dialogue, it’s almost like watching a play. But I still can’t believe they’ve made a show about the police, and it’s so bloody good. My sister keeps saying I’ve gone completely off the rails, but I can’t stop.      I’d say you’re just living life to the fullest, then. But seriously, I do love the way they use the décor in the pub scenes. It’s so authentic, like it’s actually a real place. I’ve been meaning to ask, have you noticed how the Guardhouse has that retro vibe?      I have, actually. It’s like stepping back in time, isn’t it? The way they’ve decorated it – the mix of old and new. I remember when I first came here, I almost thought I was in a museum. The lighting, the walls, the music... it all just feels right.      Absolutely. It’s the kind of place where people come to unwind. And speaking of which, have you seen the new cat that’s been hanging around? I think it’s been there for a few weeks now. I’ve been feeding it, actually.      Oh, you’re the one who’s been giving it treats? I thought you were just staring at it from the bar. It’s adorable, though. I bet it’s a stray that’s found its way here. I hope it stays. It adds a bit of charm to the place.      I think it’s starting to get used to us. It even follows me around sometimes. Although, I’m not sure if it’s more interested in my coat or the bar snacks. Either way, it’s a nice touch. I think the pub’s go-to charm is that it feels like a real community hub.      Definitely. And between us, the background music is spot on.

Aye, I’ve been thinking about the Highlands again, ye know. That’s where I was last summer, makin’ a wee trip up to Inverness. Stumbled on this little village called Plockton, and the views from the cliffs—man, it’s like een the sky’s just fallin’ down.      Aye, I remember you talkin’ about that. You said the weather was a bit of a shocker, though. I thought for sure you’d be chuffed with the skies, but I suppose you’re used to Edinburgh’s drizzle.      Oh, I’m well used to it. But that day, though—sunny as a summer’s day, right? Drove up the A83, the road’s all twisty, but the view from the top? Just— magnificent . I took a few pictures, though I’d be the first to say I’m not a pro. Just a wee hobby, ye know.      I’ve been up there myself, actually. Got a few photos from a few years back. I did a project on Scottish landscapes during my postgrad studies. You know how it is—told myself I’d be a proper photographer, but ended up just takin’ a few snaps here and there.      Aye, well, I suppose that’s the thing. It’s not about bein’ a pro, it’s about the experience. I mean, the Highlands have a way of gettin’ under yer skin, no? I’ve been there a few times now, and every time it’s like the place just speaks to ye.      I’ll say. I remember the first time I went to the Isle of Skye. It was late autumn, and the weather was a sod. Rain comin’ down like a bastard, but I still thought it was worth it. You ever been there?      No, not yet. I’ve been told it’s a doozy. Too far for me, honestly. But I’ve got the map marked. I’ll get my bike and take the ferry. Think I’ll do it this summer. Just me and the camera.      Sounds like a plan. You’ll be takin’ pictures of the weather, too, I reckon. Skye’s got more than its fair share of mist and rain.      Aye, but that’s part of the charm. You can’t beat the magic of the Highlands. Even on a bad day, it’s still a good day.      To the Highlands, then. And to the weather—give it a bit of a chance, eh?      Aye, to the Highlands, and to the wild, welly weather.

So, I’ve been thinking about our week ahead, and honestly, I’m already overwhelmed. You’ve got this nursery appointment on Monday, and I’ve got this meeting I need to go to for the community group. I feel like I’m juggling a gazillion things.      I know, Mum. I feel the same. I’ve been trying to plan my day around the baby’s naps so I can actually get some work done. It’s so easy to let things slip when you’re trying to manage a new baby and your job.      I couldn’t agree more. I remember when you were little, how we used to plan everything so meticulously. Now, it’s like everything is chaos, but somehow we keep on top of it. It’s a bit of a miracle, really.      Yeah, it feels like I’ve been living on a tightrope. But I have to say, I love the way it’s going so far. The baby is sleeping through the night now, which is a huge win. Although, I still can’t believe how quickly he’s growing. One minute he’s just a tiny bundle, and now he’s already got this little personality.      I know, and I can’t wait to see what the next few months bring. You know, I was thinking about what we could do this weekend. Maybe we could go for a walk in the park or something. Just a way to get some fresh air and maybe catch up with some friends.      That sounds great. I’d love that. Although, I have to make sure I’m not too exhausted. But I think it’s important to take some time for ourselves. You know, even if it’s just a short walk.      Exactly. We need to take care of ourselves too. I know it’s easy to forget, but it’s essential. Also, I’ve been meaning to ask you – did you get the new TV show that came out last week? I heard it’s really good.      Oh, yes, I did. It’s a comedy, and it’s so funny. I’ve been watching it every night before bed. You should really give it a go. It’s the kind of thing that makes you laugh all the way through.      I’ll consider it, but I’m not sure I’ve got the energy for another show this week.

So, I’ve been thinking, do you ever just  not  want to go to work? Like, sometimes I’m like, “I could just stay in bed all day and not see another person!” But then I remember the coffee machine and the fact that I can’t make proper tea without it.      Yeah, I get that. Sometimes I just feel like I should be working from home, you know? But then I remember I’ve got to go out and do actual physical work. I mean, what am I even doing? Shovelling gravel or something. It’s not even like I’m doing anything  important .      My job is definitely not as physically taxing, but it’s not exactly fun either. I mean, I get to push buttons and make sure the production line doesn’t crash, but honestly? It’s like breakfast, lunch, and dinner with a coffee machine in between. And don’t get me started on the corporate politics.      I can relate. I do events, so it’s like, “Oh, I’m going to a fancy hotel and meet interesting people,” and then I’m just shuffling people around, getting coffee, and then cleaning up. It’s like –  ha  – the opposite of glamour. I just want to wear something that doesn’t cost me a fortune, like a T-shirt and jeans. But then I’m like, “Wait, is this too casual for an event?” And then I end up buying another dress.      I know, I’m the same. I’ve got this  old  pair of jeans that I wear everywhere, but every time I go out, I feel like I should be wearing something a bit nicer. Like, “Do I look like I belong here?” And then I remember that the only people I’m trying to impress are my mates.      You know, I think I’ve got the easiest job of all. I can just wear whatever I want, even if it’s a tracksuit. But then again, I’m a woman, so I have to do extra. Like, you can wear a tracksuit and be fine, but if you go out in one, you’re like, “I’m not trying to look like a pirate.” It’s complicated.      Yeah, I’ve been there. I’ve had to wear a suit once for a client meeting and then came home and just collapsed in my PJs. I mean, I’m not even sure I’m allowed to go back to work in them.

Well, I’ve been waitin’ for this tea for ages, old girl. I got the tin out, and the mugs, and I even managed to find a biscuit or two. Though I’m not sure they’re still called biscuits round here.      Oh, I’ve got some very nice ones, actually. My gran used to make them. She called them "shortbread," but I think they’re more like cookies. Still, they’re good. You’re not going to be offended if I say I’m sorry I didn’t bring any, are you?      Oh, don’t worry about it. My wife still has the old tin from my mother’s house. I think it’s from the 1950s. She’s the one who started the tradition, really. You know, I remember when she’d make this tea every afternoon. She’d call it “the cuppa” and it was the heart of the day.      I can relate to that. My mother used to make tea with a proper teapot, not just a mug. She’d always say it was the way to start the day. Though I must say, I’ve never been able to get that same taste again. Now I just make it strong and add a splash of milk. Works for me.      That’s the way to do it, lass. Strong tea, a bit of milk, and plenty of biscuits. You can’t be too choosy when you’re in a place like this. I remember when I used to work, we had this place called The Red Lion. Used to be a real busy spot. People would come in after work for a pint and a cuppa. Now it’s just a pub with more walls than customers.      I know. I used to work at a childminding centre, and I’d take the kids over to the pub sometimes. They’d always ask for the “honey tea.” I think it was the way it was served, with a spoon and the sugar on the side. They loved that.      I remember that. It was a bit of a ritual, really. You’d get your tea, add the sugar, and then stir it with a spoon. It was like a little ceremony. You could tell someone was a regular by the way they handled the tea.      I think that’s what makes it special. It’s not just about the drink, it’s about the company and the routine.

So, I was at the pub last night, and this guy comes in with a baby in a carrier. I thought, “Oh, what a lovely sight.” But then he starts talking about how he’s “cutting the ties” and “freedom from the past.” I was like, “Mate, you’ve got a baby in a   carrier  . You’re not exactly making a statement about freedom.”      Oh, I know. It’s like someone’s trying to be edgy, but they’ve just arrived from the Tesco car park.      I saw a guy like that once in Cardiff. He was in a pub, shouting about “natural living” and “the power of the individual.” I didn’t know what he was talking about, but he kept saying he didn’t “need a hand.” I thought, “Well, he’s got a baby in his arms, mate. Maybe he needs a bit of help.”      That’s the thing, isn’t it? People think you have to be rebellious to be free. But really, freedom is just being able to enjoy a pint without someone trying to tell you how to raise your kids.      Exactly. I remember when I was at uni, there was this guy who thought he was “anti-establishment.” He used to rant about the government and the system. Then one day, he ended up in a hospital because someone got drunk and hit him. He said it was a “political statement.” I said, “You were drunk and got hit.” He said, “It’s part of the struggle.”      That’s the same guy who used to leave his phone in the pub and then couldn’t find it. Said it was “a sign of the times.”      I’ve got a friend who used to do that. He’d leave his phone in the pub and then write a letter to the pub owner about how he was “freeing the phone from the system.” He’s now a customer services rep with a phone that never rings.      I think the real freedom is just being able to enjoy a good meal and not have to worry about a CRB check. I had to do one for a job once. It’s like, “Oh, what’s your history? Did you have any accidents? Did you ever have a bike?” It’s so weird.      I get that. I did one for a lecturing job. They wanted to know if I’d ever been in a car accident or had any criminal record.

So, I just got back from my holiday in Cornwall, and I’m still in a bit of a haze from the sun and the sea. How are you, by the way? I've been meaning to ask you how your week was.      Honestly, I’ve been surviving. Work’s been a bit intense—another shift at the hospital, and then I had this meeting with the team about a new mental health initiative. I think I’m more exhausted than I’ve ever been. How was your trip?      It was amazing. The beach was absolutely perfect, and the food was just what I needed. I had this really good fish and chips from a local place, and then I went to a festival that night. There was live music, and I got to meet this guy who was into the same kind of music as me. I think he might be a musician, actually.      Wait, really? That’s interesting. Was he someone you’d be into hanging out with?      He was pretty cool. We talked for ages, and he shared some of his music with me. I even got a copy of one of his tracks. But I’ve been trying not to get too caught up in it. I mean, I’m still over here, right? I’ve got a partner and a flat to come back to. Though, honestly, I’ve been thinking a lot about maybe doing something different next year. You know, travel more or maybe even take a gap year.      That’s a big decision. You’d have to be careful though. I know what it’s like to have a life and then suddenly be tempted to run away from it. But it’s not all bad, is it?      No, it’s not. It’s just a thought. I think I need to explore more. I mean, I’m not one of those people who just wants to stay in the same place forever. I’ve been feeling a bit stagnant lately, you know?      I get that. I think I’ve been feeling the same. Maybe we should plan something together. Like, maybe a weekend trip? Or a little getaway? I’ve been thinking about going to the coast for a couple of days.      That sounds perfect. I could use a break from the city, and I could even take my dog. She’s been really bored since I came back.

So, I just heard from Jess yesterday. She’s really struggling. The chemo’s taking a toll on her, and she’s not been herself lately. I don’t know how she’s managing with everything.      I know, it’s heartbreaking. I tried to reach out last week, but she said she was too tired to talk. I feel awful. I mean, I know she’s strong, but this is a lot to handle alone. Have you spoken to her family? I’m sure they’re worried sick.      They’re all over it, but she’s insisting on doing it herself. It’s like she doesn’t want to burden them. I think she’s still holding on to that stubbornness she’s always had. I just hope it doesn’t end up backfiring on her.      I hope not. I’m just so worried she’ll push herself too hard. You know, I was thinking earlier this week about how she used to joke about being the last one to die in the group. Now it’s the opposite. I feel like we’ve all been hit with this sudden reality.      I know. It’s surreal. We were all just laughing about something stupid last month, and now—it’s all so different. I was going to suggest we all meet up this weekend, just to check in and make sure she’s okay. I think she’d appreciate that.      That sounds good. I’ll message her and see what she thinks. I just don’t want to intrude. She’s been so private lately. I can’t even remember the last time she opened up about how she’s feeling.      Yeah, she’s been so closed off. I think part of it is just the treatment, but I also think she’s scared. Maybe she’s afraid of what people will think if they know how bad it is. I don’t know. It’s hard to tell.      It’s just so unfair. You know, I was also thinking about the house we saw in the village the other day. We could maybe look into it. If things get too bad, we’d want to be close to her, you know? It’s not like we’re going to run away or anything.      Yeah, I thought about that too. If we go through with it, we’d have a good location.

Man, I'm so fed up with this place. I swear, if I had a penny for every time someone leaves their stuff everywhere, I could buy a new flat. It’s not like we don’t have bins or lockers or anything—some people just can’t be bothered.      Yeah, I get that. I mean, I’ve got a drawer full of keys from people who just walk in and out like it’s their own home. It’s not even like we’re short of space, but for some reason, it’s always the same people who don’t take responsibility.      Right, and don’t even get me started on the noise. I’m trying to get some sleep, and there’s always someone either playing their music loud or shouting at the top of their lungs. I mean, I’m not even sure if it’s a problem with the building or just people not respecting the quiet hours. Either way, it’s a pain in the backside.      I know, I know. Last week I was trying to study and someone started doing karaoke in the communal room. Like, in the middle of the night. I had to knock on their door three times before they finally turned it off. I swear, I thought the building was going to collapse.      You’re not the only one. I had a guy in my flat last week who kept opening and closing the door like he was testing the lock. I don’t know if he was trying to get me to move out or just had a screwdriver and a need for attention. Either way, it was annoying as hell.      Honestly, I think about quitting sometimes. I mean, I’m not even paid that much, and I’m expected to put up with all this nonsense. I barely have time to breathe, let alone deal with the drama.      I know, I know. But we’re stuck here, aren’t we? We might as well make the best of it. I mean, the view from the window is alright, and at least the rent’s not too bad.      Yeah, I guess. Still, I’m going to keep complaining about the noise and the mess. It’s better than just sitting there and letting it happen.      Agreed. I’ll keep on my list: noise, mess, and people who think they’re the only ones in the building.

So, I was in Antwerp last week, and I bumped into this guy I went to university with. We hadn’t seen each other in years, and I was just walking through the Christmas market, enjoying the mulled wine, when he walked up and said, “Debbie, is that you?” I nearly dropped my hot chocolate.      Oh, that’s typical of you. You always end up running into someone from your past, even when you’re just trying to enjoy a quiet coffee. I remember when you said you were going to Antwerp for the Christmas markets. You said it was going to be like a British Christmas but with more cobblestones.      Yeah, and the people were different too. I mean, I’ve been to Herne Bay shopping every Christmas, but Antwerp had this real European vibe. They had these cute little stalls selling handmade things, and everyone was so friendly. I even got a puppy collar as a gift, which was weird but adorable.      I know, right? I loved it. But I couldn’t help but think about how much I’ve changed since uni. Back then, I was always worrying about passing my finals and getting into a good university. Now I’m just trying to keep up with my boys’ birthdays and not forget their names. It’s wild how time flies.      Time flies, but so do your kids. I remember when you were complaining about the rush of Christmas shopping. Now you’re the one running around trying to get everything for the holidays. I still can’t believe you’ve got three boys. I’ve got two, and I’m still trying to figure out what they want for Christmas.      I know, it’s a whirlwind. I do miss the days when I just had to worry about my own birthday. Now it’s all about planning the perfect party for the kids, buying the right presents, and making sure the cake is just right. It’s exhausting.      Yeah, I feel you. But it’s also the best part. I remember when I was in university, I used to dream about having a family. Now it’s here, and it’s everything I ever imagined. I just wish I had more time to enjoy it.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. I’m retired now, and sometimes I feel like I missed out on things.

So, I was just thinking about that equality vote thing, you know the one that's been all over the news. You've been talking about it a lot lately, haven't you?      Oh, don’t get me started. I’ve been following it like a hawk. It’s such an important topic, really. I mean, it’s about fairness, isn’t it? Equal rights for everyone, regardless of gender or anything else.      Yeah, I get that. But I still don’t understand why it's such a big deal. Didn’t we already have equality in the workplace? I mean, I guess it's not just about jobs, is it?      Oh, it’s more than just jobs, love. It's about representation, about making sure women have the same opportunities as men, in politics, in education, in all areas of life. And don’t forget the LGBTQ+ community—this vote is about more than just gender.      Right, I guess that's true. But I still think people are overreacting. It's not like it's some huge change, is it? I mean, if we already have laws in place, why the need for a vote?      Because it's not just about laws. It's about culture, about changing attitudes. And let's be honest, some people are still holding on to old-fashioned views. You know how some of the older generation still think women should stay home and take care of the kids. It's not just about legal rights—it's about social change.      I guess that's one way to look at it. But I still feel like it's a bit of a joke. I mean, I'm not saying it's not important, but it's like, how much more equality can we have? I mean, we’re in Ireland, not a country with laws that treat women like second-class citizens.      That’s what I’m saying. We can’t assume we’re there yet. We have to keep pushing for change, even if it seems small. And honestly, I think it’s a good way to start a conversation about equality in general. I’ve been trying to talk to my sister about it, but she just says it's all a bit of a buzz.      Well, maybe. But I guess it's better than nothing. I mean, if we can get people to talk about it, even if they don’t fully agree, it’s a start, right?      Exactly.

Aye, I was just thinkin’ about the lathe tools. I got me a couple of them in the shed, down by the garden. You know how it is, lass. Not much use now, but they’ve got a bit of a story to ’em.      Oh, I remember when you used to work with wood. I used to watch you do that in the shed, back when we had the old bench. You were always so precise with it. I still remember when you made that little rocking horse for the kids. Was that you?      Aye, that was me. It took me weeks, but it was worth it. The kids loved it. Still do, I hear. You know, they even used it in the school play.      I remember that. It was a real showstopper. Though I do wonder, did you ever finish the rest of the tools? I mean, you had that whole set—spindles, chisels, everything.      Aye, I got half of ’em. The others… well, they got lost in the move. Or maybe they were taken by the new lads who came to help with the garden. I can’t remember. It’s all a bit hazy now.      I suppose that’s the life. You get so many things, and then time just moves on. I was thinking about something else, though. Did you ever cook that hamster in the microwave?      What? You’re joking, lass. That’s not proper. You can’t put a hamster in the microwave. That’d be cruel.      Oh, I heard about that. Someone told me they tried it and it didn’t go well. I think the hamster survived, but the microwave did not.      Aye, I heard the same. It was a real mess. I think the point is, no one should try that. You can’t just put anything in the microwave. So, I was just thinking about that mirror-writing thing in the paper the other day—the one about the typist who used to write backwards in the margins because she thought it was more efficient.      Oh, that’s one of those quirky stories, isn’t it? But it’s interesting how some people develop such idiosyncratic habits. But I think it’s more common in older generations. My grandmother used to write in the margins of her letters, and she always said it was a way to keep her mind sharp. She’d even do puzzles in the margins, like cryptic crosswords. I used to love watching her do that.      That must have been fascinating. I’ve always found mirror-writing fascinating in a way. I think there’s something about it that appeals to people who want to be different. Though I can’t imagine writing backwards in my job. I mean, I’m an administrator, and clarity is everything.      Exactly. And yet, there’s something romantic about those kind of quirks. Like the cat story in the news the other day—that one about the tabby who was allegedly a detective? But the article made it sound so dramatic, like a mystery novel.      It was a bit of a farce. But I have to say, the idea of a cat solving a crime is sort of irresistible. It’s like the perfect middle finger to human arrogance.      Well, I do have to say, I think it’s a reflection of our growing obsession with the unusual. Whether it's mirror-writing, cryptic crosswords, or cat detectives, people seem to be drawn to the eccentric.      And what about all the technology we have now? I mean, we can’t even go out without a phone, yet we’re still obsessed with things that don’t make sense.

So, I was just telling Anna how we got lost in the countryside on our holiday. Ugh, don’t be like that. You’re just not adventurous enough. I tried it and it was actually decent. I mean, it’s not going to change the world, but it’s not bad.      I’m not saying it’s bad. So, what’s the word on the street? You lot haven’t mentioned Transylvania yet. I’ve been meaning to ask—what’s the vibe there? I’ve heard it’s a bit scary, but also like,  so  cool?      Oh, it’s  weird , honestly. I was there last year with my cousin. It’s got this kind of medieval vibe, but then you walk into a castle and suddenly you’re like, “Wait, is that a real vampire or just a tourist?” And don’t even get me started on the hotels. They’re mostly  old  buildings, like, the walls are still wet from the 1600s. You’ve got to be careful with the stairs.      I’ve been there too. But I did it for the  food . The cheese there, it’s like,  liquid gold . You know, like, the kind you can’t pronounce but sounds like it’s from a dream? And the people? They’re  so  into their traditions. You’re not wrong. I was in Transylvania once, but only for a day. I was just passing through on my way to Budapest. The only thing I noticed was that everyone was  so  into the folklore. One guy tried to convince me that the  Dracula  legend was real. I said, “Mate, I’ve seen the show. It’s just a show.” He said, “No, this is real. I’ve seen the  vampires .”      You’re joking, right? I thought the only vampires were the ones in  Twilight . Speaking of vampires, though, I’ve been thinking about doing some laser eye surgery. My vision’s gotten  so  bad. I can’t even tell if the sun’s coming up or going down anymore.      That’s a  big  move. You know you’re not going to be able to read the menu in the café without your glasses anymore. You’re gonna be the one holding up the line at the counter.      Yeah, and don’t forget, I’ve got a  very  strict policy on eye health. No blurry vision in my café. I’ve been known to make people hold their coffee until they can read the label. But, hey, if you want to try it, I can help you find a good clinic.

So, I was just tellin’ Ann about the time I tried to park the car in the village and ended up in the field. Blimey, I thought I’d found a shortcut, but it turned out to be a cow path!      That sounds like you, Bob. You always did have a bit of a knack for making a mess of things.      I remember when I was a teacher, I once tried to drive to a school meeting and ended up in a layby because I misread the map. It was a Saturday, and I was the only one there. I just said, “I think I’ve done it, sir.” And the examiner said, “Well done, you’ve passed.”      That’s brilliant! I’d love to get a licence too. I think I could do it.      You know, I was just thinkin’ about the other day when I went to the shop and saw a sign for a flu jab. I thought, “I’d better get one.”      Aye, I’ve been meaning to do that too. So, I was just telling Dad about that time I tried to explain Chinese chess rules to a group of kids at the local library. They thought it was like regular chess, just with more pieces. All my travels have been within England.      It’s amazing how much you can see just within the UK, though. I grew up in St Neots, and I’ve never really left. It was fascinating to see how he used language to inspire people during the war.      I never got around to university. I started work straight away as a customer services agent. I’ve always preferred practical work over academic.      You’re not the only one. I went to sixth form, but I never seriously considered university. I wanted to get out and start working. But I have to say, it’s strange how much people still talk about it, even now.

So, I heard you mentioned working abroad? That’s a big move, isn’t it? I know you’ve got that teaching job in Prague, right?      Yeah, it’s been a while now. I left last year. Wasn’t sure at first, but the timing was right. I needed a change, and the job offer was pretty good. Plus, I wanted to get out of the UK for a bit. It’s been nice, honestly. The people are friendly, the cost of living is lower, and I’m not stuck in the same old routines.      That does sound like a decent move. I mean, I’ve been thinking about it myself, actually. You know, about working abroad. Just, I’ve never really had the opportunity. I’ve been unemployed for so long now, it’s hard to get back into the job market. It feels like the system doesn’t want me to come back.      I can imagine. It’s tough, isn’t it? I mean, even though I had a job, I had to go through so much red tape just to get the visa and everything. It’s not like you can just walk in and start teaching. You need proper qualifications, references, and sometimes even a language test. I was lucky, but I know a lot of people aren’t.      Yeah, and the student loans issue is getting worse too. I mean, I never even got to finish my degree, and now I’ve got this debt that I can’t even get rid of. It’s like the system is designed to keep people like me trapped.      I know. It’s so frustrating. I’ve been talking to my students about it too. They’re all young, and they’re worried about the future. Some of them are already taking out loans, and they don’t even know what they’re getting into. It’s just a mess.      It really is. I was thinking about pensions too. You know, I was going to retire early, but now I’m not even sure I can afford to live on my savings. I mean, I’ve got some money, but with the cost of living here in Poland, it’s not like I can just come and live permanently.      That’s true. I know a few people who have moved here for the cheaper cost of living, but they still have to work part-time to make ends meet.

So, I heard you got into that Human Sciences course at University of Manchester? That’s pretty cool, right? I’m still trying to decide between Maths and something more... creative.      Yeah, it’s gonna be awesome. I mean, I’m not exactly sure what it’s gonna entail yet, but I liked the idea of studying human behaviour and stuff. You still not decided on your choices?      Not really. I keep thinking about doing Maths, but then I get scared of all the equations. Maybe I should go for something that’s not too intense? Like, you know, not too much pressure.      Honestly, if you’re into numbers, Maths is the way to go. It’s not all equations though. There’s a lot of logic and problem-solving. Plus, it’s one of the most respected courses. You’ll have a solid foundation for any career.      I guess. But I’d hate to waste my time if I’m not passionate about it. I mean, I do like sports, especially rugby. I was thinking about doing something related to that.      Oh, you’re still playing rugby? I thought you were more into drinking these days.      Heh, yeah, I still play. It’s a good way to stay fit and meet people. But I’ve been thinking about maybe doing something in sports science or something like that. You know, combine rugby with studies.      That’s a good idea. You could even do it part-time. I mean, you don’t have to be a pro to get into that kind of course. Plus, it’s better than just playing and not having a plan after.      Yeah, I guess. I just don’t want to end up doing something I hate. But then again, I can’t just do nothing.      You’re not gonna do nothing. You’re going to uni. That’s something. And once you get there, you’ll figure it out. Just stick with your friends, and we’ll figure it out together.      Thanks, man. I appreciate that. By the way, are you going to the rugby match on Saturday?      Yeah, I’m going. You should come too. It’s gonna be a brutal game.      I’ll see. Maybe I’ll bring some beer.      That’s the spirit. Let’s not forget why we’re here—drinking, rugby, and figuring out the rest later.      Exactly.

So, lass, I’ve been thinkin’ about the money stuff again. It’s one o’ those things that’s on my mind more than ever these days. But let’s see… you know, I’ve always been an accountant. So I’ve had to keep up with the numbers. But this lot? It’s like they’re trying to make it harder for people like us. I mean, the tax system—it’s not what it used to be.      You mean the way they’re taxing the middle class? I’ve heard a lot about that. And don’t get me started on the National Insurance. It’s gone up a few times now, and I can feel it in my pocket.      I’ve noticed that. My students are all talking about how their take-home pay is shrinking. But I thought the government was supposed to help people, not take more from them.      That’s the thing, lass. They say they’re trying to fund services, but sometimes it feels like they’re just squeezing people for more. I don’t know if it’s right. You’ve got to balance the books, but I keep thinkin’—what’s the point of it all if people are getting less?      I guess that’s the dilemma. I wonder if the government is even listening to the people. I mean, the more they raise taxes, the fewer people are willing to pay. It’s a bit of a loop, isn’t it?      Exactly. And that’s why I’ve been telling you, lass, to always keep an eye on your finances.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to cook that lasagna and ended up with a fire? It was chaos, I tell ya. It’d be cheaper if we split costs.      That’s a good idea. I’d love to go with someone I know, especially someone who’s into the same stuff.
