Oh, you’re not the only one. I tried once, and it was like a biscuit from the bottom of the bag. I nearly threw it in the bin. But I didn’t. I ate it. And it tasted like regret.      Well, that’s the spirit. I think we’re both just here to eat, not to cook. I mean, we’ve got the movie on, the food’s ready, and we’ve got each other to keep us company. That’s what matters, innit?      Yeah, I reckon. We’re lucky to have a night like this.

So, I just watched  The Banshees of Inisherin  again—what a masterpiece. I don’t know how Colm Dáírdheáin did it, but it’s so heavy, you know? Yeah, it’s one of those films that makes you think. I mean, the script is so sharp. I like how it’s not just about the friendship, it’s about the  meaning  of friendship. You know? Anyway, I think the best part is how the film ends. Like, it just... ends. No resolution. You’re left thinking, “What now?” It’s so real. You know what I mean?      Definitely. Oh come on,  Zoolander  is a  classic . Plus, it’s got the most iconic bad guy ever. Wait, so what’s your favorite film of all time? I’m always looking for something new to watch. Maybe we can make a movie night?      I’d say  Roma  by Alfonso Cuarón. It’s so raw, and the cinematography is  incredible . I mean, it’s got this  feeling —like, it’s not just a film, it’s an experience. It’s not for everyone, but if you’re into it, it’s  unreal .      I’ll take that as a compliment. I mean, I like  Roma  too. It’s just that... I’m not sure if I’d ever watch it all in one go.

So, I'm telling you, I think I've got the worst hangover of my life. I mean, I went to Paris with my sister, and we had this  huge  meal at this fancy restaurant. I don’t even know what it was, but it came with a champagne flute, and I  drank  it all.      Oh my God, you’re such a lightweight. I told you, you can’t just go to Paris and think it’s a holiday to drink. You’re going to chase your own tail with that.      Oh, come on, I’m not that bad. I mean, I  did  walk around for three hours in my heels. And I had to go to the Eiffel Tower, and then I got lost.      Wait, you got lost? I thought you were with your sister.      Yeah, she’s the one who got lost. I was walking around with a map, and she was just taking selfies. This thing called  croque monsieur  that came with a side of cheese. And then we had this chocolate tart. I swear, it was like eating a cloud.      Sounds like you had a good time, though.      It was  okay . But my feet were killing me. I’ve never worn heels that high before.      I know, I’ve been through that. My feet were like concrete blocks by the end of the day. Oh, I’ve been there. I tripped over my own scarf in the Louvre.      You’re all obsessed with Paris, aren’t you?      It’s a beautiful city, but honestly, I think I’d rather go to Brighton next time. Maybe do some surfing?      That sounds more like your pace. You know, not too much going on, just relaxing.      Yeah, maybe. Although I still want to go to Nice. Somewhere with the beach and not too many people.      That sounds perfect. But you’ll have to take me. I’m still not ready to walk three hours in heels.      Deal.

Hey, Sally! Nice to see you before class. How’s everything going?      Oh, hi, James! Just catching up on some emails. I’ve been swamped with the end-of-month reports. How about you?      Not too bad, honestly. Got a bit of a backlog from the weekend, but I managed to get through it. You know how it is—this time of year always feels like a rush.      Absolutely. I’ve been trying to catch up on my own stuff too. Didn’t you go to Chichester last weekend? I heard there were some fireworks.      Yeah, I did! My sister and her family were there. It was amazing—just the kind of thing you’d expect from a small town. I even got a few photos. Do you want to see them?      Definitely! I’d love to see. I’ve been meaning to get back to Chichester for a while. I remember when I was a student there, I used to go to the theatre quite often.      Oh, I love the theatre. Are you into musicals?      I used to be. I saw  Les Misérables  last year. It was incredible. But with the job, I don’t really get to go much anymore.      That’s a shame. I actually got into creative writing last year, and I’m thinking of writing a novel. It’s a bit of a dream, but I’m enjoying it.      That’s awesome! I’ve always wanted to write too, but I’ve never found the time. I guess with the retail job and everything, it’s hard to balance.      Yeah, it’s tough. I’ve been thinking about doing a master’s in linguistics, actually. I’m fascinated by dialects and how they shape identity.      That sounds really interesting. I mean, I’ve always been curious about the British National Corpus. Do you study that?      A little. I use it for teaching—helps with grammar and referencing. Still, I think it’s a bit too formal for the average student.      Fair enough. I mean, I’m just a supervisor, so I don’t get too deep into the academic side. But I do like how you guys can make things so accessible.      It’s all about making learning engaging. And I think that’s something we should always keep in mind.      Absolutely. I’ll be sure to drop by your next class. Maybe I can even get a few tips on how to approach the writing module.

So, I tried to cook this rice and curry thing for the first time, and it got a bit… weird. I think I made my own personal apocalypse with that.      Oh no! I had a similar experience once. My mom always said that cooking is a way to show you care, even if it’s just rice and curry. I mean, it’s not like I’m a professional chef or anything.      You’re not, but you’re trying. That’s what matters. And if you want, I can help you next time. I’ve got a few tricks up my sleeve, like how to make the rice just right and not too sticky.

So, I was just telling my cousin about the meeting I had with the venue last week. You know, trying to book the conference hall for next month. So, lads, what have you been up to today? I’ve been sorting out some proofing for a client, but I couldn’t help but notice how you two have been glued to your phones all evening.      We were just scrolling through Instagram, Dad. You know, the usual. But you haven’t been on it all day. What’s up?      I've been keeping busy with some operations stuff. Yes, I heard about the match. It was absolutely thrilling. The way the players fought for every point, it’s like they’re almost playing for something bigger than just the trophy.      Yeah, I saw the match too. But I still think Serena is the best. She’s like, you know, the GOAT.      Yeah, but you’ve only been on Instagram for three hours, and you’re already arguing about who’s the best tennis player. Shouldn’t you be doing your homework?      Oh, come on, lads. Hey, we’re not kids anymore. We’re 15 and 16. You can’t just expect us to clear up every time.      I know, lads, but you’re growing up, and with that comes responsibility. Oh, I’ve been trying to keep that a secret, if you don’t mind. It’s a bit early to be talking about that, don’t you think?      Yeah, but you’ve got to start sometime. Besides, I reckon you’re gonna end up with someone who’s got a bit of facial hair. I mean, that’s how it works, isn’t it?      Yes, facial hair.

So, I was just thinking about that time we had to buy new furniture for the flat after the big move. You remember, it was all so chaotic. I was trying to find a sofa that wouldn’t cost a fortune, and I ended up at that one shop in Stockport. Got a bit obsessed with that grey sofa that looked like it was made of clouds.      Yeah, I remember that! You were so excited about it, and then when you got it home, it looked like it was made of plastic. I swear, it didn’t even match the room. You were like, “This is so cosy!” and then the next day you were complaining about the cushions.      Oh, I remember that! You two were so keen on the furniture, I think you even screamed when it came in. I’ve never seen such excitement over a couch. You were like a kid again.      Well, you didn’t have to be there. One of the guys said it was a bit of a joke, but it turned out to be real. He said it was a way to keep the shop open while the owner was on holiday.      Oh, really? That sounds like a good idea. I mean, people always complain about the cost of living, but maybe there are ways to make things work without breaking the bank.      I’ve heard of that before. It’s going to be a real change for the area.      Really? I haven’t heard about that. I guess it’s another thing to add to the list of changes in the town.      It’s all part of the process. Change is everywhere these days. You’ve got to adapt, you know. Even if it means dealing with new things like dementia, or people who get overexcited about new furniture.

So, I just got a message from my boss saying that there’s a possibility of redundancy in the next couple of months. I’m so confused, I don’t know what to do.      Oh no, really? That’s serious. You’ve been there a while, haven’t you?      Yeah, about two years. I mean, I’ve done a lot of work, and I’m pretty much the go-to person for coordination. But it’s just so sudden. I don’t even know where to start.      I know, it’s really daunting. I’ve been in that position before, when I was working in the school system. It’s not just about being qualified—it’s about fitting into the structure, and if the school is going through a restructuring, it’s hard to predict who will stay and who will go.      I guess that’s the thing, though. I’ve been planning to go back to my old job, but if I lose this one, I’m not sure what I’ll do.      Have you spoken to your manager about it yet?      Not really, I’m too nervous. I don’t want to seem desperate or make it worse. I’m hoping for a chance to negotiate or maybe even a transfer somewhere else.      That makes sense. You should definitely talk to them. And maybe start looking at your options—like those job portals, or even your network. I know you’ve been saying you want to move into a more strategic role, so maybe that’s a good time to explore it.      Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that. I’m also thinking about taking a short break, maybe take a few days off and just chill. My sister is coming to visit this weekend, and I’m planning on going to the gym, too. I need to get back in shape before I start job hunting.      That sounds like a good plan. You should take some time for yourself. I’m going to my grandad’s this weekend as well. He always has the best homemade pies and chips. I’ve been trying to get him to start eating more vegetables, but it’s a tough sell.      That sounds lovely. I’m going to try and make my own veggie meals this week. I’ve been eating out too much, and it’s not good for me.

So, what do you think we should do today, Micky? I know it’s got to be something good, but I’m not sure what.      Well, I was thinking we could go to the beach. The weather’s been so nice lately, and I bet there’ll be a good crowd. But I’m not sure if that’s what you want.      No, no, no! I want to watch Stick with Mick! I like the part where he chase the goat!      Yeah, I mean, that’s a good show. But I don’t think we have time to watch the whole thing. We’ve got to plan something for the day. I’m thinking about maybe swimming. But I’m not sure if the pool’s open today.      Let me check… Yeah, it’s open. And they’ve got a kids’ programme today, which is perfect for Micky. So why don’t we go to the pool and then maybe have a picnic?      That sounds like a plan. But wait, what about the guitar? I’ve been practising a lot lately, and I was thinking about maybe doing a little session with the neighbours, like the ones down the road who are into music.      That’s a good idea. I’m not sure what the neighbours are doing though. But if you go over, they might be happy to have some company. Also, you know, we could ask if they need any help with jobs around the house. We’ve been meaning to do a bit of cleaning up after the weekend.      Yeah, I was going to ask them that. Speaking of which, have you heard about the new Japanese restaurant that opened up near the park?      No, not really. I was too busy taking care of the toddler. But I’m curious. Do you think we could go there for dinner this week?      Well, if we can’t go to the beach, maybe we can go to the restaurant. But I go back to my original thought about Stick with Mick. Maybe Micky could watch an episode after we come back from the pool.      Yeah! I like Stick with Mick! I like when he says “Wot’s that?” and then he explains it!      Well, I’m not entirely sure what that means, but I think we’ll get there. Just make sure to take him to the pool and then maybe a little snack, okay?

Man, I just watched that bit where the dentist was like, "You know, I got a lot of patients who don't like me." I was like, "Oh no, what's wrong with you?" He's like, "I think I'm a bit of a jerk."      Yeah, I remember that. It was one of those films that’s like, "Oh, this is a horror movie, but it’s also a comedy." You know, the kind of film where the dentist is like the main character, but he's just not doing it right.      Exactly. I mean, the whole point of the film is that everyone is just a bit messed up, right? And the dentist is like the guy who’s trying to help, but he's just doing it wrong.      Yeah, and it’s funny because you’re like, "Wait, this isn’t a horror movie. It’s just a drama about a dentist who’s got issues." But then it becomes this weird combination of both.      I think that’s the point. It’s like, why even make a horror movie? Just make a drama about a dentist.      Exactly! But I guess it’s also kind of a commentary on how people in certain professions don’t always have the best bedside manners. Like, you know, the dentist, the doctor, the therapist. Everyone’s got their quirks.      Yeah, and the dentist in the film is basically the worst at his job. He’s got all this fancy equipment, but he’s like, "I don’t care if you’re scared, I’m going to do what I want."      And then the patient just sits there, like, "Why am I here?" It's like a satire of the entire dental industry.      I mean, I’ve had some weird dentists. One time, my mate had this dentist who would just jab at your teeth with a pick and not even ask if you were okay.      That's the kind of guy you really need to avoid.      I think I’m going to write a story about that. A dentist who goes too far. It’s like, "The Dentist: The Sequel."      Sounds like a hit. Maybe you should do it. I’d buy it.      Yeah, I’ll write it, and you’ll be the first to read it.      Deal. But only if you throw in a joke about my dental hygiene.      Oh, you're getting your teeth checked, aren’t you?

So, I heard you're starting your new job as a primary school teacher. How’s the transition going? You’ve been doing your PGCE, right?      Yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, but I think I’m beginning to get the hang of it. I actually started last week, so it’s still all very new. I taught a class of six-year-olds this morning, and they were a handful, but I couldn’t help but laugh at their energy.      You always had a way with kids, even when you were little. I remember when you were in primary school, you used to bring home little drawings of the teachers you adored. I still have one of them in my office.      That was you, wasn’t it? You were the one who made sure we never felt lonely. I think I used to draw you every time. You were like a superhero to us.      I was trying to be, yes. But I think you’ve got it in you. You’ll do great. And tell me, what kind of classes are you teaching? Are you working with young kids all day?      I’m teaching Reception, which is the youngest kids, so yeah, they’re all under six. It’s challenging, but I love it. I mean, they’re just so full of life and curiosity. I’ve already made some friends with the other staff, and the headteacher’s very supportive.      That’s great to hear. I’m so proud of you. You’ve always been passionate about helping others, and this is the perfect path for you.      Thank you. I think I’m going to be okay. And I’ve already got my first Easter cake planned. I’m going to make those little sugar roses you loved as a kid.      Oh, you’re going to make those again? I’d love to see that. I think it’s time we had a family Christening, you know, something to celebrate your new role.      That sounds amazing. I’d love that. When would you like to do it? Maybe after Easter?      That sounds perfect. I’ll start planning the cake and the venue. I think we should have a proper celebration, just like when you were little.      You always did love throwing parties. I think I’m going to need a bigger kitchen, though.      Well, I’ve got you.

So, I heard you mentioned your daughter’s new job in Manchester. How’s she settling in?      Oh, she’s doing well, thank you! She’s working as a language teacher, just like me. It’s funny, really. We both started our careers in different places, but now we’re both teaching English in the same city. It’s like fate.      That’s amazing! I still can’t believe I got a teaching job in Nottingham. It was a bit of a journey from Hitchin, but the people here are lovely. Did you ever think you’d end up teaching in London?      Honestly, no. I always thought I’d stay in the Midlands. But then I got this opportunity at a local school, and I fell in love with the community. It’s a bit sad, though. My husband’s still in London, and we’re not together anymore. He moved back there a few years ago after the kids grew up.      Oh, I’m sorry to hear that. I know how hard that can be. But I have to say, I’m impressed you’ve managed to keep your career going. I’ve been struggling with the workload lately. Between teaching and my little dog, Max, I’m pretty much fried.      You’re not alone. I’ve had my share of ups and downs. But don’t get me started on my new skincare routine. I’ve been using this serum from a local business, and it’s been a game-changer. You should try it, really.      I’ve been meaning to, but I’m always so busy. I’ve got this new business idea brewing in my head—something related to language learning apps. I just haven’t had the time to take it seriously.      That sounds exciting! You’ve always had such a good head for business. Maybe you should talk to your colleagues about it. They might have some ideas too. Oh, and don’t forget to take care of yourself, you know. You can’t pour from an empty cup.      You’re right. I keep forgetting that. I’ve got this new puppy, and he’s a handful, but he’s also the light of my life. I need to find a better balance.      That’s the spirit! You’ll get there. And if you ever need a break, you know where to find me. I’ve got a great cup of tea waiting.

So, I was just telling my mates about the Ortolan we had in Paris last year. You know, that little bird they serve with a sauce? I was like, "Is this for real?" and the guy said, "Yep, it's a tradition." I was like, “You’re joking, right?” But then they actually handed me this tiny bird on a plate. It was like something out of a movie.      Oh man, I remember that. You were so taken aback. I swear, when you took the first bite, you looked like you’d just swallowed a live mouse. I nearly fell off the chair laughing.      I remember that too. But honestly, I think the real story is how you ended up in Paris in the first place. It wasn’t just a whim, was it? You said you were going to see some films and then—boom—Ortolan.      Yeah, I had this whole plan. I was going to see  Amélie  and then maybe check out some Jewish restaurants. But then I got a call from my cousin, and suddenly I was on a plane. I don’t know, it just happened. Anyway, that Ortolan was a bit of a moment, but I’ve been dying to try it again.      I heard you were even trying to find a recipe for it back in London. I saw you scrolling through some obscure food blogs. You’re definitely not the typical foodie, are you?      Oh, I’m not. I’m more about the Passover Seder than I am the Ortolan. I mean, I’ve been trying to make my own matzo ball soup, and it’s a disaster. I think I’ve burned the broth twice now.      Come on, you’re not the only one. I tried to bake my own challah and ended up with a cake that looked like it had been through a war. My mum said it was “good enough for a Seder.” I almost believed her.      That’s the spirit. I remember when I was younger, I used to try to make my own Passover dishes, and they always ended up tasting like something from a box. But you know what? It’s the act of cooking with family that matters, not the perfect recipe.      Definitely. I mean, I’m an engineer, not a chef, but I tried to make my own gefilte fish last year. It was like a science experiment.

So, I just finished this really amazing book,  The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo  — it’s got such a powerful narrative about love, fame, and sacrifice. I thought you two might like it. I mean, it’s not exactly the sort of thing you’d expect from a historical romance, but it’s definitely got depth.      Oh, I’ve heard about that one. I think I’ve seen it on the shelf at the library. I’ve been meaning to read it, but I’ve been so busy with the admin stuff. You know how it is, always chasing deadlines. But I do like books that have strong, complex female leads. I think I’ll borrow it from the library next week.      I’ve actually read it. I thought it was fantastic, too. I mean, the way the author wrote about Evelyn Hugo’s career and personal life was so nuanced. It made me really think about how women in the entertainment industry have had to navigate so much more than just their craft.      Exactly. And I thought,  this is the kind of book that really makes you reflect . I’ve been thinking about it a lot lately. It reminded me of  The Picture of Dorian Gray , in a way. Both are about how fame and desire can corrupt. Though, of course,  Dorian  is a bit more gothic and dramatic.      True, but  Evelyn Hugo  is more modern, more grounded. It’s kind of like someone took the themes of  Dorian  and applied them to the world we live in now — with the added complexity of race, gender, and identity. I think that’s what makes it so compelling.      I agree. And I think the author really captured the tension between public and private life. Evelyn’s public persona is so different from who she is behind the scenes. It’s a great reminder that we can’t always judge people based on what they present to the world.      That’s such a good point. I’ve been meaning to talk about that with the book club. I think that’s what makes books so powerful — they can make you think about your own life and the people around you. Though, I must say, I’m a bit tired of the gothic themes lately. Maybe I need a change of pace.      Oh, I hear you. I’ve been reading more non-fiction lately.

So, what’s the deal with this new phone you’ve got, Lizzie? I’ve been trying to figure out why you’re so obsessed with it. It’s not even that much better than your old one, is it?      Oh, it’s not just about the specs, Tom. It’s the feel of it. The way it fits in your hand. Plus, I’ve got this new feature—this AI assistant thing. It’s like having a personal assistant in your pocket. You ever tried one of those?      Not really. I stick to my old ways. I like the simplicity of my Nokia. You know, like my granddad used to have. It worked, didn’t break, and I didn’t need to charge it every hour. Now I’ve got this smart phone—too many apps, too many notifications. I get distracted.      I get that, but it’s amazing how much you can do with one device. Like, I can set up meetings, send emails, and even translate things on the fly. I’m working on a PhD about language and tech, so I’ve got to stay on top of everything.      Yeah, I can see that. You’re like a walking encyclopedia. But I’ve got a question—how do you even set all that stuff up? I got mine out of the box, and it just worked. No need to tweak anything. Just switch it on and go.      Well, it’s a bit more involved. I had to set up my Google account, sync my email, and even choose a wallpaper. You can do it all from the settings, but it takes a bit of time. Oh, and you can customize the home screen. Want to see?      Yeah, actually. I’ve been meaning to get more into this. I’ve got this new phone I bought last week, and I’ve been leaving it in the box. Maybe I should try setting it up. But wait—what about the camera? I heard these new phones have amazing cameras.      Oh, they do! I took some photos last week, and they looked really good. I even tried some filters. It’s like a little photo studio in your hand. You can edit them on the go. I showed my mates, and they were impressed.      Alright, you’ve convinced me. Maybe I should give it a go. But I’m not getting rid of my Nokia just yet.

So, what do you think, Dad? Should we get a red panda?      Are you  trying  to get me into trouble? You know how much that would cost.      I was just thinking—red pandas are super cute. They’re like… little fluffy pandas with red fur.      Yeah, and they’re also one of the most expensive animals to keep. You’d have to build a special habitat and feed them bamboo every day.      I know, but I think it’d be the best birthday present for my friend. She said she’s been wanting one for ages.      You’re eleven, not eleven thousand. Do you even know how much responsibility that would be?      Well, I’ve taken care of my cat, Marmalade, for months now. She’s not that hard to look after.      Marmalade? I thought her name was Fluffy.      No, she’s got this weird little stripe on her tail. My friend said it looked like a marmalade jar, so I named her that.      Alright, I’ll give you that. But you can’t just decide someone gets a red panda on a whim. You need a plan.      I know. I was thinking maybe we could get a Malamooche, like the one in the movies. They’re not as expensive, and they’re friendly.      Oh, I see. So you’re not just talking about a red panda, you’re planning a whole new kind of pet.      Yeah, and I think I might have a present for you too. I saw this cool game called  Minecraft  on the iPad.      Oh no, not another game. You already have  Animal Crossing  and  Roblox  on your laptop.      I know, but this one’s different. It’s like a big building game where you can make your own town.      Well, if you can keep it clean, I suppose it’s okay. But I still think you need to be more responsible about your birthday plans.      I know. I was thinking maybe we can do a board game night. I have some new ones from the library.      You’re growing up, aren’t you? I remember when you were just learning to ride a bike.      Yeah, and I still can’t do it without training wheels.      That’s what I like about you, son. You’re always thinking about your friends and planning things.      And I still love my Malamooche, by the way. He’s the best.

So, I was just telling my mates about the Christmas I had when I was like... ten, maybe? We had this massive tree in the garden, and my dad tried to put a whole bunch of lights on it. He thought it was like a Christmas market.      Oh, I’ve seen that. My mum used to do that too. She’d string up all these lights and then one day, the whole thing would short out. It would be like a Christmas light fire.      Oh, I remember those days too. My husband and I used to have a tree that looked like a Christmas tree made of fairy lights. It was so bright, people would stop by just to take a look.      Yeah, but I think the best Christmas I ever had was when I was a kid. We lived in Bognor Regis, and every year, my gran would make the most incredible Christmas cake. It was always so heavy, and we had to bring it to the church for the carol service.      Oh, that sounds amazing. I’ve never seen a Christmas cake like that. My gran used to make a little one, but it was nothing compared to what you guys had.      Yeah, she was a proper baker. She always said the cake was the real Christmas spirit. And the way she pronounced “cake”—like “kayk”—it was like a whole different language.      Oh, I’ve heard that accent before. I think it’s called the “Barrow-In-Furness accent,” right? My mum grew up there, and she always said it was the most difficult to understand.      Yeah, I think that’s where I’m from. Barrow-In-Furness. I have that sort of accent, you know? Like, the way I say “churro” or “cough.”      Oh, I can tell. You say “churro” like it’s a curse word.      Yeah, that’s the thing about accents. They’re like little fingerprints of where you’re from. I always thought it was interesting how people from different regions of England speak so differently.      I’ve never really thought about it like that. I mean, I’ve heard people from London talk differently from people from Manchester. But I never really noticed the impact it had on the way people communicate.      It does, though. Like, when you’re in a group and someone from London is there, it’s like they’re speaking a different language.

So, I just got my new Kindle, and I’ve been really into this detective series. I think it’s got to be one of the best ones I’ve seen in a while. The pacing is just right, and the twists are all over the place. You’ve got to admit, it’s pretty good.      I’ll admit, it’s good. I’ve been catching up on it too. I’ve only got a few episodes left, and I’m really looking forward to seeing how it all ends. I’ve been trying to keep up with the show, but it’s been a bit of a challenge with work. I’ve had these deadlines that just keep piling up.      Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve been working on a novel, and it’s been a real grind. I can’t even get through a whole chapter without stopping to check emails or take a break. But honestly, I’ve been trying to make time for the Kindle. I’ve been reading some of the mystery novels that came with the device. They’re a bit more straightforward, but they help me get into the rhythm of reading again.      Yeah, I’ve been using the Kindle to keep up with reading while I’m on the move. I’m a transcriber, so I spend most of my time at my desk, but I still need to stay flexible with my schedule. I’ve been trying to find ways to balance work and personal time. It’s not always easy, but I think it’s worth it.      That sounds like a good approach. I’ve been trying to do something similar, but with the demands of being an administrator, it’s hard to find time. I’ve had to cut back on socialising a bit, just to keep up with work. It’s a bit of a balancing act.      I can totally relate. I’ve had to do the same. I’ve been trying to get back into the habit of going out with friends, but the pressure of finishing the novel has been a bit intense. I think I need to take a step back and just enjoy the process a little more. Maybe even take a break for a couple of days to clear my mind.      That does sound like a good idea. I’ve been thinking about taking a short holiday, maybe a weekend trip to somewhere nearby.

Well, I’ve been thinking, Bill. I was just down at the corner shop, and the lass behind the counter was chattering away about all sorts of things. She said she was doing a course on mindfulness or something like that. I said, “Mindfulness? I’ve heard of that. Is that like being in a state of calm?” She said, “Oh, no, it’s more like being present. Not worrying about the past or the future.” I said, “Aye, sounds a bit like what I try to do when I’m in the garden, blooming my flowers.” She laughed. I think she thought I was being a bit cheeky, but I reckon it’s the truth.      Oh, you always did have a way with words, Frank. I used to think you were just being cheeky, but now I think you’re almost right. I’ve been trying to do some mindfulness myself, in my own way, you know. Just sitting by the window, looking at the sky. It’s like the birds are telling you something, if you listen properly. Although, I have to say, it’s not like the lads in the pub who talk about the weather like it’s the most important thing in the world.      I wouldn’t say it’s the most important thing. I’ve been telling people that the weather is just a part of the day, like the tea. It’s the tea that makes the day. But I’m not trying to be a prat here. I’ve got to admit, I’d like to try this mindfulness thing. I’ve been too busy running the business, and now it’s closed, I’ve got more time on my hands than I know what to do with. Maybe I should start taking some courses. I was thinking of doing something like that. You know, to keep my mind sharp.      Aye, and it’s not like it’ll cost you a fortune. There’s a few courses you can do online, or maybe the library has books. I’ve seen one or two in the local shop. I think it’s more about being in the moment than anything else. I’ve been trying it with my gardening. When I go out there, I don’t think about the bills or the problems. I just think about the plants and how they’re doing.

Right, I think I’ve got everything sorted for the party tomorrow. The venue is confirmed, and the caterers are on board. But I’m still waiting on the RSVPs from the team. I’m a bit nervous about the numbers—some people might not be able to make it.      Yeah, I got the same message. I’ve sent a couple of reminders, but I know the last-minute stuff can be tricky. If we don’t get enough people, we might need to adjust the menu or the space. But don’t worry, I think we’ll be fine.      Wait, I just saw a message from someone about saving an insect. Did you hear about that? There’s a group of us who’ve been trying to catch a ladybug and put it somewhere safe. We’re thinking of making a tiny bug hotel in the garden, but we’re not sure where to put it.      That sounds adorable. I’ve seen similar projects in schools. I think it’s a great idea—especially if we can get some kids involved. But if we’re not careful, the ladybug might escape, and then we’ll have a real problem.      Oh, I remember that one from university. I once tried to save a bumblebee from the puddles on the car park, and it ended up on my shoulder for the whole day. It was a bit of a funny story, but I also got a lecture from the biology department.      That’s a great story. I’ve been doing some research on how people interact with wildlife in urban areas. It’s fascinating how even small actions can have a big impact. But I also know that sometimes you end up creating more issues than you solve.      Speaking of which, I heard about the last twenty minutes of  Horace  on the bus. I think it’s a really good idea to read that together. It’s such a clever way to reflect on language and meaning. Do you think we should plan a group reading session next week?      That sounds like a brilliant idea. We could even make it a regular thing. I think it would help us all connect better and see the research from a more personal angle.      I’m on my way to a meeting, but I can definitely support that. I’ve been trying to encourage more collaborative reading in our team.

Right, so I just got my results back from the mock exams. I was so nervous, like,  really  nervous. But I think I did okay, actually. Not great, but better than I expected.      Oh, you did? That’s good! I’m still waiting for mine. My teacher said they’re going to send them out next week. I just hope they’re not too bad. I’ve been so stressed about them.      Oh, don’t worry, you’ll be fine. I mean, I got a B in English Literature, which is  nothing  to be proud of, but I actually  liked  the book we read. I found it really interesting. You know that one with the time machine?      Yeah, that one! I was like, “Why would anyone write a book about a time machine?” But I guess it’s a classic. Wait, did you actually like it? Because I was just trying to get through it, you know?      I did. I mean, once I got into the story, it was pretty cool. I loved the way the characters reacted to the different times. It was like,  “Oh, look at this—this is so different from now!”  And then the ending? Absolute bummer. I almost cried.      Oh no, really? I thought the ending was kind of pointless. Like, what’s the point of all that time travel if nothing actually changes? I mean, it’s just a book. But I guess that’s the point, right?      Yeah, I guess. I mean, it’s supposed to make you think about time and how we live our lives. I don’t know. Maybe I just need to read more books like that. I’ve been trying to get into more fiction. My mum says it’ll help with my writing.      That’s true. I mean, I don’t really read much, but when I do, I notice how the authors structure their sentences. It’s kind of cool. I think I’m gonna try  Pride and Prejudice  next. I heard it’s a classic, but I’m not sure if I’ll like it.      Oh, you  have  to read that! I think it’s about a girl who falls in love with a guy, but they’re too proud to admit it. It’s all about misunderstandings and stuff. I think it’s totally worth it. I’ll help you if you’re stuck.

So, I just got a text from my mum saying she’s got the flu again. She’s been like this for weeks. I’m starting to think she might have a chronic condition or something. It’s not like her to be so fragile.      Yeah, I remember her getting sick last winter. She was bedridden for a good two weeks. But I think it’s just her body not coping with the cold anymore. I mean, she’s in her early 50s, right? Her immune system might be a bit more delicate than it used to be.      You know what I think, luv? I think she’s just been overdoing it with the work. She’s been working late at the shop, and I’ve seen her eating takeaway more than proper food. You can’t sustain yourself on chips and burgers, not for long.      Yeah, and she’s been breakfasting on cereal and toast every morning. I told her last week she needs to eat more properly. Maybe even get some protein in. But she just says she doesn’t have time.      That’s what I told her too. You don’t need time to cook, you just need to plan. Like, if you want to eat healthy, you can prepare meals in advance. I used to do that when I was working in the office. I’d batch-cook on Sundays and freeze portions for the week.      Exactly. And don’t even get me started on the food she buys. I saw her yesterday with a pack of crisps and a litre of cola. That’s not even dinner. It’s just junk. I told her she needs to make a change, or she’ll end up with something serious.      I agree. She’s had a few scares in the last few years. I’m worried about her health. And now we’re planning to take her out for dinner this weekend. I was thinking maybe we could cook something nice and healthy for her. Maybe a slow-cooked stew or something with plenty of vegetables.      That sounds good. I could help. Let’s make it a family meal. We can all join in and make sure she gets some proper food. That sounds busy. I’m actually planning to visit my sister in London next week. I’ve been meaning to do that for ages. She’s got a new flat and wants me to see it. I’ve got to get the money sorted with the building society.      Oh, that’s nice. I’d love to come with you, but I’m swamped with work. Still, I’m happy for you. So, I’ve been thinking about my job again, you know, since I got back from shift last night. It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, but I reckon I’m getting the hang of it now.      Yeah, I can imagine. I’ve been meaning to ask you, how’s the bar doing? Is it still as busy as it was before?      It’s alright, I guess. I mean, everyone’s got their own quirks, but it’s not like you’re working with a bunch of strangers, you know?      That’s true. I mean, I’ve got to deal with all sorts of people, from students to tourists, and every night is different. Sometimes it feels like I’m in a TV show.      Oh no, are you a regular in the bar?      Not exactly a regular, but I’m definitely a familiar face. One of the regulars even gave me a nickname – “The Hull Bartender.” I think it’s because I’m from up North, and the locals like to give nicknames.      I can imagine. You know, I was thinking about getting a job like that when I finish sixth form. Maybe something in hospitality? It’s not like I’ve got anything else planned.      Yeah, I’d say it’s a good option. It’s not the most glamorous, but it’s steady work, and you meet all sorts of people. Plus, it’s not like you’re stuck in a nine-to-five office.      You’re right. I’d rather be working somewhere where I’m actually interacting with people than sitting in a meeting all day.      Exactly. I think that’s what I like about it – the social side. Plus, I get to make people happy.

So, I was thinking, do any of you get time off for holidays? I’m trying to plan mine, and I’m not sure if I should take a few days or just stay in.      Oh, I took a break last year—went to the Lake District. It was lovely. I got to hike up to the top of a mountain and just sit there for an hour. The view was breathtaking.      That sounds amazing. I went to the south of France last year with my family. We rented a villa near Nice. The weather was perfect, and the food was out of this world.      The south of France, you say? I’m jealous. You must have had the best holiday ever.      It was great, but I had to take a lot of photos for Instagram. My niece’s birthday was there too, so it was a bit of a hassle.      Oh, I went to Spain with my girlfriend. We stayed in a little town near Seville. We went to the Alhambra and had tapas every night. It was a dream.      You’re the one who works in e-learning, right? I’d think you’d already be on holiday by now.      I’ve been working on a big project, so I took a week off in May. I didn’t do anything really special—just relaxed and caught up with friends.      And you’re from London, right? I imagine you’d be used to taking holidays.      Yeah, but I do miss the countryside. I’ve been meaning to go somewhere like the Lake District or the Scottish Highlands.      If you ever go to the Lake District, you’ll have to take me. I’ve never been there, and I’ve been living in Yorkshire my whole life!      That’s the spirit! You go, and I’ll be your guide. I’ve been there a few times.      Well, I might just take a trip to the coast. I’ve been meaning to visit the North Sea. Maybe somewhere like Scarborough or Whitby.      That sounds nice. You should do it. I’ve been meaning to go to Whitby too. I’ve heard the old legends there are spooky.      Spooky or not, it’s a lovely place. You’ll have to take me there too.      Alright, alright, we’ll all go together. It’s a holiday, after all.      Deal. Let’s plan it.

You’ve got to be kidding me. That ref just let that goal through. I swear, the whole match’s been a mess.      I know, right? I can’t believe the way they handled that corner. If it wasn’t for that one player who got a bit too close to the keeper, I reckon it would’ve been a clear goal.      Yeah, but this is the top tier, isn’t it? You’d think they’d have better control. I mean, when you're in the Premier League, you can’t just let those sort of mistakes happen.      You’re telling me. My uncle still talks about that goal his team scored against us last season – I think it was a free-kick, and the keeper was asleep on the job.      That’s the kind of thing that happens when you’re in a team full of players who haven’t quite got the sharpness they had when they were younger. Speaking of which, I saw a few of them on social media last week.      Yeah? What did they say?      Well, one of them was complaining about the diet at the club. I mean, I can see why – they’re all eating fast food and junk. It’s not like they’re getting proper meals.      Oh, that’s a laugh. I saw a video of them at a training session, and the chef was flinging burgers at them like it was some kind of competition.      I know, right? It’s all about the image. They want to look like they’re out there doing the hard work, but the truth is, they’re just grabbing a burger and a cola.      And don’t get me started on the weight gain. Last time I saw one of them, they looked like they’d been living off pizza and chips for a month.      I can’t believe I’ve been watching the same team for years and I’ve never noticed that. I mean, I’ve been eating fast food for years, but I’m not walking around like a giant pizza.      Well, maybe it’s all in the genetics. Or maybe it’s because they’re paid to do it.      Either way, I’m over it. I’ve got my healthy meals, and I’m not about to start eating like they do.      Right, you’re a real health nut. I’ll be over here eating chips and watching the game, while you’re off chasing kale.

Right, so I was watching  The Favourite  the other night, and I thought, “This is one of those films that’s going to be a classic.” You know, the kind that people will be talking about for years.      Oh,  The Favourite  was a good one, love. I’ve seen it twice. The way they played with the politics and the class stuff, it was quite something. Though I did find it a bit too dark for my taste. Not that I don’t like drama.      Yeah, I get that. It’s not for everyone, but the performances were top-notch. I mean, that one actress, Olivia Colman—she just oozes this kind of cunning, you know? Like, she’s got this whole world of her own in that house, and you can just feel it.      Hmmm, I don’t usually go for that sort of thing, but I did see it. It made me think of that time I went to a village fair and saw this old woman in a rickshaw, dressed like a queen. She had this look in her eye, like she knew everything.      That sounds like a real character. You know, I was thinking, maybe we should all go to a film festival sometime. You could take us to one of those, Mum. I could show you some of the newer ones.      Oh, I wouldn’t want to go to a film festival, love. I’d be too nervous. I’ve got enough trouble trying to remember which key goes to which drawer in this flat. But I’d love to see the films you like, though. I’ve got a soft spot for old-timey stuff.      I do like a good film. I’ve got a few old VHS tapes. They’re all in a box under the bed. I think I might have a copy of  Get Carter  or something like that. You know, that one with Michael Caine.      That’s a classic. I’ve seen it a few times. It’s got this gritty edge that you don’t see in modern films. But it’s still pretty good. Maybe one day I’ll show it to the lads. Although I doubt they’ll sit through it.      I remember when we first watched it. We were all squashed in the back of the car, and it was raining like mad. We didn’t even know what was going on half the time.

So, I’ve been thinking about Pancake Day again. You know, when we all got together and made those giant pancakes. It was chaos, but it was fun.      Yeah, I remember! We had to use the biggest pan we could find, and it spilled everywhere. But it was so good.      I got covered in syrup! I had to change my shirt.      Oh, I remember that. Didn’t you, Tom? You were the one who tried to flip it over and ended up burning your fingers.      I did! I thought I was being clever, but I just ended up with a pancake on my hand.      It was a mess, but it was worth it. Anyway, I was thinking about the school assembly this week. The kids were talking about growing up and how they want to be scientists when they’re older.      Yeah, I heard about that. I think the teacher said something about the Science Museum. Maybe we could go there this weekend?      That’s a good idea. I’ve been meaning to take the kids there. It’s a great way to learn and have fun.      Can we? I love the Science Museum! They have all those cool experiments.      Yeah, and the planetarium! I want to see the stars.      We can do that. But first, we need to make sure the kids brush their teeth. It’s important for their health.      Ugh, I don’t like brushing my teeth.      I know, but it’s for your benefit. Speaking of benefits, I was also thinking about the Festival Hall events this weekend. Maybe we could go to one of those short stories readings?      That sounds cool. I like stories.      I know. I think it’s a great way to spend the weekend. We can also go to the beach if we want, but let’s make sure we all eat our food first.      I didn’t eat my breakfast.      Oh, that’s not good. We need to make sure the kids are eating properly, especially with all these plans.      I think I’m full.      Well, let’s just enjoy the meal and then make some plans for the weekend. And maybe we can talk about the Green Knowe story later. I think it’s a great one.      Yeah, it’s about a girl who lives in a house with a secret. Sounds exciting.      I’m sure it will be. Now, let’s finish eating, and then we can start planning our adventure.

So, I just got the latest news about the funeral for that old lady from the corner shop. You remember her, right? Mrs. Thompson?      Oh yeah, she was one of the regulars at the local butcher’s. Was it the one at the end of the street?      Yeah, that’s the one. It was quite a thing. Everyone was there—neighbors, old friends, even a few from the village. I mean, she lived alone, so it was a bit of a surprise when she passed. They had this little service in the church.      That’s sad. I couldn’t go, though. I had to work late. Still, I managed to send a card and a bit of money. I hope the family is coping.      I heard they had a great turnout. They even had a speech from the local councillor. He said something about how she was a real community pillar. Reminds me of my grandmother. She used to always have that little stall at the market.      Yeah, that’s the thing with people like her—those who are quietly there for everyone. Sometimes it’s not until they’re gone that you realize how much they meant. It’s kind of heartbreaking, but also a reminder to not take people for granted.      I guess that’s the thing about life. You never know when someone’s going to be gone. You know what’s funny is, I saw Bob the Builder the other day. He was doing a TV advert. That’s like the first time I’ve seen him since he was a kid. Still looks the same.      Oh no! You mean the one with the yellow bucket and the plastic digger? I can’t believe he’s still on TV. I used to watch him when I was little. Still, I guess it’s a classic. You can’t just stop a show like that.      I think he’s been on for years. I remember when he was all over the place, even in the news. I think he’s the reason we all know how to build a treehouse.      That’s what I’ve always thought. Bob the Builder set the standard for building with sticks and imagination. Though I can’t believe he’s still around. It’s like he never aged.      It’s like a nostalgic trip, isn’t it? Anyway, we’re talking about funerals, not Bob.

So, I was just thinking about my gran, she always used to say that if you wanted to know what a person was like, just look at the way they ate. She had this incredible nose for a good meal, and she knew every restaurant in the village.      Aye, that’s typical of her, I used to think the same. She had this way of making every meal feel like a celebration. Even when we were short of money, she’d somehow manage to turn a simple meal into something special.      She always said that when you're cooking, you're not just feeding people—you're feeding your soul. I remember her making those rice krispy cakes with the marshmallows and cereal, it was like magic.      Oh, I remember those! We’d all gather round the table, the house would be filled with the smell of butter and marshmallows, and she’d tell us stories about how she used to make them when she was a girl. She even used to say that the first time she made them, she burnt the kitchen down.      Aye, I remember that. She said it was a bit of a fire alarm, and the neighbours came running out. But she laughed it off, said it was just a sign that she was meant to be a chef.      I think she actually got quite a few letters from people saying they’d tried to replicate her recipe and failed. She was proud of that.      And she always made sure we had enough for the next meal, too. She used to say, “If you’ve got enough for today, you’ve got enough for tomorrow.” I think she was right.      She had a way of looking at things differently. She always said that life was like a meal—you have to take the good bits and not be fazed by the bad.      And she was right. She used to say that even if you didn’t have much, you could always make something out of it. I think that’s what made her so special.      I miss her talking about the old days, about the village, about the way things used to be. She had so many stories, and I think it was her way of keeping everyone connected.      She was a real character, wasn’t she? And she always had a way of making everyone feel at home.

So, I was just telling the kids about Chinese New Year—the dragon thing, you know. You've got to have a dragon for luck, right?      Yeah, I remember when we had the dragon drawing at school. I tried to make it look like a real dragon, but it ended up looking like a spaghetti monster.      That’s not just you! I made mine with crayons and then it looked like a blob. My sister said it was the most amazing dragon she’d ever seen.      Oh, you’re both so creative. I think the real magic is in how you add your own style to it. I remember my mum used to make these really intricate dragons, all glitter and gold, with little sequins.      Did you ever make one? I’d love to see it.      I actually didn’t, to be honest. I was more into the legends and the stories. I think the dragons are part of the bigger story—like how they’re guardians of the sky and water and all that. But I did buy some Chinese New Year decorations for the house. They look really nice in the living room.      Can we put up the red paper cuttings too? I saw them in the shop and they looked super cool.      Of course. We’ll do that. And maybe even have some dumplings. I got some recipe from my cousin—she says they’re the best she’s ever had.      I can’t wait! I’ve been craving Chinese food all week. Especially the spring rolls. My teacher said they are part of the New Year feast, right?      Yes, and you’re right. They’re a big part of it. Speaking of which, have you all thought about what you want for the Year of the Rabbit?      I want to learn how to play the piano. I told my mum I want to play like Beethoven.      Me too! And I want to take drum lessons. I think I can be the best drummer in the whole world.      That’s wonderful. You both have such big dreams. I think you’ll make it. And maybe, just maybe, we’ll start planning a little New Year celebration over the weekend. We can do some drawing, maybe even have a mini feast.      That would be awesome! I’ll bring my crayons. And maybe some of my stickers too.      I’ll bring my toy drums.

So, I'm telling you, I've never seen such a beautiful place in my whole life. Rome, man. It’s like stepping back in time. I've been walking around the Colosseum and the Pantheon, and it’s just... wow.      I know, right? It’s like every corner has a story. I was just telling Speaker_3 about how I got lost in Trastevere and ended up in this little piazza with a guy selling wine. He was from somewhere in the south, and he had this really thick accent. It was like listening to a character from a film.      Yeah, you know, I’ve met a few people here with different accents. I think Speaker_4, who’s the barista at the café where we’re staying, is from Australia. He speaks like he’s trying to be British, but he still sounds Australian in his own way.      Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. It’s interesting how people here, even if they’re British, still have that sort of posh or northern accent. I think Speaker_2 has that kind of London accent, but it’s not the same as the way I grew up in Birmingham.      Oh, come on, I don’t have a ‘posh’ accent. I just speak English as it’s spoken in the UK. Though I have to say, I’ve been trying to pick up a few Italian words. I think I said “ciao” the other day and it got me a weird look.      I know what you mean. I tried to order coffee this morning and said "cappuccino" with that London drawl, and the barista just stared at me. I think I got the look of “are you high?”      You should’ve asked me. I speak Italian, you know. I run a café, so it’s part of the job. And I always tell people that if they want to survive here, they need to learn a few phrases.      Yeah, and if you don’t, you risk getting lost or confused. I’ve seen it happen. I had a friend from the US who said “taxi” and ended up at the airport.      I think we all have our own mishaps here. Speaking of which, we should probably plan dinner tonight. I’m thinking of going to that little trattoria near the Piazza Navona. The food there is amazing.      That sounds good. I was going to suggest it, too.

So, I just got an email from Lucy saying she’s going to be in town next week. She wanted to know if we could plan a hen do for her wedding. I think it’s next month, right?      Yeah, I think it’s the 15th. She’s got a friend who’s doing the venue, so we just need to pick the date and then start planning. I’ve been thinking about doing something creative—maybe a craft day or something?      Oh, that sounds fun. I’ve been meaning to do some pottery myself. I saw a workshop at the local community centre. Maybe we could do that? It’s the kind of thing that people would enjoy and it’s not too expensive.      That could work. I’m actually looking for a venue for a friend’s event next month, so if you’re up for it, maybe we can get some details from them? I mean, if you’re in, that is.      Absolutely. I’d love to do that. I’ve always thought pottery was a great way to get people together—it’s relaxing and people can take something home. Plus, it’s not the kind of thing that’s too messy or anything.      Exactly. I was also thinking about adding a baking element. Maybe after the pottery, we could have a little bake-off or something. I’ve got some new recipes from a magazine I got last week.      That sounds amazing. I could help with the baking. I’ve been practicing my scone-making lately—though I’d say I’m still at the beginner stage.      That’s adorable. I think about baking as well. I’ve been trying to improve my cake decorating skills. Maybe we could have a competition between us?      Oh, a competition? I’d be up for that. I’ve been meaning to try my hand at making cupcakes. I have this new cupcake recipe I got from my sister.      You’re getting somewhere with the baking, aren’t you? I’ve seen your Instagram posts with your homemade cookies. They’re incredible.      Thank you, I try. I think I’ve got the hang of it now. But I’m still trying to get the texture right.      You’ll get it. I think the key is just to keep practicing. I’ve been doing it for a while and I still mess up sometimes.

Man, I'm so glad we're not cooking this for the whole house. I’d be in a right pickle if Mum walked in and saw this mess. I've been feeling absolutely knackered all week, like I’ve got a cold or something. Just can't seem to shake it.      Yeah, I reckon you’ve got something going on. You’ve been off your food and your eyes look a bit puffed. You should probably take a day off or something. You can’t just keep pushing through like you're some kind of superhero. Look, I get it. You’re trying to be responsible, but you’re not being kind to yourself. You could always take the day off and get some rest. I mean, you’re not the only one who needs to get this done. You know I can help out with the project if you need me to.      You'd do that? I’d really appreciate that. Honestly, I’m just trying to keep up with everything. It’s been a bit of a hectic time.      No worries. We’re in this together. Speaking of which, have you thought about where you're going on holiday this year? I heard you mentioned something about France.      Yeah, I was thinking about it. Maybe somewhere near the coast. I always feel better when I’m by the sea. But I’m worried about the hotels. I don’t know if I can trust the ones online. I remember last time I booked a hotel in Spain, the place was a bit of a dump.      You’re not the only one who’s had that experience. I always read reviews and check the location before I book. But if you’re thinking about France, I heard there are some amazing places in the south. You should try a place with a good view and a decent breakfast.      Yeah, maybe. I’ll look into it. I just need to get this project done first, though. I can’t afford to be sick on holiday.      Fair enough. Just take care of yourself, mate. You’re not invincible, you know. And if you need help with anything—keeping up with work or planning the trip—just let me know.

So, I was sorting through the kitchen drawers the other day, and I found this old birthday card from when I was about ten. It had my age written on it in crayon, and it said “Happy 10th Birthday, Annie!” — well, that’s what my mum called me then. I mean, I still call myself Annie, but I reckon I’ve had a few more birthdays since then.      Oh, I remember those days! You were the one who used to draw the most elaborate cards. I still have one with a picture of a space ship and a little alien. I think it was for your 7th birthday. You were obsessed with that one.      Yeah, and I still have that! I kept it in a box for years. It’s in the attic now. I was just thinking about how times have changed. I mean, those birthday cards back then were so simple — no digital photos, no fancy designs. Just sticks and glue and crayon. Now, we just send them through WhatsApp or something.      True. I was just talking to one of the younger people the other day about how we used to make our own stuff. They don’t know what a “calendar fob” even is. I told them, you know, those little things you wear on your wrist with the numbers and the month and everything. I still have one from when I was in primary school.      Oh, I remember those. You had a red one with a little cow on it. I’d always pretend it was a watch. But seriously, I was thinking the other day, how do we even do things like that now? I mean, the other week I had to buy some hockey boots for the kids, and it was all online. I didn’t know where to start.      I know. I passed by the computing museum the other day, and it was just full of all those old gadgets. I thought about how much things have changed. I mean, you used to have to know how to use a typewriter to get into university, and now it’s all about coding and sound recording.      Exactly. I was thinking about applying to do some sound recording at university, just for fun. I mean, I’m retired now, but it’s something I’ve always been interested in. I remember in school, we had to do art and craft, and I never had a real hobby.

So, I was just telling ANON that the first time I walked through the woods behind the house, I thought I'd stepped into a Bond movie. All these paths, and not a soul in sight. Not even a squirrel, for God's sake.      That sounds dramatic. I mean, it’s just a bit of countryside. Though I have to say, I love the quiet. I used to be a city girl, but now I can't get enough of the peace here. The only thing that's a bit of a pain is the lack of shops. You have to walk all the way to Holsworthy for anything.      My first week here, I thought I’d left my keys in the car, so I went to the post office to get a new one. Turns out I had them in my hand the whole time. I still haven’t figured out how that happened.      That's the kind of thing that happens when you’re still getting used to the rhythm of the place. I remember when I first moved in—there I was, trying to work out whether the water pressure was off or if the tap was broken. Took me two days to figure out it was just a faulty washer.      I had a similar thing with the garden. I thought the plants were dying, but it was just the wrong type of soil. I ended up getting a soil test kit, which turned out to be a bit of a waste of money. But at least I learned something.      I still don’t know how to use the wood burner. I mean, I’ve watched the videos, but when the real thing is in front of me, it’s like I've been transported to another era. ANON says it’s all about the draft, but I’m not sure I believe her.      You need to get the fire going right. I fell into that trap myself. I started too hot, and the whole thing just went out. It took me two weeks to figure out the right way to do it. Now, I’ve got a little routine going.      I think the real test is the local walking group. I was invited to join, and I thought it’d be a nice way to get to know people. But when I showed up, it was all about the trail, and I was just the odd one out.

Man, I'm so fed up with this online shopping thing. I tried to order a new pair of boots last week, and it took me  three  days just to get the right size. I mean, we live in the 21st century, right? You’d think it’d be easier than ordering a takeaway.      Yeah, I know, I’ve been through that too. I ordered this new laptop for my uni course, and it was supposed to be delivered in three days. Turns out it took a week and a half. I almost gave up on the internet.      I know the feeling. But you know what's even worse? Trying to get help from customer service. I called the shop and they put me on hold for  twenty  minutes. I ended up just giving up and going to the local shop instead.      “Ah, yes, I’m sorry for the inconvenience, can I get your name and address?” No, I don’t want to give them my name and address, I just want my boots!      Exactly! It's like they're deliberately making it hard. I tried to get a job once, you know. Online – like, remote work. I thought it'd be easy, but the application process was like a game of snakes and ladders. You apply, then you wait, then you get rejected, then you try again.      Yeah, I tried that too. Some guy sent me this email asking if I could work from home as a virtual assistant. I thought, "That sounds easy enough," but then he sent me a 50-page questionnaire about my “digital skills.” I didn’t even know what that meant.      I know, I know. I just feel like there’s no way forward. I’m stuck at home, not working, not studying, just… waiting. I tried to apply for some courses, but I couldn’t even afford the fees. It’s a real catch-22.      Yeah, I get it. I mean, it’s tough out there. But you know what? Maybe it’s not all bad. I mean, I’ve got my course, and I’m learning new things, even if it’s just about how to use a computer properly.      I guess. Maybe I should just start learning some skills. I mean, I’ve been on TikTok for ages, so I know how to make videos. Maybe I could do something with that. Or upload some stuff online?

So, I’ve been thinking, do you reckon we should get rid of that old boiler in the house? I mean, it’s been going since the 80s, and it’s still kicking. Not sure if it’s even worth fixing.      Yeah, I’ve been meaning to bring it up. I reckon it’s about time we sorted it out. I don’t want to be stuck in the dark again during a cold snap. It was a bit of a shock last time when the heat died and we had to rely on the electric fire. You know what I mean?      I remember that night. You were trying to knit and the fire was flickering like a candle. It’s one thing to be cold, but it’s another to feel like you’re in a cave. But then again, it’s not like we’re going to be here forever. I mean, everyone has a certain age when they start needing more modern things.      That’s true, but I like the idea of keeping some of the old stuff. There’s something nostalgic about that broken toaster that’s still working and the chair from my dad’s house. It’s like part of the rhythm of the house.      I get that, but I think we need to balance it. We’re not moving out, but we are planning to go on that coastal walk next weekend, and I want to make sure we’re not also dealing with a broken heating system. Besides, we’re thinking of buying some new furniture anyway.      Exactly. I was looking at some stuff online today about vintage chairs and modern sofas. You know, the kind that blend the old with the new. Maybe we could do that with the house. I mean, it’s not like we’re trying to be trendy for the sake of it. It’s more about making it feel like home.      Fair point. I’ve been meaning to do a bit of DIY anyway. I had that idea of putting up some shelves in the kitchen. I think it would help with the storage and also make the place look a bit more lived-in. I’ve been watching some videos on YouTube on how to do it properly.      That’s brilliant! I can help you with that. I’ve got some tools and I’m pretty handy with a hammer and a drill.

So, I was just thinking about how things have changed since we first started working on this project together. It’s been almost three years now, and I’m still not sure if I made the right decision to take this post-doc role. You know, the one that moved us from Guildford to Manchester?      Yeah, I remember that. You were really hesitant at first, weren’t you? But I think it was the right move in the long run. I mean, the research opportunities here are top-notch, and you’ve been making some solid contributions. Plus, we’ve got the kids settled now.      That’s true. The kids are great, and the school’s pretty good. But sometimes I worry about whether I’m being ambitious enough. I mean, I’m doing good work, but I’m not sure if I’m on the right track for a professorship or if I’ve got the right network. I feel like I’m just going through the motions.      You’re not going through the motions, love. You’ve got the skills, the drive, and the passion for this work. You just need to be more strategic about your next steps. Why don’t you start by reaching out to some of the academics you’ve worked with? Maybe even consider a few collaboration opportunities. It’s all about building those relationships.      That’s what I was thinking. But it’s hard to know where to start. I feel like I’m stuck in this cycle, doing the same things, not getting the recognition I deserve. I know it’s part of the process, but sometimes it gets frustrating.      I get it. I’ve been in that place too. Remember when we were both just starting out? You used to talk about your goals all the time, and I used to think you were too focused on the future and not enough on the present. Maybe that’s the thing, though—being too focused on the future can make you miss the things that matter right now. Like family time, or just enjoying the moment.      You’re right. I’ve been so caught up in work that I’ve barely had time to breathe. I’ve been thinking about taking a short break, maybe a holiday, something to reset.      That sounds like a great idea. You deserve some time off. And besides, you’ve got the kids, so you need to make sure you’re looking after your own mental health.

So, I was just telling my sister about the cat that ran into the garden and got stuck in the hedge. It was  so  dramatic, like a movie scene. She said, “You’re not serious,” and I said, “Oh yes, I am. It was like it was trying to escape from the world.”      Sounds like a typical cat. I had one once that would escape from the house every morning, like it was going on a mission. One day, it was gone for three days. We thought it was lost. Then came back with a big, muddy paw print on the kitchen floor. We knew it had been on an adventure.      I swear my left hand is like a separate entity. I try to use it, and it just does its own thing. I told my mum about it once, and she said, “That’s just how you are, love.” But honestly, it’s so frustrating. I can’t even write with it without making a mess.      I’ve had that problem too. My left hand’s like a rebellious teenager. It’s got its own agenda. I’ve tried everything—therapies, exercises, everything. But no matter what, it just won’t cooperate. Sometimes, I think it’s trying to prove a point.      I think it’s just a left-handed thing, you know? I mean, we’re all born with a dominant hand, but some of us are left-handed. It’s like the universe is testing us.      I’ve never been left-handed, but I’ve always been interested in how people manage. I mean, I had to use my right hand for everything growing up. My mum used to say it was a sign of strength to be right-handed. But I think left-handedness is just as natural.      I think it’s all about how you use your hands. You can train your brain to use the other hand. I’ve seen people do it. It takes time, but it’s possible. I’ve even seen a few left-handed people in my department.      Yeah, but it’s not just about using the other hand. It’s about the whole body. I mean, my left hand isn’t the only one that’s stubborn—it’s like my whole body resists change. I’d rather write with my right hand and make a mess than try to be left-handed.

So, I was just telling my mates about the best meal I had when I was in Newcastle last month. It was this tiny little place down by the quayside, right? You know, the kind of place that only the locals go to. The fish and chips were just... wow. The batter was  crispy , the chips were  golden , and the beer? Oh, it was a proper real ale. I haven’t had anything like that since I was a kid.      Sounds like a proper chase. I remember when I was young, I used to go to the pub with my dad every Sunday. We’d have a few pints, and then he’d take me to the fish and chip shop. The only difference now is, I can’t even afford a pint anymore. I mean, I’m retired, but I’m not rich. I still remember when I was working at BT, I’d take a week’s holiday and go to the coast. You know, the Northumberland coast. There was this little village, I think it was called Amble, and the fish and chips there were next-level.      Yeah, I remember that. My gran used to take me there when I was a kid. She’d say it was the best in the county, and I believed her. But these days, I’m too busy with work to go anywhere. I was in Manchester last week, though. For a meeting. And I had this chicken tikka masala. It was just... incredible. I mean, I know it’s a British invention, but it was delicious. I told my mates I should open a restaurant, but they all laughed. They said I was being too dramatic.      I’ve been thinking about that. I was in Dubai a while back, and the food there was amazing. But I couldn’t get the same taste of home. I mean, I tried to find a proper English pie and mash, but it was just... not the same. You can’t replicate the taste of home, can you?      No, not really. I’ve tried, but it’s like trying to get the smell of the old house back. You can go back, but it’s not the same. I still remember the smell of the fish and chips, the smell of the ale, the smell of the pub. It’s like a part of you.

So, I just got an email from the university about the new module we’re supposed to co-teach. It’s on post-war European literature—sounds like a good topic, but I’m not sure how we’re going to structure it. You’ve got more experience with that, haven’t you?      Yeah, I mean, I’ve taught some of those texts before. But honestly, I think we need to be careful not to just list the authors and novels. We should really focus on the historical context and how the political climate influenced the writing. You know, like how the Cold War shaped some of the themes in those books.      That’s a good point. I was thinking we could start with a seminar on the fall of the Berlin Wall and then move into the post-war period. But I’m worried we might be too focused on the Western European angle. Should we include some Eastern European perspectives too?      Absolutely. That’s something I’d like to bring up. I think it’s important to show the diversity of the region. Maybe we could invite a guest speaker from a different university, or at least include some secondary sources from Eastern Europe. It would make the module more balanced.      That sounds like a solid plan. But I’m curious—how are you feeling about the workload? I know we’ve both got other classes to teach, and this one’s going to take a lot of preparation.      Honestly, I’m a bit nervous. I mean, it’s a big responsibility, but I think it’s a good challenge. I’d love to work with you on this. Plus, I think the students will really benefit from our combined expertise. You’re so good at making complex ideas accessible—maybe you can help me with the lectures?      That would be great. I’d love to collaborate more. Speaking of which, I was thinking we should go out for dinner tonight. I found this new restaurant near the campus that serves some amazing modern British cuisine. You know, proper fish and chips, but with a twist.      Sounds good. I’ll bring the wine. Although, I do have to mention that I tried the fish and chips last week and it was  way  overpriced. But the chips were good. Maybe we can split a platter and save some money.      Fair enough.

You know, I’ve been thinking about that coffee machine we’re supposed to get rid of. I mean, I’m not sure we can even afford the removal and storage costs these days. I remember when we had the old one—grind, brew, and it was good enough for the whole house.      Yeah, I’ve been tracking the quotes. The removal company said it’s going to cost over £200 just to get it to the storage unit. And then there’s the storage fee. I’m not even sure if we should keep it. I mean, we don’t even use it that much anymore.      I agree. I think it’s time to let go of the past. I mean, I used to love the smell of coffee in the morning, but now? I just make breakfast and call it a day. Plus, with the state of the economy, I don’t want to be stuck with unnecessary expenses.      It’s not just the coffee machine, though. I’ve been thinking about the whole idea of holding on to things. You know, like we used to do—everything had to be kept, everything had to be saved. Back when we had a job, a house, and a future. But now? I’m not sure if we even have a future.      I know. I’ve been thinking about that too. I mean, I’m not in a bad place, but with the cost of living going up, and the job market being what it is, I’m starting to feel like we’re just treading water. I don’t know if it’s the right time to be spending money on things we don’t really need.      It’s funny, isn’t it? We used to talk about the Labour leadership all the time. I remember when Tony Blair was in charge, and everyone thought we were going to be alright. But now? I don’t know what to think. I mean, I still believe in the ideals—equality, justice, fairness—but I’m not sure where they’ve gone.      I think some of us still believe in those ideals, but the reality is different. I mean, I’m retired now, and I’m not working, but I can still see the struggles of people my age. We’re the ones who were promised a better life, and now we’re the ones who are struggling to make ends meet.

So, I was just telling the others about the restaurant we stumbled upon. It was this tiny place tucked between two shops, and the owner’s name was  Reuben . You gotta love that name—sounds like a character out of a  Harry Potter  book.      I like that. I was just saying that if I had a café, I’d name it  Reuben’s  too. It’s got that kind of classic, slightly mysterious vibe.      Yeah, but I’m still not sure about the name  Reuben . It sounds more like a nickname for a guy who’s into vintage vinyl than a café. Though I’ll admit, it does give you a sense of character.      Exactly. And the menu? They had this weird thing with  kosher law  on it. I thought it was a joke at first, but apparently, they’re trying to be  kosher-certified .       Kosher ? I thought that was something you had to be  very  specific about. Like, you couldn’t even have a  microwave  in the kitchen?      Oh no, you can have a microwave. But it has to be  certified .
