I mean, I’ve never even thought about it before, but I guess it’s about the principles.      “Oh, but this  condiment  is not  kosher , and this  Italian  sauce is  kosher  because it’s made in a  certified  kitchen.”      That’s the thing. It’s like,  if you are doing it right, you’re doing it right . Maybe I should start a chain of  kosher  takeaway places. All I’d need is a  microwave  and a  license .      You’d be a  certified   kosher   microwave   owner . That’s the kind of tagline that’ll make you go viral.      I go to a  club  near my flat that’s  Italian  and  kosher —it’s like a  condiment  on a  canal boat . You can have  pasta  with  olive oil  and  chickpeas  and still be  kosher .      It’s all about  context , isn’t it? Like, if you’re in a  canal boat  in  London , you can pretty much  do anything , as long as you don’t  break the law .      That’s the spirit. Break the law, but don’t break the  salad .      I’m just glad the  law  didn’t stop us from having  Italian   pasta  for lunch today. Even if we had to eat it out of  microwave  containers.      To the  canal boat  crew and the  kosher   law —may we never  break  it.

So, I'm telling you, I've been swiping left and right on Tinder for like, what, three weeks now, and I still haven't met someone who isn’t a total numptie. I mean, honestly, I saw a bloke who said he loves  kale —I thought, "Oh, he’s got good taste!" But then he wanted to meet up and said he only eats "clean" food. I’m like, "Alright, then, what about a bit of toast and butter?"      I know, right? I saw someone who said they’re into  science —okay, cool—but then they only liked people with PhDs. My uni degree is a first-class in English Lit. I’m not a PhD, but I’m not a  numptie , either. I mean, I can spell  'numptie'  if I want to.      You're both being too picky. I mean, it’s not like you're looking for someone who can help you with your thesis, is it? I mean, I’ve been on Tinder for a month now and I’ve only met two people who aren’t in their thirties. One was a guy from Manchester who said he was a “home cook” but I didn’t even know what  ‘home cook’  meant. It was just takeaway and a litre of lager.      Oh, that’s the same bloke I saw. He sent me a photo of himself doing a  'side hustle'  and it was just him painting a picture of a cat in a house. I thought, “Is he about to sell this?” I mean, I’m not looking for an artist, I’m looking for someone who knows how to use a plug socket without burning it down.      I’ve been trying to find someone who actually wants to  cook  together. I saw a guy who said he was into  “healthy eating”  and I thought, “Great, I can teach him how to make a decent stir-fry.” But then he told me he doesn’t like onions. I’m like, “Okay, then, what about garlic? Or gochujang? Or…” and he said, “No, I’m just not into that.” I don’t know, I’m starting to think he just wants to eat at the same time as me.      I’m not even trying to find someone. I’m just trying to avoid getting a heartbreak like last time. I had this guy who said he was "into  university life "—which is basically just binge-watching  Friends  and drinking cider.

Well, I’ve been thinking about this benefits situation again, Bill. I know it’s been a tough few years, and I don’t know about you, but I feel like the system’s gone from bad to worse. It’s not like we’ve done anything wrong—just living our lives, trying to get by on what we can.      Yeah, I reckon you’re right, Harry. I mean, we’re not asking for much, just a bit of support to keep the lights on and put food on the table. But it’s like the government doesn’t care anymore. I keep hearing about how they’re cutting back, and it’s just made things harder for people like us.      I agree, lads. I’ve been through this before. I remember when things were different, and the support was more consistent. Now, it’s like you’re expected to jump through hoops just to get what you’re entitled to. And I’ve got to say, I’m not a fan of the new TV programme that’s been on the telly about benefits. It’s full of blokes like us, but they don’t show the real story. I mean, we’re not all scroungers, you know.      That’s right, Karen. I was watching it last night, and it made me really angry. I mean, they take people’s stories out of context and paint them as lazy, when in reality, we’ve spent our lives working hard. I was a civil engineer, and someone like me should be able to get a bit of a hand up, not be treated like a criminal.      I can’t say I disagree with that, Harry. I spent most of my life on the land, and I’ve had a rough go of it. I used to be a farm worker, and now I’m just trying to make ends meet. I think the system’s not just broken—it’s designed to keep people like us down.      Exactly. And the TV programme just adds to the stigma. People don’t want to admit they need help, but the truth is, we’re just trying to live our lives. I’ve got a couple of grandkids now, and I want to make sure they know that their grandparents are not scroungers—we’re just people who’ve had a hard time.      I couldn’t agree more, Karen.

So, I was just thinking about that charity event you had last week. You looked absolutely exhausted after it. I mean, I’m not saying I wouldn’t have done the same, but you’re not exactly the type to go all out like that.      Oh, come on, I’m not that bad. I reckon I kept up with the energy level. Besides, I had a decent amount of support from the team. Still, it was a long day, and I had to do the speeches, the set-up, and then the actual event. You know how it is.      Yeah, and I know you’re not one for unnecessary drama, but I could tell you were really pushing yourself. It’s not like you to take on so much. But I guess you wanted to prove something. Or maybe you just needed a bit of a challenge.      Maybe. I mean, I’ve been in that job for a while now. It’s not like I’m going anywhere, but I do like to keep things interesting. Plus, the people I work with are a great bunch. It’s not just about the fundraising — it’s about the relationships, the impact we make. You know how I feel about that.      Of course I do. You’ve always been passionate about that. But you have to remember, you’re not just fundraising for the sake of it. You’re doing it for real people. And you’re doing a good job of it. I just worry you’ll burn out.      I know. I’ve been thinking about that too. I’m not sure if I’m ready to step down just yet, but maybe I need to take a break. I’ve been working more than I should. And I haven’t even mentioned the time I’ve been spending on the family stuff. I know you’ve been helping out a lot with the kids.      You know I’d do anything to help. But I’m not doing it for you. I’m doing it because I love my kids and I love our family. Still, I think you need to take a step back. Maybe go for a walk, or just sit and talk about something other than work for a bit.      Okay, fair enough. I’ll take your word for it. Although, I’d still like to go to that new comedy show on Friday.

I’ve been feeling so rotten lately. I think I’ve caught something from the cat. It’s been sneezing and coughing like mad. I’ve been lying in bed all day, just hoping it’ll pass. I don’t know what’s worse—being sick or trying to convince myself that I can still do the things I used to do.      That’s rough. I had a bit of a cold last week, but it wasn’t as bad as that. You’re lucky the cat doesn’t chase you around the flat anymore. You know, I’ve been thinking about how weird it is that we’re both stuck in Poland, not really in our own homes.      It’s strange, isn’t it? I’ve been back to Cambridge a couple of times for the funeral, but it’s not the same. You’re not really ‘home’ when you’re returning for a funeral. It’s like you’re just visiting a place you once knew.      Yeah, it’s like a ghost town. I mean, I left Bury quite a while ago, but when I go back, everything’s just… different. The people, the rhythm of the town—it’s like I’ve forgotten how to breathe in that place.      It’s that sense of belonging, isn’t it? I used to think that if I just worked in teaching again, I’d feel more settled. But now, I’m not even sure what I’m working toward. I’ve got a few hours of TEFL here and there, but it’s not enough to make a difference.      I know what you mean. I’ve been doing this teaching job for years, but I still feel like I’m running on autopilot. My sister’s got a therapy group for people like us—those of us who feel disconnected. I’ve been going a few times, and it’s actually helping. I mean, it’s not a cure, but it’s something.      I tried to do something like that, but I just couldn’t get around to it. I think I was too ashamed to admit I needed help.      It’s not shameful. It’s just human. You’re not the only one. I mean, have you seen the photos on my social media? I’m always posting about holidays and where I want to live next. But the truth is, I’m not sure where I want to live.

Right, so I was thinking – have you noticed how much more expensive it is to buy food in London now? I mean, I can’t even afford a proper meal without breaking the bank. Not that I’m complaining, but sometimes it feels like we’re just paying for the privilege of being here.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to save up for that new laptop, and every time I go into a café or even a supermarket, it feels like I’m losing money. But it’s not just the cost – it’s the choices. Like, you can’t just grab a sandwich and a coffee anymore without feeling like you’re being scammed.      Exactly! I tried this new place near the station last week, and I think the sandwich was like £5.50. For what? A piece of bread with some random filling? I mean, I’m not a food snob, but I thought we were supposed to have better things in London. I guess it’s just the cost of living, though.      You’re not the only one. I’ve been trying to buy groceries on a budget, but even the cheapest loaf of bread is like £1.50 these days. I mean, I know the cost of living is high, but it’s not just the food. I’ve been working part-time as a survey programmer, and even then, I can’t afford to eat out more than once a week.      I’d love to be in your position. I’m in a lower managerial role, and it’s not easy. I mean, I’m not in debt or anything, but I feel like I’m always just scraping by. I think it’s easier to save up when you’re a student, even if you’re not earning much. At least you’re not paying rent.      Yeah, I know. I mean, I’m not complaining, but I do feel like I’m working harder and still not being rewarded properly. It’s funny because we’re both in the same city, but the way we live is so different. I guess it’s just the difference between being in a higher professional occupation versus a lower managerial one.      I know. I’ve been thinking about moving out of London for a while, but I can’t afford it. Plus, it’s not like I can just up and leave without a plan.

Oh, I'm so sorry, Love. I know it's early, but I just got up and thought I'd check on you two. I didn't mean to wake you up!      Mmm… it’s like 7 a.m. I was just dreaming about glitter and jumping on trampolines.      I was dreaming about flying! Or maybe I was riding a unicycle. It was a bit of both.      That sounds like a circus dream. You two are going to the Neon Moon event today, aren’t you?      Yeah! It’s at the town hall, right? I think it’s like a night market with tents and fire dancers.      And there’s a ring of fire! I saw something about it on the flyer.      Oh, right! The circus skills display. I remember reading about it in the local paper. It’s a family-friendly event, so you’ll be fine.      What about lunch? Do we need to bring anything?      No, they have food stalls. You can get hot dogs, burgers, and even vegan options. I think there’s a guy selling lemonade with a neon sign.      Can I learn to juggle? I saw a poster about circus skills workshops.      Absolutely! You can try juggling, balancing, or even acrobatics. It’s a great way to burn off some energy before the event.      I’d like to try the hula hoop. I’ve always wanted to do that.      Perfect! I’ll make sure to sign you both up for the workshop. Oh, and don’t forget—there’s a “Australian phrases” game at the event.      What’s that?      It’s where you learn all the slang from Australia. Like “arvo” for afternoon or “barbie” for barbecue. I’ve been practicing them with the kids at the park.      That sounds fun. I think I’ll say “g’day” to everyone at the event.      You’ll be the star of the show. Now, go get dressed and grab your snacks. We’ll leave in ten minutes.      Alright, but only if you promise not to sleepwalk again.      I won’t. I’ve had enough sleepwalking to last a lifetime. Now, off you go!      I’ll be back in five!      Don’t forget your bucket for the lemonade!      And your hula hoop!      We’ll be back!      I love this family. Being woken up at 7 a.m. is worth it.      Mom! We’re ready!      Alright, let’s go! Time for some circus magic!

So, I was just thinking about that election result last year—the way it all panned out, it felt like a complete mess. I mean, I’ve been editing books for years, and I’ve seen how people can be so passionate about things, but this... it just felt like a farce.      I couldn’t disagree more. It was a very clean result, actually. The party got the majority they deserved, and the people who voted for them trusted their judgment. You can’t just call it a “mess” when the numbers clearly showed otherwise.      I don’t know, Tony. I still think people were confused about what they were voting for. I remember my niece telling me she voted for the party because her teacher said they’d cut the school budget. She didn’t know they were actually proposing to increase funding for better facilities. It was a total misunderstanding.      Yeah, I saw that too. My mate in the village actually got confused and voted for the wrong one, and now he’s got this really weird guilt about it. He’s like, “I think I’ve let the whole country down.”      That’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve heard all week. You can’t let the whole country down for one vote. You don’t even know what the whole country wants.      Well, someone has to. But seriously, I think the real issue is that people are so disengaged from the political process. It’s like we’re being told what to think all the time, and there’s no real debate. I mean, I’ve had arguments with my brother about this stuff for years. He’s always been more socialist, and I’m more of a traditionalist. But we both still have respect for each other’s views.      I think that’s the key—having respect. I mean, I’m a student, so I don’t have much say, but I do vote. I’ve seen how people in the village talk about politics, and it’s mostly just gossip. Like, “Oh, so-and-so’s a leftie,” or “They’re really on the up.” It’s not about policy at all.      That’s exactly the problem. People don’t engage with the actual content. They just pick sides based on who they think is “in.” It’s like a football match—everyone’s cheering for their team, but no one cares about the rules.

So, what do you think of our story so far? We’ve got this little girl, Lila, who’s got this magical compass that only points north when it’s time for a real adventure. I think we’re getting somewhere, don’t you?      Yeah, I think it’s really cool that the compass only points north when it’s time for an adventure. Like, it’s not just a normal compass, it’s got a special purpose. I mean, you know, I read that book about the Linton Book Festival last week, right? That’s where Helen Moss does her stories. I think she’s the one who inspired us to write our own.      Yeah! I remember her talking about how she used to write stories with her brother when he was little. She said she’d make up all sorts of adventures. I wish I could do that. I mean, I’m not really good at writing, but I like to imagine things. I think Lila should go to the Linton Book Festival one day.      I think that’s a great idea. You know, Helen Moss is such an inspiration. She’s got that magic in her stories, like the way she makes you feel like you’re right there with the characters. I remember reading one of her stories where the main character was trying to find a way home, and it was so vivid. It made me want to write something like that.      Yeah, and I think we should make our story as vivid as hers. I mean, we’ve got Lila, but we need more characters. Maybe a talking animal or something. I think I remember the talking fox from one of her books. I think he was really clever.      A talking fox? That could work. It could be a guide for Lila. Or maybe even a guardian. You know, it could help her on her journey. We could call him something like... Arlo. That sounds good, doesn’t it?      Yeah! Arlo! That’s a cool name. I think he should live in the forest. I mean, the compass points north, so maybe the adventure is in the north woods. I could draw a map of the forest. I’ve got a big piece of paper in my bedroom.      You’re already planning the map! I think that’s brilliant. And I’ll help you with the story.

So, I just read this article about shmeat, like lab-grown meat, and it made me really think. I mean, I’ve been vegetarian for years, but this idea of lab-grown meat is kind of… weird. I don’t know, it feels like a fake solution to a real problem.      I get that, but haven’t you heard about all the environmental benefits? Like, if we’re not farming animals, we’re not using so much land, water, or emitting as much methane. Plus, it’s not like animal farming is sustainable, especially with the population growing.      Yeah, but is it really ethical? I mean, even if it’s grown in a lab, it’s still using animals. You’re just taking cells from a cow and growing them, but doesn’t that still involve some form of exploitation? Or is it just about the end result?      That’s a good point. I mean, if you’re using cells from an animal, you’re still kind of using that animal. It’s not like you’re just getting a plant-based product. I think I’d still prefer a fully plant-based diet. Plus, I’ve started taking vitamin tablets to make sure I’m not missing out on nutrients.      Yeah, I do that too. I mean, I’m vegetarian, but I’ve had a hard time getting enough B12 and iron. I’ve been experimenting with spirulina and chia seeds, but it’s not always enough. I’ve even read about some supplements that mimic the nutrients in meat—kind of like synthetic versions.      I’ve been thinking about that too. I started writing a piece about how our food choices reflect our values, and how we’re all caught in this weird middle ground between tradition and progress. Like, some people are okay with killing animals for food, others are against it for moral or environmental reasons, and then there are people like us who are trying to figure it all out.      That’s exactly it. I think the biggest issue is how we view animals. If we’re okay with hunting, but not with slaughterhouses, then we’re being inconsistent. I mean, I know a lot of people say that the animals are killed inhumanely, but I’ve also heard that some abattoirs are very regulated.      Yeah, I’ve seen some documentaries that show how some farms are really clean, and the animals are treated well.

So, I was just telling my sister about the washing machine—the one we had when I was a kid. It was this massive thing, like a giant beast, and every time it went off, it sounded like a train crash. I swear, it used to wake the whole street up. I still remember my mum screaming, “John, turn that bloody thing off!” every time it finished a cycle.      Oh, I remember that too. My mum had one like that. She used to call it the “flying saucer” because it looked like it was going to lift off the floor when it started. And you’d think the water supply would run out if it didn’t have a leak somewhere. Still, it worked reliably—until it gave up the ghost and we had to get a new one.      You’ve both got such vivid memories. I remember when I was a kid, my parents had a “modern” washing machine—like, a Kenmore or something. It was the first one with a timer, and I thought it was magic. I’d stare at it like it was a spaceship.      You were probably too young for the old ones. I was all about “the sound of the machine” growing up. I even tried to replicate it with a drum and some water once. It was a disaster. The whole kitchen was soaked.      You had a full-blown water crisis in the kitchen? That’s not bad for a kid. I think I’d have just been scared and ran out.      Yeah, I was about five. My dad tried to explain it to me, and I just thought it was a robot doing laundry. I was so confused.      You were just a ‘robot’ yourself back then. You’d probably still be washing clothes if you weren’t a copywriter now.      You’re getting your copywriting skills mixed up with something else. But seriously, speaking of robots… I keep thinking about that new smart fridge we saw. It even tells you when the milk’s going off.      That sounds cool. I’d love one. But I’m scared it’ll start talking to me like the box in  The IT Crowd .      Oh, you’d be the one talking to it. You’re the one who thinks the kettle’s ‘bubbling up’ and the fridge is ‘trying to keep things fresh’—like it’s got a personality.

So, I was just telling the boys about the butterfly fork—the one that’s like... got to be the most useless object I’ve ever seen. I mean, sure, it’s a fork, but it’s shaped like a butterfly. You know, with those little legs and everything.      Yeah, I saw that thing at the museum last year. I didn’t even know it was a real thing. I thought it was just a joke.      I think it’s called a "butterfly fork" because it’s like, literally, a fork that looks like a butterfly. You know, like, if a butterfly had a handle.      Exactly! And I’m not sure why anyone would ever use it, but apparently, it’s been around for decades. I remember seeing it in a Victorian kitchen. You know, all those fancy things they used to have.      Maybe it’s for people who want to eat their food while also admiring the design? Like, you get your meal and a little art in one?      Or maybe it’s for people who are just really into...  fancy  things. I mean, I don’t know. I’d rather have a regular fork.      It’s not just about the fork, though. I was also telling them about the two minutes of silence we did at the memorial for the girls in Russia. That was really moving. I mean, two minutes isn’t long, but it feels like forever.      Yeah, it’s about remembering, isn’t it? You just sit there, and it’s like... everything slows down.      I think it’s important. I mean, even though it’s just two minutes, it helps you process what happened.      Exactly. And I think it’s something we should do more often. Like, for birthdays too. You know, sometimes we just jump into celebrating without taking a moment to really think about what we’re celebrating.      You know, I think my mum used to do that with my birthday. She’d make a big deal out of it, but I never really thought about why it was important until now.      Maybe we should do a two-minute silence for birthdays too? Like, to appreciate the person and what they mean to us.      That’s a great idea. Maybe we’ll start a tradition. Two minutes of silence, then a toast.      I’m in. But before that, let’s finish this meal.

So, I was just telling the boys about the time I took them to Adventure Island... remember when we got stuck on the roller coaster?      Oh, yes! You were so stressed, and then we all ended up laughing when it finally stopped. I still remember the way you screamed.      You were a mess, Mum! I think Dad was more scared than you.      Please, you were the one who screamed when the ride started. I was just trying to hold you both together. But it was hilarious—still one of my favorite memories.      I think that’s why I still love going on rides. I’m not scared anymore, even though I used to be.      Yeah, I used to be scared of everything. Now I’m like,  what’s the worst that could happen?       That’s the spirit! I think that’s why we need to plan a holiday soon. You know, a real adventure.      Can we go to Cornwall? I’ve always wanted to see the cliffs and the beaches.      Yeah, and the seaside! We could take the ferry and go to Plymouth or something.      Cornwall sounds great—but we need to also think about the V&A exhibition. I’ve been meaning to take you both there, and it’s a bit of a walk from here.      Is it worth it? I mean, I’ve never been to a museum like that.      It’s amazing! The design stuff, the artefacts... you’ll love it. Plus, it’s a good way to get out and learn without going too far.      Can we go on a trip too? Like, somewhere that’s not just a museum?      Of course! We could even think about a short break in Devon or somewhere. Maybe even a campsite? I think it would be perfect for you both.      I’d love that. I’ve always wanted to try camping.      Me too! And maybe we can even take some pictures to show Grandma.      Oh, you’ll have to be careful with that. She’s got an eye for anything unusual.      She’s got  your  eye for weirdness!      Exactly. Well, as long as we get to see some real adventure and not just a museum, I think we’re all set.      Then let’s plan it! I can’t wait!      Me neither. Let’s make it a proper holiday.      I’ll start saving up!      Me too! I’ll ask my gran if she can give me some pocket money.

So, I just got my coursework back from Mrs. Thompson. She gave me an F. Again. I can’t believe it. I spent  hours  on that essay about the industrial revolution. It was a disaster.      No way! You’ve got to be kidding me. I thought you were doing better. What did she say exactly?      She said it was “lacklustre” and “not up to the standard expected of a sixth-former.” It was basically a slap in the face. I was so proud of myself when I finished it. I even checked it twice.      Man, I can relate. Mrs. Clark gave me a C on my history project last week. I was so upset. I thought I’d done really well. I even asked her for feedback, and she just said, “You need to be more detailed.” Ugh.      Yeah, it’s so frustrating. I feel like I’m doing everything right, but somehow I keep getting poor grades. I mean, I’m not even getting detention, which is a relief, but it’s still annoying.      I know. I’ve been trying to be more responsible with my time. I even started using the school library more. It’s got way better resources than my house. Plus, I’ve been hanging out with the prefects more. They’re actually pretty cool.      You know what? I might try joining the prefects too. I mean, I don’t want to be a bad influence, but maybe it’ll help me get better grades. Plus, I heard there’s a party next week at the community centre. I’m in, right?      Definitely. I’ve already told the others. It’s going to be a blast. Maybe we can all go together. Speaking of which, have you heard about the new movie coming out?      Yeah, I heard about it. It’s supposed to be epic. I’m going to see it on the weekend. I hope it’s not too long. I’ve got a lot of coursework to finish.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve got a ton of stuff due next week. I’m so stressed. I even got a warning from my teacher about my behavior. I think I got a little too loud in the classroom last week. I didn’t mean to.      Look, I’ve been there. Sometimes you just get carried away. But you’ve got to keep your head down and focus on your studies, especially with this party coming up and all.

So, I was just thinking about that A34 stretch near Chester-le-Street—ever since that accident last year, it’s like the whole road’s been on edge. I swear, every time I pass it, I half-expect to see a motorbike gone off the side.      Yeah, I remember that. I was on my way to a meeting in Durham when it happened. The road’s got a weird vibe since then. Makes me think about that old bike I had in university. You know, the one that always seemed to take the long way round.      That’s the spirit! Still, I can’t help but think about how much better it would be if they just fixed the potholes and the blind corners. I mean, I’ve got a little sister who’s learning to ride a bike, and I can’t exactly tell her to take the A34 for fun.      Exactly. I told her I’d take her along once I got my bike back from the shed. She’s obsessed with the idea of riding with me. I’ve got to say, it’s funny how we all get attached to these things. I mean, when I got my first bike at sixteen, it was like a second home.      It’s not just bikes, though. I remember the first time I went to the cricket ground in Sunderland. Felt like I was walking into a different world. The rush of the crowd, the smell of the pitch—there’s something about it that makes you feel alive.      I know what you mean. I used to play club cricket when I was younger. It’s one of those things you don’t really think about until you’re out of it. You’re so focused on the game, you don’t notice the weather or the time.      Yeah, it’s weird how something you loved when you were younger can just… fade. I mean, I still watch matches, but it’s not the same. I guess the world changes, and so do you.      Yeah. But then again, life’s full of those kinds of changes. You just have to appreciate the moments when you’re in the middle of something you love.      True. So, what’s next for you? I mean, aside from your engineering stuff—do you still play cricket?      Only on the weekend, mostly. But I’m thinking of joining a local team again.

So, I just got the delivery app on my phone, but I’m not sure how it works. I mean, I’ve used food delivery before, but never for Chinese food specifically. I think I might need some help.      Oh, it’s not that bad. I use it all the time. You just select the restaurant, choose your meal, and then it sends it to your address. I’ve ordered from that place down the road that does all the classics—sweet and sour chicken, egg foo yung, and that amazing crab rangoon. Didn’t you say you wanted to try some of that?      Yeah, I did. I’ve been craving it for weeks. I even made a list of the things I want—sweet and sour chicken, beef and broccoli, and the chicken with cashew nuts. I think it’s the only place in the area that does that. But honestly, I’m not sure if I should go for the bigger portions or just stick to the standard ones.      That’s a good point. I’m not sure how much I want to order, but I don’t want to waste money on something I won’t eat. I’ve tried ordering Chinese food before, and sometimes it’s not what you expect. I remember once I got fried rice instead of the sweet and sour chicken I ordered, and it was just… okay. Not the best experience.      Oh, that’s funny. I had a similar thing. I ordered the General Tso’s chicken and got something that looked like it was dipped in soy sauce and left in the fridge for a day. I had to laugh about it later. But still, it’s better than nothing.      I’m not sure I want to risk that. Maybe I should just go for a smaller portion and see how it goes. Or maybe I should call the restaurant and ask what’s the most popular dish. I mean, if I’m going to order, I might as well make sure it’s something I’ll actually enjoy.      That sounds smart. I could do that too. I’ve never called the restaurant before—just used the app. I think it would be better to do a bit of research first. I mean, I’m not a big fan of surprises, especially when it comes to food.      Yeah, I agree. I think that’s a good idea.

So, I was just talking to one of the lads from the university about the NHS, and I thought you might want to hear it. I mean, I've been over there a few times, and it's alright, but I can't say I'm a big fan of the way it's run now.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been working in the NHS for years now, and honestly, it’s gotten a lot worse. I mean, just last week, I had a patient who called in with a broken arm, and they had to wait for over an hour just to be seen. It's not like in the old days when you could get an appointment the same day.      I heard about that. I was in the city the other day and saw a poster saying "NHS is under strain – we need your support." You know, they’re trying to get people to donate more, but I don’t think that’s the answer. People are working harder, but the system is just too overburdened.      Right, and it’s not just the hospitals. The GPs are in a mess too. I work with a few of them, and they’re constantly being told to do more with less. I mean, one of the nurses at my clinic nearly had a breakdown last month because she was working 12-hour shifts every day. It’s not fair.      I can imagine. I had a friend who used to work in a hospital in Germany, and they had a different system altogether. You could book appointments, and they had more resources. I mean, I’m not saying the NHS is bad—there are a lot of good people in it—but the system is just not up to scratch anymore.      I agree. But then again, I can’t complain too much. I mean, I was lucky enough to get into the NHS, and I’ve got a good job. It’s just the way things are now. I suppose it’s a bit of a thankless job, but I love working with people.      That’s the spirit. I think that’s what keeps people going, even when things get tough. I’ll admit, I don’t go to the NHS much myself, but when I do, I try to be understanding. I mean, I live in a council house, and I know how things can get when you’re not on the same page.

So, I heard the latest about the police and the immigrants in the area. It’s got me thinking, you know? I mean, I’ve got a few students who come from all over, and they’re all polite, respectful, and—get this—actually help out when someone’s in trouble. But I guess some folks still don’t get that.      I know, I know. I’ve had a few letters from the council about “untidy immigrants” or whatever. You’d think after all these years, people would get used to it. I mean, I’ve lived here all my life, and I’ve seen changes. You know, when I was young, everyone was English, and now it’s a bit of a mix. But I’ve always said, as long as they’re not causing trouble, let ‘em be.      Exactly! And I think the real problem is this welfare system. You know, people don’t want to work, and then they expect to get paid for not working. I’ve got a bloke in my class who’s been on benefits for ten years. I mean, don’t get me wrong, he’s got a family, but he’s got a degree, and he’s got a brain. He just doesn’t wanna use it. It’s a real shame.      Oh, I know that one. He’s a regular at the pub, always talkin’ about the old days. He says he’s too old to work now, but I’ve seen him doing a bit of gardening for the old folks on the road. Maybe it’s not the same as a job, but it’s something.      Yeah, but you know what the real issue is? It’s not just immigrants and welfare—it’s the whole system. People are getting lazy, and the government’s not doing enough. I’ve got a friend who’s been passed around from one job to another, and now he’s just not got the skills. It’s a shame, really.      I’ve seen that too. My nephew’s in a similar boat. He was a decent lad, but he lost his job after a few years, and the system just doesn’t support him. He ended up getting a job in a factory, and now he’s stuck. I suppose it’s the same for a lot of people these days.      I suppose it is.

So, I heard you were in Cambridge last week? Did you get to see the new art installation in the library?      Yeah, I did. It was amazing. They’ve got this huge sculpture made of recycled paper. It’s like a giant tree, but made out of old books and magazines. I tried to take a photo, but the light was so bad.      I remember seeing something about it on social media. They said it was part of a sustainability drive. Do you think it’s just for show or do you think they’re really trying to make a change?      It’s a bit of both, I think. They’re definitely using it as a marketing tool, but I can’t deny it’s a powerful statement. I mean, if you’re a university press, you’re already in the business of knowledge and paper, so it makes sense.      I guess. But isn’t it a bit ironic that they’re promoting sustainability when, like, the printing house is still powered by fossil fuels?      Exactly. I read something about that the other day. They’re doing some green initiatives, but the infrastructure is still pretty traditional. I mean, it’s a start, but there’s a long way to go.      I suppose we can’t expect them to switch overnight. But I also think they’re trying to appeal to the younger generation. People are more conscious about the environment now.      Yeah, and it’s not just about the environment. It’s also about image. Universities and publishing houses want to be seen as progressive. It’s like, “We care about the planet and our future.”      I’d say it’s more about branding than anything else. But hey, it’s a positive step. I mean, I’m not going to knock it. If they’re using their platform to raise awareness, even if it’s a bit performative, it’s better than nothing.      I guess. But I still can’t go past the fact that their printing house is in Cambridge. I mean, I love the city, but I don’t know how they can say they’re eco-friendly when they’re still part of this massive, carbon-heavy industry.      Oh, come on. It’s not like they’re not doing anything. They’re hiring more green staff, and they’ve started recycling their paper waste. It’s incremental, but it’s something.

You know, I’ve been thinking about how much the internet has changed the way we communicate. It’s like, you could be in Bath or Hull, and you can still chat about the same things as if you were sitting next to each other. It’s pretty wild, innit?      Yeah, I mean, it’s made a massive difference, especially for people like us who are always moving around. But it’s also messed up the way we talk. You know, I’ve seen so many people using text speak and slang now that it’s like,  what even is proper English?       You’re not wrong. My lectures are full of students who write “u” instead of “you” and “2” instead of “to.” I think it’s because of all the social media stuff. But honestly, it doesn’t bother me that much. I mean, I grew up reading Shakespeare and all that, so I can handle some slang. But I still think it’s important to keep the language alive.      Yeah, I agree. I’ve been teaching English as a second language, and I’ve seen how much people value the language. It’s not just about words; it’s about culture. Like, when you’re teaching someone how to say “I’m sorry,” you’re also teaching them how to apologize properly, which is part of the culture.      Exactly. I remember when I first moved to London, I thought I’d be able to communicate just fine, but there were so many layers to the language. Like,  what’s the difference between "chuffed" and "pissed off"?  And the accents—sometimes you couldn’t even tell where someone was from just by listening.      You’re not the only one. I’ve been in Hull for most of my life, and I still hear accents from all over the country. It’s crazy how different people speak, but it makes the country so interesting. Like, when I’m in London, I always feel like I’m in a different world.      That’s the beauty of it, man. Yeah, it’s a bit of a headache sometimes, but it’s also what makes us unique. I think that’s why we should keep exploring different cultures and languages. It’s like, the more you learn, the more you see the world.      To the endless journey of learning, then.      To the endless journey of learning.

So, I was just telling my granddaughter, Ellie, about the time I tried to fix the fuse box in the old house in Hull. Blimey, I thought I’d be a proper DIY genius, but honestly, I just made it worse!      That sounds like the kind of thing my gran would have done. She once tried to clean the roof and ended up with a serious case of frostbite.      Oh, I remember that. She said she was “just clearing out the leaves and bits of grime.” But she ended up stuck on the roof for hours, and the fire department had to come and rescue her. My husband had to take the day off work to help her down.      I’ve got a story about that too. I was about nine and I thought I could help her. I brought her a ladder, a bucket, and a cup of tea. She was so proud, didn’t she?      Oh, you were the pride of the family! I remember you used to call her “the Queen of the Roof.” She still remembers that.      She said it was the best compliment she ever got. I think she still swears by it.      Anyway, enough about the past. We’ve got more pressing matters. The old man says the fridge’s broken again.      Oh no, not the fridge again. It’s been acting up since last week. I thought I’d wait till the weekend to fix it, but I’m not sure I can manage it.      You should have let me take it to the shop. I’ve got the contacts, and I know the guys who do the repairs. They’ll fix it up in no time.      Yeah, you’ve always been good with gadgets. I mean, you could fix a microwave with one hand and a teapot with the other.      He did once fix a washing machine with a hairdryer. I still don’t know how that worked.      That’s a bloke’s story for another day. But in all seriousness, I’ll call the shop and see if they can get someone over. Just don’t let it go on too long, ‘cause this time of year, the fridge is essential.      Fair enough. I’ll make sure the kids take it easy on the fridge while we’re waiting.      You know what they say – if you don’t fix it, you’ll lose it.

So, I found these old photos from last summer, and I just had to show you. You were supposed to be in one of them, but you were too busy drinking wine with your mates to even notice the camera.      Hey, I remember that! I was  so  into that one moment. I think it was the beach in Phuket—those sunsets were unreal. I still have that photo on my phone.      Oh, I know, you always say it's the best photo you've ever taken. But I saw one of the ones I took, and it’s just me standing there, arms out like a madwoman, and the sun was setting behind you. So dramatic.      You were trying too hard. I think you were trying to get that "I'm free and wild" look. But honestly, it’s just a memory. You know, like all the times we got lost in different countries, trying to find the best street food.      Yeah, that’s another thing. I still remember the time in Hanoi when we got to this tiny noodle shop, and the guy didn’t speak English, but we managed to communicate with a combination of gestures, broken Vietnamese, and a lot of hand waving.      And then we got the most amazing pho of our lives. You were so proud. You even said it was better than the one in London.      Oh, you were  definitely  right. I still say that. You know, I was thinking the other day—if we had kept those photos, we’d have a whole album of our travels. It’s funny how you can remember the details of that one meal or that one walk, but not the names of the places we went.      Yeah, I think it’s the memories that stick. The people, the food, the way you felt when you were there. Not the actual places.      Except for the one in Kyoto, where we got lost for hours and ended up in a temple. You remember? We had to ask for directions in Japanese, and I think we managed to say “I’m sorry” and “thank you” without breaking down.      And we ended up with a free shrine cleaning. You were so happy.      It was a win. I still have that photo too. The one where I’m half in the temple, half outside, like I was trying to take a selfie but failing.

So, I was out last night with the lads, and we ended up at this new bar in Bethnal Green. I’m telling you, it was chaos.      Did you finally get that drink you’ve been eyeing up for weeks?      Yeah, I did. But it was basically just a glass of water with a lime wedge and a little umbrella. I was like, “I’m not even gonna lie, I think it’s just a gimmick.”      You’re not the only one. My cousin tried that last week and said it was the worst thing she’d ever had. She said it tasted like a sunset.      I’m not sure if that’s a compliment or not. Anyway, after that, we went to this tiny club down the road. I thought it was going to be cool, but it was like a GCSE dance.      Are you serious? That’s worse than the last time you tried to DJ at a house party. I still don’t know how you managed to play the whole night without someone turning the music off.      It was a miracle. I swear, half the people there were there because they thought it was a free pub quiz.      I can imagine. You know, I was out with my mates last week and we ended up at this vegan burger place. The guy behind the counter was so into his job, he told us the whole story of how he started the place.      That’s nice. I like that. I think the thing I miss most about being out is just being with people. Like, even if you’re not really doing anything, it’s still fun.      Totally. I was thinking about my family the other day. My mum’s got this new cat, and it’s already taken over the house. You’d think it was the only one in the world.      Oh no, I feel that. My sister got a dog, and now it’s like the whole house is just a dog park.      I’m telling you, it’s the only thing that can make you feel like you’re not alone.      Yeah, but I’m still not sure how we’re going to survive the next few weeks with all these animals around.      Yeah, we’ll be lucky if we can find the stairs without stepping on a paw print.      Well, I think we’ll manage.

So, I was just telling my partner about the last time my mum came to visit. It was the summer she came to stay with us after her operation. I remember she insisted on making us tea in that old-fashioned teapot, and then she turned around and said, “I’ve had a bit of a  bend  today.” I nearly choked on my chips.      That’s typical of your grandmother. She always had a way of mixing up words, but it was part of the charm. I remember when she visited last year. She was telling me about the time she tried to make a pie and ended up setting the kitchen on fire. Still, she managed to save the turkey.      Yeah, she was always full of stories, even when she was just trying to keep warm. I remember she once told me about how she used to play football with the lads in the village when she was younger. She’d say she was “the best passer in the county,” but I think she just liked the idea of being part of a team.      Oh, she did have a bit of a passion for football. I used to tease her about how she used to play when she was young. She’d always say, “I could have been a proper player if I’d had the chance.” But she was more of a supporter, really. Still, she could talk about every match for hours.      I think she really loved FIFA. She used to watch the World Cup every year, even when she couldn’t move much. I remember she was really upset when England didn’t do well. She even tried to argue with the commentator on the telly. I had to stop her before she got into trouble.      That’s typical. She always thought she knew more about football than anyone else. Still, I have to admit, she had a point about the penalties. She could predict them better than most people I know.      It’s funny, isn’t it? She’s been through so much, but she still has this spark. I think it’s because she’s still got that sense of adventure. Even if she’s not going out anymore, she’s still in her head, planning her next trip, or the next match, or the next story to tell.      I think that’s what makes her special.

You know, I’ve been trying to set up my Blackberry phone again, and I’m getting so frustrated. It’s like it’s got a mind of its own.      You’re not the only one. My brother tried to set up his phone last week and ended up downloading a bunch of random apps. He’s been trying to delete them all day.      It’s all that voice recognition software. You think you’re being clever, but it just starts doing stuff you didn’t ask it to. I tried it once and ended up asking it to play the radio, and it started singing “I’m a survivor” by Garth Brooks.      Oh, I remember when I used to set up the SAT NAV. It used to take me down the wrong roads, and I’d end up in a field with a cow staring at me. I still have nightmares about that.      That’s worse than my laptop. I’ve had this problem with it breaking down every time I try to do something simple. I think it’s like the laptop’s got a rebellious streak.      I know what you mean. I almost lost my glasses the other day while trying to find the USB port. I was like, “Where the hell is this?” and then I found them in the cereal box.      That’s classic. I once put my glasses in the bin because I thought I lost them. Two hours later, I found them in the bin, right in front of me.      I’ve had a bin strike going on for weeks. I can barely find the bin, let alone throw anything in. My neighbour’s got a bin that’s got a fancy lock on it. I think it’s a security bin or something.      You know, I’ve been trying to figure out why my tap water tastes different. Is it because of the water company? I’ve been thinking about switching.      I’ve heard that the water in Brighton is pretty good. I mean, it’s not like London, but it’s still clean. I think it tastes better than the tap water in my town.      I’d say the tap water in Brighton is better than what I had back in London. But I still bought a Brita filter. I’m not taking chances.      You know, I always find it weird how you can walk around Brighton and see all those places, but I can’t remember the names of half of them.

I can't believe it's already October. I've been feeling so low lately, you know? The days are getting shorter, and I can't shake this sense of being stuck in a rut. I’ve been thinking about how things were back home in Cambridge — the bright autumn days, the leaves falling, the smell of the coffee shop on the High Street. It's so different here in Tarnow. The coffee is good, but it doesn't quite taste the same.      I know what you mean. It's the homesickness, isn't it? I’ve been feeling it too. I miss the rain and the way the sky looks in the North of England. Even though I’ve been teaching here for a while, I still get this ache for home, especially around this time of year. I’ve been trying to stay busy — I’ve got a few students, and I’m helping them prepare for exams. It's hard work, but I feel responsible for them, you know?      It must be tough, especially if you're used to a more stable life. I’ve been teaching part-time, but I'm not sure how much longer I can keep it up. I'm worried about the students, too. I remember when I was teaching in Cambridge, I had one student who was really struggling. I ended up spending hours after class helping them through their work. It was frustrating, but I felt like I was making a difference.      That's the thing, isn’t it? Even if you're not working full-time, you still feel like you owe it to the students. I’ve been trying to balance work with my own life — I even started reading again. I’ve been going through a few books from the local library. It's a way to escape, a bit.      That’s a good idea. I used to love reading, but life got in the way. I think I’ll have to start again. I’ve been getting into some gardening too — I’ve got a few plants in my flat. It’s not much, but it helps. I also love the way the birds sing in the mornings. It’s such a contrast to the quiet here in Tarnow.      I love that about you. You always have this way of finding beauty in the simplest things. I’m planning to go to the market tomorrow — it’s a bit of a local tradition here.

So, I’ve been thinking, do you ever just  not  want to go out with someone because they're just… not you? Like, I mean, sure, they might be nice, but you don’t feel  anything  when you’re with them.      I get that. I had this girl once, she was all about the weekend plans—like, “Let’s go to that new bar, then maybe see a film, then maybe a restaurant.” But when we were actually doing it, it was like, “Okay, done. Let’s get back to my place and just  talk .” And she’d say, “I don’t know, I’m just not feeling it.”      That’s the worst. It’s like, you’re out spending money on wine and snacks, and then you’re just sitting there, awkwardly eating them.      Exactly! And I’m not saying I’m not into casual stuff—it’s just that sometimes, I feel like I’m not even  present  when I’m with them. Like I’m just waiting for the night to end.      You know what’s even worse? When you’re out with someone and they’re trying to impress you with their job, but they’re not even  interested  in yours. Like, “Oh, you work in events? That’s cool! What do you do exactly?” And you’re thinking, “Yeah, I book conference rooms, arrange caterers, and occasionally get stuck in a toilet at 2 a.m. with a client.”      I’ve been there. I once went out with a guy who said he was “in tech.” I was like, “Cool, what does that mean exactly?” And he said, “Oh, I just code for a living.” And I was like, “Right. Cool. What do you code?” And he was like, “I code for a gaming company.” And I was like, “Right. Cool. What do you do for a living?” And he said, “I’m a  developer .” And I was like, “Oh, right. Cool.”      That’s not even real. You could say you’re in tech and not even be in tech.      I’ve had that too. I’ve met people who think that “tech” is like, “I’ve got a laptop and I type.”      I think we need to start a dating app called “Real Jobs.” Where you can only see people who actually do what they say.      To real jobs and real feelings.      And to not having to explain what a conference co-ordinator does to a date.

So, I was just thinking about that time I was teaching in China, and I had this student who insisted on calling the panda a “bear.” I mean, sure, they are both in the same family, but I told him, “You can’t just call a panda a bear, mate—pandas are more like… fluffy, black-and-white bears.” He didn’t get it, but I’ve got a soft spot for that one.      I know what you mean. I remember when I was teaching TEFL in Shanghai, I had a Chinese student who thought the word “panda” was a type of meat. I nearly died laughing. Still, it’s amazing how the language can be so different, isn’t it?      Absolutely. It’s like when I was in the UK, teaching English to some German students. They kept calling breakfast “tea.” I said, “No, that’s not right.” They said, “But in Germany, we have  tee  for tea.” I had to explain that “tea” in British English is the same as “tee” in German, but the context is different. It’s funny how language can be so context-sensitive.      That’s the thing about language—it’s not just about words, it’s about culture. I mean, the other day, I was at the park and saw a group of Chinese tourists taking photos with a couple of pandas. They were all dressed in matching red and gold outfits. It was like they were at a cosplay convention. Some guy was even trying to feed the pandas chocolate. I told him, “No, you can’t do that,” and he just said, “But the pandas like chocolate!”      Oh, I know that one. I’ve seen it all. At the zoo, the pandas are like celebrities. They’ve got their own Instagram accounts, for God’s sake. I think the one in Chengdu got 10 million followers. It’s wild.      Yeah, and the panda is such a symbol of China. It’s everywhere—on mugs, t-shirts, you name it. I’ve even seen a panda-shaped coffee cup in a café on Oxford Street. It’s like they’re everywhere, and I just can’t get enough of it.      I’ll tell you something—when I was in Devon, I met this guy who grew up in rural China, and he said the biggest thing about living there was the quiet.

So, I was just thinking, do you remember that time we tried to cook that lasagna and ended up with a fire? It was  so  dramatic, like we were on a cooking show or something.      Oh yeah, I still remember the smoke alarm going off and you trying to put it out with a saucepan. Classic. You were like a knight in shining armor with that ladle.      I was just trying to save the day, you know? I thought I was being resourceful. But honestly, I think we’ve both learned our lesson—no more cooking experiments unless we have a fire extinguisher on hand.      Yeah, and I think we should start a rulebook for cooking. Like, "No more lasagna unless we’ve got a backup plan."      Agreed. Rule number one: No fires. Rule number two: No lasagna unless it’s a planned event. And rule number three: Always have a fire extinguisher.      You’re starting to sound like a real kitchen supervisor.      Well, I  am  a corpus administrator. I’ve got to be organized, even if it’s just for cooking.      I can see that. You’re always bringing structure to everything. Even when we’re just hanging out.      Well, you know, I think that’s what makes us work well together. I bring the structure, and you bring the... what’s the word? The  engineer  touch?      Yeah, I bring the  problem-solving . You bring the  planning . It’s like a team.      And if we ever open a restaurant, it’ll be called  Fire and Structure .      Sounds like a disaster waiting to happen.      Exactly. But it’ll be a  good  disaster.      You know, I think we should actually go out and find a recipe that’s not going to set the house on fire.      Yeah, and maybe we can start a cooking club. Strict rules, no fires, no drama. Just…  clean  cooking.      You’re on. I’ll bring the recipe book.      And I’ll bring the fire extinguisher.      Deal. No more lasagna unless we’re  totally  prepared.      Deal. Now, let’s go find that recipe. I’ve got a feeling it’s going to be good.      I don’t know what you’re talking about. I’m not sure I trust you with a recipe.      Oh, you’ll see. I’ve got a  plan .      That’s what I like to hear. I’m always impressed by your  plans .      Thank you.

So, I’ve been feeling really off for the past few days, like I’ve got this weird bug or something. I tried to push through it, but I was so tired, I just fell asleep at my desk last night.      You should’ve taken the day off, lass. You look like you’re about to collapse. Have you been eating properly?      Honestly, I haven’t. I’ve been too busy with the conference prep. I’m so stressed, I just want to keep going. You know how it is.      I know what you mean. I’ve been like that too. Just got back from a meeting and I was so drained, I couldn’t even think straight. It’s like your brain’s gone on strike.      That’s what happens when you’re trying to run a business on your own. You end up pulling double shifts and not even noticing when you’re burning out.      Yeah, and it’s not just work. I’ve been feeling quite down as well. Like, I don’t even want to go out or see people. It’s like this invisible weight on my chest. I don’t know what to do.      Maybe you should talk to someone? Like a therapist or something? I’ve been meaning to do that for a while. It’s not just about work, it’s about how you’re feeling. You deserve to feel better.      Yeah, and you’re not alone in that. I’ve been there too. I mean, I’m not the best at talking about mental health, but I know it’s important. If you need someone to listen, I’m here.      Thanks, guys. I really appreciate that. I just feel like I’m drowning in it all. But I don’t want to be like this for long.      You’re not drowning, you’re just swimming. And we’re all here to help you float. You don’t have to do it alone.      To life, and surviving it, even when it’s a bit of a mess.      To surviving, and to getting through this.      And to not ignoring your own needs for too long. You’re worth it.      I know. I just hope I can remember that soon.      You will. It’s just a matter of time, and a few good cups of tea, maybe some fresh air, and a bit of rest.

So, I just had this meeting with the project team, and honestly, I was so frustrated. The client kept changing their mind about the timeline, and it felt like we were going in circles. I mean, we’re already behind schedule, and now they want us to add another feature. It’s just so stressful.      I can totally understand. I’ve been having similar issues with the mental health ward. The management keeps shifting priorities, and it’s making it really hard to keep track of what’s actually important. Plus, we’ve got these new regulations coming in, and it’s like we’re trying to juggle three things at once.      Yeah, it’s like no one’s in control anymore. My boss keeps saying we need to be more flexible, but I feel like we’re just being pushed around. I don’t know how long I can keep doing this without burning out.      I know exactly what you mean. I’m starting to feel like I’m not even being heard. I told my manager last week that the workload was unsustainable, but they just said I need to "adapt" or something. It’s really frustrating.      It’s so sad, isn’t it? I’ve been thinking about how much I miss the days when we had more structure. Back when we had a clear plan and people actually followed through. It’s like we’re all just trying to survive now.      I miss that too. I’ve been trying to stay positive, but sometimes I just feel so overwhelmed. I even had a conversation with one of my colleagues the other day about how we’re all just trying to get through the week without breaking down.      I heard about that. I think she mentioned something about the break-up too. I mean, it’s not just work, right? I’ve been trying to figure out how to move on from that relationship, but it’s like the emotional stuff is just as draining as work.      Yeah, it’s exhausting. I’m trying to focus on my friends more now. I’ve been out with Jess and Sam last week, and it was good to laugh and not have to think about anything else for a while. You should come along sometime.      I would love to. I really need that. I’ve been so caught up in work and my own head, I haven’t even had time to socialize properly.

So, you two, what do you think about the idea of good versus evil? I mean, it’s such a big topic, isn’t it?      I think it’s really important, especially when we’re little. Like, if you do good things, you get rewarded, and if you do bad things, you get punished. It makes sense, doesn’t it?      But what if there’s no real good or evil? Like, what if it’s just people making choices?      That’s a good point, love. It’s not always black and white. Sometimes things are more complicated than that. Like, in the stories we used to read, the good guys weren’t always perfect, and the bad guys had their reasons.      Yeah, like the witch in the tale. She was scary, but she was just trying to protect her village, right?      Exactly! And the hero wasn’t always the bravest person—sometimes they were just brave enough to make the right choice.      So, what if we’re both good and bad? Like, we can do good things, but sometimes we mess up?      That’s the beauty of it, isn’t it? We’re all learning, and it’s okay to make mistakes. What matters is that we try to do the right thing.      So, if I hit my brother, is that bad?      Well, it’s not good, but it’s not the end of the world. What matters is that you learn from it and try not to do it again.      Okay. So, if I do something bad, I have to be sorry?      Yes, you have to be sorry, and you have to try to fix it. That’s what makes us better people.      So, like, if I tell a lie, I have to tell the truth?      Exactly. And if you’re brave enough to admit when you’re wrong, that’s a real sign of being a good person.      So, we’re like heroes in our own stories?      Yeah, we are. And even though we’re not in any legends or tales, we’re still making our own versions of good versus evil every day.      So, I can be a hero?      You already are, my dear. You just don’t realize it yet. You’re already doing good things every day.      I want to be a hero when I grow up.      That’s the best kind of hero. One who wants to do good and learn from their mistakes.

So, I just got a text from the school about ANON’s filming trip. They said they’re filming in the countryside and it’s going to be a bit of a trek. I was thinking, are we going to need to pack extra clothes or anything?      Oh, I’ve already packed a few extra jumpers and a waterproof jacket. I know the weather can be all over the place. I’ve also got a couple of small thermos mugs for tea, just in case.      That’s good. I was also wondering if the kids are okay with the idea of being filmed. I mean, they’re still little, so it’s not like they’re used to being in front of the camera.      Yeah, I know. I told them it’s just a school project, and I think they’re excited. They’ve been talking about it all week. Wait, isn’t ANON’s leg still hurting?      Yes, the doctor said it’s just a minor strain, but they still need to be careful. I was going to tell them not to run around too much. I mean, we all know how they are.      I know. I’ve been watching them run around like little tornadoes. I’m thinking maybe we should get them a pair of compression socks. That might help.      That’s a good idea. I was also thinking about the gym. I’ve been meaning to go this week. I’ve been so busy with work, but I really need to get back on track with my running.      Hey, you know what I just thought? I’ve been meaning to try out those new running machines at the gym. I heard they’re pretty good for people who don’t like running outside.      Yeah, I’ve heard about them too. I think they’re called ellipticals or something like that. I’ve seen people using them, but I’ve never tried it myself.      I think they’re a bit like the old treadmills, but they’re smoother and less jarring on the joints. I’m thinking about trying it next week.      That sounds like a plan. Oh, and I just remembered—Dad mentioned he’s going to bring some doughnuts to the gym. I think they’re the ones with the caramel drizzle.      Oh, I love those. You know, I think those doughnuts are what got me through my first week of teaching.

Well, I’ve just read this article about the Green Party launching a new initiative for community gardens in Brighton. It’s all about promoting local food production and reducing carbon footprints, you know.      Aye, I heard about that. Seems like a good idea. But with the economy how it is, I don’t know if people have the time or the money to get into that sort of thing.      That’s a fair point, but I think it’s more about pulling together as a community. You know, like boot sales or local markets, where people can swap and share what they’ve got.      That’s true. I’ve been thinking about starting a small community garden myself, but I’ve got enough on my hands running the café. I’m always trying to keep up with the bills and the customers.      I can imagine. You’ve got the pressure of running a small business. I’ve been in teaching for over thirty years, and while it’s not the easiest job, it’s more stable than being your own boss.      Aye, I’ll say that. Sometimes I think I’ve got more stress running the place than I did in my old job. But it’s all part of being your own boss, isn’t it?      I suppose so. But I’ve seen a lot of people in that position struggle through the tough times. I remember back when the economy was bad, a lot of small businesses in Brighton closed down.      That’s right. I lost a few friends to that. It’s tough when the market’s not great and you’ve got overheads to pay. I’ve been lucky so far, but I’m always on edge.      I can only imagine. You know, I’ve been worrying about my own health lately. I’ve got this back problem that’s been troubling me for years. I think it’s from all the standing around in the classroom.      That’s not good. You need to take care of yourself, mate. You’ve done a lot for this town.      Thanks, but I’m not sure how much longer I can keep it up. Maybe it’s time for a bit of a change. I’ve been thinking about taking up some part-time work, maybe something more flexible.      That sounds like a good move. If you can get something that suits you better, then go for it.

So, I was at the supermarket the other day, and this bloke in front of me was trying to buy a pasty. He looked like he’d just woken up from a three-day sleep. I said, “Mate, you’ve got to be joking,” and he goes, “No, it’s the only thing I’ve got left. My wife said I’ve got to eat something with some meat in it.” I couldn’t help but laugh.      Pasty? You’re in Cambridge and you’re talking about pasties? I thought you were supposed to be all about baked beans and cider.      Oh, come on, you know it’s not just me. The whole North East’s got a thing for pasties. It’s like our national dish. I mean, if you’re not eating a pasty, you’re not really from around here. My mum still sends me one every Christmas. It’s like a love letter wrapped in pastry.      Yeah, I get it. I’ve had some of those—bit of a greasy, meaty mess, but it’s comforting. I still remember the first time I had one in Sunderland. I was like, “What is this? A brick wrapped in a crust?” But now I’m sort of addicted. Though I reckon the pasty’s got more depth than most of the politics we’re hearing these days.      Oh, you say that now. But don’t let me start on Trump—everyone’s got an opinion these days. I mean, what’s next? A pasty in every political debate? I swear, the only thing he’s good for is talking about walls and trade deals.      Oh, I’m not touching that. I’m still trying to understand why anyone would vote for him. I mean, he’s like a walking conspiracy theory. You can’t even trust him with a banana.      Yeah, and I’m not even going to get into the fashion stuff. I mean, the man wears a hat like he’s going to a funeral. But hey, if it’s a pasty and a goatee, I’ll take it.      You’re a pasty connoisseur, then. I’ve got to say, I think you’ve made me a convert. Although I still think the best one is from the butcher in nearby Milton Keynes. They’ve got this swirl of meat in the middle that’s like a masterpiece.

So, I was just thinking about that episode of  Blue Peter  we watched last night. You know, the one where they were talking about killer whales. It was so interesting, wasn’t it? I mean, I always thought they were just these big, kind of dumb creatures, like the ones in the old  Flipper  TV show. But they’re actually really intelligent, aren’t they?      Oh, definitely. I remember reading that they can learn complex tasks and even communicate with each other in ways that are pretty advanced. But I also remember when I was teaching, I had a student who thought killer whales were just like dolphins, but bigger. I tried to explain the difference, but they kept calling them “whale sharks,” which is obviously wrong. It got so frustrating.      I know, it’s so easy to mix them up. But then again, I’ve always been fascinated by marine life, especially since I grew up in Norfolk. You know, there’s a lot of seabirds and seals around here, and the occasional pod of dolphins. I’d love to see a killer whale, though. I’d say it would be the highlight of my life.      I’d love that too. But I’ve also been thinking – what about all the TV shows that feature killer whales? Like  Flipper  or even  The Grey Seal ? I mean, they’re often portrayed as aggressive or even violent. I remember one episode where they attacked a boat, and the whole thing was dramatised to the max. Is that real? Or just for show?      That’s a good question. I think it’s a bit of both. I’ve read that killer whales are actually very social and intelligent, but they can be aggressive when they feel threatened or when they’re hunting. But I think a lot of the violence we see on TV is exaggerated for drama. It’s like how they show the violence in some action shows – it’s not realistic, but it’s supposed to make you watch.      Yeah, exactly. You know, I’ve also been hearing a lot about squatting in London lately. It’s weird, right? Like, people are moving into empty buildings and living there. I mean, it’s a bit of a grey area, isn’t it? But I can’t help but think about the kids who do it, they’re just trying to make a home.

Aye, it's a real shame what's happening to the hostel down by the train station. I was there a few years back when it was still running proper. Not like now, it's all been turned into flats. Don’t know if it’s better or worse, but I can tell you, it’s not the same.      I know, I used to take the kids there when they were little. It was like a second home to me. I remember the woman who ran it, she was a real character. Always had a cup of tea ready for anyone who walked in. Now it’s all gone, and I miss that bit of community.      You’re not the only one who remembers. I used to go there too when I was younger. It was a place where you could meet people, no matter where you came from. Even after I left, I used to go back sometimes to catch up with old friends. It was a real heart of the town, wasn’t it?      Aye, and now it’s all changed. I tell you, it’s like the town’s losing its soul. But then again, maybe it’s just me getting old and sentimental. Still, I can’t help but feel a bit sad about it.      I understand. You don’t get that sense of community in modern housing. It’s all about the money, isn’t it? Everyone’s looking out for themselves, not each other. I think the hostel was one of the few places where people really looked out for one another.      That’s true. It’s funny, I remember a time when even the local abattoir had a kind of camaraderie. The workers would have a laugh, talk about the day’s work, share a few drinks after hours. Not like now, it’s all about efficiency and profit.      Yeah, I remember when my dad ran the shop. He always said the best thing about the place was the people. Some of them were like family. Now, it’s all just a place to buy things, no real connection.      I suppose that’s why I keep these photos. They remind me of the good old days. I still see some of the same faces in the pictures, and I wonder where they are now.      I think that’s the key. No matter how much the world changes, those memories stay with us.

So, I heard you were in recruitment before you became an associate lecturer? That’s interesting. I mean, I used to work in educational publishing, so I guess I’ve seen a few different roles over the years. But recruitment? That’s a bit different from what I did.      Yeah, I did that for a few years. It was actually pretty eye-opening. I mean, I used to think that people were all just looking for the best candidates, but it was more about how you presented yourself and what you could sell. It was like a different side of academia, if you like. You had to talk up the benefits of working in higher education, even if the reality was a bit more complex.      I can imagine. I remember when I left teaching to do some admin work, I thought I'd be more in control of the day-to-day. But you know, it’s still part of the academic world—just a different angle. Anyway, I was just thinking about the course you’re running. I saw some of the student feedback about the academic literacy component. Some were really impressed, others found it challenging.      I know, it’s a bit of a mixed bag. I think it’s because the course is designed for students who may not have had much exposure to academic writing before. I mean, some of them come from very different educational backgrounds. It’s not like they’re used to writing essays or engaging with complex theories.      Absolutely. I remember when I was starting out, I had a student who struggled with academic writing so much that I had to give them extra support. It was frustrating, but also a good learning experience. I think the key is to make it interactive and not just assign essays. Maybe use some peer reviews or workshops?      I’ve been thinking about that. I was actually considering introducing some group work where students have to present their ideas, so they can get feedback in real time. It might help them feel more confident. But the challenge is time. I don’t want to overload the syllabus.      Fair enough. I mean, it’s a delicate balance. But I think the students appreciate when you show you care about their development. Even if it’s a bit extra work for you. That’s what makes a good lecturer, isn’t it?

So, I just sat down, and there’s this guy in front of me who’s got a massive stack of books. I’m like, “Are you doing a degree in philosophy or something?” He goes, “No, I’m just trying to find a good novel to read on the train.” I thought, “Well, that’s not really a degree, is it?”      I think that’s more of a social experiment.
